title: 15  Optimal contributions and the \(\alpha\) constraint
section: 15.3 Relation to the standard OCS formulation
text:
15.3 Relation to the standard OCS formulation
Gómez-Romano et al. (2016) write the general optimal-contribution problem, for a vector of continuous contributions \(\mathbf{c}\) (their eq. 1a-1d), as
\[\text{minimise} \quad \mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\,\mathbf{c}
  \qquad \text{subject to} \qquad
  \mathbf{c}'\mathbf{s} = 0.5,\;\; \mathbf{c}'\mathbf{d} = 0.5,\;\; c_i \ge 0, \tag{15.4}\]
with \(\mathbf{s}\) and \(\mathbf{d}\) the indicators of the two sexes. The paper writes the coancestry matrix chosen for managing diversity \(\mathbf{G}\); it is written \(\mathbf{f}\) here, because \(\mathbf{G}\) is the VanRaden relationship matrix of this book (used for prediction only). The form that maximises gain subject to a bound on \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}\) is the one Chapter 4 reports from the Methods of Meuwissen et al. (2020) (Meuwissen (1997) reported through it and not read for this book), up to the constant \(\tfrac12\) in their group coancestry.
Equation 15.2 is that constraint form restricted to \(c_i \in \{0, 1/n\}\): a fixed number \(n\) of candidates contribute equally, none partially, and the bound is set from the random-subset baseline through Equation 15.3. The restriction makes the problem combinatorial, which moves the solution method from convex quadratic programming to search. It is not arbitrary: a commercial hybrid programme plants a whole plot of a hybrid or does not plant it.






NoteWhat the contributions are attached to



Three objects can carry a contribution: an individual, a line, a cross. In this chapter \(c_i\) is attached to a hybrid, that is, to one \(A \times B\) cross (Equation 15.2), and the diversity side of that problem is optimal-contribution selection on lines under three further restrictions (Section 12.1). The per-sex sum constraint of Equation 15.4 becomes, for hybrids of two pools, one sum per pool. “Cross” here is the \(A \times B\) hybrid. Assigning contributions to the within-pool crosses that make the next generation of lines is the problem named optimal cross selection in the title of Gorjanc et al. (2018), cited here for the name only: that paper was not read for this book, and nothing in this chapter rests on its content. The mating-design part (Chapter 18) does not solve that assignment: it treats which \(A \times B\) crosses to make and test under a field limit as a sampling problem for estimation, and reviews the literature on the other in one paragraph.
crumbs: 15  Optimal contributions and the $\alpha$ constraint

title: 15  Optimal contributions and the \(\alpha\) constraint
section: 15.4 The continuous relaxation, and what it bounds
text:
15.4 The continuous relaxation, and what it bounds
Drop \(c_i \in \{0, 1/n\}\) to \(0 \le c_i \le 1/n\) with \(\sum_i c_i = 1\). For \(\lambda \ge 0\) let
\[V(\lambda) \;=\; \max_{\mathbf{c}}\; \mathbf{c}'\mathbf{u} - \lambda\,\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}
  \qquad \text{over} \quad \sum_i c_i = 1,\;\; 0 \le c_i \le 1/n, \tag{15.5}\]
attained at \(\mathbf{c}_\lambda\), with \(\bar u_\lambda = \mathbf{c}_\lambda'\mathbf{u}\) and \(\theta_\lambda = \mathbf{c}_\lambda'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}_\lambda\), so that \(V(\lambda) = \bar u_\lambda - \lambda\,\theta_\lambda\). ocs_relaxation() solves it by projected gradient, with the projection below. The cap \(c_i \le 1/n\) keeps the relaxation from putting all weight on the best candidate.


Show code
project_capped_simplex
#> function (v, cap) 
#> {
#>     lo <- min(v) - 1
#>     hi <- max(v)
#>     for (i in 1:60) {
#>         tau <- (lo + hi)/2
#>         if (sum(pmin(pmax(v - tau, 0), cap)) > 1) 
#>             lo <- tau
#>         else hi <- tau
#>     }
#>     pmin(pmax(v - (lo + hi)/2, 0), cap)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x7a7b19c040>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>


Two statements about \(V(\lambda)\) hold and one that looks like them does not.

No budget (\(\lambda = 0\)). \(V(0)\) is the mean of the \(n\) largest \(u_i\), the truncation plan: the relaxation is exact when there is no constraint.
Weak duality. The equal-weight vector of any set \(S\) with \(|S| = n\) is feasible in Equation 15.5, so for every \(S\) and every \(\lambda \ge 0\)
\[\bar u_S \;\le\; V(\lambda) + \lambda\,\theta_S \;=\; \bar u_\lambda + \lambda\,(\theta_S - \theta_\lambda). \tag{15.6}\]
Hence a relaxation point bounds every discrete plan at least as diverse as itself (\(\theta_S \le \theta_\lambda\) gives \(\bar u_S \le \bar u_\lambda\)). For a plan with less diversity than the point, Equation 15.6 is the tangent of slope \(\lambda\) at the point, which rises above the point’s height.
What does not follow. A budget limits \(\theta_S\) from above, and a plan that spends it has \(\theta_S\) close to \(\theta_{\max}\). For a relaxation point inside the budget (\(\theta_\lambda < \theta_{\max}\)) such a plan is less diverse than the point, and its index can exceed the point’s height. The height of “the best relaxation point whose own \(\alpha\) falls inside the budget” is therefore not an upper bound on the constrained problem. The book once used that construction; Section 17.4 shows it falling below a feasible plan.

The valid statement is Equation 15.6 evaluated at the budget and minimised over \(\lambda\). For every \(S\) with \(\theta_S \le \theta_{\max}\),
\[\bar u_S \;\le\; \min_{\lambda \ge 0}\,\bigl[\,V(\lambda) + \lambda\,\theta_{\max}\bigr], \tag{15.7}\]
and every \(\lambda\) gives a valid bound, so a coarse grid of \(\lambda\) costs tightness, not validity. By Lagrangian duality for a convex programme (linear objective, \(\mathbf{f}\) positive semi-definite, Slater’s condition holding when a feasible \(\mathbf{c}\) has \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c} < \theta_{\max}\); Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004), section 5.2.3) the minimum over all \(\lambda\) equals the optimum of the continuous problem \(\max\,\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{u}\) with \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c} \le \theta_{\max}\) in the same box, the continuous frontier at the budget, and taking \(\theta_{\max} = \theta_S\) in Equation 15.7 shows that a discrete plan lies on or below that frontier at its own \(\alpha\). The frontier is concave in the budget, so the chord between two points of a \(\lambda\) grid lies below it, and the height of the last grid point inside the budget is below it by an amount that depends on the grid. ocs_bound() returns the minimum over a grid (one row per \(\lambda\) in Table 15.2), doubles the number of projected-gradient iterations until the bound value \(V(\lambda) + \lambda\theta_{\max}\) changes by less than a relative tol = 1e-3, and carries a converged attribute (a stalling criterion on the doubling, not a certificate); the iteration count that converges at this scale does not at \(N = 10{,}000\) (Section 17.7).


Show code
# One call returns the grid of lambda, the converged relaxation points and the bound.
lam_grid <- 10^seq(0, 2.5, by = 1 / 6)           # 16 multipliers, 1 to 316
am <- 0.01                                       # the budget alpha_max
gd <- null$gd_ref
bound <- ocs_bound(ctx, n_sel, am, gd, lambdas = lam_grid)
relax <- attr(bound, "relaxation")               # one row per lambda, converged
a_relax <- (gd - relax[, "GD"]) / gd
theta_max <- 1 - gd * (1 - am)
u_top <- mean(sort(ctx$index, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_sel)])
stopifnot(attr(bound, "converged"),
          abs(u_top - mean_index(tr, ctx)) < 1e-12,       # V(0) = truncation
          abs(relax[1, "index"] - mean_index(tr, ctx)) < 1e-6,  # lambda = 1 already is
          isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(bound),
                           min(relax[, "index"] - relax[, "lambda"] * relax[, "theta"] +
                               relax[, "lambda"] * theta_max))))




Show code
tab_relax <- cbind(as.data.frame(relax), alpha = a_relax,
                   bound_term = relax[, "index"] - relax[, "lambda"] * relax[, "theta"] +
                                relax[, "lambda"] * theta_max)
knitr::kable(fmt(tab_relax, 4),
             col.names = c("$\\lambda$", "$\\bar u_\\lambda$", "$\\theta_\\lambda$", "$GD_\\lambda$",
                           "$\\alpha$", "$V(\\lambda) + \\lambda\\theta_{\\max}$"))

The first row of Table 15.2 coincides with the truncation plan (statement 1; the chunk asserts it); \(\alpha\) then falls as \(\lambda\) rises. The last column is the quantity of Equation 15.7 at each \(\lambda\) of the grid; its minimum, 1.5532, is at \(\lambda^* =\) 68.1, reached with 8000 iterations (converged is TRUE). \(\lambda^*\) is the multiplier the 1% budget implies on this grid, in index units per unit of \(\theta\); per percentage point of \(\alpha\) it is 0.22 index units.
The other discrete plans are the greedy sweep over the index weight \(\omega\) (argument w of sel_greedy(), score \(\omega u_i - \theta\)), on a logarithmic grid of 60 values from \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{-1}\). The grid is logarithmic because the increments of \(\theta\) are of order \(10^{-3}\) and the differences of \(u_i\) of order 1, so \(\omega\) above about \(10^{-2}\) returns the truncation plan and \(\omega\) below about \(10^{-5}\) returns nearly the maximum-diversity plan: the frontier lives between.


Show code
ws <- 10^seq(-6, -1, length.out = 60)
front <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ws, function(w) {
  s <- sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = w)
  data.frame(w = w, alpha = alpha_loss(s, ctx, gd), index = mean_index(s, ctx),
             Ne_par = ne_parents(s, ctx),
             theta = theta_group(s, ctx))
}))
a_trunc <- alpha_loss(tr, ctx, gd)               # alpha of the truncation plan
n_trunc <- sum(abs(front$alpha - a_trunc) < 1e-9)  # grid values that return truncation
key <- round(front[, c("alpha", "index")], 8)
n_distinct <- sum(!duplicated(key))
stopifnot(n_distinct >= 20,                      # the frontier is not degenerate
          n_trunc < nrow(front))                 # ... and it leaves truncation
inb <- front$alpha <= am
best_greedy <- max(front$index[inb])
best_relax  <- max(relax[a_relax <= am, "index"])
stopifnot(best_relax < best_greedy, best_greedy < as.numeric(bound))


At the 1% budget three numbers are in play. The best relaxation point of the grid with \(\alpha \le\) 1% has index 1.3473; the best greedy plan inside the budget, at \(\alpha =\) 0.00685, has index 1.4226; the bound of Equation 15.7 is 1.5532. The chunk asserts the order relaxation point \(<\) feasible plan \(<\) bound. A feasible plan above a relaxation point inside the budget shows that the height of that point is not a ceiling (Figure 15.1); the bound, which is one, lies above both. The gap between the greedy plan and the bound, 0.131 index units, is an upper limit on what a better search could gain at this budget on this dataset, and only if converged is TRUE, as it is here; closing it is the subject of Chapter 17.


Show code
set.seed(42)
sels <- list(random = sel_random(ctx, n_sel), trunc_cap = sel_truncation_cap(ctx, n_sel),
             truncation = tr)

  c(alpha = alpha_loss(s, ctx, gd), index = mean_index(s, ctx))))

     xlab = "gene diversity loss, alpha (%)", ylab = "mean index (s.d.)",
     xlim = range(c(a_relax, pts[, "alpha"], front$alpha) * 100),
     ylim = range(c(relax[, "index"], pts[, "index"], front$index, as.numeric(bound))))
points(front$alpha * 100, front$index, pch = 20, cex = 0.7, col = book_pal[["loss"]])
points(pts[, "alpha"] * 100, pts[, "index"], pch = 19, col = book_pal[["loss"]])
text(pts[, "alpha"] * 100, pts[, "index"], rownames(pts), pos = c(2, 2, 1), cex = 0.7)

points(front$alpha[j] * 100, front$index[j], pch = 1, cex = 1.6, col = book_pal[["loss"]])

abline(v = am * 100, lty = 3)
legend("bottomright",
       c("relaxation, one point per lambda", "greedy sweep and selections",
         "best greedy plan inside the budget", "Lagrangian bound at 1%"),
       col = c(book_pal[["mid"]], book_pal[["loss"]], book_pal[["loss"]], "black"), pch = c(1, 20, 1, 2),
       lty = c(2, NA, NA, NA), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
grid()








Figure 15.1: The continuous relaxation (grey circles, one per \(\lambda\) of Table 15.2, joined by chords) and discrete plans (red: the greedy sweep of 60 index weights and three selections) on the plane of gene diversity loss \(\alpha\) against mean index. Dotted vertical line: the 1% budget. Triangle: the Lagrangian bound of Equation 15.7 at that budget, from ocs_bound() (\(\lambda\) grid of 16 values, converged). Open red circle: the best greedy plan with \(\alpha \le\) 1%, which lies above the highest relaxation point inside the budget and below the triangle. The height of a relaxation point is not a ceiling for plans that spend more of the budget; the triangle is. Teaching scale (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, \(n\) = 60, \(N\) = 625), simulation seed 1; random: one random subset, set.seed(42).











WarningAn under-converged relaxation reports a value that is too small



Projected gradient approaches \(V(\lambda)\) from below, so an under-converged relaxation understates \(V(\lambda)\) and, with it, the bound of Equation 15.7, which then stops being one. The diagnostic is the penalised value \(V = \bar u_\lambda - \lambda\,\theta_\lambda\) (Table 15.3), not the index: by Equation 15.6 \(V(\lambda) \ge \bar u_S - \lambda\theta_S\) for every discrete plan, so a relaxation whose \(V\) is below a discrete plan’s is not converged. The index of a converged relaxation can lie below that of a discrete plan with no contradiction, because the relaxation is the more diverse and pays \(\lambda\) per unit of \(\theta\).




Show code
lam <- 10
its <- c(50, 500, 4000, 16000)
conv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(its, function(it) {
  r <- ocs_relaxation(ctx, n_sel, lam, iters = it)
  data.frame(iterations = it, index = r[, "index"], theta = r[, "theta"],
             V = r[, "index"] - lam * r[, "theta"], row.names = NULL)
}))
disc <- data.frame(iterations = NA, index = mean_index(tr, ctx),
                   theta = theta_group(tr, ctx),
                   V = mean_index(tr, ctx) - lam * theta_group(tr, ctx))
rel_change <- abs(conv$V[4] - conv$V[3]) / abs(conv$V[3])
stopifnot(conv$V[1] < disc$V,                # 50 iterations: V below a feasible plan
          conv$V[3] >= disc$V,               # 4000 iterations: V above it
          all(diff(conv$V) >= 0),            # V rises with iterations
          rel_change < 1e-3)                 # the tol of ocs_bound(), applied here to V
# weak duality (eq. ocs-weak) for every discrete plan of the chapter, lambda = 10
plans <- c(sels, lapply(seq_len(nrow(front)), function(i) sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = front$w[i])))
Vplan <- vapply(plans, function(s) mean_index(s, ctx) - lam * theta_group(s, ctx), numeric(1))
stopifnot(all(Vplan <= conv$V[4] + 1e-8))
knitr::kable(fmt(rbind(conv, disc), 4),
             col.names = c("iterations", "$\\bar u_\\lambda$", "$\\theta_\\lambda$",
                           "$V = \\bar u_\\lambda - \\lambda\\theta_\\lambda$"))

At 50 iterations \(V\) is -5.1939, below the discrete plan’s -4.884; at 4000 it is -4.8748, above; from 4000 to 16000 it moves by \(1.8 \times 10^{-4}\)% (Table 15.3). The chunk asserts that ordering, that \(V\) does not fall as iterations grow, that the relative change in \(V\) from 4000 to 16000 iterations is below \(10^{-3}\), and that no discrete plan of the chapter (all 63 of them) has a penalised value above the converged \(V\). The tolerance is the same relative \(10^{-3}\) as the tol of ocs_bound(), but ocs_bound() applies it to the bound value \(V(\lambda) + \lambda\theta_{\max}\), not to \(V\) at \(\lambda = 10\). “Converged” here means that relative change at \(\lambda = 10\) at this scale: a stalling criterion, the value stopped moving as the count grew, not a certificate that it equals \(V(\lambda)\). This chapter does not measure larger \(\lambda\) or larger \(N\); ocs_bound() doubles the count and checks the change in the bound value at each \(\lambda\) grid it is given, rather than assuming that a count that stalls here stalls there.

title: 15  Optimal contributions and the \(\alpha\) constraint
text:
15.5 Setting the budget
The budget should not be chosen a priori. Pure truncation, the unconstrained optimum of the index, has loss \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\): the \(\alpha\) at which the constraint stops binding. It is not the largest \(\alpha\) any \(n\)-subset reaches (a minimum-diversity selection would exceed it); it is the largest a gain-maximising selection ever needs (Section 11.9). A budget \(\alpha_{\max} \ge \alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) restricts nothing, and stage2_select() warns about any requested \(\alpha\) above this ceiling rather than return an unconstrained plan that looks constrained. Here \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}} =\) 0.0412 for \(B\) = 400 random subsets; it depends on \(B\) in the third decimal.
Figure 15.2 traces what each budget costs: the greedy frontier over the index weight \(\omega\) of the grid above. The frontier is the set of feasible plans the greedy finds; it is a lower bound on the constrained optimum, not the optimum. Table 15.4 lists a subset of its plans.


Show code
fd <- front[!duplicated(key), ]
fd <- fd[order(fd$alpha), ]
plot(fd$alpha * 100, fd$index, type = "b", pch = 19, col = book_pal[["ink"]],
     xlab = "gene diversity loss, alpha (%)", ylab = "mean index (s.d.)")
abline(v = a_trunc * 100, lty = 2, col = book_pal[["loss"]])
abline(v = am * 100, lty = 3)
text(a_trunc * 100, min(fd$index), "truncation", pos = 2, cex = 0.7, col = book_pal[["loss"]])
grid()

Dashed red line: \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\), the loss of the truncation plan; dotted: the 1% budget of Figure 15.1. Teaching scale, simulation seed 1, \(n\) = 60, \(N\) = 625; \(\alpha\) against gd_ref from \(B\) = 400 random subsets (seed 7).

Of the 60 values of \(\omega\), 39 give distinct plans and 11 return the truncation plan (Table 15.4). Linear interpolation of the distinct plans gives, between \(\alpha\) = -1, 0, 1, 2, 3% and \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\), a secant slope of 0.52, 0.31, 0.22, 0.15, 0.1 index units per percentage point of \(\alpha\). This shows that on this dataset the cost of diversity is largest at low \(\alpha\) and falls towards \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\); the greedy frontier is a heuristic, not the optimum, and the slopes are secants of a noisy curve. It does not locate a sharp knee, and none is claimed. Where along it to set the budget is the committee’s decision. A grid of \(\omega\) in the wrong units (the integers \(1, 2, 3, \dots\), say) returns the truncation plan for every value and the frontier collapses to one point; the grid has to be in the units of \(\omega\) that move the plan, which is why the chunk asserts that the sweep has at least 20 distinct plans.

15.5.1 How \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) moves when \(\mathbf{f}\) moves
\(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) is quoted to four decimals, which invites more confidence than the marker panel supports. The same panel feeds \(\mathbf{f}\) and therefore \(GD_{\text{ref}}\) and \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\). In the experiment below \(\mathbf{f}\), the null and \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) are rebuilt under a minor-allele-frequency (MAF) filter, a density and an ascertainment scenario (Table 15.5), but the index is not: ctx$traits stays the one made from all markers, so A5 (the panel is the causal set) is dropped here and the result concerns a fixed index with a thinned \(\mathbf{f}\), not a change of genotyping platform. Each panel’s null is null_distribution() with its default seed 7, so the random subsets are the same draws of hybrids in every panel.


Show code
ceiling_for <- function(keep, label, B = 250) {
  Xs <- ctx$X[, keep, drop = FALSE]
  ck <- build_ctx(X = Xs, f = molecular_coancestry(Xs), G = NULL,
                  traits = ctx$traits, ped = ctx$ped, n_lines = ctx$n_lines,
                  pool = ctx$pool, fL = NULL, cfg = ctx$cfg)
  nl <- null_distribution(ck, n_sel, B = B, B_full = 1)
  data.frame(panel = label, markers = ncol(Xs), gd_ref = nl$gd_ref,
             alpha_trunc = alpha_loss(sel_truncation(ck, n_sel), ck, nl$gd_ref))
}
maf <- pmin(ctx$p0, 1 - ctx$p0)
polyA <- colMeans(simulate_lines(book_cfg)[seq_len(book_cfg$n_pool_A), ] / 2)
sens <- rbind(
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.10),
    function(t) ceiling_for(maf >= t, sprintf("MAF >= %.2f", t)))),
  ceiling_for(polyA > 0 & polyA < 1, "ascertained in pool A"))
knitr::kable(fmt(sens, 4),
             col.names = c("panel", "markers", "$GD_{\\text{ref}}$", "$\\alpha_{\\text{trunc}}$"))

Across the 20 draws \(GD_{\text{ref}}\) moves by a mean of 19.1% (range 17.7 to 21.3%) and \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) by a mean of 7.8% (s.d. 4.4, range 1.3 to 16.8%), about 2.5 times less than the level; seed 1, the draw of Table 15.5, is 4.7%, below the median of 6.7%. The chunk asserts that the seed-1 value of this file equals the live value of Table 15.5. This measures that the budget ceiling moves less than the diversity level it is computed from, not that it does not move. A ratio of two diversities measured on the same panel cancels the part of the shift that numerator and denominator share; the table shows that cancellation is partial. A budget is therefore more portable across panels than \(GD_{\text{ref}}\), not invariant to them, and the spread is a property of this simulator at this scale (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers), not measured at another.
Density adds noise (Table 15.7). Each draw’s panel was thinned to 250, 500 and 1000 markers, six independent subsets each, the subsets drawn before any null_distribution() call (the callout on null_distribution() below).

}

At 250 markers the mean over six subsets differs from the full-panel value by -0.0004 on average (s.e. 0.0011 over draws), inside one s.d. of the six subsets in 20 of 20 draws; the s.d. itself is a median of 36% of the estimate (range 10 to 81%) (Table 15.7). That is a measurement on six subsets per cell, with no interval on the s.d. itself. What it supports is that no bias of a thin panel’s \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) was detected over founder draws, at a resolution of about 0.002 (two standard errors at 250 markers, against a mean full-panel \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) of 0.037), so a bias of a few percent of \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) is not excluded; and that a single study gets an estimate with a relative spread of a third. A single thin-panel study cannot tell which side of the full-panel value it landed on.






Warningnull_distribution() reseeds, and will freeze a resampling loop



It calls set.seed(seed) on entry, with seed = 7 by default, so the random stream is reset every time it is invoked. Any sample() written after it inside a loop draws the same values on every pass, and a replication study becomes one replicate reported with a spurious standard deviation. The chunk checks the mechanism.


Show code
draw_after_null <- function() {

title: 15  Optimal contributions and the \(\alpha\) constraint
section: 15.6 A caveat carried over from the OCS literature
text:
15.6 A caveat carried over from the OCS literature
Gómez-Romano et al. (2016) (p. 7, their Fig. 1 and p. 8, their Fig. 2) study contributions optimised under a restriction on the rate of regional genomic coancestry (the whole genome except one chromosome, strategy CHR_ove), with populations of \(N = 20, 100, 200\) candidates. They compute the expected rate of coancestry in the next generation as follows (Equation 15.8):
\[E(\Delta f_{t+1}) \;=\; \frac{\mathbf{c}_t'\,\mathbf{G}_{x,t}\,\mathbf{c}_t - f_t}{1 - f_t}, \tag{15.8}\]
with \(\mathbf{c}_t\) the contributions, \(\mathbf{G}_{x,t}\) the coancestry matrix of the candidates computed from marker genotypes (for the region in question) and \(f_t\) the mean coancestry of the candidates’ generation (written \(\mathbf{f}\) and \(\bar f\) elsewhere in this book). Two measurements are reported.

Fig. 1: with the restriction set at 0.1%, the realised rate was approximately 1.4%, 0.3% and 0.2% for \(N = 20, 100, 200\), always above the restriction while the expected rate met it; the gap between expected and realised rate tended to grow as \(N\) fell.
Fig. 2: for three sets of parents with the contributions held fixed, 1000 offspring generations were drawn; the realised average coancestry was always above the expected value, and the observed rate was approximately double the intended rate (at \(N = 20\)).

The paper’s Discussion (p. 11) states that the predicted value “was consistently biased downward” and that the bias grew as \(N\) fell, and suggests that terms from Mendelian inheritance variance are missing from an equation derived for the infinitesimal model with pedigree coancestry; that is the authors’ suggestion, not a derivation. No single factor of two follows from these: it is about 2 in one resampling analysis at \(N = 20\) and about 14, 3 and 2 against the restriction at \(N = 20, 100, 200\). Whether the same bias holds for the whole-genome \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}\) of this book, at other \(N\) and for hybrids, is not shown by that paper.
This does not affect the \(\theta_S\) computed in this book: \(\mathbf{f}\) is measured on the marker genotypes of an already-realised hybrid population, with no forward-prediction step. It becomes relevant when the pipeline plans a further generation from the selected hybrids, predicting their offspring’s coancestry from a contribution vector: the direction of the bias reported is that \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}\) underestimates the realised coancestry, and a budget on a predicted coancestry would need a margin whose size is not measured here.

section: 15.7 Quadratic programming, when contributions are continuous
text:
15.7 Quadratic programming, when contributions are continuous
Where the problem genuinely is continuous (composing a synthetic, assembling a core collection, setting seed proportions) it is solved as a quadratic programme (QP) rather than by search: optimal_contributions() of Chapter 3, with ocs_quadprog() adding the merit term. The example below (Table 15.8) uses all 50 lines, with \(\mathbf{f}^L\) the line coancestry and, as the merit of a line, the mean index of the hybrids that use it as a parent (line_merit). That is a value of the line against a tester, the other pool as a whole (not the line alone), computed on the known index and not on a prediction. quadprog is a Suggests package; the chunk runs only where it is installed.


Show code

line_merit <- vapply(seq_len(ctx$n_lines),
                     function(a) mean(ctx$index[pa == a | pb == a]), numeric(1))
front_qp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(10^seq(-1, 2, length.out = 8), function(lam) {
  o <- ocs_quadprog(ctx$fL, line_merit, lambda = lam, upper = 0.20)
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(o$c_i), 1, tolerance = 1e-4)),
            all(o$c_i <= 0.20 + 1e-5))
  data.frame(lambda = lam, merit = o$merit, coancestry = o$coancestry,
             n_used = sum(o$c_i > 1e-6), share_A = sum(o$c_i[ctx$pool == "A"]))
}))

upper = 0.20 is a share of the pooled contribution, which sums to one over the 50 lines, with a single margin: the QP of Chapter 3 has no per-pool sum, and the share of pool A shows what that permits (the hybrid problem requires each pool to carry one half; Section 12.1). The cap max_use of the discrete problem is a count of hybrids; in contribution weights \(w_a = k_a/(2n)\) (with \(k_a\) the number of times line \(a\) is a parent of the \(n\) selected hybrids, so \(\sum_a w_a = 1\)) it is \(w_a \le \texttt{max\_use}/(2n)\), so upper \(= \texttt{max\_use}/(2n)\) puts the two on one scale, and upper = 0.20 at \(n\) = 60 corresponds to max_use = 24. They are the same restriction in kind, an operational ceiling on one line’s use that is easier to defend than the \(\lambda\) that produced it, not the same constraint: the first caps a share of a continuous vector, the second a count in a discrete selection enforced in the decoder (Chapter 16). The chunk asserts that each solution sums to one and respects the cap.
As \(\lambda\) falls the solution concentrates on fewer lines, which the lines-used column shows, down to the five lines that the 20% cap allows at least. The same mechanism makes \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) a second restriction in the discrete problem of Section 12.6; the fitness printed above carries only the budget (and, when set, max_use), not \(N_{e,\text{par}}\). The merit here has no correlated prediction error, so the concentration shown is the concentration of the truth; the effect of selecting on predicted values, where error is correlated with relatedness, is Section 12.5.

section: 15.8 What belongs in the inner loop
text:
15.8 What belongs in the inner loop
The optimiser performs on the order of \(10^5\) to \(10^6\) evaluations (the defaults of sel_de() give NP x itermax = 600,000 fitness calls at most), so the cost per call decides what goes into the objective and what waits for validation. Section 12.2 times the metrics and reports that the matrix route and the line route of Section 12.1 agree to numerical precision, that the line route is slower per call at \(N = 2{,}500\), \(n = 50\) and cheaper only for large \(n\), and that it is the only one that exists at \(N = 22{,}500\): it is the route that scales, not a faster call at the scale of this chapter. This chapter times nothing. What Section 12.6 puts in the objective is \(\theta\) (by the matrix or line route) and \(N_{e,\text{par}}\); allelic richness and A-NE (accession-to-nearest-entry distance, Chapter 11) are kept for validation of the returned plan. This chapter computes none of them, nor Nei’s \(G_{st}\) (gst()); where they are computed, and at what cost, is Section 12.2 and Section 12.6.

title: 16  Combinatorial selection
text:
16.1 Four baselines before any optimiser
Chapter 15 posed the problem – choose \(n\) of \(N\) hybrids to maximise the mean index \(\bar u_S\) subject to \(\alpha(S) \le \alpha_{\max}\) (Equation 15.2) – and bounded it from above (Equation 15.7). It left to this chapter the discrete side: the decoder that turns a real-valued optimiser vector into \(n\) distinct hybrids, the per-line cap max_use, and the order in which to try methods. The chapter builds the strategies from the two that need no optimiser (truncation, and truncation under a per-line cap), through a greedy swept over an index weight, to differential evolution (DE), and measures each at the book scale.
What it finds depends on the evaluation budget of the DE, and the introduction says so rather than promise otherwise. Evaluations are counted nominally as NP \(\times\) itermax. The chapter runs sel_de() at 30,000 evaluations (NP = 120, itermax = 250) and, for its five-budget frontier, at 18,000 (NP = 100, itermax = 180); the printed defaults of sel_de() are NP = 300, itermax = 2000, that is 600,000. At the chapter’s budgets, and with the default warm start, the mean of the DE’s index over repeated seeds is below the best feasible greedy plan at each of the five diversity budgets tried (Section 16.5). At the 1% diversity budget, the only one run at a larger evaluation budget, that order reverses at 120,000 and at 600,000 evaluations (Section 16.4.2); the other four diversity budgets were not run above 18,000. The warm start is worth a measured amount over a cold start at 30,000 evaluations, the only budget at which a cold start was run, and the DE does improve on a greedy plan when that plan is among its seeds (Section 16.4.1; 1% budget, 30,000 evaluations). What the DE offers at the chapter’s budgets is a budget as its interface; the last section states what the three budgets do and do not support, within the limits of these measurements, which are one simulated dataset at the book scale.
The decision is a concrete one, and it is the last of a cycle in a cross-pollinated crop. Two heterotic pools, A and B, hold \(L_A\) and \(L_B\) inbred (or doubled-haploid) lines. Every candidate is one cross \(A_a \times B_b\), so the candidate set is the factorial \(N = L_A \times L_B\) – in maize, the set of single crosses that could be made from the current elite lines without introducing anything new. The \(n\) you keep are the crosses that go forward: into multi-location testing, into seed increase, and – through their parents – into the next recycling cycle. Keeping too few distinct parents is not a statistical inconvenience, it is a decision to narrow the pool that the programme will breed from next.
What has to be in hand before any line of this chapter runs is the three-object contract of Chapter 6:
Assumptions, declared once and not violated afterwards. They are those of Chapter 15, restated for the claims made here.
Scale. “Book scale” is 25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, simulation seed 1, \(N =\) 625, \(n =\) 60, and is what every number below refers to unless a sentence names another scale. Four other scales are named where they occur, because the word “production” has been used for more than one of them: the benchmark book scale and the benchmark production scale of search_benchmark.csv (Chapter 17; regenerated in this repository by book/scripts/regenerate.R search), which the file records as \(N =\) 625, \(L =\) 50, \(n =\) 60, cap 5 and \(N =\) 10,000, \(L =\) 200, \(n =\) 200, cap 4; the cached-run scale of de_constraints.csv, \(N =\) 3,600 hybrids with \(L = 120\) lines (an external file, below); and the package production scale, 71 + 71 lines and \(N =\) 5,041, used only to count dimensions. The benchmark book scale has this chapter’s \(N\), \(L\) and \(n\) but a cap of 5, where this chapter’s capped truncation uses 4.
The per-line usage cap, defined once. A line \(a\) is used once by each selected hybrid it parents, so the number of uses is \(k_a\), with \(\sum_a k_a = 2n\) (Appendix A). The cap, \(k_{\max}\), is the largest \(k_a\) a plan may have: at most \(k_{\max}\) of the \(n\) selected hybrids may share a line as a parent. It is a count of crosses, not of seeds or plants. The argument that carries it is called cap in sel_truncation_cap() and max_use in sel_greedy(), make_fitness(), sel_de() and stage2_select() (and in decode_lines(), make_fitness_fast(), sel_de_fast(), sel_local_search() and ocs_round() of Chapter 17); it is one quantity under two argument names. max_use = NULL is the default everywhere and means no cap; it reproduces the behaviour before the cap existed bit for bit. sel_truncation_cap() has no NULL and defaults to ceiling(2 * n_sel / n_lines) + 1, one above even use. The realised value of a plan is max_line_use(), printed as max_line. In make_fitness() the cap enters as the number of parent slots above \(k_{\max}\), summed over lines and divided by \(2n\), added to the violation of \(\alpha\) and charged at the same penalty (R/03_de_select.R); in the greedy it is a feasibility test on the move.
The instance this chapter runs on:
Read it as a breeder would. 60 crosses are kept out of 625, which is 9.6% of the factorial. The 60 crosses consume \(2n =\) 120 parent slots spread over 50 lines, so a perfectly even plan would use each line 2.4 times – the scale against which any per-line cap has to be set. gd_ref is the gene diversity of a random subset of exactly this size, with its resampling standard deviation next to it. The last row is \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) (Chapter 15), the loss of the truncation plan: pure truncation loses 4.12% of gd_ref. A budget \(\alpha_{\max} \ge \alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) constrains nothing, because truncation, which maximises the index, already meets it; that is the first thing to check and the subject of Chapter 15.
Four families – random, truncation, truncation under a per-line cap, and greedy – in six rows, because greedy is shown at three index weights.

Three of those six rows are the same plan. greedy_w1 and greedy_w3 return exactly the truncation set (the chunk asserts it) – same index, same \(\alpha\), same max_line – because both index weights sit far above the crossover measured in the w-units chunk below, where the merit term swamps the coancestry term and the greedy argmax degenerates to the index ranking. Read them as one row until that measurement has been made; it is the reason an \(\omega\) grid of round numbers is a trap.
Read the columns in this order, because each answers a different question and three of them are routinely skipped:
Truncation is the plan of maximum mean index: the optimum with no constraint, and the reference for the budget (\(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\)). It is what every programme does by default, and the interesting question is not whether it loses diversity but how little index a constrained plan has to give up relative to it. It is not the \(n\)-subset of lowest diversity (Chapter 15): a plan confined to fewer lines loses more.
Show code
# The top n crosses among those of the first three A lines (3 x 25 = 75 crosses).
a3 <- which(ctx$ped$a %in% 1:3)
s3 <- a3[order(ctx$index[a3], decreasing = TRUE)][seq_len(n_sel)]
a_trunc <- alpha_loss(sels[["truncation"]], ctx, null$gd_ref)
a_three <- alpha_loss(s3, ctx, null$gd_ref)
stopifnot(a_three > a_trunc)
fmt(100 * c(alpha_trunc_pct = a_trunc, alpha_three_A_lines_pct = a_three), 3)
#>         alpha_trunc_pct alpha_three_A_lines_pct 
#>                   4.122                   6.867
Truncation’s max_line here is 23: one line parents that many of the 60 selected crosses, against 2.4 under even use. That is the concentration a cap is meant to remove, and it is visible without any coancestry matrix. The plan confined to three A lines loses 6.87% against truncation’s 4.12%, so truncation is not the floor on diversity; it is the reference that a gain-maximising plan never needs to go beyond.
Truncation with a per-line cap is the cheap baseline that deserves more attention than it gets. It needs no coancestry matrix at all – only counting:

The default cap is ceiling(2 * n_sel / ctx$n_lines) + 1, one above even use, which is 4 here. Filling 60 slots under it required scanning 413 of the 625 ranked candidates, and only 16 of the resulting crosses are also in the truncation set: the cap does not trim the top of the ranking, it reshuffles most of it. The last two rows count the same reshuffling in lines rather than in crosses, and they are the reason \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) is not a line count: the capped plan touches 32 distinct parent lines against truncation’s 33, out of 50 available – to within one line, the same set size – while its effective number of parents is 31 against 13. What the cap changes is how evenly the 120 parent slots are spread over the lines that are used, not how many lines are used at all.
What that buys and what it costs, separately. The cap cuts the diversity loss from 4.12% to 0.33% and raises the effective number of parents from 13 to 31, at 41% of truncation’s index. Whether that is a good trade is a programme decision, not a statistical one – but note that the capped plan is feasible at a 1% budget while truncation is not, and it was found by counting alone.
Before reaching for an optimiser, run this. If a per-line cap already meets your constraint at an acceptable index, you are done. The failure mode at this step is silent: a returned vector shorter than n_sel, which every downstream metric will happily evaluate on the wrong set size – length() it.

title: 16  Combinatorial selection
text:
index, in standard deviations of the candidate set – what the plan is worth.
alpha_pct, the loss of gene diversity relative to a random subset of the same size – what it costs, on the lens the constraint will pin. Negative means more diverse than random.
Ns, the status number \(N_s = 1/(2\theta)\) (Section 11.3). On the molecular coancestry \(\mathbf{f}\) it lies in \([1/2, 1]\) and is a monotone rescaling of \(\theta\), not a head count; unlike \(\alpha\) it carries no reference to a random subset of the same size.
Ne_parents, the effective number of parent lines, which is computed from counts alone and is the metric that catches “\(\theta\) looks fine but twelve lines did all the work”.
max_line, the largest number of selected crosses sharing one parent, the realised \(k_{\max}\) – the operational number, because that line is a seed parent and has to be increased, maintained and, in a CMS system, converted.








Rank all 625 candidate crosses by index, best first.
Walk down the ranking. Admit a cross only if both its parents are still below the cap.
Stop when n_sel crosses have been admitted, or when the ranking is exhausted – in which case the returned vector is shorter than n_sel and the cap was infeasible for this set size.
A cap \(k_{\max}\) admits at most \(L_A k_{\max}\) crosses through pool A and at most \(L_B k_{\max}\) through pool B, so \(n \le k_{\max}\min(L_A, L_B)\) is necessary for the walk to reach \(n\): here 60 against

It is not sufficient, because the walk is greedy and can exhaust the ranking while admissible slots remain on lines that no remaining cross uses together:

title: 16  Combinatorial selection
text:
16.2 Greedy, with incremental updates
Adding hybrid \(j\) to an existing set changes the submatrix total by \(2 s_j + f_{jj}\), where \(s_j\) is the sum of \(f_{ij}\) over the already-chosen. That makes each step \(O(N)\) instead of \(O(n^2)\), and the whole construction affordable.


Show code
S <- sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel = 10, w = 1)
j <- setdiff(seq_len(ctx$N), S)[1]
f <- ctx[["f"]]
recomputed  <- sum(f[c(S, j), c(S, j)])                 # O(n^2), from scratch
incremental <- sum(f[S, S]) + 2 * sum(f[S, j]) + f[j, j] # O(n), the update
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(recomputed, incremental)))
c(recomputed = recomputed, incremental = incremental)
#>  recomputed incremental 
#>    87.07925    87.07925




Show code
sel_greedy
#> function (ctx, n_sel, w = 0, max_use = NULL) 
#> {
#>     f <- ctx[["f"]]
#>     d <- diag(f)
#>     s <- numeric(ctx$N)
#>     avail <- rep(TRUE, ctx$N)
#>     out <- integer(n_sel)
#>     total <- 0
#>     if (!is.null(max_use)) {
#>         pa <- as.integer(ctx$ped$a)
#>         pb <- as.integer(ctx$ped$b)
#>         cnt <- integer(ctx$n_lines)
#>     }
#>     for (k in seq_len(n_sel)) {
#>         theta_new <- (total + 2 * s + d)/k^2
#>         score <- w * ctx$index - theta_new
#>         score[!avail] <- -Inf
#>         j <- which.max(score)
#>         if (!is.finite(score[j])) {
#>             out <- out[seq_len(k - 1L)]
#>             break
#>         }
#>         out[k] <- j
#>         avail[j] <- FALSE
#>         total <- total + 2 * s[j] + d[j]
#>         s <- s + f[, j]
#>         if (!is.null(max_use)) {
#>             for (a in c(pa[j], pb[j])) {
#>                 cnt[a] <- cnt[a] + 1L
#>                 if (cnt[a] >= max_use) 
#>                   avail[pa == a | pb == a] <- FALSE
#>             }
#>         }
#>     }
#>     out
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x76d82d5d58>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>


One step \(k\), in the order the code performs it:

theta_new <- (total + 2 * s + d) / k^2 is the group coancestry the set would have, for every candidate at once, with total the current submatrix sum, s the running vector of coancestry sums against the chosen set and d = diag(f). The normaliser is \(k^2\), the size after the addition.
score <- w * ctx$index - theta_new – merit against relatedness.
Candidates already chosen are set to -Inf; with max_use set, so is every hybrid of a line that has reached its cap. The cap is therefore a feasibility test on the move, never a penalty on the result – the partition-matroid treatment of Chapter 17.
The argmax is taken, total and s are updated in \(O(N)\), and the parent counts incremented.
If no finite score remains, the loop exits early and the returned vector is short – the same check as for the capped truncation.

The score is \(\omega\,u_i - \theta_{\text{new}}\), where \(\omega \ge 0\) is the index weight of Appendix A and w is its argument name in the code (it is not the line-usage vector \(\mathbf{w}\) of Section 12.1). At \(\omega = 0\) the greedy returns the most diverse plan it can build – a heuristic, with no certificate that it is the minimum of \(\theta\) over all \(n\)-subsets – at near-zero gain. As \(\omega \to \infty\) it converges to truncation. Sweeping \(\omega\) traces a frontier – but only if the grid is in the right units, and that is the trap at this step.
\(\omega\) is an exchange rate. Under the score \(\omega\,u_i - \theta_{\text{new}}\) two candidates are indifferent when \(\omega\,\Delta u = \Delta\theta\), so \(\omega = \Delta\theta / \Delta u\), in units of group coancestry per index standard deviation: the greedy argmax accepts, for one standard deviation of index, a rise of \(\theta\) of up to \(\omega\). The multiplier \(\lambda\) of Equation 15.7, in \(V(\lambda) = \max\,\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{u} -
\lambda\,\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}\), has the reciprocal dimension, index units per unit of \(\theta\); how the numerical values of the two relate is not examined here. The two quantities \(\omega\) converts between differ by four orders of magnitude, and that ratio is measurable before any sweep is run:


Show code
S30 <- sel_greedy(ctx, 30, w = 0)
theta_if_added <- (sum(f[S30, S30]) + 2 * colSums(f[S30, ]) + diag(f)) / 31^2
w_crossover <- diff(range(theta_if_added)) / diff(range(ctx$index))
c(index_spread = diff(range(ctx$index)),
  theta_spread = diff(range(theta_if_added)),
  w_crossover  = w_crossover)
#> index_spread theta_spread  w_crossover 
#> 6.055856e+00 3.293444e-04 5.438446e-05


w_crossover is the weight at which the two terms of the score have equal range, measured at the 31st pick of the \(\omega = 0\) plan (S30), not at the \(n = 60\) problem: it is a scale for the sweep and not a threshold, and the sweep below measures where the plans actually change relative to it. Two grids appear in this book, and the best feasible greedy plan depends on which is used.


Show code
alphas    <- c(0, 0.0025, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02)    # the five budgets of the frontier
alpha_max <- 0.01
grid_bench <- c(0, 10^seq(-5, 1, length.out = 19))  # book/scripts/regenerate.R, @sec-advanced
grid_fine  <- 10^seq(-6, -1, length.out = 60)       # the grid of @sec-ocs
sweep <- function(ws) {
  plans <- lapply(ws, function(w) sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = w))
  list(w = ws, plans = plans,
       alpha = vapply(plans, alpha_loss, numeric(1), ctx = ctx, gd_ref = null$gd_ref),
       index = vapply(plans, mean_index, numeric(1), ctx = ctx))
}
gb <- sweep(grid_bench)
gf <- sweep(grid_fine)
# the best plan of a sweep whose own alpha is within a budget
best_within <- function(g, a) {
  ok <- which(g$alpha <= a)
  ok[which.max(g$index[ok])]
}
summ <- function(g) {
  is_tr <- vapply(g$plans, setequal, logical(1), sels[["truncation"]])
  a_in  <- sort(unique(c(0, g$alpha[g$alpha > 0 & g$alpha < a_trunc], a_trunc)))
  c(values = length(g$w),
    distinct_plans = sum(!duplicated(round(cbind(g$alpha, g$index), 8))),
    return_truncation = sum(is_tr),
    flat_from = min(g$w[is_tr]),
    from_x_crossover = min(g$w[g$w > 0]) / w_crossover,
    to_x_crossover = max(g$w) / w_crossover,
    largest_alpha_interval_pct = 100 * max(diff(a_in)))
}
grid_summary <- rbind(benchmark_20 = summ(gb), fine_60 = summ(gf))
fmt(grid_summary, 4)

The benchmark grid is 0 and 19 values log-spaced from \(10^{-5}\) to 10; it is the grid of the benchmark of Chapter 17 and of Chapter 12, so those chapters report this greedy. It runs from 0.18 to 183,876 times w_crossover: it starts below the crossover, by a factor of 5.4, and lies almost wholly above it. The grid of Chapter 15 is 60 values log-spaced from \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{-1}\), which runs from 0.018 to 1,839 times the crossover. The plan is the truncation plan from \(\omega =\) 0.0215 upward on the benchmark grid and from 0.0142 upward on the fine one; on the benchmark grid that is 2.6 decades above w_crossover. A grid of round numbers such as \(\{0.25, 0.5, \dots, 30\}\) – the one this chapter used before it was measured, and the one sel_de() hard-codes for its warm start – lies entirely above the weight from which the plan is truncation and returns the same selection at every value, which makes greedy look an order of magnitude worse than it is.


Show code
plot(NA, xlim = 100 * range(c(gb$alpha, gf$alpha)),
     ylim = range(c(gb$index, gf$index)),
     xlab = "gene diversity loss, alpha (%)", ylab = "mean index (s.d.)")
points(gf$alpha * 100, gf$index, pch = 19, cex = 0.6, col = "#1f5f8b")

       pch = c(2, 19), col = c("#d98e04", "#1f5f8b"), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

The greedy frontier at book scale (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, n = 60, N = 625, simulation seed 1): mean index against gene diversity loss alpha. Triangles: the 20 plans of the benchmark grid of omega; dots: the 60 plans of the finer grid of the optimal-contributions chapter. omega = 0 is the most diverse plan the greedy builds; large omega converges to truncation (cross). Dotted vertical line: alpha = 0. The points are not joined, because no plan exists between two grid values.






Show code
# Where the sweep leaves the omega = 0 plan and where it reaches truncation, in units
# of w_crossover. "Same as omega = 0" means the same index and alpha to 1e-9; the sets
# of hybrids may still differ, and usage_same checks that the line usage then agrees.
usage <- function(s) tabulate(c(ctx$ped$a[s], ctx$ped$b[s]), ctx$n_lines)
w0 <- sels[["greedy_div"]]
a0 <- alpha_loss(w0, ctx, null$gd_ref); i0 <- mean_index(w0, ctx)
ends <- function(g) {
  lo   <- which(g$w < w_crossover)
  at0  <- abs(g$index - i0) < 1e-9 & abs(g$alpha - a0) < 1e-9
  set0 <- vapply(g$plans, setequal, logical(1), w0)
  use0 <- vapply(g$plans, function(s) all(usage(s) == usage(w0)), logical(1))
  tr   <- vapply(g$plans, setequal, logical(1), sels[["truncation"]])
  c(below_crossover = length(lo),
    distinct_below = length(unique(lapply(g$plans[lo], sort))),
    same_set_as_w0 = sum(set0[lo]),
    same_index_alpha_as_w0 = sum(at0[lo]),
    same_usage_as_w0 = sum(use0[lo]),
    index_below_min = min(g$index[lo]), index_below_max = max(g$index[lo]),
    first_rise_x_crossover = min(g$w[g$w > 0 & !at0]) / w_crossover,
    index_at_first_rise = g$index[which(g$w == min(g$w[g$w > 0 & !at0]))],
    truncation_from_x_crossover = min(g$w[tr]) / w_crossover,
    neither_w0_nor_truncation = sum(!at0 & !tr))
}

Two readings, and the second is the argument for everything that follows. First, the plan is not constant below the crossover and the frontier does not begin at it. Result (the window-ends chunk). On the benchmark grid 4 of the 20 values lie below w_crossover (\(\omega = 0\) and 3 positive values, up to 0.85 times it); they return 4 distinct plans, with mean index from 0.134 to 0.499, so only the \(\omega = 0\) value returns the \(\omega = 0\) plan. On the fine grid 21 of the 60 values lie below it, from 0.018 times w_crossover; the lowest 3 return plans with the index and \(\alpha\) of the \(\omega = 0\) plan, to \(10^{-9}\) (they are not the same set of hybrids – none of the 21 is – but they have the same line usage), and from 0.033 times w_crossover the index rises (0.165 there, 0.549 at the highest value below the crossover). At the upper end the plan is truncation from \(\omega =\) 0.0215 on the benchmark grid and from 0.0142 on the fine one: 396 and 261 times w_crossover. 9 of the 20 benchmark values and 11 of the 60 fine values return truncation; the benchmark grid has 12 distinct plans, and 10 of its values return neither the \(\omega = 0\) plan nor truncation: these are the plans of the frontier. Interpretation, and what limits it. The transition from the \(\omega = 0\) plan to truncation spans about 3.9 decades on the fine grid, from 0.033 to 261 times w_crossover: neither end is within an order of magnitude of it, so w_crossover is a scale inside the range and not a locator of either edge (it is measured at one pick of one plan, above). The lowest end is resolved only to the spacing of the fine grid, and the benchmark grid, which has no value between \(\omega = 0\) and 0.18 times w_crossover, does not resolve it at all. Second, the sweep is parameterised by \(\omega\) and the breeder’s constraint is not. Within \([0, \alpha_{\text{trunc}}]\) the largest interval of \(\alpha\) with no plan of the sweep in it is 1.53 percentage points on the benchmark grid and 0.59 on the fine one; a budget falling inside such an interval cannot be requested of a greedy sweep at all, only stumbled upon, and the best feasible plan for it is the one at the interval’s lower end. A finer grid shrinks the intervals, it does not remove them. An optimiser parameterised by \(\alpha_{\max}\) can be asked for the budget directly.
Greedy plans also seed the initial population of the differential evolution; what that is worth is measured in Section 16.4.1.

title: 16  Combinatorial selection
text:
16.3 The encoding problem
Differential evolution searches a box of real numbers, and an encoding turns a point of the box into a set of \(n\) distinct hybrids. Three encodings appear in this book, and they differ in dimension and in what a coordinate means:

\(n\) keys (decode()): \(n\) coordinates, each naming a candidate by its integer part. This is what sel_de() searches; the dimension is \(n =\) 60 here.
\(N\) keys (decode_rank()): one random key per candidate, the \(n\) smallest keys selected; the dimension is \(N\), which is 625 here, 3,600 in the cached run below and 5,041 at the package production scale. A 0/1 vector of length \(N\) has the same dimension; the package implements the key form and I did not test the 0/1 form.
\(L\) line weights (decode_lines()): one weight per line, dimension \(L\).

The package searches \(n\) coordinates, not \(N\), because the dimension of the \(N\)-key search grows with the candidate set. Whether that makes the \(N\)-key search infeasible, or only under-powered at a given budget, is not settled by anything in the book: the only measurement of the \(N\)-key encoding is the cached external run below, at one budget, and its limits are stated with it.


Show code
decode
#> function (par, N, n_sel) 
#> {
#>     k <- as.integer(par)
#>     k[k < 1L] <- 1L
#>     k[k > N] <- N
#>     dup <- duplicated(k)
#>     if (any(dup)) 
#>         k[dup] <- setdiff(seq_len(N), k[!dup])[seq_len(sum(dup))]
#>     k
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x76d827dd90>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>


The decode of the first encoding, step by step:

as.integer(par) truncates each coordinate toward zero, so the real interval \([i, i+1)\) maps to candidate \(i\). sel_de() searches the box \([1,\, N + 0.999]\), so candidates \(1\) to \(N-1\) each own a full unit interval and candidate \(N\) owns \([N,\, N + 0.999]\) – narrower by one part in a thousand, because the upper bound stops just short of \(N + 1\) instead of reaching it.
Coordinates outside the box are clamped to the ends.
duplicated() marks every coordinate after the first that lands on an already-used candidate.
Each duplicate is replaced by the lowest index not otherwise in use, so the result always has exactly n_sel distinct candidates.

A worked case, small enough to check by hand:


Show code
d <- decode(c(3.9, 3.2, 1.1, 7.5), N = 10, n_sel = 4)
stopifnot(all(d == c(3, 2, 1, 7)))
d
#> [1] 3 2 1 7


Truncation gives \((3, 3, 1, 7)\); the second coordinate is the duplicate; the lowest index not in \(\{3, 1, 7\}\) is 2; the repair returns \((3, 2, 1, 7)\). The same mechanism is what lets a warm start be injected exactly: a seed is written into the population as index + 0.5, the middle of its own interval, and decodes back to itself.


Show code
s0 <- sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = 1)
seed_roundtrip <- all(decode(s0 + 0.5, ctx$N, n_sel) == s0)
stopifnot(seed_roundtrip)
c(box_lower      = 1,
  box_upper      = ctx$N + 0.999,
  width_typical  = 2 - 1,                       # candidate 1 owns [1, 2)
  width_last     = (ctx$N + 0.999) - ctx$N,     # candidate N owns [N, N+0.999]
  seed_roundtrip = seed_roundtrip)
#>      box_lower      box_upper  width_typical     width_last seed_roundtrip 
#>          1.000        625.999          1.000          0.999          1.000


Duplicates are repaired deterministically. A stochastic repair would make the fitness noisy, and a noisy fitness stops DE converging – the same parameter vector must always score the same.


Show code
set.seed(3)
p1 <- runif(n_sel, 1, ctx$N + 1)
p2 <- runif(n_sel, 1, ctx$N + 1)
d1 <- decode(p1, ctx$N, n_sel)
d2 <- decode(p2, ctx$N, n_sel)
stopifnot(length(unique(d1)) == n_sel, length(unique(d2)) == n_sel,
          all(c(d1, d2) >= 1 & c(d1, d2) <= ctx$N),
          identical(d1, decode(p1, ctx$N, n_sel)))
c(unique_1 = length(unique(d1)), unique_2 = length(unique(d2)),
  collisions_repaired = sum(duplicated(as.integer(p1))))
#>            unique_1            unique_2 collisions_repaired 
#>                  60                  60                   2








NoteA bias in the repair, measured



The repair fills in the lowest free indices. It is marked in the source with a ponytail: comment naming the limit and the upgrade path – switch to “nearest free” if the DE ever stalls. What the bias is can be measured on random vectors:


Show code
set.seed(3)
rb <- t(replicate(2000, {
  p   <- runif(n_sel, 1, ctx$N + 1)
  dup <- duplicated(as.integer(p))
  fill <- decode(p, ctx$N, n_sel)[dup]                 # the repaired members
  c(n_dup = sum(dup), same_B_line = sum(ctx$ped$b[fill] == min(ctx$ped$b)))
}))
c(vectors = nrow(rb), duplicates_per_vector = mean(rb[, "n_dup"]),
  share_repaired_on_one_B_line = sum(rb[, "same_B_line"]) / sum(rb[, "n_dup"]))
#>                      vectors        duplicates_per_vector 
#>                    2000.0000                       2.7585 
#> share_repaired_on_one_B_line 
#>                       1.0000


Over 2,000 random vectors there are 2.76 duplicates per vector, and 100% of the repaired members are crosses with the same B parent (line 26), because candidates \(1, \dots, L_A\) are the crosses of that line with each A line. So the bias is not a diffuse tilt toward low-numbered candidates: it adds about 2.8 uses of one B line to each random vector, which interacts with the cap. Whether it changes the plans the DE returns is not measured here; the line usage of the returned plans was not examined.



16.3.1 A third encoding: one weight per line
Section 12.1 showed that \(\theta\) depends only on the line-usage vector. That makes the third encoding available, and one that changes what the coordinates mean: one weight per line, dimension \(L\). Against the \(N\)-key vector that is a collapse from 3,600 coordinates to 120 in the cached run below. Against the \(n\) coordinates sel_de() actually searches it is a different trade, which the cached run does not record (\(n\) is not in the file), and the numbers below say which of the two comparisons is which.


Show code
decode_lines
#> function (p, ctx, n_sel, max_use = NULL, w_div = 3) 
#> {
#>     par <- ctx$parents
#>     sc <- ctx$index + w_div * (p[par[, 1]] + p[par[, 2]])
#>     ord <- order(-sc)
#>     if (is.null(max_use)) 
#>         return(ord[seq_len(n_sel)])
#>     sel <- integer(n_sel)
#>     cnt <- integer(ctx$n_lines)
#>     k <- 0L
#>     for (h in ord) {
#>         a <- par[h, 1]
#>         b <- par[h, 2]
#>         if (cnt[a] < max_use && cnt[b] < max_use) {
#>             k <- k + 1L
#>             sel[k] <- h
#>             cnt[a] <- cnt[a] + 1L
#>             cnt[b] <- cnt[b] + 1L
#>             if (k == n_sel) 
#>                 break
#>         }
#>     }
#>     if (k < n_sel) {
#>         rest <- setdiff(ord, sel[seq_len(k)])
#>         sel[(k + 1L):n_sel] <- rest[seq_len(n_sel - k)]
#>     }
#>     sel
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x76d8285460>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>


The line weight shifts each hybrid’s score by the weights of its two parents, and hybrids are taken greedily subject to the per-line usage cap – so the cap is satisfied by construction rather than by penalty. In detail:

Each candidate scores ctx$index + w_div * (p[a] + p[b]), with p the line-weight vector being searched and w_div = 3 by default. A line’s weight therefore moves every cross it parents, which is what makes the decision a line decision.
Candidates are taken in decreasing score, skipping any whose parents have reached max_use.
If the cap makes n_sel unreachable, the selection is topped up ignoring it, and the fitness function’s penalty term then sees the violation – so an infeasible cap degrades gracefully instead of returning a short vector.

At p = 0 the decoder is exactly capped truncation, which is the natural zero of the encoding; Chapter 17 verifies that identity numerically where the encoding is actually driven.


16.3.2 The four restrictions
The only measurement of the \(N\)-key encoding in this book is a cached run (Section 12.4 previews it) under four simultaneous restrictions on the plan. They are defined here once; Section 12.4 points to this section. With \(k_a\) the number of uses of line \(a\) (above), \(\sum_a k_a = 2n\):


Show code
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Restriction = c("Diversity loss", "Effective number of parents",
                  "Per-line usage cap", "Pool balance"),
  Quantity = c("$\\alpha$ of @eq-ocs-alpha",
               "$N_{e,\\text{par}} = (\\sum_a k_a)^2 / \\sum_a k_a^2$",
               "$\\max_a k_a$, the cap $k_{\\max}$",
               "$\\lvert \\sum_{a \\in \\mathcal{A}} k_a / (2n) - 1/2 \\rvert$"),
  Limit = c(sprintf("$\\alpha \\le$ %s%%", lim[["loss_pct"]]),
            sprintf("$N_{e,\\text{par}} \\ge$ %s", lim[["ne_par"]]),
            sprintf("$k_{\\max} =$ %s", lim[["k_max"]]),
            sprintf("$\\le$ %s", lim[["pool"]])),
  Argument = c("`alpha_max`", "`ne_par_min`", "`max_use`", "`pool_tol`")),
  escape = FALSE)




Table 16.1: The four restrictions of the cached run of de_constraints.csv. Columns: the restriction; the quantity it limits (\(k_a\): uses of line \(a\), \(\sum_a k_a = 2n\); \(\mathcal{A}\): the lines of pool A); the limit of the cached run as Section 12.4 states it (the file records outcomes, not limits); the argument of make_fitness_fast() that carries it. In make_fitness_fast() (R/04_fast_metrics.R) the first, second and fourth enter the fitness as a violation divided by its own limit, and the cap as the number of parent slots above \(k_{\max}\), summed over lines, divided by the total number of uses \(2n\) (not by \(k_{\max}\)); all are charged at one penalty multiplier, and the multiplier of the cached run is not recorded.












Restriction
Quantity
Limit
Argument




Diversity loss
\(\alpha\) of Equation 15.1
\(\alpha \le\) 0.5%
alpha_max


Effective number of parents
\(N_{e,\text{par}} = (\sum_a k_a)^2 / \sum_a k_a^2\)
\(N_{e,\text{par}} \ge\) 50
ne_par_min


Per-line usage cap
\(\max_a k_a\), the cap \(k_{\max}\)
\(k_{\max} =\) 6
max_use


Pool balance
\(\lvert \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} k_a / (2n) - 1/2 \rvert\)
\(\le\) 0.05
pool_tol








The fourth restriction cannot bind in a factorial of \(A \times B\) crosses: every selected hybrid has one parent in pool A and one in pool B, so the \(2n\) slots are split exactly \(n\) and \(n\) for every plan, and the quantity in the last row is 0 identically.


Show code
set.seed(5)
share_A <- replicate(500, {
  s <- sel_random(ctx, n_sel)
  k <- tabulate(c(ctx$ped$a[s], ctx$ped$b[s]), ctx$n_lines)
  sum(k[ctx$pool == "A"]) / sum(k)
})
stopifnot(all(share_A == 0.5))

#>       plans min_share_A max_share_A

The cached column pool_imbalance is 0 in 9 of 9 rows, which the identity requires; I infer that the cached run’s candidate set was such a factorial (\(N =\) 3,600 \(= 60^2\) is consistent with 60 + 60 lines, but the file does not record it). The restriction therefore carries no information in this setting, and the “four simultaneous restrictions” are at most three.


16.3.3 What the cached run compares, and what it does not
The claim that an \(N\)-key search is infeasible at this scale would be a claim about every budget; the cached run measures one. It is an external file: book/data/de_constraints.csv (9 rows: three configurations, three seeds) has no producer in this repository – no target of book/scripts/regenerate.R writes it, and its code is not available here – so it cannot be regenerated or re-run, and nothing below is reproducible from this repository beyond arithmetic on the stored values (Chapter 12 lists the files of this kind). It is worth being exact about what it compares, because neither arm of it is sel_de(). Both are driven through make_fitness_fast(), at the cached-run scale, under the four restrictions above. One arm is decode_rank() – one random key per hybrid, dimension 3,600. The other is decode_lines(), dimension 120. Neither is warm-started. The file does not record the number selected \(n\), the DE population size NP, the iteration count or the penalty multiplier.

Result. At the same budget of 60,000 evaluations the \(N\)-key search reaches a mean index of 0.351 (seed range 0.343 to 0.358) and the line-weight search 1.988 (1.956 to 2.017): a difference of 1.64 index units, with non-overlapping seed ranges. (No ratio is quoted: the index has no natural zero.) In the \(N\)-key arm every restriction is slack: \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) is 75.8 to 77.2 against a floor of 50, loss is 0.05 to 0.07% against 0.5%, and the largest use is 5, 6, 6 against a cap of 6 (reached in 2 of 3 seeds). In the line-weight arm \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) is 50 to 50.25 and loss 0.42 to 0.5%, at the \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) floor and near the loss limit, and the largest use is 6 in every seed – which the decoder guarantees by construction. Penalty and repair returned numerically identical outcomes in the \(N\)-key arm for all three seeds (the file stores outcomes, not plans); no line-weight arm with a penalty was run.
Interpretation, and what limits it. Feasible plans with index 1.99 exist for this problem (the line-arm plans), so the \(N\)-key plans at 0.35 with every restriction slack are not constrained optima: a slack restriction at the end of a run is here the sign of an unconverged search, not of a conservative plan (Section 12.4 reads it the same way). That follows from the table; it is not a general rule. Four limits apply.

Budget. With NP at least ten times the number of parameters, the guidance of the DEoptim.control help page (the package is described by Mullen et al. (2011)), 3,600 parameters call for 36,000 population members, so 60,000 evaluations are 1.67 generations; at 120 parameters they are about


The NP of the cached run was not recorded, so I cannot say that either arm followed the guidance. The \(N\)-key search is under-powered by construction at this budget; the result is a statement about that budget, not about the encoding at any budget.


Handlers. The comparison is between two encodings through the same fitness, not between two constraint handlers. The identity of penalty and repair in the \(N\)-key arm is not explained. One candidate, an inference from the package code and not a test (the cached run’s own code is not available): the \(N\)-key fitness calls decode_rank(), which takes no max_use (R/04_fast_metrics.R), so for that arm “penalty” and “repair” would be the same function. The line decoder satisfies the cap by construction, so “uses = 6” in the line arm is not evidence that the search found the boundary, and nothing here says that the constraint handler does or does not matter.
Replication. Three seeds, one setup, no interval.
Not sel_de(). The benchmark of Chapter 17 is the measurement closest to the question of which encoding wins in the setting this chapter uses:

Uncapped, sel_de() is ahead of the line-encoded DE by 0.3 (s.e. 0.009) at the benchmark book scale, 35 standard errors with all three seed differences positive, and by 0.11 (s.e. 0.032) at the benchmark production scale, 3.4 standard errors on 2 degrees of freedom (two-sided \(p =\) 0.08): not resolved by three seeds. The cached run’s verdict is on the \(N\)-key encoding at its budget, not on sel_de().

The cached run shows that, at its budget, one random key per hybrid reaches far less than one weight per line under four restrictions, with every restriction slack in the former. It does not show that an \(N\)-dimensional encoding is infeasible at larger budgets, and it does not compare constraint handlers in the encoding that works. Which of two viable encodings wins in the setting of this chapter has to be measured, and Chapter 17 measures it.

title: 16  Combinatorial selection
text:
16.4 Differential evolution
The run, as a procedure:

Fix n_sel first, then obtain gd_ref from null_distribution() at that same size. A reference computed at another size is a different quantity and every \(\alpha\) downstream is wrong by a fixed factor.
Choose \(\alpha_{\max}\) below \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\), printed at the top of this chapter, by the procedure of Chapter 15.
Call sel_de(). It builds its warm start, injects it into the initial population, and hands DEoptim the fitness \(-(\bar u_S - 1000 \cdot \text{viol})\) to minimise, with \(\text{viol} = \max(0, \alpha - \alpha_{\max})\), an absolute excess in units of \(\alpha\) – plus, when max_use is set, the cap term defined above.
Check the returned plan before using it: realised \(\alpha\) against the budget, max_line, \(N_{e,\text{par}}\), and the gap to the bound. The diversity constraint is a penalty, so a returned plan is not guaranteed feasible – the violation is only made expensive.



Show code
sel_de
#> function (ctx, n_sel, alpha_max, gd_ref, NP = 300, itermax = 2000, 
#>     seeds = NULL, trace = FALSE, max_use = NULL) 
#> {
#>     fit <- make_fitness(ctx, n_sel, alpha_max, gd_ref, max_use = max_use)
#>     if (is.null(seeds)) 
#>         seeds <- lapply(c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16), function(w) sel_greedy(ctx, 
#>             n_sel, w = w, max_use = max_use))
#>     seeds <- Filter(function(s) length(s) == n_sel, seeds)
#>     initial <- matrix(runif(NP * n_sel, 1, ctx$N + 1), NP, n_sel)
#>     for (i in seq_len(min(length(seeds), NP))) initial[i, ] <- seeds[[i]] + 
#>         0.5
#>     ctrl <- DEoptim::DEoptim.control(NP = NP, itermax = itermax, 
#>         trace = trace, initialpop = initial)
#>     res <- DEoptim::DEoptim(fit, lower = rep(1, n_sel), upper = rep(ctx$N + 
#>         0.999, n_sel), control = ctrl)
#>     decode(res$optim$bestmem, ctx$N, n_sel)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x76d54ff9a0>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>




Show code
set.seed(9)
de_idx <- suppressWarnings(
  sel_de(ctx, n_sel, alpha_max = alpha_max, gd_ref = null$gd_ref,
         NP = 120, itermax = 250))

fmt(c(index      = mean_index(de_idx, ctx),
      alpha_pct  = 100 * alpha_loss(de_idx, ctx, null$gd_ref),
      budget_pct = 100 * alpha_max,
      Ns         = status_number(de_idx, ctx),
      Ne_parents = ne_parents(de_idx, ctx)), 3)
#>      index  alpha_pct budget_pct         Ns Ne_parents 
#>      1.330      0.978      1.000      0.738     22.857


The realised loss sits just inside the budget, which is the sign that the constraint is active and the penalty correctly scaled: with penalty = 1000 multiplying the absolute violation, one tenth of a percentage point of excess loss costs a full index standard deviation. A plan that comes back well inside the budget at a low index usually means the opposite – that the penalty dominated and the search never approached the boundary.

16.4.1 The warm start
sel_de() seeds its initial population with a greedy sweep, and the package keeps that seeding as a design decision. An earlier version of its documentation stated a stronger form – that at roughly 100 integer dimensions \(4.5 \times 10^5\) evaluations are not enough to beat greedy without it; the current documentation calls that a historical figure of which no run is recorded in this repository. I did not rerun it and it is not used here. What is measured below is the effect at book scale, 20 seeds per arm, with the chapter’s own calls (NP = 120, itermax = 250, i.e. 30,000 evaluations); that is the only evaluation budget at which a cold start was run.
Five initial populations, each NP = 120 rows with the first rows overwritten by the seeds: cold, one random plan; w = 0 only, the maximum-diversity plan; truncation only; default, the eight greedy plans sel_de() builds for itself (seeds = NULL); and default + best greedy, those eight and the best feasible plan of the fine \(\omega\) grid. In every arm the rest of the population is uniform random keys. The arms share the seed and NP; they do not share the random part of the initial population (the cold arm draws its one plan before the keys, the others do not), so pairing by seed removes no initial-population variance, and the standard errors below are of differences by seed for convenience only.


Show code
best_fine <- gf$plans[[best_within(gf, alpha_max)]]       # best feasible greedy, 60-value grid
best_bench <- gb$plans[[best_within(gb, alpha_max)]]      # ... and on the benchmark grid
seed_w <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16)                 # the grid sel_de() hard-codes
default_seeds <- lapply(seed_w, function(w) sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = w))
arms <- list(`cold` = NULL,
             `w = 0 only` = list(default_seeds[[1]]),
             `truncation only` = list(sels[["truncation"]]),
             `default` = default_seeds,
             `default + best greedy` = c(default_seeds, list(best_fine)))
wa_runs <- lapply(1:20, function(sd_) vapply(names(arms), function(a) {
  set.seed(sd_)
  sd_arg <- if (a == "cold") list(sample.int(ctx$N, n_sel)) else arms[[a]]
  r <- suppressWarnings(
    sel_de(ctx, n_sel, alpha_max, null$gd_ref, NP = de_cfg$NP[1],
           itermax = de_cfg$itermax[1], seeds = sd_arg))
  c(index = mean_index(r, ctx), alpha = alpha_loss(r, ctx, null$gd_ref))
}, numeric(2)))
pick <- function(what) data.frame(seed = 1:20, t(vapply(wa_runs, function(m) m[what, ],
                                                         numeric(length(arms)))),
                                  check.names = FALSE)
wa <- pick("index")          # one row per seed, one column per initial population
wa_alpha <- pick("alpha")    # the alpha of the same plans, against `alpha_max`
# the `default` arm at seed 9 is the plan `de_idx` of the previous chunk: same call, same seed
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(wa[["default"]][wa$seed == 9], mean_index(de_idx, ctx))))
arm_names <- names(arms)
wtab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(arm_names, function(a) {
  d <- wa[[a]] - wa[["cold"]]
  data.frame(arm = a, mean = mean(wa[[a]]), sd = sd(wa[[a]]),
             min = min(wa[[a]]), max = max(wa[[a]]),
             `minus cold` = mean(d), `s.e.` = sd(d) / sqrt(length(d)),
             `seeds above cold` = sum(d > 0),
             `over budget` = sum(wa_alpha[[a]] > alpha_max), check.names = FALSE)
}))

Mean index of the DE plan at the 1% budget for five initial populations (Table 16.4), book scale, 20 seeds each (points; horizontal jitter only), NP = 120, itermax = 250 (30,000 evaluations). Horizontal lines: the best feasible greedy plan of the 60-value omega grid (solid) and of the 20-value benchmark grid (dashed).




Result. The default arm averages 1.34 (standard deviation 0.0225) and the cold arm 1.201 (0.0291); the difference by seed is 0.139 (s.e. 0.008), positive in 20 of 20 seeds, about 12% of the cold mean. The ratio of the two standard deviations is 1.29 (variance-ratio test \(p =\) 0.27). The default plan is below the best feasible greedy plan of the 60-value grid (1.4226) in 20 of 20 seeds, and below that of the benchmark grid (1.3782) in 20. The one-plan arms recover 5% (w = 0 only, s.e. 0.01) and 47% (truncation only) of the default difference. Adding the best feasible greedy plan to the default seeds raises the mean to 1.482, that is 0.059 above that plan on average (range 0.028 to 0.075). The diversity constraint is soft, so the improvement has to be read together with the feasibility of the plans: 0 of the 20 default + best greedy plans exceed the 1% budget (their \(\alpha\) runs from 0.973 to 0.999%), and the numbers of plans over budget are cold 1, w = 0 only 0, truncation only 0, default 0, default + best greedy 0.
Interpretation, with its limits. The warm start is worth about the difference above at this scale and budget, in the direction of the package’s design decision, and a single cold run is not reportable (the cold arm’s range, 0.117, is 84% of the difference being measured). A smaller spread of the warm arm is not established: a ratio of 1.3 is what these 20 seeds show. The DE can improve on a greedy plan when that plan is among its seeds (a DE cannot return a worse plan than the best of its initial population, so the informative number is the size of the improvement, which is positive in every seed, with 0 of those plans over the budget). The default seeds are not that: the grid sel_de() hard-codes lies above the crossover except for \(\omega = 0\), and the best feasible greedy plan is not among them. Which feature of the seeds carries the effect is not identified by these arms: the default seeds contain few distinct plans (Table 16.5), w = 0 only is not distinguishable from cold at 20 seeds, and truncation only recovers part of the effect, so the number of copies of the infeasible truncation plan in the population (several in the default, one in truncation only) may matter; an arm that varies it was not run, and a “dimensional” explanation of the effect was not tested. All of this is one dataset at book scale and one evaluation budget, 30,000: the cold arm and the five-arm ablation were not run at another evaluation budget (the next subsection runs the default warm start alone at two larger ones) and I did not measure either at another scale. Widening the seed grid is a change to the package rather than to the call, and it is not made here: every number in this book was produced with sel_de() as it stands.

fit <- make_fitness(ctx, n_sel, alpha_max, null$gd_ref)
seeds <- default_seeds
n_trunc_seeds <- sum(vapply(seeds, setequal, logical(1), sels[["truncation"]]))
n_distinct_seeds <- length(unique(lapply(seeds, sort)))
knitr::kable(fmt(data.frame(
  w         = seed_w,
  index     = vapply(seeds, mean_index, numeric(1), ctx = ctx),

  fitness   = vapply(seeds, function(s) fit(s + 0.5), numeric(1))), 4),
  row.names = FALSE)

A method that beats both on index, at a fraction of the wall-clock, is in Chapter 17.


16.4.2 The evaluation budget
Every sel_de() run above has NP \(\times\) itermax = 30,000 evaluations, and the frontier below has 18,000, against the printed default of 600,000 (the sel_de listing above). The same function and the same call, changing only NP and itermax, was run at three evaluation budgets at the 1% diversity budget, seeds 1 to 10, with set.seed() immediately before each run and the default warm start (seeds = NULL) in every one. Evaluations are nominal, NP \(\times\) itermax; DEoptim also evaluates the initial population. The first configuration repeats the default arm of Table 16.4 for seeds 1 to 10, which the chunk asserts.

    r <- suppressWarnings(sel_de(ctx, n_sel, alpha_max, null$gd_ref,

               alpha = alpha_loss(r, ctx, null$gd_ref),
               secs = proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0)
  }))))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(bud$index[bud$config == "chapter"],

}))

Result. The mean index is 1.334 at 30,000 evaluations, 1.438 at 120,000 and 1.481 at 600,000; the best feasible greedy plan of the 60-value grid is 1.4226. The number of the 10 plans above it is 0, 10, 10 in that order, and 0, 1, 0 of the 10 plans exceed the budget (largest excess 0.000057 percentage points). Among the plans within budget, the numbers above the fine-grid greedy plan are 0 of 10, 9 of 9, 10 of 10 in that order.
