Interpretation, and what limits it. “The DE is below the best feasible greedy plan” is a statement about 18,000 to 30,000 evaluations at the 1% budget; at four times the chapter’s budget and at the printed default the DE is above that plan in all 10 seeds, so the sentence does not hold at the budget of the printed defaults. The chapter applied the same objection to the cached \(N\)-key run (“a statement about that budget”); it applies here. What the table does not show: the other four diversity budgets of the frontier were run at 18,000 evaluations only, so their position at a larger budget is not known; the cold-versus-warm effect and the ablation were run at 30,000 evaluations only, so whether the warm start is worth anything at 600,000 is not known; whether the gain at the larger budgets comes from the evaluations or from the seeds working together with them was not separated; the wall-clock of a DE run was not compared here with that of the greedy sweep; and it is one dataset, one simulation seed, one budget of diversity, 10 optimiser seeds.


16.4.3 Checking convergence against the bound
Section 15.4 derived the bound. For every plan \(S\) with \(\theta_S \le
\theta_{\max}\), where \(\theta_{\max} = 1 - GD_{\text{ref}}(1 - \alpha_{\max})\) (Equation 15.3) and \(\bar u_S\) is the mean index (Equation 15.2),
\[\bar u_S \;\le\; \min_{\lambda \ge 0}\,\bigl[\,V(\lambda) + \lambda\,\theta_{\max}\bigr]\]
(Equation 15.7, with \(V(\lambda)\) the optimum of the continuous relaxation, Equation 15.5; \(\lambda\) the multiplier on \(\theta\), in index units per unit of \(\theta\)). Every \(\lambda\) gives a valid bound, so a coarse grid costs tightness, not validity. ocs_bound() returns the minimum over a grid of \(\lambda\), doubles the number of projected-gradient iterations until the value changes by less than a relative \(10^{-3}\), and sets a converged attribute: a stalling criterion on that doubling, not a certificate (Section 15.4). An under-converged relaxation reports \(V(\lambda)\) too small, which makes the “bound” too small, so the attribute has to be read before any gap is quoted (Section 17.7).


Show code
lam_grid <- 10^seq(0, 2.5, by = 1 / 6)            # 16 multipliers, as in @sec-relaxation
bound <- ocs_bound(ctx, n_sel, alpha_max, null$gd_ref, lambdas = lam_grid)
relax <- attr(bound, "relaxation")                # one row per lambda, converged
a_relax <- (null$gd_ref - relax[, "GD"]) / null$gd_ref
stopifnot(attr(bound, "converged"))
theta_max <- 1 - null$gd_ref * (1 - alpha_max)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  as.numeric(bound),
  min(relax[, "index"] - relax[, "lambda"] * relax[, "theta"] +
        relax[, "lambda"] * theta_max))))
c(upper_bound = as.numeric(bound), lambda_star = attr(bound, "lambda"),
  iterations = attr(bound, "iters"), converged = attr(bound, "converged"),
  theta_max = theta_max)
#>  upper_bound  lambda_star   iterations    converged    theta_max 
#>    1.5532442   68.1292069 8000.0000000    1.0000000    0.6774198


The gap of the DE plan (seed 9, 30,000 evaluations) to the bound is 14.4%, and that of the best feasible greedy plan (fine grid) 8.4%. Here the stalling flag is TRUE, at 8000 iterations. A gap is the sum of two shortfalls, that of the plan from the best discrete plan and that of the best discrete plan from the bound (the bound is that of a continuous relaxation of a discrete problem), and the gap alone does not separate them. At the book scale the second is limited by the benchmark of Chapter 17: its simulated-annealing plan reaches 1.528 against its own bound 1.554, a gap of 1.7% (3 seeds; the benchmark computes its reference from \(B\) = 500 random subsets, this chapter from 400, hence the slightly different bound). So at this scale and evaluation budget most of the DE’s gap is the optimiser’s, not the relaxation’s; that reading holds only where the bound is certified and the relaxation is known to be tight. At the benchmark production scale the flag is FALSE in 36 of 36 rows, so no gap there is quoted, and “a large gap means the optimiser has not converged” cannot be applied.






TipIf the DE ever looks unconvincing on real data



De Beukelaer et al. (2018), optimising core-collection subsets with stochastic search rather than DE, rank three search algorithms of the Core Hunter framework on the same objective across four crop datasets – rice, coconut, maize and pea – in the Results section “Optimizing E-NE and A-NE with local searches”: parallel tempering first, a genetic algorithm second, and random descent – a plain stochastic hill-climber – third, with all twelve pairwise comparisons significant under a Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon test. The objective of that comparison is E-NE only, the average distance from each selected entry to its nearest other selected entry (the authors state they ran these experiments only for E-NE): a distance-based diversity measure, not allele coverage. The genetic algorithm therefore does beat the hill-climber on raw score. What it does not do is win, and the method that wins is the one assembled from many simple local searches run in parallel, not the one with the more elaborate update rule.
The inference, stated separately from that result and limited by it: extra sophistication inside a single-solution algorithm bought a rank there and not the win, which is a weak reason to spend complexity on the optimiser and no reason at all to expect a DE to be the right one. It is one application, on a distance-based objective without an index or a coancestry budget, so it transfers as a prior about where effort pays and not as a result. That direction is taken up in Chapter 17, which builds the local search on the O(L) swap this package already had and measures it against the DE at equal wall-clock.

title: 16  Combinatorial selection
text:
16.5 The full frontier
One optimisation per budget, which is the \(\varepsilon\)-constraint method of Haimes et al. (1971): maximise one objective (the index) subject to a bound on the other (\(\alpha \le \alpha_{\max}\)). Each point is a plan that can be put in front of a committee, described by the budget it respects rather than by an exchange rate nobody can interpret. Each budget is run with 10 seeds, at NP = 100 and itermax = 180: 18,000 evaluations, against the 600,000 of the printed defaults of sel_de().


Show code
seeds_front <- 45:54
fr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(alphas, function(a) do.call(rbind, lapply(seeds_front, function(sd_) {
  set.seed(sd_)
  r <- suppressWarnings(sel_de(ctx, n_sel, a, null$gd_ref, NP = 100, itermax = 180))
  data.frame(alpha_max = a, seed = sd_, alpha = alpha_loss(r, ctx, null$gd_ref),
             index = mean_index(r, ctx), Ne_par = ne_parents(r, ctx))
}))))
front <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(fr, fr$alpha_max), function(d) data.frame(
  alpha_max = d$alpha_max[1], DE_mean = mean(d$index), DE_sd = sd(d$index),
  DE_min = min(d$index), DE_max = max(d$index), alpha_mean = mean(d$alpha))))
rownames(front) <- NULL
front$greedy_fine  <- vapply(front$alpha_max, function(a) gf$index[best_within(gf, a)], numeric(1))
front$greedy_bench <- vapply(front$alpha_max, function(a) gb$index[best_within(gb, a)], numeric(1))
front$seeds_above_fine  <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(front)), function(i)
  sum(fr$index[fr$alpha_max == front$alpha_max[i]] > front$greedy_fine[i]), integer(1))
front$seeds_above_bench <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(front)), function(i)
  sum(fr$index[fr$alpha_max == front$alpha_max[i]] > front$greedy_bench[i]), integer(1))
over <- fr$alpha - fr$alpha_max                        # > 0: the soft constraint is violated
n_within <- sum(over <= 0)
# the claim of the introduction: the DE's mean is below the best feasible greedy of the fine grid
stopifnot(all(front$DE_mean < front$greedy_fine))




Show code
plot(NA, xlab = "gene diversity loss, alpha (%)", ylab = "mean index (s.d.)",
     xlim = 100 * range(c(fr$alpha, gf$alpha, a_relax)),
     ylim = range(c(fr$index, gf$index, relax[, "index"], as.numeric(bound))))
lines(sort(a_relax) * 100, relax[order(a_relax), "index"], type = "b", pch = 1,
      lty = 2, col = "grey55", cex = 0.7)
points(gf$alpha * 100, gf$index, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "#1f5f8b")
points(fr$alpha * 100, fr$index, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "#b2182b66")
lines(front$alpha_mean * 100, front$DE_mean, type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2, col = "#b2182b")
points(alpha_max * 100, as.numeric(bound), pch = 2, cex = 1.4, lwd = 2)
abline(v = 0, lty = 3); abline(v = alpha_max * 100, lty = 3)

       c("constrained DE (mean, and seeds)", "greedy sweep, 60 plans",
         "continuous relaxation", "Lagrangian bound at 1%"),
       col = c("#b2182b", "#1f5f8b", "grey55", "black"), pch = c(19, 19, 1, 2),
       lty = c(1, NA, 2, NA), lwd = c(2, 1, 1, 1), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

Three things to read, in this order.
The constraint does its job, softly. In 48 of 50 runs the DE plan’s \(\alpha\) is within its budget; the other 2 exceed it by at most 0.0011 percentage points, which the penalty prices at 0.011 index units at most – the constraint is a penalty, as the procedure above says, and the returned plan has to be checked. The mean realised \(\alpha\) is -0.02, 0.24, 0.46, 0.97, 1.95% for budgets 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2%: the optimiser spends nearly the diversity it was allowed and no more. A plan that lands far inside its budget has not been constrained by it, and whatever else is limiting it – the cap, the penalty scale, an unconverged search – has to be identified before the frontier is read as a price list.
The comparison against greedy depends on the greedy grid. Result: against the best feasible plan of the 60-value grid the DE’s mean is lower at all 5 budgets, by 0.217, 0.123, 0.141, 0.101, 0.109 index units from the smallest to the largest budget, and 0 of the 50 DE runs are above it. Against the 20-value benchmark grid the DE’s mean is above the greedy at 4 of the 5 budgets, with 40 of 50 runs above it; there the greedy has no point near the budget (between two consecutive values of \(\omega\) the sweep steps over the whole interval, and the best feasible plan is one from far inside it). Interpretation: the count of budgets at which the DE is ahead is a property of the greedy grid, and it reverses on a finer one. At this scale, on this dataset, with sel_de() and its default warm start at 18,000 evaluations, the DE buys the ability to hit a requested budget, not a better plan than a fine greedy sweep. That statement is about that evaluation budget: at the 1% budget the mean DE index passes the fine greedy plan at 120,000 evaluations (Section 16.4.2), and the other four diversity budgets were not run above 18,000. The 10 seeds give the DE side a measured spread (standard deviation 0.032, 0.025, 0.033, 0.029, 0.021 across the five budgets); the greedy side has none because it is deterministic; the grid resolution is a tuning choice that moves the verdict; and this is one dataset and one simulation seed, not measured at another scale.
The dashed curve is the relaxation; the triangle is the bound. Each grey point is the index maximiser of the continuous problem at its own diversity, so by weak duality (Equation 15.6) it bounds every discrete plan at least as diverse as itself. What does not follow is a bound for a plan that spends the whole budget when the point lies strictly inside it (Section 15.4, statement 3): there the height of the point depends on the grid of \(\lambda\). In this run the highest relaxation point inside the 1% budget is 1.347, below the best feasible greedy plan (1.423), and the bound (1.553) lies above both; Section 15.4 shows how this height moves with the grid, and Section 17.4 shows that the construction “best relaxation point inside the budget” is not a bound. The vertical distance to the bound at \(\alpha_{\max}\) is what Chapter 17 spends its effort on.

The cap binds there (max uses equals the cap) and the budget does not. At the benchmark book scale the capped routes reach 1.106 to 1.112 with \(\alpha\) near the budget (0.88 to 0.98%); de_hybrid_cap returns the tempering_cap row and de_lines_cap the ocs_round_cap row to the four decimals of the table, in index and in \(\alpha\). greedy_cap needs the \(N \times N\) matrix, which at \(N =\) 10,000 is 0.745 GiB in double precision. an optimiser. sel_de() for a budget: at the 1% budget its mean index was below the best fine greedy plan at 18,000 to 30,000 evaluations and above it at 120,000 and at the default 600,000 (Table 16.6); the other four diversity budgets were run at 18,000 evaluations only (below it), so for them the table supports no recommendation of sel_de() over a fine greedy sweep. Seeding it with the best greedy plan improved on that plan at 30,000 evaluations, 1% budget only. sel_de_fast() for an \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) floor, the only route of Chapter 17 with an argument for it








As an order of operations at the end of a cycle:

Build the contract objects and print the instance panel at the top of this chapter. Confirm gd_ref was computed at the n_sel you will actually use.
Compute \(\alpha_{\text{trunc}}\) from truncation. If it is below your intended \(\alpha_{\max}\), stop: the constraint is inactive and truncation is the answer.
Run sel_truncation_cap(). It costs nothing and needs no matrix. If it meets the budget at an acceptable index, stop.
Sweep sel_greedy() over an \(\omega\) grid that begins well below the crossover measured from your own data (here the index starts rising about 30 times below it) and ends above the point where the plan becomes truncation, not a grid of round numbers. Read the frontier and locate the knee.
Only if a specific budget has to be hit, or an \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) floor applies, run an optimiser, with an evaluation budget of the order of the printed default of sel_de() (at the 1% budget of this chapter’s dataset 30,000 evaluations did not pass the best fine greedy plan and 120,000 did) – and warm-start it, with the best feasible greedy plan among the seeds (measured at 30,000 evaluations only).
Whatever returned the plan, validate it on the second lens and on allelic richness before it leaves the analysis (Chapter 25).

The summary, within what was measured here, which is one simulated dataset at the book scale. At the chapter’s evaluation budgets (18,000 to 30,000), a fine greedy sweep reaches a higher index than sel_de() at each of five budgets, and at those budgets what the DE offers is a budget as its interface. At the 1% diversity budget, the only one run at larger evaluation budgets, the DE’s mean index is above the best fine greedy plan at 120,000 evaluations and at the printed default of 600,000 (Table 16.6), at a wall-clock cost that rises with the budget; seeded with the best greedy plan it improved on that plan at 30,000 evaluations (Table 16.4). The worth of the warm start at the larger budgets, and the five-budget comparison there, were not measured, and nothing here is measured at another scale. For the capped case at the benchmark production scale something simpler is as good on index, and the cost table of Section 12.2 is the reason to check which row you are in before writing any optimisation code. The claim that a restriction a greedy cannot test (an \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) floor) rules the cheap routes out rests on the argument of Chapter 17, not on a measurement in this chapter.

text:
Reproduce this chapter
All the code of this chapter, in order and with the explanation kept as comments, is one script: 10-combinatorial-selection.R. Download it, install hybdiv, and run it top to bottom in an empty directory; cached results are fetched on first use.

title: 17  Advanced selection: structure, bounds and scale
text:
17.1 Three facts about this problem
Chapter 16 stops at a warm-started differential evolution (DE). That is a reasonable place to stop if the problem is a black box. It is not one. This chapter names the structure, and then spends it: on cheaper moves, on genuine approximation guarantees, on a bound that is actually a bound, and on an oracle that says how far from optimal the heuristics really are.
The target throughout is the scale the method has to survive: 200 hybrids chosen from 10,000, a full factorial of 100 by 100 lines. That is an ordinary size for a hybrid maize programme at the end of a cycle: two heterotic pools of a hundred inbred or doubled-haploid lines each, every cross between them a legitimate candidate, and a few hundred of them going into the next round of multi-location testing.
That is a different – and deliberately larger – “production scale” from the “package production scale” Chapter 16 uses to count dimensions: the real dataset this package was written for, 71 + 71 lines and \(N = 5041\) candidates. (Chapter 16 also quotes this chapter’s two benchmark scales, by name, and the cached run at \(N = 3{,}600\) from 120 lines, which is where its encoding measurement was made.) Here it is the 100 + 100 factorial the scaling study and the head-to-head benchmark are run at, because a cost curve needs a span of \(N\) wider than one point provides. They are not interchangeable: every per-evaluation cost and every memory figure in this chapter is at \(N = 10{,}000\).
Scales, replication and provenance. The names are those of Chapter 16. “Book scale” is the live instance of this chapter: 25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, simulation seed 1, \(N =\) 625, \(n =\) 60 (the teaching scale of Chapter 15). The rows book and production of search_benchmark.csv are the benchmark book scale – the same \(N\), \(L\), \(n\) and dataset, with the reference gd_ref resampled \(B = 500\) times against \(B = 400\) here, and a per-line cap of 5 – and the benchmark production scale: \(N =\) 10,000, \(L =\) 200, \(n =\) 200, cap 4. The unit of replication in that file is the optimiser seed (1 to 3) on one simulated dataset per scale: the deterministic methods (greedy, greedy_cap, ocs_round, ocs_round_cap) return three identical rows, and every capped row has a seed standard deviation of 0 at the benchmark production scale. “Mean of 3 seeds” below means that, and a standard error over three seeds is a statement about the optimiser, not about the dataset.
The files read here – search_benchmark.csv, search_scaling.csv, search_anytime.csv, search_exact_gap.csv, search_anytime.png and search_scaling.png – are written by book/scripts/regenerate.R search (about 15 minutes; the exact oracle by search_exact), which quarto render never calls. They are reproducible in this repository, unlike the cached external files of Chapter 18; the indices of the deterministic methods reproduce to the digits printed, the timings (secs, us_*) come from one machine and do not. sel_exact() needs the highs package and ocs_quadprog() the quadprog package, both Suggests of hybdiv.
The evaluation budget of the differential evolutions. In the benchmark sel_de() and sel_de_fast() run NP = 100 and itermax = 300, that is 30,000 nominal evaluations (the evals column), against 30,000 proposed moves for each local search; the anytime curve of Section 17.3 runs the DE from 2,000 to 80,000 evaluations. Every statement about the DE in this chapter is about those budgets. Section 16.4.2 runs sel_de() at four times the first of them and at the printed default of 6e+05 evaluations, and finds its mean index above the best fine greedy plan there at the 1% budget, below it at 30,000; this chapter’s “DE below greedy” is the 30,000 reading and not a property of the method.
What has to be in hand, beyond Chapter 16’s three objects, is the line-level route: fast_ctx() adds ctx$parents, the \(N \times 2\) matrix of parent indices, to a context that already carries ctx$fL, the \(L \times L\) coancestry between lines. Everything in this chapter that scales is a function of those two and of nothing else.
The assumptions are Chapter 16’s, unchanged and worth restating because two of them are load-bearing here: parent lines are homozygous, which is what makes \(f_{ij}\) a function of the four parental coancestries and hence collapses the problem to \(L\) dimensions (Section 12.1); and f is molecular coancestry in \([0, 1]\), not a centred relationship matrix, which is what makes it a Gram matrix with the properties Section 17.1 needs.
Everything below follows from three properties of the problem, each of which takes three lines to check. The first, the Gram form of f, is stated in Section 6.2.1 and checked there numerically (and Section 10.7.7 asserts the related form \(\mathbf{f} = \tfrac12 + 2\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}^\top/m\), \(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{X} - \tfrac12\)); here it is used for convexity. The second and third, the submatrix sum and the matroid, are stated here for the first time.
crumbs: 17  Advanced selection: structure, bounds and scale

title: 17  Advanced selection: structure, bounds and scale
text:
17.1.1 f is a Gram matrix
Molecular coancestry is \(f_{ij} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_k [x_{ik}x_{jk} + (1-x_{ik})(1-x_{jk})]\), which is an inner product of the stacked vectors \([\mathbf{x}_i;\, \mathbf{1}-\mathbf{x}_i]\). So f is not merely symmetric, it is a Gram matrix, exactly:


Show code
V  <- cbind(ctx[["X"]], 1 - ctx[["X"]])
ev <- eigen(ctx[["f"]], symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ctx[["f"]], tcrossprod(V) / ctx$m, tolerance = 1e-12)),
          min(ev) > -1e-10 * max(ev))     # positive semi-definite up to rounding
c(max_abs_difference = max(abs(ctx[["f"]] - tcrossprod(V) / ctx$m)),
  min_eigenvalue     = min(ev),
  min_over_max_eig   = min(ev) / max(ev))
#> max_abs_difference     min_eigenvalue   min_over_max_eig 
#>       0.000000e+00      -4.275667e-13      -1.018142e-15


The check is the whole argument, and the chunk asserts it: the difference is zero to rounding, and the smallest eigenvalue is zero to the eigensolver’s own rounding – its sign is arbitrary, 15 orders of magnitude below the largest eigenvalue. A negative eigenvalue large enough to see on that scale would mean f had been centred, rescaled, or built on the wrong marker coding – and every method in this chapter would silently lose its justification.
Two consequences carry the rest of the chapter. First, \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}\) is a convex quadratic, so the diversity budget is a convex constraint – which is what makes the exact method of Section 17.6 possible at all. Second, \(\psi_{ij} = f_{ii} + f_{jj} - 2f_{ij}\) (not the distance \(1 - f_{ij}\) of E-NE and A-NE, Appendix A) is a squared Euclidean distance, hence a distance of negative type, which is the precise hypothesis the strongest approximation results require.


17.1.2 Maximising diversity is minimising the submatrix sum
\(\theta_S = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i,j \in S} f_{ij}\) (Equation 11.1; Cockerham (1967)), and at fixed \(n\) the normaliser is a constant:


Show code
s <- sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = 1)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(theta_group(s, ctx) * n_sel^2, sum(ctx[["f"]][s, s]),
                           tolerance = 1e-12)))
# the max-sum identity of @eq-advanced-maxsum, below
fS  <- ctx[["f"]][s, s]
psi <- outer(diag(fS), diag(fS), "+") - 2 * fS
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(psi[upper.tri(psi)]),
                           n_sel * sum(diag(fS)) - n_sel^2 * theta_group(s, ctx),
                           tolerance = 1e-12)))
c(theta_times_n2 = theta_group(s, ctx) * n_sel^2,
  submatrix_sum  = sum(ctx[["f"]][s, s]),
  difference     = theta_group(s, ctx) * n_sel^2 - sum(ctx[["f"]][s, s]))
#> theta_times_n2  submatrix_sum     difference 
#>   2.475329e+03   2.475328e+03   1.818989e-12


So the objective of the greedy score of Chapter 16, \(\omega\,\bar u_S - \theta_S\), is, up to the positive constant \(n^{-2}\), \(n\omega \sum_{i \in S} u_i -
\sum_{i,j \in S} f_{ij}\). Here \(u_i\) is the index of hybrid \(i\) (index standard deviations), \(S\) a set of \(n\) hybrids, \(\bar u_S\) its mean, and \(\omega \ge 0\) the index weight of Appendix A, in units of group coancestry per index standard deviation. The first term is modular; the second is submodular, because \(f_{ij} \ge 0\) makes the marginal cost of adding a hybrid, \(f_{ii} + 2\sum_{j \in S} f_{ij}\), grow with the set. Writing the same thing through \(\psi_{ij}\),
\[\sum_{i<j \in S} \psi_{ij} \;=\; n\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{f}_S) - n^2\theta_S, \tag{17.1}\]
with \(\mathbf{f}_S\) the \(n \times n\) submatrix of \(\mathbf{f}\) on \(S\) and \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{f}_S) = \sum_{i \in S} f_{ii}\) (an identity of the definitions, asserted in the chunk above), identifies it as the max-sum diversification problem of Borodin et al. (2017). I have not found it named that way in the plant-breeding literature, and this book makes no claim about what a systematic screen would find – no such screen was run. The structural identity is the load-bearing part, and it holds whether or not anyone has written it down before.
The practical content of “fixed \(n\)” is worth spelling out: it is only at a fixed set size that maximising gene diversity and minimising the submatrix sum are the same instruction. Comparing \(\theta\) across selections of different sizes compares two different things, which is the same reason gd_ref has to be resampled at the size actually being used (Section 11.9).


17.1.3 The per-line cap is a partition matroid
“No line may parent more than max_use of the selected hybrids” is one partition matroid per heterotic pool. Together with the cardinality constraint that is an intersection of matroids – not an arbitrary combinatorial restriction, but the single best-understood constraint class in discrete optimisation.
The structure comes from the mating design, not from the mathematics. Every candidate is a cross between one pool-A line and one pool-B line, so each selected hybrid contributes exactly one use to a pool-A line and one to a pool-B line, and the counts within each pool sum to \(n\) by construction:


Show code
cnt <- line_counts(s, ctx)
stopifnot(sum(cnt[ctx$pool == "A"]) == n_sel, sum(cnt[ctx$pool == "B"]) == n_sel)
c(uses_pool_A     = sum(cnt[ctx$pool == "A"]),
  uses_pool_B     = sum(cnt[ctx$pool == "B"]),
  n_sel           = n_sel,
  distinct_A_used = sum(cnt[ctx$pool == "A"] > 0),
  distinct_B_used = sum(cnt[ctx$pool == "B"] > 0))
#>     uses_pool_A     uses_pool_B           n_sel distinct_A_used distinct_B_used 
#>              60              60              60              10              23


That is exactly the ground-set partition a partition matroid needs. It also gives the feasibility condition for any cap \(k_{\max}\) (the per-line cap of Chapter 16, max_use in the code) directly: a plan of \(n\) crosses exists under the cap only if \(n \le L_A k_{\max}\) and \(n \le L_B k_{\max}\), with \(L_A\) and \(L_B\) the numbers of lines in the two pools. In a programme the cap is rarely chosen for theoretical reasons – it is set by how many seed-production fields a female line can support – and the point of naming the structure is that a constraint arriving from the field turns out to be the one class of constraint discrete optimisation handles best.






NoteWhy naming the structure is worth a section



Three named properties buy three concrete things (Table 17.1), and it is worth being blunt about which is which.

section: 17.2 What lazy greedy would not buy
text:
17.2 What lazy greedy would not buy
The obvious first move on a submodular objective is the accelerated, or “lazy”, greedy of Minoux (1978): keep stale marginal gains in a priority queue and re-evaluate only the top one, which is valid precisely because submodularity makes a stale gain an upper bound on the current one. Two distinct results are easy to conflate here, so name them apart: the acceleration is Minoux’s, while the worst-case guarantee for the plain greedy it accelerates is Nemhauser et al. (1978)’s and is quoted separately below. It is the standard accelerator for this objective class, and here it is worthless.
sel_greedy() already carries the running vector s of coancestry sums against the chosen set, so every candidate’s marginal gain is \(O(1)\) and the whole step is one vectorised pass. Lazy evaluation optimises precisely the cost that is already free. Reaching for it would add a heap, add bugs, and save nothing.
The guarantee is worth stating even so, because it settles a question rather than improving a number: greedy under our constraints cannot do worse than \(1/(p+1)\) of optimal, with \(p\) the number of matroids intersected – here the cardinality constraint plus one partition matroid per pool.
State it with its hypotheses, though, because they are not all met. The \(1 - 1/e\) and \(1/(p+1)\) results of Nemhauser et al. (1978) and Fisher et al. (1978) are proved for monotone, non-negative submodular functions. Our objective is neither in general: the index is standardised to mean zero over the candidate pool, so \(\bar u_S\) can be negative, and adding a hybrid increases the coancestry term, so the objective is monotone only where the merit term dominates. The guarantee therefore belongs in this chapter as a statement about the constraint class – the cap is not an arbitrary restriction – and not as a guarantee for any particular run. The bound this chapter actually uses is the Lagrangian bound of Section 17.4, and Section 17.6 measures what the local search does in fact achieve.

text:
17.3 The move that was already paid for
Section 12.1 established \(\theta_S = \mathbf{w}'\mathbf{f}^L\mathbf{w}\) (Equation 12.2), and theta_state()/theta_swap() have been in the package ever since, maintaining group coancestry in \(O(L)\) per swap. Nothing consumed them. Chapter 16 even ends with a callout recommending local search, citing De Beukelaer et al. (2018) – and then does not run one.


Show code
theta_swap
#> function (st, out_h, in_h, ctx) 
#> {
#>     cnt <- st$cnt
#>     v <- st$v
#>     po <- ctx$parents[out_h, ]
#>     pi_ <- ctx$parents[in_h, ]
#>     for (a in po) {
#>         cnt[a] <- cnt[a] - 1L
#>         v <- v - ctx$fL[, a]
#>     }
#>     for (a in pi_) {
#>         cnt[a] <- cnt[a] + 1L
#>         v <- v + ctx$fL[, a]
#>     }
#>     s <- st$s
#>     list(cnt = cnt, v = v, s = s, theta = sum(cnt * v)/(s * s))
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x78a09ace78>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>


Four rank-one column updates. No N x N matrix is touched, and the cost depends on neither \(N\) nor \(m\). The state it maintains is three objects: the line-count vector cnt, the product v = fL %*% cnt, and their inner product divided by \(s^2\), which is \(\theta\). Removing a hybrid subtracts the two columns of fL belonging to its parents; adding one adds the two columns of the entrant’s parents. Because a swap keeps the set size fixed, the normaliser \(s = 2n\) never changes.
It is an exact update, not an approximation, and that is checkable in three lines:


Show code
st    <- theta_state(s, ctx)
out_h <- s[1]
in_h  <- setdiff(seq_len(ctx$N), s)[1]
st2   <- theta_swap(st, out_h, in_h, ctx)
after <- c(setdiff(s, out_h), in_h)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(st2$theta, theta_group(after, ctx))),
          isTRUE(all.equal((2 * n_sel)^2 / sum(st2$cnt^2), ne_parents(after, ctx))))
c(incremental = st2$theta, recomputed = theta_group(after, ctx))
#> incremental  recomputed 
#>   0.6863819   0.6863819


If that identity ever fails, the state and the selection have drifted apart – the usual cause being a move that was accepted in the selection vector but not applied to the state, or the reverse.
That last property is the one that matters, and it is worth being precise about where the saving actually comes from, because the obvious answer is wrong. The line encoding does not make an evaluation cheaper. Taking two rows of Table 17.18, in Table 17.2:

The line encoding is slower per evaluation, because decoding a weight vector into a selection has to rank every candidate. What it buys is a smaller search space, not a cheaper objective. The order-of-magnitude saving belongs to the swap – and the swap is available only to a method that moves in the space of selections rather than decoding one from scratch each time.


Show code
args(sel_local_search)
#> function (ctx, n_sel, alpha_max, gd_ref, start = NULL, max_use = NULL, 
#>     mode = c("hill", "anneal", "tempering"), iters = 20000, n_chains = 8, 
#>     penalty = 5, t0 = NULL, swap_every = 50L, seed = NULL, trace = FALSE) 
#> NULL


Three modes, one driver, differing only in the temperature schedule. The driver does the following, and each step is a decision a breeder can inspect:

Start from a plan, never from noise. start = NULL builds a warm start: capped truncation, plus the greedy sweep whenever an \(N \times N\) f is present (the test is that ctx[["f"]] is a matrix with \(N\) rows), and it is worth being accurate about which branch produced the numbers in this chapter: the production benchmark of Section 17.7 deliberately forms the 0.745 GiB matrix so that the routes needing it can be timed at all, so its rows took the greedy branch. Among the candidates it takes the highest-index one that meets the budget, and if none does, the one with the smallest loss. As in sel_de(), NULL never means “start cold”.
The greedy branch is guarded, but the ranking that follows it is not: the warm start scores every candidate with alpha_loss(), which reads ctx[["f"]]. So start = NULL needs the \(N \times N\) matrix whichever branch it takes, and on a context built without one it stops with the message ctx[["f"]] (hybrid coancestry) is missing, as Table 17.19 shows. Supplying an explicit start = skips the whole function, and from there the search is fL-only; that is the call to make if f does not fit in memory, and Section 17.7.1 is where the two are run side by side.
Build the state. theta_state() on the starting selection, plus the running index sum and a logical membership vector, so that every later question is \(O(1)\) or \(O(L)\).
Calibrate the temperature. With t0 = NULL and a stochastic mode, the driver proposes up to 200 random swaps, records the median absolute change in the objective, and uses that as the starting temperature. Nothing about the scale of the index is assumed, so the same call transfers between datasets. mode = "hill" skips this entirely, since it never accepts a worsening move.
Propose a feasible move. Pick one of the \(n\) selected crosses at random to leave; draw entrants at random until one is found whose parents stay under max_use once the leaving cross is removed, giving up after 20 attempts. The cap is tested, never punished.
Score it in \(O(L)\). theta_swap() for the new \(\theta\), one addition and one subtraction for the new index sum, and the objective is \(\bar u_S\) minus penalty times the budget violation expressed in units of the budget itself – the violation is divided by alpha_max, so a 5 becomes an effective slope of 500 index standard deviations per unit of relative loss at a 1% budget, and 5000 at 0.1%. The tighter the budget, the harder a violation is punished, which is the behaviour you want and is not what make_fitness()’s fixed multiplier of 1000 on the absolute violation does.
Accept or reject. Improving moves are always accepted; worsening ones with probability \(\exp(\Delta / t_k)\) at the current temperature. The best-ever selection is tracked separately from the current one and is what is returned – so a chain that wanders away at high temperature loses nothing.

Two design points are worth stopping on.
The cap is tested, not punished. Whether a swap keeps every line under max_use is an \(O(1)\) question given the count vector, so infeasible moves are never proposed. Penalising them instead spends the evaluation budget on being rejected – with a tight cap that was the difference between the search improving on its warm start and not moving at all.
The temperature calibrates itself. A constant would not transfer between datasets, so t0 = NULL samples the median absolute objective change over a short burn-in and uses that.
One run of each is not a comparison. Twenty seeds (1 to 20) of each mode, at 20,000 and at 30,000 proposed moves – 30,000 is the budget of the benchmark of Table 17.5. The seeds are the same at both budgets but the draws are not, because the number of moves differs; sel_local_search() sets the seed itself, immediately before its own draws. Table 17.3 gives the indices and the paired differences, and Table 17.4 the realised loss, \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) and largest line use of each mode at 20,000 moves.


Show code
modes <- c("hill", "anneal", "tempering")
ls_run <- function(iters)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:20, function(sd_) do.call(rbind, lapply(modes, function(m) {
    s <- sel_local_search(ctx, n_sel, am, gd, mode = m, iters = iters, seed = sd_)
    data.frame(seed = sd_, mode = m, index = mean_index(s, ctx),
               alpha_pct = 100 * alpha_loss(s, ctx, gd),
               Ne_par = ne_parents(s, ctx), max_line = max_line_use(s, ctx))
  }))))
ls_raw <- lapply(c(`20000` = 20000, `30000` = 30000), ls_run)
ix <- function(d, m) d[["index"]][d[["mode"]] == m]          # ordered by seed
ls_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ls_raw), function(k) {
  d  <- ls_raw[[k]]

             hill = mean(ix(d, "hill")), anneal = mean(ix(d, "anneal")),
             tempering = mean(ix(d, "tempering")),

}))

Note that iters is the total number of proposed moves summed over chains, so the three modes cost about the same wall-clock at equal iters: at the benchmark book scale their mean times are 0.222 to 0.232 seconds for 30,000 moves. In tempering mode those moves are split across n_chains replicas on a geometric temperature ladder spanning three decades, exchanging adjacent rungs every swap_every moves.
The realised alpha of Table 17.4 sits against the 1% budget in every mode: the constraint is binding, and the search is spending the diversity it was allowed.
Three checks before a plan from this function is used, in this order: realised \(\alpha\) against the budget (a plan far inside it means the search never reached the boundary, or the penalty was too steep); max_line against the cap you set; and \(N_{e,\text{par}}\), which is free and catches the case where \(\theta\) is satisfied by a handful of lines used many times each.
Result. At 20,000 moves the mean indices are 1.5227 (hill), 1.5218 (anneal) and 1.4997 (tempering), with seed standard deviations of 0.0037, 0.0039 and 0.0069; at 30,000 moves 1.524, 1.5249 and 1.5091. Hill minus anneal, paired over the 20 seeds, is 0.93 thousandths of an index unit (standard error, s.e. 1.41; hill ahead in 10 of 20 seeds) at 20,000 moves and -0.91 (s.e. 1.1; hill ahead in 8 of 20) at 30,000. Tempering is below both in 20 of 20 seeds at 20,000 moves and in 20 of 20 at 30,000. Seeds 1 to 3 alone, the three-seed comparison an earlier version of this chapter read, give 6.2 thousandths at 20,000 moves; the other seeds do not repeat it.
Interpretation, and what limits it. Neither paired difference between hill and anneal is as large as two standard errors, and the two have opposite signs, so this run does not separate the two schedules at either budget; it also does not show that they are equal – a standard error of about one thousandth bounds what 20 seeds on one dataset can resolve. A change of sign between the budgets is therefore not evidence of an ordering that depends on the budget. Tempering’s shortfall is resolved at both budgets (below both in every seed). A candidate cause is the splitting of a fixed move budget across the replicas; that was not tested (no run at a larger budget, and n_chains and the ladder were not varied), so the shortfall is a measurement of this implementation at its default settings, on 625 candidates, and not of parallel tempering. What this panel supports is that at a fixed move budget the schedule is a second-order choice (the three modes differ by at most 1.5% of the index, and the spread is tempering’s). One dataset, one simulation seed: a different dataset is not measured.

17.3.1 Against the differential evolution, at equal wall-clock
Equal evaluations is the wrong comparison when one evaluation costs several times what another does. At the benchmark book scale a nominal DE evaluation costs 28 microseconds (seconds divided by evaluations, de_hybrid, which includes DEoptim’s own overhead) and a local-search move 7.5 (hill, which includes the driver’s), a ratio of 3.8; and the hybrid-encoding fitness costs 12 and 32 times the swap at \(N = 3{,}600\) and \(10{,}000\) (Section 17.7). The honest axis is seconds (Figure 17.1).








Figure 17.1: Best index reached (in standard deviations of the candidate pool) against wall-clock seconds on a log axis, at the benchmark book scale (N = 625, n = 60) under a 1% diversity budget. Grey circles: independent differential-evolution runs of 100 members and 20 to 800 generations (2,000 to 80,000 evaluations), one per budget and joined by a line; they are drawn as the running maximum over increasing budgets, so a run that ended below a cheaper one is drawn at the cheaper run’s value. Dashed line: the Lagrangian bound of Section 17.4. One run per arm: no dispersion is shown. The vertical axis of the image is labelled ‘mean index (s.d.)’: it is the index in standard deviations of the candidate pool, not a dispersion.

Read Table 17.5 by columns rather than by rank. index orders the methods; loss % says which of them actually spent the budget; max uses says which were capped, since the capped variants are solving a strictly harder problem and must not be compared with the uncapped ones on index alone; seconds is the axis the ranking is conditional on; and, among the uncapped rows, gap to bound % is the only column that says whether the leader is near optimal or merely ahead of the others. The greedy row is the one to keep in view. On the benchmark grid of 20 values of the index weight \(\omega\) (c(0, 10^seq(-5, 1, length.out = 19))) it reaches index 1.378 in 8 ms, which is 9.8% below the leading method (anneal) at about 29x less wall-clock. On the finer 60-value grid of Chapter 16 (10^seq(-6, -1, length.out = 60)) the best feasible greedy plan against the same gd_ref reaches 1.4226, which is 6.9% below the leader: the two greedy numbers of this book at one budget and scale differ by the grid, and the percentage depends on which is used. Whether the remaining shortfall is worth 0.23 seconds is a question about the programme, not about the algorithm. At the benchmark production scale the cost ratio is not the book-scale one: the mean times are 0.221 s for the greedy sweep and 0.341 s for hill, a ratio of 1.5, while the greedy index is 17% below hill’s (1.5 against 1.816) there, so the economy of the greedy sweep is a book-scale property of this file and not a production one.
The same file lets the local searches be set against the two differential evolutions, with the replication it has: three optimiser seeds on one dataset per scale, so a standard error below is over seeds and says nothing about the dataset (Table 17.6).

}))

Result. Both differential evolutions are run at 30,000 nominal evaluations (NP = 100, itermax = 300), the local searches at the same number of proposed moves. hill is ahead of sel_de() by 0.168 index units (s.e. 0.011) at the benchmark book scale and by 0.37 (s.e. 0.009) at the benchmark production scale, and ahead of the line-encoded sel_de_fast() by 0.468 and 0.48. The three local-search schedules span 0.014 and 0.127 at the two scales, with a within-mode seed standard deviation of at most 0.0059. Each local search also takes less wall-clock than either DE at both scales (asserted in the chunk; the seconds columns of Table 17.5 and Table 17.20 give the seconds).
Interpretation, and what limits it. At these budgets the swap-based local search reaches a higher index than both DE in less time, by a margin larger than the spread among its own schedules. That is a comparison of whole algorithms: a swap neighbourhood with an annealing or hill-climbing acceptance rule and a warm start from the greedy sweep against DEoptim’s operators on a decoded vector, with a different warm start. No arm runs the same search on the other neighbourhood, so the comparison does not isolate the neighbourhood from the rest of the algorithm; what the cost argument above supports is the mechanism for time (a swap is \(O(L)\), a decode sorts \(N\) candidates), not for index. Two further limits. The DE arms are at 30,000 evaluations, where Section 16.4.2 finds sel_de() below the best fine greedy plan (1.423 here) and above it at four times that budget and at its printed default: the DE results of this chapter are not results about sel_de() at its default. And the local search was not rerun against the DE at those larger budgets, so whether the ordering of the figure persists there is not measured here; the wall-clock of the DE rises with the budget (Table 16.6).






NoteWhat the literature says about picking a metaheuristic



De Beukelaer et al. (2018), on core-collection subsets, report that a basic stochastic hill-climber (random descent) already yields high-quality cores and that their genetic algorithm gave no further advantage over it as a global optimiser; the genetic algorithm did outperform random descent, but “is not as effective as parallel tempering”, which they prefer and which runs several cooperating local searches in parallel. Parallel tempering therefore beat both there. The twenty-seed run above does not reproduce that ordering: tempering is below both simpler modes. It is not a test of their result, because the move budget is split across the replicas and n_chains and the ladder are left at the package’s defaults, untuned.
Yadav et al. (2025) compared a genetic algorithm (GA), DE, particle swarm optimisation (PSO) and simulated annealing (SA) on parent selection in wheat and, for the selection function the source names OPV (its acronym, not expanded here), ranked them by convergence area under the curve (AUC) at 0.879, 0.860, 0.820 and 0.769; DE took longer to run than GA and performed comparably in final fitness. TrainSel (Akdemir et al. 2021) uses a genetic algorithm in conjunction with simulated-annealing steps, and MateR (Fernández-González et al. 2026) is optimised with it.
None of these compares a swap-based local search with a differential evolution on this objective, so they do not decide the question of Section 17.3.1. They are consistent with its result, that a simple local search is a serious competitor of the population methods; the warm start and the cheap move are this chapter’s explanation, not theirs.




17.3.2 The encoding, wired up at last
Chapter 16 measures the line encoding against a fully \(N\)-dimensional one – one random key per hybrid – and finds the line encoding far ahead at an equal budget, with every restriction slack in the \(N\)-key arm. That is a verdict on the \(N\)-key encoding at that budget, not a verdict on sel_de(), whose search space is \(n_{sel}\) coordinates wide. The paired comparison of the two encodings the package ships, sel_de() and the line-encoded sel_de_fast(), is given in Table 17.7 from this chapter’s benchmark (and per seed in Table 16.3); uncapped, it goes the other way. What is true regardless is that decode_lines() and make_fitness_fast() have been exported since the line route was written with nothing driving them. sel_de_fast() closes that:


Show code
sel_de_fast
#> function (ctx, n_sel, gd_ref, alpha_max, ne_par_min = NULL, max_use = NULL, 
#>     pool_tol = NULL, NP = 300, itermax = 2000, seeds = NULL, 
#>     trace = FALSE) 
#> {
#>     if (is.null(ctx$parents)) 
#>         ctx <- fast_ctx(ctx)
#>     L <- ctx$n_lines
#>     fit <- make_fitness_fast(ctx, n_sel, gd_ref, alpha_max, ne_par_min = ne_par_min, 
#>         max_use = max_use, pool_tol = pool_tol)
#>     if (is.null(seeds)) {
#>         v <- -rowMeans(ctx$fL)
#>         v <- (v - min(v))/max(max(v) - min(v), 1e-12)
#>         seeds <- lapply(seq(0, 1, length.out = 8), function(s) s * 
#>             v)
#>     }
#>     initial <- matrix(stats::runif(NP * L), NP, L)
#>     for (i in seq_len(min(length(seeds), NP))) initial[i, ] <- seeds[[i]]
#>     ctrl <- DEoptim::DEoptim.control(NP = NP, itermax = itermax, 
#>         trace = trace, initialpop = initial)
#>     res <- DEoptim::DEoptim(fit, lower = rep(0, L), upper = rep(1, 
#>         L), control = ctrl)
#>     decode_lines(as.numeric(res$optim$bestmem), ctx, n_sel, max_use)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x789e709b98>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>


What the call does, in order:

Builds the fast fitness: decode the line weights into a selection, tabulate the parent counts, evaluate \(\theta = \mathbf{w}'\mathbf{f}^L\mathbf{w}\) on the used lines only, and add one proportional penalty per active restriction – diversity budget, minimum \(N_{e,\text{par}}\), per-line cap, pool balance. No \(N \times N\) matrix is formed or indexed anywhere.
Builds the seeds. They sweep a line-diversity direction, not a merit weight: p proportional to the negated mean coancestry of each line, at eight increasing strengths from zero to one.
Searches the box \([0, 1]^L\) with DEoptim, and decodes the best member.

The zero-strength seed is worth isolating, because it is the natural origin of the encoding: with every line weight at zero the decoder ranks on index alone and takes crosses greedily under the cap, which is capped truncation exactly.


Show code
cap <- ceiling(2 * n_sel / ctx$n_lines) + 1
zero_w <- decode_lines(rep(0, ctx$n_lines), ctx, n_sel, max_use = cap)
stopifnot(identical(as.integer(zero_w),
                    as.integer(sel_truncation_cap(ctx, n_sel, cap = cap))))
c(cap = cap, index = mean_index(zero_w, ctx),
  alpha_pct = 100 * alpha_loss(zero_w, ctx, gd),
  max_line = max_line_use(zero_w, ctx))
#>       cap     index alpha_pct  max_line 
#> 4.0000000 0.8203555 0.3257287 4.0000000


The seeds sweep a line-diversity direction rather than a merit weight, but the principle is Chapter 16’s unchanged: seeds = NULL builds the sweep and never means “start cold”. The practical consequence of the identity above is that the population always contains at least one plan that respects the cap by construction, whatever the diversity penalty later does.

17.3.2.1 What it is actually for
sel_de_fast() is the only route in this package that accepts more than a budget and a cap: it also takes an \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) floor and a pool-balance tolerance. The case for it therefore has to be made where those extra restrictions are active. The first of them cannot be:


Show code
pool_share <- function(s) mean(ctx$pool[as.vector(ctx$parents[s, ])] == "A")
# Every candidate is one A x B cross, so any n-subset uses n slots in each pool.
stopifnot(all(ctx$pool[ctx$parents[, 1]] == "A"), all(ctx$pool[ctx$parents[, 2]] == "B"))
set.seed(3)
pool_random <- vapply(1:5, function(i) pool_share(sample.int(ctx$N, n_sel)), numeric(1))
stopifnot(all(pool_random == 0.5))
pool_random
#> [1] 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5


Pool balance cannot bind. make_fitness_fast() measures the share of line uses that fall in pool A, and every candidate hybrid has one pool-A and one pool-B parent (asserted above), so the share is 0.5 for any set of \(A \times B\) crosses, a complete factorial or not: five random subsets of the \(n\) = 60 crosses give 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5. pool_tol is vacuous for every candidate set this package builds. The other three restrictions are the budget, the cap and the floor, run next, all four set at once (Table 17.8), followed by an annealed local search at the same cap and no floor (Table 17.9):


Show code

A plan that meets the floor exists and is cheap to find. The capped greedy sweep over the 20-value benchmark grid of \(\omega\) contains 5 plans with \(\alpha \le 1\)% and \(N_{e,\text{par}} \ge 30\); the best has index 0.673, and on make_fitness_fast()’s own penalised objective (penalty 5, floor 30, asserted against the function above) it scores 0.815 against 0.391 for the DE plan. The DE returned a plan that is worse on its own objective than a one-line greedy plan: the route accepts a floor, it did not satisfy one here. The greedy plan that meets the floor has an index 0.432 units below the DE plan that violates it; how much better a search that honoured the floor could do than that greedy plan is not measured.
And it does not lead on index where a floor is slack. Under the same budget and cap, with no floor argument, a plain annealed local search reaches 1.11 at \(N_{e,\text{par}} =\) 25.1, against sel_de_fast()’s 1.106 at the floor of 25.
The recommendation therefore narrows. sel_de_fast() is the one route whose signature accepts an \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) floor; in the single instance run here it did not satisfy a floor that binds, and a capped greedy sweep filtered on \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) did. Check ne_parents() on whatever it returns. That the swap neighbourhood “cannot test” a floor is not a structural limit. With \(k_a\) the number of times line \(a\) is used as a parent in the selection (\(\sum_a k_a = 2n\); the count vector cnt of theta_state()), so that \(p_a = k_a/2n\) in Equation 11.5,
\[N_{e,\text{par}} = \frac{(2n)^2}{\sum_a k_a^2} \tag{17.2}\]
is a function of cnt, which theta_state() already carries, and it can be updated in \(O(1)\) per swap because four counts change (asserted in the swap-identity chunk above, against ne_parents()). What sel_local_search() lacks is an ne_par_min argument – an implementation gap, not a property of the move. This is one instance, one seed per floor, 30,000 and 150,000 evaluations; it is a measurement of this run, not of the route in general.

section: 17.4 The bound was not a bound
text:
17.4 The bound was not a bound
Section 15.4 introduces the continuous relaxation and its two statements, Equation 15.6 (weak duality) and Equation 15.7 (the Lagrangian bound). The convergence check of Chapter 16 was originally written to take, as an upper bound, the best relaxation point whose own \(\alpha\) falls inside the budget. As used, that construction is not valid, and this section shows it with the experiment that found it – and says what the experiment does and does not show.
The relaxation at a given \(\lambda\) maximises \(\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{u} - \lambda\,\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}\) (Equation 15.5), a penalised objective, not the index. By Equation 15.6 a relaxation point bounds every plan at least as diverse as itself, and at exactly equal diversity a plan cannot beat it. What Equation 15.6 does not give is a bound for a plan that spends the whole budget when the point lies strictly inside it: that plan is less diverse than the point, and the bound it satisfies is the tangent of slope \(\lambda\) at the point, which lies above the point’s height (Section 15.4, statement 3). A grid of \(\lambda\) values makes “strictly inside” the rule: the last grid point inside the budget is the one the construction uses. Table 17.11 gives the experiment.


Show code
lam   <- 10^seq(-1, 3, length.out = 12)
rel   <- ocs_relaxation(ctx, n_sel, lam, iters = 2000)
a_rel <- (gd - rel[, "GD"]) / gd
V     <- rel[, "index"] - lam * rel[, "theta"]     # the relaxation's dual value

# The eight plans of every row: one annealed local search and seven greedy weights.
cmp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.0025, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02), function(a) {
  ok  <- a_rel <= a
  j   <- if (any(ok)) which(ok)[which.max(rel[ok, "index"])] else NA_integer_
  old <- if (is.na(j)) NA_real_ else rel[j, "index"]
  new <- min(V + lam * (1 - gd * (1 - a)))  # the Lagrangian form, under-converged
  best <- max(vapply(
    Filter(function(s) alpha_loss(s, ctx, gd) <= a + 1e-12,
           c(list(sel_local_search(ctx, n_sel, a, gd, mode = "anneal",
                                   iters = 8000, seed = 1)),
             lapply(c(0, .5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16), function(w) sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = w)))),
    mean_index, numeric(1), ctx = ctx))
  data.frame(alpha_max = a, feasible_plan = best, old_bound = old,
             point_lambda = lam[j], point_alpha_pct = 100 * a_rel[j],
             old_valid = old >= best - 1e-9, lagrangian_2000 = new,
             lagrangian_valid = new >= best - 1e-9)
}))

Show code
# Move the relaxation point onto the budget: bisect lambda so that alpha(lambda) is
# at the 1% budget (alpha falls as lambda rises), 4000 iterations per point.
at_lambda <- function(l) {
  r <- rbind(ocs_relaxation(ctx, n_sel, l, iters = 4000))
  c(lambda = l, alpha_pct = unname(100 * (gd - r[1, "GD"]) / gd),
    index = unname(r[1, "index"]))
}
lo <- 10; hi <- 158
for (i in 1:10) {
  mid <- sqrt(lo * hi)
  if (at_lambda(mid)[["alpha_pct"]] > 100 * am) lo <- mid else hi <- mid
}
pt_budget <- at_lambda(hi)
plan_1pct <- cmp[["feasible_plan"]][cmp[["alpha_max"]] == am]
pb <- fmt(rbind(grid_point_inside_budget = c(lambda = cmp[["point_lambda"]][3],
                                             alpha_pct = cmp[["point_alpha_pct"]][3],
                                             index = cmp[["old_bound"]][3]),
                point_on_the_budget      = pt_budget,
                feasible_plan            = c(NA, NA, plan_1pct)), 4)
stopifnot(pt_budget[["alpha_pct"]] <= 100 * am, pt_budget[["alpha_pct"]] > 0.99,

Interpretation, and what limits it. What the experiment shows is a statement about finite grids: on a grid of 12 values of \(\lambda\) the last relaxation point inside the budget lies below a plan that spends the budget. It does not show that a relaxation point at the budget fails to bound a plan, and the second chunk is consistent with Equation 15.6: the same relaxation at the \(\lambda\) for which the point sits on the 1% budget (\(\alpha =\) 0.992%, bisected, 10 steps) has index 1.5373, above the feasible plan (1.5202); that is one point against one plan, and Equation 15.6 allows it for a point that is on the budget to within the 0.008 percentage points by which it lies inside. It does not show that a point at the budget bounds every plan. The construction is therefore a bound only if its grid is fine enough to put a point at the budget – a property nobody checked – and that is why the Lagrangian form, which does not ask where a point lies, replaces it. One dataset, one budget for the bisection, a 4000-iteration relaxation that is not tested for convergence here.
lagrangian_2000 is the Lagrangian form evaluated at a deliberately cheap setting – 12 multipliers, 2,000 projected-gradient iterations – and it is here only to show that the form survives where the construction does not. Its validity needs \(V(\lambda)\) to be computed to convergence, which this setting does not guarantee, so nothing downstream of this chunk quotes it; the value quoted as the bound comes from ocs_bound() below.
The correct statement is Equation 15.7, derived from Equation 15.6 in Section 15.4 and not re-derived here: for every \(\lambda \ge 0\) and every plan \(S\) of \(n\) hybrids with \(\theta_S \le \theta_{\max}\), \(\bar u_S \le V(\lambda) + \lambda\,\theta_{\max}\), with \(V(\lambda)\) the optimum of the relaxation. The tightest such statement is the minimum over \(\lambda\), and a coarse grid costs tightness, not validity – unlike the old construction, where a coarse grid could silently produce a “bound” below the achievable.

To use it: translate the budget into \(\theta_{\max} = 1 - \text{gd\_ref}(1 - \alpha_{\max})\) (Equation 15.3); solve the relaxation at each \(\lambda\) to get \(V(\lambda)\); take the minimum of \(V(\lambda) + \lambda\,\theta_{\max}\); and read the converged attribute before quoting anything. The function doubles its iteration count until the value stops moving by more than a relative tol = 0.001, because the value rises monotonically with iterations, so an under-converged run reports the bound too small – the one failure mode that turns a bound into a wrong number rather than a loose one. converged is a stalling criterion of that doubling, as in Section 15.4, and not a certificate: a value that has stopped moving by 0.1% on doubling has not been proved to be at its limit. Its default grid is 25 multipliers, log-spaced from 0.1 to 1000, and every bound quoted in this chapter is on that grid unless stated. Table 17.13 compares it with the cheap setting of the experiment above.


Show code

th_max <- 1 - gd * (1 - am)
lam25  <- eval(formals(ocs_bound)[["lambdas"]])
hand   <- function(lams, it) {                 # the same formula, a chosen grid and count
  r <- ocs_relaxation(ctx, n_sel, lams, iters = it)
  b <- r[, "index"] - lams * r[, "theta"] + lams * th_max
  c(value = min(b), lambda = lams[which.min(b)])
}
h12_2000 <- hand(lam, 2000); h12_8000 <- hand(lam, attr(bound, "iters"))
h25_2000 <- hand(lam25, 2000)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(h12_2000[["value"]], min(V + lam * th_max))))
bg <- fmt(rbind(`12 multipliers, 2000 iterations`   = h12_2000,
                `12 multipliers, ocs_bound iterations` = h12_8000,
                `25 multipliers, 2000 iterations`   = h25_2000,
                `25 multipliers = ocs_bound()`      = c(as.numeric(bound), attr(bound, "lambda"))), 4)
knitr::kable(cbind(grid_and_iterations = rownames(bg), bg), row.names = FALSE)

Result. At \(\theta_{\max} =\) 0.6774, the first row of Table 17.13 is the cheap sweep of Table 17.11 (1.5355); the fourth is bound, 1.5532, 1.16% higher, with converged TRUE after 8000 iterations. The two differ in the grid (12 against 25 multipliers) and in the iteration count (2,000 against 8000), and the second and third rows separate them: raising the iterations on the 12-multiplier grid moves the value by 0.28%, changing the grid at 2,000 iterations by 0.74%. Interpretation, and what limits it. Under-convergence does lower the value, in the direction the paragraph above gives, but it is the smaller part of the difference here; the larger part is the grid, and its effect is not a one-way correction: the 12-multiplier grid contains a multiplier near the minimiser (81.1) that the 25-multiplier grid skips (68.1), so at equal iterations the 25-point bound is the looser one by 0.87%. Both are valid bounds if their relaxations are converged; the second is looser. One dataset and one budget: how the two effects trade at other budgets is not measured. Everything this chapter quotes as a bound from here on is bound, the converged object of the fourth row of Table 17.13.
Two practical consequences. Every \(\lambda\) gives a valid bound, so a coarse grid costs tightness and never validity. And the bound can be used as a stopping rule within what it supports: when the converged bound exceeds the best plan found by a small margin, the margin is the most that further search can gain on this dataset and budget – an upper limit, conditional on the stalling criterion having signalled convergence.






WarningThis changes a number in Chapter 16



The convergence check in Chapter 16 once used the invalid construction, and the gap it reported was not a gap. That chapter now calls ocs_bound(), and the number there is the Lagrangian one; its qualitative conclusion survived the correction – the bound lies above the best feasible greedy plan and above the warm-started DE at its chapter budgets, and the size of that shortfall is what Section 17.3 closes. The lesson is the one that generalises: a quantity is only a bound if a feasible solution can never exceed it, and that is a property to test, not to assume.
Section 15.4 has been rewritten to match: it states the relaxation as a penalised optimum at each \(\lambda\), shows the order relaxation point \(<\) feasible plan \(<\) bound at the 1% budget, and takes its bound from ocs_bound().

title: 17  Advanced selection: structure, bounds and scale
section: 17.5 Rounding the relaxation into a plan
text:
17.5 Rounding the relaxation into a plan
With a bound in hand, the relaxation stops being only a diagnostic. Solve the optimal-contribution programme in line space, where quadprog returns instantly because the dimension is \(L\), round the contributions to integer line usage, and assign concrete crosses under both pools’ caps. That two-stage shape – contributions first, mate allocation second – is exactly Waldmann (2025)’s, whose mate-allocation stage solves in under 0.01 seconds.
The five steps inside ocs_round(), in the order they run:

Line merit. Each line is scored by the mean index of the hybrids it parents in the candidate set, the line_merit of Chapter 15. That quantity is a general combining ability: a property of the line against the opposite pool as represented in this factorial, never a property of the line alone (Section 5.11). Change the tester pool and the score changes.
Contributions. ocs_quadprog() on ctx$fL with those merits, at a given \(\lambda\), with each line’s contribution capped at \(\texttt{max\_use} / 2n\) – the cap expressed as a share of the \(2n\) parent slots, as in Chapter 15. As there, the quadratic programme has a single margin (the contributions of all \(L\) lines sum to one) and no per-pool sum; the two pools’ totals are equalised only in step 4, because every cross spends one slot of each pool.
Rounding. Contributions times \(2n\), floored, and the shortfall handed to the largest remainders; then clipped at max_use again.
Mate allocation. Walk the candidates in decreasing index and take each cross whose two parents still have quota and are under the cap – a greedy b-matching. If quota runs out before \(n\) crosses are found, top up on the cap alone, because the quota is a rounding artefact and the cap is the real restriction.
Choose \(\lambda\) by budget, not by preference. The whole sweep is evaluated and the plan returned is the best-index one whose realised \(\alpha\) respects alpha_max. The exchange rate stays an internal detail; the budget remains the interface.

Table 17.14 gives the plan returned on the live instance, and Table 17.15 sets it against the cached benchmark row of the same method.

Interpretation: the quadratic programme is doing what an optimal-contribution scheme is supposed to do – allocate more crosses to better general combiners and stop where relatedness makes the next cross expensive. Note that this call passes no max_use, so the plan’s max_line is whatever the coancestry term alone permits; with a cap set, the bound stays valid but goes loose, because the relaxation it comes from carries no cap and therefore bounds an easier problem.
It is not the best method here, and it is not meant to be. What it gives is a plan and a bound in one call, at a cost that does not grow with \(N\) in the part that matters – and a sanity check on everything else.

title: 17  Advanced selection: structure, bounds and scale
section: 17.6 Exact, and how far the heuristics really are
text:
17.6 Exact, and how far the heuristics really are
Everything so far is a heuristic with a bound. The remaining question is what the true optimum is, and the honest answer requires solving the problem exactly at a scale where that is possible.
The obvious route is closed. Maximising a linear index subject to a quadratic diversity constraint over binary variables is a mixed-integer quadratically constrained programme, and HiGHS – like most open solvers – does not accept a quadratic term together with integer variables at all.
Convexity opens a different one. Because f is positive semi-definite, \(\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{x}\) is convex, so its tangent at any point is a valid linear under-estimate. Write \(\mathbf{x}\) for the 0/1 indicator vector of the selection (\(N\) binary variables) and \(b = n^2\,\theta_{\max}\) for the budget in submatrix-sum units (step 1 below); at any point \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\) the tangent gives the cut
\[\bar{\mathbf{x}}'\mathbf{f}\bar{\mathbf{x}} + 2(\mathbf{f}\bar{\mathbf{x}})'(\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}) \;\le\; b \tag{17.3}\]
and Equation 17.3 is a linear relaxation of \(\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{x} \le b\). Solve the resulting mixed-integer linear programme (MILP), add a cut wherever the solution violates the true constraint, re-solve. This is outer approximation (Duran and Grossmann 1986), it needs only a MILP solver, and it terminates: each cut strictly removes the infeasible point that generated it.


Show code
args(sel_exact)
#> function (ctx, n_sel, alpha_max, gd_ref, max_use = NULL, start = NULL, 
#>     max_cuts = 200L, time_limit = 60) 
#> NULL


The loop, step by step:

Translate the budget. The diversity constraint becomes \(\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{x} \le n^2\,\theta_{\max}\) with \(\theta_{\max} = 1 - \text{gd\_ref}(1 - \alpha_{\max})\) – the same quantity as in the Lagrangian bound, expressed in submatrix-sum units because that is what the solver sees.
Write the structural rows. One cardinality row summing to \(n\), and one row per line for the partition matroid when max_use is set. Those are linear and exact; only the quadratic needs approximating.
Carry an incumbent from the start. The warm start is the same sel_local_search() warm start; if it satisfies the budget it becomes the incumbent and is handed to the solver as a starting point, so that a run stopped by the clock still reports a real interval.
Solve, cut, repeat. If the MILP solution satisfies the true quadratic constraint, it is optimal for the current relaxation and the loop can stop; otherwise a gradient cut at that point is added and the MILP re-solved.
Read the dual bound from the right field. objective_value is an upper bound only for a MILP solved to optimality; the moment the solver hits its own time limit the bound must come from mip_dual_bound. Cuts only tighten the relaxation, so the running minimum over iterations stays valid.



Show code

# The runs of the table below carry no max_use: one structural row.

  budget_xfx                   = n_sel^2 * (1 - gd * (1 - am)),
  binary_vars                  = ctx$N,
  structural_rows_no_cap       = 1,
  structural_rows_with_max_use = 1 + ctx$n_lines)
#>                    theta_max                   budget_xfx

#>                  binary_vars       structural_rows_no_cap 
#>                  625.0000000                    1.0000000

Result. On the tiny instance (\(N =\) 36, \(n =\) 8) the loop proved optimality at all three budgets, in 20 to 73 cuts, and the local search equals the proven optimum to the largest gap in Table 17.17 (2e-14%). At the benchmark book scale (\(N =\) 625, \(n =\) 60) the loop stopped at the time limit after 4 cuts at both budgets. At the 1% budget the interval is [1.528, 1.6995], a gap of 10.1% for the local-search plan. Two valid bounds are therefore on the table for the same budget and scale: the oracle’s dual bound, 1.6995, and the Lagrangian bound of Section 17.4, 1.5543 (the benchmark’s, \(B = 500\)). The same plan has a gap of 1.7% against the second. Neither is called a certificate here: the Lagrangian bound’s converged is a stalling criterion (Section 17.4), and the oracle’s dual bound is that of a relaxation with four cuts.
Interpretation, and what limits it. On this one tiny instance, at three budgets and with no cap, the local search is not leaving anything on the table, which is evidence that the move and the objective are right at that size. It is not evidence about another instance, about a plan under a cap (no oracle run carries max_use), or about 625 or 10,000 candidates, where the true optimum is unknown. At 625 the tighter valid interval is the one against the Lagrangian bound, and the 10.1% against the oracle’s dual reads as the looseness of a four-cut relaxation, not as the heuristic’s distance from optimal. Why the loop stalls at 625 was not diagnosed: 20 to 73 cuts were enough at \(N =\) 36 and 4 fit in 300 s at \(N =\) 625, which does not say how the number of cuts needed grows; and the oracle was not run at \(N = 10{,}000\), where the matrix alone is 0.745 GiB, so nothing here says what it does there. At that scale neither bound converged in this file (Section 17.7), so no interval is reportable. Ahadi et al. (2024), solving an integer programme for mate selection with a commercial solver, write that massive datasets could make optimal solutions unrealistic, that they may consider decomposition techniques, and that they would likely settle for “sub-optimal (but good quality) feasible solutions”; that is a statement of the same kind, about another problem, not a measurement of this one.






ImportantWhat the oracle is for



Not production. sel_exact() forms the N x N matrix and scales like the mixed-integer programme it is. It belongs with the ref_* functions of Appendix C: deliberately slow, deliberately literal, and the only way to know whether the fast route is right. Run it once, small, when the data changes; do not put it in a pipeline.

Figure 17.2: Cost per objective evaluation (microseconds, log-log axes) against the number of candidate hybrids, one timing per N on one machine; N = 22,500 has no timing because the matrix is not formed there. Only the incremental swap is flat. Both encodings grow: the line route by 9.4x, dominated by decode_lines()’s O(N log N) sort over all candidates, and the hybrid route by 20x – but that arm is confounded, because the sweep sets n_sel to 2 percent of N (20 crosses at N = 400, 200 at N = 10,000) and mean(f[idx, idx]) is quadratic in the selection, not in N.





Three things scale badly, and they are worth separating because only one of the three is fixed by the line encoding.
Memory. f is \(8N^2\) bytes: 0.745 GiB at \(N = 10{,}000\) and 3.8 GiB at \(N = 22{,}500\), which is why Chapter 12’s benchmark refuses to form it there. \(\mathbf{f}^L\) is \(200 \times 200\), or 0.3 MiB. Fixed by the line route.
Search dimension. Not what the line encoding fixes – not for the two differential evolutions, at any rate. sel_de() searches \(n_{sel}\) continuous coordinates and sel_de_fast() searches \(L\); at this chapter’s target both are 200, which is also the figure Section 17.9 quotes. The 10,000-dimensional alternative is one key per hybrid, the encoding Chapter 16 rejects and no route in this package uses. What the collapse genuinely moves to \(L\) is the contributions space: ocs_quadprog() inside ocs_round() solves a 200-variable quadratic programme where ocs_relaxation() works on a 10,000-variable contribution vector, which is why ocs_round() (uncapped, no max_use) sweeps its ten \(\lambda\) values and returns a plan in 157 ms at the benchmark production scale. That number includes the ten per-\(\lambda\) quadratic programmes, the rounding, the mate allocation and the ten alpha_loss() evaluations of the frontier against the 0.745 GiB matrix; which of them dominates was not measured. The benchmark passes bound = a value computed once, outside the timed block, and at \(N = 10{,}000\) that value did not converge, so the plan is what is fast here and there is no converged bound at this scale to be fast about. Section 17.7.2 is where that is measured. Fixed for the quadratic programme; already true for the DE.
Cost per evaluation. mean(f[idx, idx]) is \(O(n^2)\) in the selection, so it degrades exactly as the problem gets interesting – but decode_lines() is \(O(N \log N)\), so the line encoding does not fix this and at these sizes is slightly worse. Fixed only by not decoding, which is what the swap neighbourhood does.
Scaling up is therefore not a matter of buying time. It is a matter of not forming f at all: build ctx$fL and ctx$parents, and use the routes that read only those. That last clause is a real restriction and not a formality, because most of this package still reaches for the \(N \times N\) matrix, and fast_ctx() does not change that – it adds parents to whatever context it is handed and neither builds f nor drops it. The constructor with the switch is ctx_from_pools(sim, with_f = FALSE), and Section 17.7.1 is what actually happens on the context it returns.

17.7.1 Which routes actually run without f


Show code
sim <- simulate_pools(n_A = 10, n_B = 10, m = 400, seed = 1)
cxF <- ctx_from_pools(sim, with_f = FALSE)   # fL + parents, no N x N matrix
cxT <- ctx_from_pools(sim, with_f = TRUE)    # the same data, f as well
k   <- 12
gdk <- null_distribution(cxT, k, B = 50, B_full = 10)$gd_ref
st  <- sel_truncation_cap(cxF, k, cap = 3)   # a valid starting selection
set.seed(1); wts <- runif(cxF$n_lines)
# Line merit as ocs_round() defines it: mean index of the hybrids a line parents.
merit <- vapply(seq_len(cxF$n_lines), function(l)
  mean(cxF$index[cxF$parents[, 1] == l | cxF$parents[, 2] == l]), numeric(1))

runs <- function(e) tryCatch({ force(e); "runs" },
                             error = function(err) paste0("ERROR: ", conditionMessage(err)))
tab_ffree_df <- data.frame(
  Route = c("`theta_state()` / `theta_swap()`", "`fast_theta()`",
            "`sel_truncation_cap()`", "`decode_lines()`", "`sel_de_fast()`",
            "`ocs_quadprog()`", "`ocs_bound()`",
            "`sel_local_search(start = st)`", "`sel_local_search(start = NULL)`",
            "`theta_group()` / `alpha_loss()`", "`null_distribution()`",
            "`sel_greedy()`", "`ocs_round()`"),
  `On a ctx with no f` = c(
    runs(theta_swap(theta_state(st, cxF), st[1], setdiff(seq_len(cxF$N), st)[1], cxF)),
    runs(fast_theta(st, cxF)),
    runs(sel_truncation_cap(cxF, k, cap = 3)),

    runs(ocs_quadprog(cxF$fL, merit, lambda = 1, upper = 1)),

    runs(sel_local_search(cxF, k, am, gdk, start = st, iters = 500, seed = 1)),
    runs(sel_local_search(cxF, k, am, gdk, iters = 500, seed = 1)),
    runs(theta_group(st, cxF)),
    runs(null_distribution(cxF, k, B = 20, B_full = 5)),

  check.names = FALSE)

# The f-free replacement for null_distribution(): the same resampling, scored
# with fast_theta() instead of theta_group(). Same seed, same draws, same gd_ref.
set.seed(7)
gd_free <- mean(replicate(50, 1 - fast_theta(sample.int(cxF$N, k), cxF)))
stopifnot(all.equal(gd_free, gdk))

# What the matrix was buying the local search: only the starting point.
objs <- c(
  with_f_start_NULL = attr(sel_local_search(cxT, k, am, gdk, iters = 500, seed = 1),
                           "objective"),
  no_f_start_given  = attr(sel_local_search(cxF, k, am, gdk, start = st, iters = 500,
