Read the second column of Table 17.19 before designing a pipeline around the scaling recipe of Section 17.7. The incremental swap, the line decoder, the line-space quadratic programme and the Lagrangian bound are genuinely f-free, and so is sel_local_search() once it is given an explicit start =: on this instance it reaches 1.5804 against 1.5804 for the default warm start with f present, a difference of 0 in the objective after 500 moves. On this instance the matrix bought a starting point and little else. That is one instance, not a guarantee – the greedy warm start is there because at book and production scale it is worth having.
sel_greedy() is the one failure that is not a named message: it opens with f <- ctx[["f"]] and dies on a NULL, with R’s own error (argument is of length zero at the time of writing; a chunk of this section asserts only that it is an error, not the named one). The four others – theta_group() and through it gene_diversity() and alpha_loss(), which reach null_distribution(), ocs_round()’s per-\(\lambda\) frontier and sel_local_search() at its documented default of start = NULL – stop with ctx[["f"]] (hybrid coancestry) is missing, a guard in theta_group() (R/01_metrics.R). ls_warm_start() guards the greedy branch with a test that ctx[["f"]] is a matrix of \(N\) rows, but the ranking that follows scores every candidate with alpha_loss(), and that call stops. So the table says what the package does today: a loud failure, with a name, wherever f is needed. The package reads the matrix as ctx[["f"]] and not ctx$f for the reason Chapter 12 gives in its callout on two implementation traps: R’s $ partial-matches, so ctx$f on a context without f would have returned ctx$fL, an \(L \times L\) matrix. That is history, not a measurement of the current code, and it is the reason the guard exists.
So the honest scaling recipe has two branches. If f fits, form it: the benchmark of Section 17.7.2 does, on purpose, and the whole chapter’s numbers come from that branch. If it does not fit, the f-free subset is the whole pipeline you get – sel_truncation_cap() for a starting plan, fast_theta() over random subsets for gd_ref in place of null_distribution() (same seed, same draws, the same gd_ref to machine precision, which the chunk above asserts), sel_local_search(start = ...) and sel_de_fast() for the search, ocs_quadprog() and ocs_bound() for the contributions and the bound – and the greedy sweep, the resampled null and the rounding route are simply not available.


17.7.2 The head-to-head at production scale
Nothing broke at 10,000 and nothing here claims it did: the benchmark of Table 17.20 forms the 0.745 GiB matrix on purpose, and the hybrid route still evaluates in 132 us. The wall is further out, and it is documented rather than predicted – at \(N = 22{,}500\) the matrix is 3.8 GiB and Chapter 12’s cost benchmark declines to form it at all, so every metric that needs it has no timing entry at that scale. The line route has one.

Two things in Table 17.20 are worth more than the ranking.
The cap binds, the budget does not. At the benchmark production scale every capped method reaches essentially the same index (the spread is given below), at a diversity loss far inside the 1% allowed. With \(n = 200\) over \(L = 200\) lines the mean usage is already 2, so a cap of 4 leaves very little to choose; the restriction that is actually deciding the plan is the one nobody wrote a budget for. Check max_line and realised alpha together before concluding that a diversity constraint is doing any work.
Read down the capped rows only, as the rule given for Table 17.5 requires. At the benchmark production scale the five capped routes span 0.0002 index units (greedy_cap 1.1225, the other four 1.1223), each with a seed standard deviation of 0 (asserted above), on one dataset. With no seed dispersion that difference is deterministic on this dataset, greedy_cap ahead by 0.0002, exactly as the book-scale differences below are. “Tie” in this chapter is therefore a statement about a margin and not about dispersion: routes are called tied when their mean indices lie within 0.001 index units, about 0.09% of the index of these rows. The margin is a convention named here, not derived from any sampling distribution (there is none to derive it from), and the five production rows satisfy it (asserted above) while the book-scale rows do not. They differ in cost, greedy_cap taking 0.329 s and tempering_cap 0.466 s. At the benchmark book scale the same five rows do not tie. They span 6.6 thousandths: greedy_cap 1.1122 in 0.008 s, de_hybrid_cap 1.1097 and tempering_cap 1.1097 (0.286 s for the latter), and de_lines_cap 1.1056 and ocs_round_cap 1.1056, the two lowest. Every one of these rows has a seed standard deviation of 0 (asserted above), so the differences are not seed noise; they are differences between routes on one dataset. Interpretation, and what limits it: at the production scale no capped route is distinguished from the others on index at that margin; at the book scale the capped greedy sweep is highest, by 2.5 thousandths over the capped hybrid DE and the capped tempering and by 6.6 over ocs_round(max_use) and the line-encoded capped DE. A seed standard deviation of 0 measures nothing about the dataset, and with one dataset per scale this file does not resolve whether that order, or the agreement within the margin at production, holds on other datasets or for capped problems in general.
The diagnosis is arithmetic and takes a minute: compare \(2n/L\), the mean number of uses per line, against the cap. If the cap is a small multiple of the mean, it is the binding restriction and the diversity budget is decoration. Raising the cap, or enlarging the candidate pool, changes the plan; tightening the budget does not, until it starts to bind.
The bound does not converge at this scale, and no gap is reported. ocs_bound() doubles its iteration count until the value stops moving by more than a relative 0.001 (the stalling criterion of Section 17.4). At the benchmark book scale it stops; at \(N = 10{,}000\) it did not within the one doubling the benchmark allowed (4,000 and 8,000 iterations, 9 multipliers; Table 17.21). The reason offered is the step size, \(1/(2\lambda \max_i \sum_j f_{ij})\), whose denominator grows with \(N\), so that the same iteration count that converges on 625 candidates is not enough on 10,000; this was not tested by running more doublings at this scale. An under-converged relaxation reports \(V(\lambda)\) too small, which makes the “bound” too small, and it stops bounding anything.

At the benchmark production scale you have heuristics that agree with each other (in the capped case, to within 0.0002 index units on this dataset, inside the 0.001 margin of the capped-routes paragraph above) and no bound that has converged, so no statement of how close any of them is: the honest position, and a better one than a gap column computed from a quantity that is not a bound.

title: 17  Advanced selection: structure, bounds and scale
text:
17.8 Multi-objective, and why not NSGA-II
stage2_select() traces the frontier by sweeping alpha_max and running a full optimisation at each point: the budget is a constraint, not a weight (Chapter 15), so each point is a plan a committee can approve, expressed in a budget rather than in an exchange rate.
A saving is available that is not a Pareto algorithm. Consecutive budgets have nearly identical solutions – an expectation, not measured here – so the plan found at \(\alpha_k\) is the obvious warm start for \(\alpha_{k+1}\), and stage2_select() does not pass one: its call to sel_de() carries no start argument (R/11_stage2.R). sel_local_search() already has a start = argument.
NSGA-II (non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II) (Deb et al. 2002) returns an approximation of the whole front in one run. I have not run it on this problem, so nothing in this book says it would give worse plans per point than the sweep. The reason not to reach for it is narrower: it is built for trade-offs with no interpretable scale for one objective, and here the trade-off is already parameterised by a budget the breeder chooses, so a front is not what is being asked for. That is a design argument, not a measurement.
crumbs: 17  Advanced selection: structure, bounds and scale

title: 17  Advanced selection: structure, bounds and scale
text:
17.9 What not to reach for
Reinforcement learning. Younis et al. (2024) cast a breeding programme as a Markov decision process, with the number of crosses made in each generation as the action and a delayed reward, in an environment they name BREEDING GYM. Those are sequential decisions with delayed reward. Choosing 200 hybrids from a fixed candidate pool, once, with a closed-form objective, is not. The tool is aimed at a different question.
Bayesian optimisation. Built for expensive black-box objectives with a handful of continuous inputs. The swap that sel_local_search() uses costs 4.2 microseconds at \(N = 10{,}000\) (a state update, not the objective); the fitness a surrogate-based method would call costs 132 to 169 microseconds (Table 17.2); and the problem has 200 integer dimensions at the target scale. I did not run a Bayesian optimiser; this is an argument from cost and dimension.
Sampling from a determinantal point process. Determinantal point processes (DPPs) (Kulesza and Taskar 2012) are the natural probabilistic model of a diverse subset, and \(\log\det(\mathbf{I} + \beta\mathbf{f}_S)\), with \(\beta \ge 0\) a free scale, is submodular, as Chen et al. (2018) state for the DPP log-probability. That it is also monotone and non-negative is the book’s own argument, not theirs: \(\mathbf{f}\) is positive semi-definite (the Gram form of Section 17.1.1), so every eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{I} + \beta\mathbf{f}\) is at least 1, and so is that of each of its principal submatrices; the Schur complement of an added element is the reciprocal of a diagonal entry of an inverse whose eigenvalues are at most 1, hence at least 1, and each added element adds at least \(\log 1 = 0\). Monotone, non-negative and submodular, the greedy then carries the \(1 - 1/e\) guarantee of Nemhauser et al. (1978) under a cardinality constraint – a guarantee for that objective, which is not the one the programme constrains. Sampling from a DPP gives diversity in distribution when what is wanted is a single best plan, and the log-determinant lens is not \(\theta\): adopting it would change the quantity the programme is constraining. The assumption that the constraint pins one lens, \(\theta\), chosen deliberately (Chapter 15, assumption 5; Chapter 16, assumption 3), applies.


Show code
# The eigenvalue half of the argument on this instance: I + beta f has all
# eigenvalues >= 1 (f is positive semi-definite), here for beta = 1.
ev_dpp <- eigen(diag(ctx$N) + ctx[["f"]], symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
stopifnot(min(ev_dpp) >= 1 - 1e-10)
c(min_eigenvalue = min(ev_dpp))
#> min_eigenvalue 
#>              1

17.10 Which method to use
Table 17.22 gives the route for each situation; the protocol after it gives the order in which to run them.




Table 17.22: Which route to use in each situation, with the figures of this chapter’s benchmarks behind each recommendation (one simulated dataset per scale; benchmark means over the optimiser seeds 1 to 3, live results at the book scale).










Situation
Use




Any scale, first thing to run
sel_truncation_cap(), then sel_greedy() swept over \(\omega\) on a grid that starts well below the crossover (Chapter 16)


A budget and a per-line cap, benchmark production scale
sel_greedy(max_use = cap) swept over \(\omega\): at the benchmark production scale it is within 0.001 index units of sel_local_search(max_use = cap, mode = "tempering"), both capped DEs and ocs_round(max_use = cap) (spread 0.0002 index units, seed standard deviation 0, one dataset; the margin is a convention, Section 17.7.2), so there the routes differ in cost, not in index at that margin (ocs_round_cap 0.214 s against greedy_cap 0.329 s, and both need the \(N \times N\) matrix); at the benchmark book scale the same rows span 6.6 thousandths, greedy_cap highest and ocs_round_cap and the line-encoded capped DE lowest, with no seed dispersion, also on one dataset


A budget the \(\omega\) grid steps over (no cap)
sel_local_search(), with start = NULL when f exists: at 30,000 moves the hill climber and the annealing reach 1.527 and 1.528 (benchmark book scale, mean of 3 seeds) against 1.423 for the best feasible plan of the 60-value greedy grid (live, one dataset). sel_de() needs a larger evaluation budget to pass the greedy plan (Section 16.4.2); the local search was not compared with it there


An \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) floor that binds
sel_de_fast() is the only route that accepts an ne_par_min argument, but in the run above it did not meet a floor of 30 (N_e,par 25.7), while a capped greedy sweep filtered on ne_parents() did (index 0.673). sel_local_search() has no such argument – an implementation gap, not a limit of the swap. Pool balance cannot bind


You need to know whether to keep optimising
ocs_bound() – an upper limit if converged (its stalling criterion) is TRUE; a small gap says little more can be gained on this dataset and budget


You need to know the true optimum
sel_exact() on a small subsample – an oracle, not a pipeline


Contributions are genuinely continuous
ocs_quadprog() – Chapter 15








As a protocol at production scale:

Build ctx through fast_ctx(), and decide up front whether the \(N \times N\) matrix is going to exist, because that decision selects the rest of the protocol (Section 17.7.1). ctx$fL and ctx$parents are required by every fast route; f is required by null_distribution(), sel_greedy(), ocs_round() and sel_local_search()’s automatic warm start. At \(8N^2\) bytes it fits at \(N = 10{,}000\) and the benchmark of Section 17.7.2 forms it. If it does not fit, steps 2-4 change as noted, and the f-free subset is what you have.
Get gd_ref from a resampling at the target n_sel, and set \(\alpha_{\max}\) below the attainable ceiling (Chapter 15). With no f, null_distribution() is unavailable and the resampling has to be mean(replicate(B, 1 - fast_theta(sample.int(ctx$N, n_sel), ctx))), which is fL-only and returns the same gd_ref at the same seed (Section 17.7.1).
Run the sweeps that cost milliseconds – sel_truncation_cap() and, when f exists, sel_greedy() over an \(\omega\) grid spanning your data’s crossover, passing max_use if a cap applies – and record what they achieve. They are the baseline every later number is judged against. Under a cap, the capped greedy sweep is within 0.001 index units of the other capped routes at the benchmark production scale (the margin of Section 17.7.2) and is the highest of them at the benchmark book scale (Table 17.5, Table 17.20 and the capped-routes paragraph of Section 17.7.2), on one dataset per scale.
Run sel_local_search() for as many seconds as you are willing to spend, with the cap passed as max_use rather than enforced afterwards. With f present, leave start = NULL and let it build the warm start; with no f, pass start = sel_truncation_cap(...) explicitly, which is the only configuration of this route that runs without the matrix. The mode is the least consequential choice in this list: over 20 seeds "hill" and "anneal" are 0.9 and 0.9 thousandths of an index unit apart at 20,000 and 30,000 moves, with a standard error of about one thousandth and no resolved sign, while "tempering" is below both in every seed. Take the simplest one unless your own data says otherwise – but those runs are uncapped, and the only mode benchmarked under a cap is "tempering".
Compute ocs_bound() and check its converged attribute. Converged and the gap small: the gap is the most further search can gain on this dataset and budget, if the stalling criterion is to be trusted; stopping is a decision for the programme. Converged and the gap large: keep going. Not converged: report no gap at all, and judge the plan by agreement between independent methods instead.
Validate the returned plan on the lens the constraint does not pin – F_drift and allelic richness – and on the pool decomposition, before it is used (Chapter 25).

What the chapter measured, and what it did not. The problem is \(L\)-dimensional in its state: \(\theta\) is a function of the line-usage vector and of nothing else. What was measured to follow from that is cost: an \(O(L)\) swap (4.2 us at \(N = 10{,}000\) against 132 to 169 us for a full fitness evaluation, Table 17.2), a 0.3 MiB matrix and a 200-variable contributions programme. What was not measured is how much of any difference in index between routes is due to the state: the swap-based local search differs from sel_de() in neighbourhood, acceptance rule and warm start together, so that comparison is of whole algorithms (Section 17.3), and no experiment here ranks the state collapse against the other changes. The comparison closest to isolating the encoding, sel_de() at \(n_{sel} = 200\) against sel_de_fast() at \(L = 200\), at 30,000 evaluations on boxes of the same width, still differs in the seeding and the decoder of sel_de_fast() (Section 17.3.2.1); it favours sel_de() uncapped, by 0.3 (s.e. 0.009) at the benchmark book scale and 0.11 (s.e. 0.032) at the benchmark production scale (the production difference is not resolved by three seeds), on one dataset per scale (capped: 0.004 and 0). The guarantees, the Lagrangian bound (converged at the benchmark book scale, not at production) and the oracle (\(N = 36\) only) bound how far a plan can be from the optimum where they apply, and no further.

Name the structure before choosing the algorithm: it changes what a move costs (4.2 us for the swap, against 132 us for a hybrid-encoding evaluation at \(N = 10{,}000\)) and, in the line encoding, what an evaluation costs (169 us: more, not less). Whether it also changes the index a method reaches is a separate claim that this chapter does not settle. The one comparison near it, sel_de() against sel_de_fast(), still differs in seeding and decoder as well as in encoding: uncapped, sel_de() is ahead by 0.3 (s.e. 0.009) at the benchmark book scale, which three seeds resolve, and by 0.11 (s.e. 0.032) at the benchmark production scale, which they do not; capped, the differences are 0.004 and 0, and a standard error of 0 does not mean the difference is known. One dataset per scale throughout.

Reproduce this chapter
All the code of this chapter, in order and with the explanation kept as comments, is one script: 10b-advanced-selection.R. Download it, install hybdiv, and run it top to bottom in an empty directory; cached results are fetched on first use.

title: 18  How few hybrids are enough? Mating designs for a two-pool programme
text:
18.1 Why the crossing plan is the binding decision
The selection problems of the Optimisation part (Chapter 15, Chapter 16, Chapter 17) start from a list of hybrids with predicted values, and Chapter 6 builds that list as the complete \(A \times B\) factorial: every cross formed once, every value known. Earlier chapters did ask where such a list comes from, and each deferred the answer to this one: Chapter 1 describes the evaluation of lines in cross, against testers or in a sparse factorial; Chapter 9 (“How many testers, how many locations”) gives a tester-design accuracy for a simulated programme; Section 5.13.6 checks that a crossing layout identifies what one intends to fit. None of them chooses the crossing plan. This chapter does, and it therefore removes the assumption, made by the Optimisation part, that the values of the whole factorial are known: what that part receives after a sparse plan is a prediction, and this chapter measures how good it is.
The list comes from a crossing plan, and the crossing plan is the most constrained decision a hybrid programme makes. Two pools of 200 candidate lines each define a factorial of 40,000 single crosses. A field holds 1,000 to 3,000 plots. Every hybrid programme is therefore choosing a sample of a factorial whose cells are overwhelmingly empty, and the classical tester – every candidate crossed to one or two lines of the opposite pool – is one sample among many. This chapter treats the choice of sample as the design problem it is, and defends three results:
One word, three objects. In the Optimisation part a hybrid is a cross between a pool-A and a pool-B line, and selection acts on its predicted value. In this chapter, unqualified, a cross is a filled cell of the design: an \(A \times B\) single cross that is made and planted to be tested; the cells not in the design are untested hybrids, which can only be predicted. A third object, the within-pool cross made to produce the next generation of lines (stage S2 of Table 1.1), is the subject of the literature reviewed in Section 18.6 and is not designed here.
The running example throughout is one simulated maize programme: two heterotic pools, 200 doubled-haploid candidates per pool, a field of 1,000 to 3,000 hybrid plots, and a winter nursery that must physically produce the seed of every cross that enters the field.
The crossing plan, not the statistical model and not the marker platform, sets the ceiling on what a hybrid programme can learn in a cycle. Which lines can be ranked, whether specific combining ability is estimable at all, how many plots each hybrid can occupy, whether untested combinations can be predicted – every one of these is fixed the moment the nursery plan is written. A mixed model fitted afterwards can only extract what the plan put there.
The arithmetic is unforgiving. A 200 x 200 factorial against 1,000 to 3,000 plots is a sampling fraction of 2.5 to 7.5 % at one plot per hybrid, and 1.25 to 3.75 % at two plots per hybrid, the minimum for replication. Three decisions are usually conflated inside “the testing plan”, and it pays to separate them:
The organising question of the chapter follows: for a fixed budget, which sample of the factorial maximises the accuracy of combining-ability estimates and the selection response they support? And one constraint is stated now, because it is the one most often forgotten: a crossing plan is not a matrix, it is a nursery. Each filled cell is a pollination that must yield enough seed for its plots.
The three canonical samples drawn over the same grid make the difference visible before any statistics. The plans below are produced by the package’s generators, at 40 x 40 so that individual cells can be seen:
Show code
set.seed(3)
grids <- list("Tester, k = 2"     = design_tester(40, 40, k = 2),
              "Circulant, c = 4"  = design_circulant(40, 40, c = 4),
              "NC II, 10 x 10 sets" = design_nc2(40, 40, 10, 10))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2.2, 1))
for (nm in names(grids)) {
  M <- matrix(0, 40, 40)
  M[cbind(grids[[nm]]$parent1, grids[[nm]]$parent2)] <- 1
  image(t(M[40:1, ]), col = c("grey96", "#1f5f8b"), axes = FALSE,
        main = sprintf("%s  (%d crosses)", nm, nrow(grids[[nm]])), cex.main = 0.9)
  box(col = "grey60")
}
par(op)








Figure 18.1: Three samples of the same 40 x 40 factorial, drawn by the package’s own generators. Rows are pool-A lines, columns pool-B lines, a filled cell is a cross that goes to the field. Left: two testers per pool (156 crosses). Centre: a circulant sparse factorial with four crosses per line (160 crosses). Right: North Carolina Design II as four disconnected 10 x 10 blocks (400 crosses).
The tester fills two full columns and two full rows: every line meets the same partners, so lines are compared on a common background but the background is narrow. The circulant design spreads the same number of crosses as thin diagonals: every line meets different partners, every line is crossed exactly four times, and – the property that the next section shows to matter – every line is linked to every other through a chain of shared partners. NC II fills more cells than either and still cannot compare a line in the first block with a line in the second.

section: 18.2 Combining ability as an estimation problem
text:
18.2 Combining ability as an estimation problem
General and specific combining ability are properties of a reference population of crosses, and a design estimates them only to the extent that it samples that population. The concepts are classically attributed to Sprague and Tatum (1942); the distinction between fixed-effect inference about a specific set of parents and random-effect inference about the population they were drawn from is classically attributed to Griffing (1956) (page-level support not checked for this book). The North Carolina layouts, in which a factorial between two sets of parents separates the components of variance, are attributed to Comstock and Robinson (1948); that attribution, and the assignment of Design II to this paper rather than to a later publication, was not verified for this book. Reciprocal recurrent selection, the scheme that uses both combining abilities, is the subject of Comstock et al. (1949), cited here for its title and existence only.

18.2.1 The model
At the level of a cross mean the model is Equation 1.1, \(\bar y_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij} + \bar e_{ij}\), with \(\bar y_{ij}\) the mean of cross \(i \times j\) over its \(r_{ij}\) plots, \(\mu\) the mean of the reference set of crosses, \(g^A_i\), \(g^B_j\) the GCA of the pool-A and pool-B parent, \(s_{ij}\) the SCA of the pair and \(\bar e_{ij}\) the plot error of the mean. This chapter adds the error variance,
\[\mathrm{Var}(\bar e_{ij}) = \sigma^2_e / r_{ij}, \tag{18.1}\]
with \(\sigma^2_e\) the plot-error variance (s2e, defined from a single-plot heritability of 0.3) and \(r_{ij} \ge 1\) the plots the cross received. The other variances are \(\sigma^2_{gA}\) and \(\sigma^2_{gB}\), over the candidate lines of each pool (vc$A, vc$B), and \(\sigma^2_s\), that of \(s_{ij}\) (vc$S; written \(\sigma^2_{SCA}\) in Chapter 5, where it is a closed form for the heterosis part). Where one GCA variance is needed, as in every closed form below, it is \(\sigma^2_g = (\sigma^2_{gA} + \sigma^2_{gB})/2\), the mean of the two pools. \(n_A\) and \(n_B\) are the candidate lines per pool, and \(n_A'\), \(n_B'\) those that receive at least one cross. In Chapter 19 and Chapter 20 the pool-A line is the female and the pool-B line the male. Two ratios will be quoted and must not be confused: the SCA:GCA ratio of this chapter is \(\sigma^2_s/\sigma^2_g\), and the SCA share is \(\sigma^2_s/(\sigma^2_{gA} + \sigma^2_{gB} + \sigma^2_s)\), the proportion of the genetic variance among cross means. In the cached run they are 0.378 and 0.159. Neither is the SCA share of the heterosis variance of Chapter 5, which excludes the additive variance and assumes neutral divergence.
Section 5.11 derived this decomposition from allele frequencies for the dominance part of the hybrid value, and showed that a pool-A line’s GCA is an average effect evaluated at pool B’s frequencies. There \(g^A_i\) is that dominance part alone, which that chapter calls the GCA for heterosis; here \(g^A_i\) is the whole GCA of the cross mean. With an additive effect \(a_k\) added to the dominance effect \(d_k\) at locus \(k\), the general combining ability of pool-A line \(i\) in the factorial of the candidate lines is
\[g^A_i = \sum_k \bigl[a_k + d_k (1 - 2\bar v_k)\bigr]\,\delta u_{ik},
  \qquad \delta u_{ik} = u_{ik} - \bar u_k, \tag{18.2}\]
with \(u_{ik}, v_{jk} \in \{0, 1\}\) the genotype of inbred pool-A line \(i\) and pool-B line \(j\) at locus \(k\), and \(\bar u_k\), \(\bar v_k\) their means over the candidate lines of the factorial, not over the pool (the two converge as the number of lines grows; the identity below holds for the former only). Genotypic value is \(a_k(u + v - 1) + d_k(u + v - 2uv)\) per locus, so the row effect of the product term \(-2d_k u_{ik}v_{jk}\) is \(-2d_k\,\delta u_{ik}\bar v_k\) and the rest is linear. The structure – an average effect of substitution against the other population – is that of Stuber and Cockerham (1966) for a cross between two populations; the equation is checked here, not taken from that paper. The additive part adds a term and changes nothing else, which is quick to confirm: the row effects of a complete factorial of genotypic values equal cU %*% a plus the gca_A of heterosis_gca_sca(), with no second implementation. The same chunk shows what the identity does not cover: with the frequencies of the pool that generated the lines in place of \(\bar u_k\), \(\bar v_k\), the two sides differ.


Show code
set.seed(7)
m  <- 300
pA <- runif(m, 0.1, 0.9); pB <- runif(m, 0.1, 0.9)
U  <- matrix(rbinom(30 * m, 1, rep(pA, each = 30)), 30)   # 30 inbred lines, pool A
V  <- matrix(rbinom(25 * m, 1, rep(pB, each = 25)), 25)   # 25 inbred lines, pool B
a  <- rnorm(m, 0, 0.3); d <- rnorm(m, 0.2, 0.2)
# Genotypic value of every single cross: a(u + v - 1) + d * heterozygosity
G  <- outer(seq_len(30), seq_len(25), Vectorize(function(i, j)
        sum(a * (U[i, ] + V[j, ] - 1) + d * (U[i, ] + V[j, ] - 2 * U[i, ] * V[j, ]))))
cs <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, d)
gcaA_formula <- drop(sweep(U, 2, colMeans(U)) %*% a) + cs$gca_A
row_eff <- rowMeans(G) - mean(G)
# @eq-mating-gca with candidate-set frequencies, and with the pool frequencies
gca_cand <- drop(sweep(U, 2, colMeans(U)) %*% (a + d * (1 - 2 * colMeans(V))))
gca_pool <- drop(sweep(U, 2, pA) %*% (a + d * (1 - 2 * pB)))
c(max_abs_diff_heterosis_gca_sca = max(abs(row_eff - gcaA_formula)),
  max_abs_diff_candidate_freq    = max(abs(row_eff - gca_cand)),
  max_abs_diff_pool_freq         = max(abs(row_eff - gca_pool)),
  sd_row_effect                  = sd(row_eff))
#> max_abs_diff_heterosis_gca_sca    max_abs_diff_candidate_freq 
#>                   2.042810e-14                   1.909584e-14 
#>         max_abs_diff_pool_freq                  sd_row_effect 
#>                   9.489157e-01                   2.165922e+00
stopifnot(max(abs(row_eff - gcaA_formula)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(row_eff - gca_cand)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(row_eff - gca_pool)) > 1e-3)


Result. The row effects of the complete factorial equal Equation 18.2 with the candidate-set frequencies, and the gca_A of heterosis_gca_sca() plus the additive term, to machine precision (asserted below \(10^{-10}\)); with the pool frequencies the largest difference is 0.95 against a standard deviation of the row effects of 2.17, at 30 + 25 lines and 300 loci. Interpretation. “True GCA” in this chapter is always the quantity on the left – the row and column effects a breeder would estimate by growing every hybrid of the candidate lines without error – and every accuracy reported is meant as a correlation with it, over all candidates of a pool, crossed or not (for the cached sweep this is the estimand as the study describes it; the repository holds only the realised factorial variances of check V2). The population GCA, at pool frequencies, is a different object, which the finite panel approximates; this chapter does not use it.


18.2.2 Four quantities that control a design



Table 18.1: The four quantities of a two-pool mating design, their closed forms and what controls them. Rows 3 and 4 hold for a tester design with \(k\) testers per pool and \(c = k\) crosses per line, every candidate crossed to the same \(k\) partners; they are not written for a sparse factorial (see the text and Table 18.2).

The third row is the quantitative form of the classical argument for using more than one tester (attributed to Sprague and Tatum (1942); not checked at page level here), and the fourth is its square root as an accuracy: the square root of the heritability, for GCA, of the mean of a line’s \(k\) cross means. Both describe least squares in a tester design, and the derivation uses that: the \(k\) partners are the same for every candidate, so their GCA is a constant that the within-pool centring removes, and the error of a line’s estimate is the mean of \(k\) independent \(s_{ij}\) and \(\bar e_{ij}\). In a sparse factorial each line has its own partners, which are themselves unknown candidates, and nothing in the derivation covers that noise. gca_accuracy_theory(c, r, ...) can nevertheless be evaluated at \(c\) crosses per line, and it is useful to see what it then returns against the cached accuracies of the two estimators, at 2,000 plots:

                     "model", "acc_gca_all")],
              idvar = c("scenario", "family", "x_axis", "reps_per_cross", "n_linesA_tested"),
              timevar = "model", direction = "wide")

fs$formula_minus_ls   <- fs$formula - fs$acc_gca_all.LS
fs <- fs[order(fs$family != "tester", fs$family, fs$x_axis), ]
is_t <- fs$family == "tester"
fmt(data.frame(design = fs$scenario, c = fs$x_axis, r = fs$reps_per_cross,
               lines = round(fs$n_linesA_tested), formula = fs$formula,
               blup = fs$acc_gca_all.BLUP, ls = fs$acc_gca_all.LS,

18.2.3 Connectivity, in one paragraph






ImportantThe rank rule



A mating design is a bipartite graph: pool-A lines on one side, pool-B lines on the other, an edge for every cross. GCA contrasts are estimable within a connected component of that graph and not between components, so the rank of the GCA design matrix is \(n_A' + n_B' - (\text{components})\), one lost constraint per component. That is the formal content of what breeders call “ties between sets”, and it was settled long ago: Weeks and Williams (1964) gave the criterion for an \(N\)-way classification and Fernando et al. (1983) an algorithm for the connected subsets of a two-way one.


design_diagnostics() computes both sides of the rule independently – the numerical rank by QR, the components by union-find over the graph – so a disagreement would be a bug, not a modelling choice:


Show code
set.seed(2026)
plans <- list("tester k=1"        = design_tester(n, n, 1),
              "tester k=2"        = design_tester(n, n, 2),
              "random sparse c=2" = design_random_sparse(n, n, 2),
              "circulant c=2"     = design_circulant(n, n, 2),
              "circulant c=5"     = design_circulant(n, n, 5),
              "NC II 10x10 sets"  = design_nc2(n, n, 10, 10))
diag_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(plans), function(nm) {
  d <- design_diagnostics(plans[[nm]], n, n)
  data.frame(design = nm, crosses = d$n_crosses,
             untested = 2 * n - d$lines_A - d$lines_B,
             components = d$components, rank_gca = d$rank_gca,
             rank_expected = d$rank_expected, df_sca = d$df_sca)
}))
stopifnot(all(diag_tab$rank_gca == diag_tab$rank_expected))

Result. The rank equals the graph prediction in every row. The NC II layout – twenty disconnected 10 x 10 blocks – has rank 380, not 399: twenty components, twenty lost constraints. The random sparse design at two crosses per line leaves 53 candidates with no cross at all and splits the rest into 11 components; the circulant design with the same number of crosses is a single component with every line crossed exactly twice. One tester per pool is connected and has zero residual df: \(n_A + n_B - 1\) crosses for \(n_A + n_B - 1\) GCA parameters. The GCA model is saturated and SCA is not merely imprecise, it is not identifiable.
What “not estimable” means is checked directly. A contrast between two lines of the same NC II block lies in the row space of the design matrix; a contrast between lines of different blocks does not:


Show code
nc <- plans[["NC II 10x10 sets"]]
l_within  <- c(0, 1, -1, rep(0, 2 * n - 2))           # A1 - A2, same block
l_between <- c(0, 1, rep(0, 9), -1, rep(0, 2 * n - 11)) # A1 - A11, next block
rbind(within  = unlist(design_estimable(nc, n, n, l_within)),
      between = unlist(design_estimable(nc, n, n, l_between)))
#>         estimable rel_residual
#> within          1 3.831056e-16
#> between         0 2.236068e-01


The within-block residual is rounding error; the between-block residual is 0.224, a contrast nowhere near the row space. Any least-squares ranking that crosses block boundaries in this design is a statement about the analyst’s centring convention, not about the lines.
BLUP does rank across blocks, and in the simulations below NC II scores well on all-lines accuracy. It can, because a random-effects model supplies the missing constraint from its prior: every block’s lines are assumed drawn from the same pool distribution, so every block mean is shrunk to the same value. That assumption is exactly true in a simulation that assigns lines to blocks at random, and exactly what fails when blocks are families, years or breeders’ sub-programmes with real mean differences. Disconnection is not repaired by the estimator; it is replaced by an assumption, and the assumption should be stated.


18.2.4 SCA and the cross-level residual are the same thing in cross means
One more property of the model must be stated before any variance component is reported. Each cross has its own SCA, so in cross-mean data \(s_{ij}\) and \(\bar e_{ij}\) occupy exactly the same position: only their sum \(\sigma^2_s + \sigma^2_e / r\) is identified. The cached study separated them by an external plot-error variance and estimating \(\sigma^2_s\) (the validation file does not record how \(\sigma^2_e\) was fixed; this is as the study describes it); an independent REML implementation (sommer) was compared with the in-house one (check V6), and the validation file records that only the sum is identified there, which the two agreed on to 2e-06 relative error. A reported \(\sigma^2_s\) from cross means is only as good as the external plot-error estimate it was separated with. fit_gca() in this package sidesteps the question by taking the components as known, and weights each cross mean by \(1/(\sigma^2_s + \sigma^2_e/r)\) for exactly this reason.
crumbs: 18  How few hybrids are enough? Mating designs for a two-pool programme

title: 18  How few hybrids are enough? Mating designs for a two-pool programme
text:
18.3 The classical tester approach
The tester design answers the sampling problem by collapsing one margin of the table. Each candidate is crossed to \(k\) testers of the opposite pool, and in the usual reciprocal arrangement each pool’s candidates are tested against the other’s testers, giving \(k(n_A + n_B) - k^2\) crosses. Evaluating inbred lines in crossbred combinations is an old practice, and Jenkins and Brunson (1932) compared methods for it; the argument for general versus specific combining ability is classically attributed to Sprague and Tatum (1942) and Hull (1945) (not checked at page level here), and the modern treatment of tester choice is Hallauer et al. (2010).

18.3.1 What a tester is for, and what it trades
A tester is a deliberate variance trade. It buys cheap seed production and perfect connectivity – every line tied to every other through the common testers – at the price of confounding a line’s GCA with its SCA to the testers used, and of a training set that covers the relationship space of the opposite pool very thinly. The testcross mean of line \(i\) estimates \(g^A_i\) plus the mean of \(k\) SCA deviations, so its error variance carries \(\sigma^2_s/k\) and \(\sigma^2_e/(k r)\). Adding testers buys down both terms; adding replicates buys down only one. That is why the allocation literature treats tester number as a decision variable jointly with lines, locations and stages (C. Longin et al. 2006), and why it is not interchangeable with replication.
The closed form and its least-squares simulation on the running example, with the truth redrawn in every replicate so that tester SCA is resampled as the theory assumes:


Show code
set.seed(42)
tester_mc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 8), function(k) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(r) {
    acc <- replicate(12, {
      tr <- simulate_factorial(n, n, vc$A, vc$B, vc$S)
      p  <- design_tester(n, n, k)
      p$reps <- r
      p  <- simulate_cross_means(p, tr, s2e)
      f  <- fit_gca(p, n, n, vc$A, vc$B, vc$S, s2e, "ls")
      mean(c(cor(f$gA, tr$gA), cor(f$gB, tr$gB)))
    })
    data.frame(k = k, r = r, acc = mean(acc), se = sd(acc) / sqrt(length(acc)))
  }))
}))
tester_mc$theory <- gca_accuracy_theory(tester_mc$k, tester_mc$r, s2g, vc$S, s2e)
tester_mc$z <- (tester_mc$acc - tester_mc$theory) / tester_mc$se
stopifnot(max(abs(tester_mc$z)) < 2)
tm_gain <- function(k0, k1) gca_accuracy_theory(k1, 1, s2g, vc$S, s2e) -
                            gca_accuracy_theory(k0, 1, s2g, vc$S, s2e)
kk <- seq(1, 8, by = 0.1)
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 8), ylim = c(0.3, 0.9), xlab = "testers per pool, k",
     ylab = "GCA accuracy (all 200 lines)", las = 1)
cols <- c("#1f5f8b", "#b2182b")
for (r in 1:2) {
  lines(kk, gca_accuracy_theory(kk, r, s2g, vc$S, s2e),
        col = cols[r], lwd = 2)
  d <- tester_mc[tester_mc$r == r, ]
  arrows(d$k, d$acc - 2 * d$se, d$k, d$acc + 2 * d$se, angle = 90,
         code = 3, length = 0.03, col = cols[r])
  points(d$k, d$acc, pch = 19, col = cols[r])
}
legend("bottomright", c("1 plot per testcross", "2 plots per testcross"),
       col = cols, lwd = 2, pch = 19, bty = "n")








Figure 18.2: GCA accuracy of a k-tester design against the number of testers, at one and two plots per testcross. Lines: the closed form of Table 18.1. Points: least-squares estimates from fit_gca() on the 200 x 200 running example, mean of 12 replicates with the truth redrawn each time; bars are two standard errors.





Result. At this seed the simulated least-squares accuracies lie within 0.88 standard errors of the closed form at every \(k\) and both replication levels (asserted below 2), the in-repo counterpart of the cached check V4. With 12 replicates the standard errors are 0.005 to 0.015, so the comparison resolves a bias of about \(\pm 0.02\) and no smaller. The gain per doubling of the testers is the same at one and at four: going from one to two testers at one plot raises accuracy by 0.122 (from 0.38 to 0.5), going from four to eight by 0.123: equal gains per doubling, one quarter of it per added tester in the second case. Interpretation. Here the plot error, \(\sigma^2_e \approx\) 42.6 at a single-plot heritability of 0.3, dwarfs \(\sigma^2_s =\) 2.9, so testers and replicates are nearly interchangeable in this simulation. In material where SCA is 20 to 30 % of the genetic variance (Giraud et al. 2017; Lorenzi et al. 2024) the \(\sigma^2_s/k\) term is no longer negligible and testers buy strictly more than replicates. Section 5.13.6 gives the finite-population version of the same curve, with \(k\) testers drawn without replacement from the \(n_B\) available.


18.3.2 Choice of tester
The long-standing debate is between broad-base testers, elite inbreds and elite single crosses. The theoretical argument against a high-performing tester is Smith (1986)‘s: for many loci with substantial dominance, favourable dominant alleles carried by a good tester mask the candidate’s alleles, reducing the variance among testcrosses and with it the correlation between testcross and line value. A good tester discriminates less. The counter-argument is operational: an elite tester produces hybrids that are themselves candidate products, so the testcross trial doubles as a product trial in the background where the line will actually be sold. Programmes have resolved the tension by staging – discriminating testers early, elite testers late, single-cross evaluation last – and the number of testers per stage is one of the levers of the scheme. In a deterministic budget model of one Zimbabwean maize programme – not a simulation of genotypes, and by its authors’ own statement not extrapolable to other programmes – replacing a 4-1-1 tester plan with a 2-2-1 plan raised gain per dollar by 8.2 % and cut the cost of a unit of gain by 7.4 %; combined with doubled haploids and a higher selection intensity at the first two stages, the figures were 43.1 % and 28.5 % (Chaingeni et al. 2025).


18.3.3 What testers cannot deliver
Three limitations recur, and the simulation bears on two of them.
No SCA in the reference population. With \(k = 1\) the GCA model is saturated and \(\sigma^2_s\) is not identifiable at all (df_sca = 0 in Table 18.4). With \(k \ge 2\) it is identified. The model gives a reason to expect it to be estimated with the testers: the testcross mean of a line contains the mean of the same \(k\) SCA deviations for every line, so what the design samples is the interaction of the candidates with those \(k\) partners, not with the population of crosses the programme will sell. Whether the cached REML estimates show a tester-specific distortion is a separate, measurable question:


Show code
sr <- subset(sm, model == "BLUP" & budget_plots == 2000 & df_sca >= 1 &
               n_linesA_tested >= 198 &
               family %in% c("tester", "sparse_circulant", "sparse_random", "nc2"))
sr <- data.frame(design = sr$scenario, df_sca = round(sr$df_sca),
                 ratio_of_means = 100 * ((sr$vc_sca / ((sr$vc_gcaA + sr$vc_gcaB) / 2)) / ratio_ref - 1),
                 mean_of_ratios = 100 * (sr$vc_ratio_obs / ratio_ref - 1))
sr <- sr[order(-sr$mean_of_ratios), ]
rownames(sr) <- NULL
stopifnot(sr$design[which.max(abs(sr$ratio_of_means))] == "circulant c=2",
          sr$design[which.max(abs(sr$mean_of_ratios))] == "circulant c=2")
fmt(sr, 1)

The file holds no replicate-level dispersion.

Result. Read as a ratio of replicate-mean components, the ratio is 0.8 % off the reference at \(k = 2\) and 5.2 % at \(k = 4\); read as the mean of the per-replicate ratios, 14.8 % and 12.8 %. For sparse designs the same two statistics give -3.1 and 0.3 % at circulant \(c = 3\) and 12.1 and 15.6 % at \(c = 5\); the errors across the table run from -7.6 to 23.9 % (ratio of means). Interpretation. The two statistics disagree by up to 14 points, as they must: the mean of a ratio is not the ratio of the means, and the former is the Jensen-biased one. Under either, circulant \(c = 5\) is at least as far from the reference as the tester designs, and the sign changes across the sparse designs, so the cached file does not show an inflation specific to testers. It also cannot show that there is none: with no replicate-level dispersion in the file, differences of a few percent cannot be called resolved. The mechanism above stays a statement about the model, not a measured effect.
Testcross ranking is not single-cross ranking. Comparing testcross progeny tests with randomly paired single-cross tests, Burdo et al. (2021) found that the top 25 lines on testcross yield and on single-cross yield coincided for only 48 % of lines in the Stiff Stalk pool and 11 % in the Iowa Dent pool – almost disjoint selections – rising to 56 % in both with genomic prediction.
A thin training set. All hybrids of a candidate share one or two partners, so the design explores a narrow slice of the hybrid relationship space. Testcross was the worst of the designs compared as a training set for predicting the single crosses of a full diallel (Fritsche-Neto et al. 2018), and simulation agrees that the deficit grows with the SCA share (Seye et al. 2020).


18.3.4 When the tester is still right
None of this makes testers obsolete. They remain the right answer when seed production rather than plot capacity binds – a tester cross is made in bulk in an isolation block or on a male-sterile female, a sparse factorial needs many small hand pollinations (Section 18.7) – when the candidate set is so large that the first screen must be cheap per line, in programmes that cannot fit a mixed model and whose field holds only two or three crosses per line (Section 18.5), and in the first cycle of a new pool, where there is no relationship information to exploit. González-Diéguez et al. (2026) make the case for a hybrid of the two logics: three to five testers allocated sparsely across families rather than every tester crossed to every line.

title: 18  How few hybrids are enough? Mating designs for a two-pool programme
text:
18.4 Sparse and incomplete factorials
Once candidates are crossed to each other rather than to a common tester, the design becomes a sparse bipartite graph, and two things matter: how many crosses each line gets, \(c\), and whether the graph is connected. Which particular partners are drawn matters much less.

18.4.1 The design family
The classical theory is the partial diallel of Kempthorne and Curnow (1961): each parent crossed to a fixed number \(s\) of others, with the sampling variances of the genetic components derived as functions of \(s\). Its two-pool analogue is the incomplete factorial, each pool-A line crossed to \(c\) of the \(n_B\) pool-B lines. The members studied here:

random sparse – \(c \cdot n_A\) cells drawn at random. Lines receive a Binomial number of crosses, some none; the graph may be disconnected.
circulant (round-robin) – pool-A line \(i\) crossed to pool-B lines \((i - 1 + o) \bmod n_B + 1\) for \(c\) offsets \(o\). With \(n_A = n_B\) every line in both pools has exactly \(c\) crosses, and choosing offsets with \(\gcd(n_B, \Delta o) = 1\) guarantees one component. design_circulant() nudges the last offset until that holds.
NC II in sets – complete \(a \times b\) factorials on disjoint line sets (the layout attributed to Comstock and Robinson (1948)); deliberately disconnected.
criterion-optimised – greedy exchange towards A-optimality, D-optimality or CDmean (Rincent et al. 2012); relationship-guided – partners chosen to minimise genomic similarity between parents. Both appear in the cached sweep only.



18.4.2 How sparse is sparse enough – the published evidence
Remarkably sparse, provided the design is structured and analysed well. The most informative single data point is operational rather than simulated: a commercial winter oilseed rape programme ran 4,000 hybrids over 61 unreplicated trials covering 1.67 % of all mother x father combinations, and a GCA + SCA model still reached accuracies of 0.63, 0.84 and 0.80 for yield, oil and protein after a further 50 % of the observations were artificially removed (Thomsen et al. 2026). Across maize, wheat and rice, training sets of 2 to 13 % of the hybrid set sufficed for genomic prediction (Guo et al. 2019). A 363-hybrid dent x flint factorial predicted an independent 951-hybrid factorial as well as or better than tester designs at equal numbers of hybrids and lines (Lorenzi et al. 2022); NC II was the best and testcross the worst training set for predicting a full diallel (Fritsche-Neto et al. 2018); and in simulation the factorial’s advantage grew with the SCA share (Seye et al. 2020).
The design principle that this chapter’s own sweep supports is to spend the hybrid budget on parents, not on depth per parent – up to the point where \(c\) is so small that connectivity and within-line precision fail – and the published evidence says that the point depends on what is to be predicted. Melchinger et al. (2023) found, in their first data set (DS1) at a training-set size of 96 hybrids, for hybrids with both parents untested (H0), the accuracy maximal at \(c = 1\), each parent in a single cross, exceeding \(c = 2\) and \(c = 4\) by about 1 to 3 % and 5 to 10 % (largest differences at high heritability); for hybrids with one or both parents in the training set (H1, H2), and for the GCA of lines that are in it, \(c = 1\) gave the lowest accuracy in DS1, and the optimum \(c\) across hybrid types depends on the size and resources of the programme. Their second data set (DS2) is described as showing essentially the same picture with some trends amplified: at 96 training hybrids the difference between \(c = 1\) and \(c = 4\) for H0 hybrids was larger than in DS1 in all six scenarios, with an attainable accuracy at \(c = 1\) of 0.50 to 0.65 at low and 0.70 to 0.85 at high heritability, while the accuracy of H1 hybrids hardly differed between \(c = 1\), 2 and 4. The percentages above are DS1 figures; no DS2 percentage is quoted here. That is a trade between predicting new lines and estimating the ones already crossed, at a fixed number of hybrids; the sweep below fixes plots, not hybrids, and scores GCA of lines in the field, so it is not a test of that paper (Table 18.15).


18.4.3 Sparse versus tester, at equal plot budget
The cached sweep puts every design at the same three plot budgets and scores GCA accuracy over all 200 candidates per pool, analysed by phenotypic BLUP:

The z-scores are 6.4, 8.7, 4.1, 3.2 at \(c = 2, 3, 5, 10\), so the margin at \(c = 10\) is a single cached run, 3.16 standard errors unpaired, a little above this chapter’s threshold of 3. A sparse factorial should be built, not sampled, at least at low \(c\).


18.4.5 What is lost
SCA is weakly estimated at low \(c\). The circulant design with \(c = 2\) has exactly 1 residual degree of freedom at cross-mean level (Table 18.4) – enough to fit a model and not enough to estimate a variance component – and the cached REML SCA:GCA ratio there is off the reference by 23.9 % as a ratio of replicate-mean components (34.4 % as a mean of ratios), the largest error in Table 18.5 under either statistic. The same table shows errors of 12.1 % at \(c = 5\), so the cached REML evidence does not by itself separate \(c = 2\) from higher \(c\); the structural fact, one residual df at \(c = 2\) against 601 at \(c = 5\) (Table 18.4), does. The recommendation therefore splits by objective: \(c = 2\) to rank lines, \(c \ge 3\) before any statement about SCA variance.
Sparsity in crosses also interacts with sparsity in environments. A parallel literature, mostly from CIMMYT, allocates entries to subsets of environments and predicts the unobserved line-by-environment cells (Jarquin et al. 2020; Atanda et al. 2021, 2022; Montesinos-López et al. 2023). When the genetic correlation between managements is as low as 0.37 (Atanda et al. 2021), a line observed only in one is weakly informative about the other. A design observing 2 % of the hybrid factorial and 30 % of the environment cells within that observes well under 1 % of the information space, and the two sparsities have not been studied together for hybrids (Section 18.9). Chapter 19 takes the environment axis on its own and Chapter 20 the two together.

title: 18  How few hybrids are enough? Mating designs for a two-pool programme
section: 18.5 The analysis is part of the design
text:
18.5 The analysis is part of the design
The sparsest factorials (\(c \le 3\) per line) are good designs only if analysed with a shrinkage estimator. The in-repo core sweep agrees for random sparse \(c = 10\) (0.76) and NC II (0.756) against a tester at 0.671, but not for circulant \(c = 10\), which is 0.615 in-repo against 0.707 in the cached sweep, below the in-repo tester; that disagreement is the one left unexplained in Section 18.10. Interpretation. The least-squares penalty makes a tester the better design only against the sparsest layouts (\(c \le 3\) per line, and circulant \(c = 5\)); with \(c = 10\) random crosses per line, or NC II sets, an unshrunken estimate is already better than the best tester’s at equal plots, in both sweeps, and so is circulant \(c = 10\) in the cached sweep only. What limits this: one budget (2,000 plots), unpaired z from a cached external sweep whose replicate unit is not known, a circulant \(c = 10\) row the in-repo sweep does not reproduce, and “best tester” and the sparse arms chosen on the same means (the winner’s-curse caveat of Table 18.6 applies).
Interpretation of the estimator contrast. At low \(c\) each GCA estimate rests on two or three cross means, each carrying a full \(\sigma^2_s + \sigma^2_e/r\) of noise, and the unshrunken estimate is dominated by it. BLUP borrows strength across the connected graph: a line’s partners are themselves estimated from their partners, and the shrinkage towards zero is proportional to how little each line was observed. That the circulant design loses more to least squares than the random one at the same \(c\) is not a contradiction of the previous section. The circulant design’s partners are each other’s partners in long chains, which is what BLUP can exploit and least squares cannot; this is a mechanism proposed here, not one the sweep isolates.
The practical consequence is conditional on \(c\) and on the layout: a programme that cannot or will not fit a mixed model should avoid the sparsest layouts (\(c \le 3\) per line, circulant \(c = 5\)) – under least squares they are worse than a tester – while a design with \(c = 10\) or an NC II layout retains an advantage over the best tester in this sweep (Table 18.11). The literature that motivated BLUP of single crosses (Bernardo 1994, 1996) and the allocation tools that assume it (Endelman et al. 2014; Mi et al. 2014) are cited here for that context; this chapter has not checked, page by page, what they state about the estimator.

18.6 Genomic information for deciding which crosses to make
Genomic information changes the question from how well can I estimate the lines I crossed? to which crosses should I make, and what can I say about the ones I did not? Its value is in extrapolation and in the choice of what to field, not in improving estimates for lines that are already there.

18.6.1 From relatedness to hybrid prediction
The idea that untested single crosses can be predicted from tested ones through marker relatedness is Bernardo (1994)’s: random subsets of 10 to 30 hybrids from a 54-hybrid factorial, and RFLP relationships recovering single-cross performance. Bernardo (1996) scaled it to operational data, with correlations of 0.43 to 0.76 for yield in heterotic patterns with more than 100 tested crosses. Massman et al. (2012) compared marker-relatedness BLUP with ridge-regression marker effects on 479 single crosses. The modern version models hybrid value as pool-specific additive kernels for GCA plus a dominance or product kernel for SCA (Technow et al. 2012; Technow et al. 2014). This book does not fit those models: Chapter 14 fits one additive GBLUP kernel over all hybrids, with no pool split, on a trait with no SCA, and Section 14.4 validates that fit by masking hybrids.
The kernel the cached sweep used for SCA follows from the algebra of Section 18.2: \(s_{ij} = -2\sum_k d_k\,\delta u_{ik}\,\delta v_{jk}\) is linear in the elementwise product of the two parents’ centred genotypes, so the natural SCA kernel is the linear kernel on that product. It is not the Hadamard product of the two pool kernels, which adds cross-locus terms the model does not contain.


18.6.2 The T0 / T1 / T2 hierarchy
The standard currency for comparing designs is the split of untested hybrids by how many of their parents appear in the training set: both (T2), one (T1), neither (T0). Grain-yield accuracies of 0.91, 0.85 and 0.77 with 300 training hybrids (Technow et al. 2014), 0.92, 0.88 and 0.80 under a GCA model on the Hohenheim series (González-Diéguez et al. 2021), and 0.28 to 0.77 with the ordering T2 > T1-female > T1-male > T0 (Kadam et al. 2016). The hierarchy also explains why a tester is a poor training set: it generates only T1-type information for new lines, because the tester is always a tested parent and the candidate never is.
These figures share a property that must be stated: they come from material with strong family structure, where an untested line has close relatives in the training set. Technow (2019) found that the difference in accuracy between two training-set types, F1 hybrids and F1:2 bulks, was largest under a divergent heterotic structure and ranged from 0.15 correlation points for hybrids that are themselves in the training set (T3) to 0.06 for T0, at constant residual variation. Published T0 accuracies are not programme-independent, and the simulated counter-example below makes the point concrete.


18.6.3 The negative result

Result. At 2,000 plots genomic kernels raised all-lines GCA accuracy in 2 of 24 designs, both of them reduced line sets of 50 per pool chosen by CDmean (+0.017 and +0.012, z = 4.5 and 4.2). Over the three budgets Table 18.13 lists 6 winning rows, but only 3 distinct cells: the rows at 2,000 and 3,000 plots of the two designs are the same data for the 50-line, \(c = 10\) design (replication is capped at three, so it fields 1,500 plots at both budgets), and the 50-line, \(c = 5\) design fields 750 plots at every budget, so its three rows are one cell. The three distinct cells have z = 2.46, 4.52, 4.25; the smallest is below this chapter’s threshold of 3, and the budgets are not replicates of one another. In every other design at 2,000 plots – all 200 candidates fielded, 50 per pool drawn at random, or 100 per pool by either rule – the genomic model was level with or below the phenotypic one, by 0.005 to 0.031: below by more than three standard errors in 10 of 22, between two and three in 6 (relationship-guided c=5, tester k=4, tester k=3, relationship-guided c=3, 100 lines/pool c=10 (random), 100 lines/pool c=5 (random)), which this chapter’s three-standard-error rule does not count as resolved, and within two in 6 (circulant c=10, random sparse c=5, 50 lines/pool c=5 (random), 50 lines/pool c=10 (random), tester k=2, tester k=1), unresolved at 30 replicates. Table 18.14 pairs the CDmean line sets with random ones of the same size: the genomic accuracy is not distinguished between the two choices (z = 0.21, 0.17, 0.03, -0.02 across the four configurations; an absolute z below 2 does not show equality: with a standard error of the difference of 0.007 to 0.008, differences up to about 0.016 are not excluded), while the phenotypic accuracy is lower for CDmean in each (z = -1.2, -0.8, -3.8, -4.2), resolved only in the two 50-line configurations. Genomic T0 accuracy, where it is defined on more than a handful of lines, was 0.1 to 0.15, against genomic T2 of 0.7 to 0.81 in the same designs, a ratio of 5.2 to 7.5; the negative value in the random sparse rows is computed over the few lines the random draw happened to leave uncrossed and means nothing.
Interpretation. Three separate statements. First, when every candidate is phenotyped in a connected design, the marker kernel has little to add to what the crosses already say, and a simplified SCA kernel (equal \(d^2\) at every locus) may cost a little (not tested separately here). Second, the two designs in which the genomic model beat the phenotypic one are the two in which CDmean chose the lines, but the genomic accuracy did not rise with CDmean: the gain over BLUP comes from the phenotypic arm falling, by 0.026 on average in the 50-line designs, not from the genomic arm rising. This sweep therefore does not show that CDmean picks better lines for a genomic model than random choice does; why the phenotypic arm falls on CDmean sets was not investigated. It is also confounded: the two designs are those with the fewest plots (750 and 1,500, against 2,000 for the 200-line designs), and they are two designs in one cached run, so “genomics gains where the field holds a fraction of the candidates” is a description of these two cells, not a generalisation. Third, the simulated T0 accuracies are 5.2 to 7.5 times below their own T2, a gap of 0.57 to 0.7 in absolute terms, against the published gaps of 0.14 (0.91 to 0.77, Technow et al. (2014)) and 0.12 (0.92 to 0.80, González-Diéguez et al. (2021)). A candidate explanation, not tested by this sweep, is that the simulated candidates are unrelated doubled haploids from two pools described by the sparsex study as diverged for 100 generations, with no family structure to carry information from a tested line to an untested one – the condition under which genomics should transfer least, and the one of a programme sampling new, unrelated material. The genomic model is the only route to a prediction for lines outside the field, where the phenotypic model gives none.


18.6.4 Which hybrids to phenotype, and which crosses to make
Once prediction is in place the design question becomes which cells to observe to calibrate it. CDmean (Rincent et al. 2012) beat random sampling and PEVmean for inbred calibration sets because it accounts for the redundancy among related individuals; for hybrids, sets built by clustering, network analysis and mating-scheme considerations beat both (Guo et al. 2019), which suggests that the structure that matters for a hybrid training set is bipartite. In a cross-validation on one Brazilian maize data set, reviewed in a roadmap paper, pre-selecting the best 30 % of single crosses on genomic prediction with additive and non-additive effects retained 85 to 95 % of the top 5 % hybrids for ear height, 75 to 85 % for grain yield and 70 to 80 % for plant height (Fritsche-Neto et al. 2021).
A different question is which within-pool crosses to make to produce the next generation of lines (not the \(A \times B\) crosses of the design sections). The usefulness criterion adds the within-cross selection differential to the predicted mean, and selecting on it added 0.14 genetic standard deviations of gain at 1 % selected per cross (Lehermeier et al. 2017); within-cross variance is usable for ranking but the marker model’s estimate was biased downward by 28 to 60 % (Lian et al. 2015). At the portfolio level, optimal cross selection chooses a set of crosses under a constraint on diversity: 15 to 78 % more genetic gain than truncation selection with four cycles per year in Gorjanc et al. (2018), and more again once within-family variance enters the objective (Allier et al. 2019). Kinghorn (2011) gives an algorithm for mate selection under a group mating permission matrix, reported several hundred times faster than penalising solutions in the scenario he tested. Whether it, or any such algorithm, makes optimising a crossing list over a 200 x 200 candidate space under nursery constraints routine is this chapter’s conjecture, not a result of that paper; nothing in this book implements it. Nor does this book solve the assignment of contributions to crosses that Gorjanc et al. (2018) call optimal cross selection (named in Chapter 15 for the within-pool crosses): the contributions of Chapter 15 attach to hybrids, one per \(A \times B\) cross, and the design problem treated here is a sampling problem for estimation, not an assignment of contributions.
The long-term caution is this book’s own: cross selection controls inbreeding and the divergence of the pools, and a design chosen once should not be held fixed across cycles. Lorenzi et al. (2024) reported SCA shares that differ by trait and between two selection cycles of one silage maize programme (up to 30 % in one cycle’s data and up to 10 % in the other, depending on the trait), so the variance structure that every design calculation in this chapter takes as given may not be stationary.


18.6.5 What the simulation adds to the literature



Table 18.15: Where the simulated programme confirms, refines or contradicts the published expectation.










Published expectation
Simulated result
Verdict




Sparse factorials beat testers as training sets (Seye et al. 2020; Lorenzi et al. 2022; Fritsche-Neto et al. 2018)
Sparse beats tester on GCA accuracy over all candidates at every budget, by 0.082 to 0.125 (Table 18.6)
Confirms, and extends beyond the training-set role


For hybrids of untested lines accuracy is highest at \(c = 1\) (DS1 and DS2); in DS1 it is lowest at \(c = 1\) for hybrids and lines already in the training set (in DS2 H1 hybrids hardly differ); the optimum \(c\) depends on programme size (Melchinger et al. 2023)
Not the same experiment: the budget here is plots, the target GCA of lines in the field. Circulant GCA accuracy under BLUP rises from 0.63 at \(c = 2\) to 0.78 at \(c = 10\) at 2,000 plots; \(c = 2\) leaves 1 residual df (Table 18.4)
Different question; not a test of the paper


Small sampling fractions suffice: 1.67 % of combinations operationally (Thomsen et al. 2026); training sets of 2 to 13 % across maize, wheat and rice (Guo et al. 2019)
Over all designs, 1 % of the factorial gives 0.61, 1.5 % gives 0.72, 2.5 % gives 0.81 (Table 18.7)
Consistent in order of magnitude; the fraction follows the accuracy target


T0 below T2 by 0.14 and 0.12 (0.91 to 0.77, Technow et al. (2014); 0.92 to 0.80, González-Diéguez et al. (2021))
Genomic T2 minus T0 of 0.57 to 0.7 in the designs with at most 100 lines per pool (Table 18.12)
Tension: a gap several times the published one; the cause is not tested here


Genomic kernels improve hybrid evaluation
Gain over BLUP in 2 of 24 designs at 2,000 plots, both 50-line CDmean sets, and in 3 distinct cells over three budgets, one with z = 2.46; genomic accuracy not distinguished between CDmean and random lines (Table 18.13, Table 18.14)
Weak: two designs, one run; the gain is the phenotypic arm falling


Structured vs random layouts at matched \(c\) not compared
Circulant ahead at every \(c\), z from 3.2 to 8.7 unpaired, the smallest at \(c = 10\) (Table 18.8)
Addresses the gap, in one simulation


Testcross ranking differs from single-cross ranking (Burdo et al. 2021); testers confound GCA with SCA to the testers
\(k = 1\): SCA not identifiable. \(k = 2, 4\): REML SCA:GCA ratio off by 0.8 and 5.2 % (ratio of means) or 14.8 and 12.8 % (mean of ratios); sparse designs are in the same range (Table 18.5)
Confirms the \(k = 1\) limit; no tester-specific inflation is shown


No published counterpart was located by the author (no systematic search)
Least squares instead of BLUP costs 0.5 at \(c = 2\) and 0.007 at most for testers (Table 18.10); the penalty is confined to the sparsest layouts (Table 18.11)
The largest estimator effect in the sweep; not shown to be new

section: 18.7 Seed production and the cost of a crossing plan
text:
18.7 Seed production and the cost of a crossing plan
The crossing plan has to be made in a nursery. Treating hybrid seed production as a scalar cost term – as the published cost models do (Marulanda et al. 2016; Longin et al. 2015) – hides the constraint that actually binds sparse designs: the seed quantity per cross limits how many plots and locations each hybrid can occupy.

18.7.1 Three cost centres
A mating design has three cost centres that scale differently. Making the crosses – pollinations, ears, nursery rows, isolation blocks – scales with the number of distinct crosses. Testing them scales with crosses x locations x replicates. Genotyping scales with the number of lines, not crosses, which is the structural reason genomics favours designs with many lines and few crosses each. A tester design makes few crosses with much seed each; a sparse factorial makes many crosses with little seed each. The two can occupy the same plots and need completely different nurseries.
cross_cost() writes the accounting chain from plots back to the nursery: seed needed per cross is plots x seed per plot; ears are that over seed per ear, never fewer than an insurance minimum; pollinations are ears over pollination success; female rows follow from the pollinations each pool-A parent carries, male rows from the pollinations each pool-B parent serves, several per plant. Four designs at the same 2,000 plots:


Show code
set.seed(8)
cost_plans <- list("tester k=4"       = design_tester(n, n, 4),
                   "circulant c=5"    = design_circulant(n, n, 5),
                   "circulant c=10"   = design_circulant(n, n, 10),
                   "NC II 10x10 sets" = design_nc2(n, n, 10, 10))
cost_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cost_plans), function(nm) {
  cc <- cross_cost(design_reps(cost_plans[[nm]], 2000), n, n)
  data.frame(design = nm, t(cc[c("crosses", "plots", "pollinations",
                                 "nursery_rows", "genotyped", "total")]))
}))
cost_par <- cross_cost_par()
cost_common <- cost_par[["cost_fixed"]] + cost_par[["cost_per_line_geno"]] * cost_tab$genotyped[1]
cost_plan <- cost_tab$total - cost_common
cost_tab

Result. Under this accounting the four plans cost within 9.7 % of each other in total, and within 13.7 % once the cost common to all four (the fixed cost and the genotyping of 400 lines, 30,000) is removed. The cheapest is the circulant design with five crosses per line, because it makes the fewest distinct crosses (1000) and spends the rest of the plots on replicates, which need more seed per cross but no more pollinations: the two-ear insurance minimum already produces enough seed for two plots. The ten-cross designs make twice as many crosses and need 6000 pollinations against 3000.
Interpretation. The tester is not cheaper here, and that is a property of the model, not of testers. cross_cost() charges every cross as hand pollinations, so it cannot credit the bulk production – an isolation block, a male-sterile female – that makes a tester cross cheap in practice, and the tester’s 1,584 crosses each pay the insurance minimum. That missing term is gap 1 of Section 18.9, and it is the term a real programme must add before comparing designs on cost. The other term is seed per cross as a cap on replication. At the placeholder levels one ear gives 250 kernels against 60 per plot, that is 4.2 plots per ear, and the two-ear minimum 8.3; so seed caps replication only above about 8 plots per cross, which no design here approaches (the sweep caps replication at three). The constraint would bind where seed per ear is small against seed per plot; at these levels it does not. Operational sparse designs such as Thomsen et al. (2026) are unreplicated; the cost model does not explain why.






WarningThe cost levels are placeholders



Every monetary and biological level in cross_cost_par() – seed per plot, seed per ear, pollination success, pollen uses per male plant, the price of a plot, a row, a pollination and a genotype – is an order of magnitude for a public maize programme, not a costed figure. The structure – which quantity multiplies which, which capacity binds – is what this section offers. Re-parameterise before any number below means anything for a real programme.




18.7.2 Budget-constrained optimisation
The cached optimiser searched over lines tested per pool, design family, \(k\) or \(c\), plots per cross and whether to genotype every candidate, subject to field, nursery and money constraints, and maximised expected response \(R = i\,\rho\,\sigma_g\) – not accuracy. That distinction is the trade-off: raising \(c\) raises \(\rho\) but, at fixed budget, lowers the number of lines tested and with it the selection intensity \(i\). It scores \(\rho\) with the least-squares closed form of Table 18.1 at the design’s \(c\), whatever the family. Table 18.2 shows that for sparse designs that score is above the cached accuracy of both estimators, so it is optimistic for them, not conservative.






Figure 18.6: Left: expected response per unit cost by design. Right: the best feasible configuration at each total budget. Cached from the sparsex optimiser; cost levels are placeholders.









Figure 18.7: The optimiser’s budget frontier. Cached from the sparsex optimiser.





Show code
ff <- subset(front, feasible)
# Tester and sparse configurations with the same lines per pool, c or k, plots per
# cross and genotyping: the optimiser's response must be the same function of them.
cfg <- c("n_test", "c_or_k", "reps", "genotype_all")
tt <- unique(subset(front, design == "tester")[, c(cfg, "resp", "n_crosses", "cost_total")])
ss <- unique(subset(front, design == "sparse")[, c(cfg, "resp", "n_crosses", "cost_total")])
mm <- merge(tt, ss, by = cfg, suffixes = c("_t", "_s"))
stopifnot(max(abs(mm$resp_t - mm$resp_s)) < 1e-9, all(mm$cost_total_t >= mm$cost_total_s))
best <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(ff, ff$budget), function(d) d[which.max(d$resp), ]))
best <- best[, c("budget", "design", "n_test", "c_or_k", "reps", "n_crosses",
                 "n_plots", "cost_total", "resp", "resp_per_1000")]
rownames(best) <- NULL
# Reading of the table used in the text below.
stopifnot(nrow(best) == 6, max(front$n_test) == 200, all(best$n_test[-1] == 200),

Result. A sparse factorial is on the frontier at every budget, and no tester configuration is optimal anywhere in the grid. The response is, however, the same for a tester and a sparse configuration with the same lines per pool, \(c\) or \(k\), plots per cross and genotyping in all 64 such pairs in the grid (largest difference 0), while the tester plan makes 2 times as many crosses (median) and costs more. The optimum at 60,000 is 150 lines per pool at \(c = 5\) and one plot per cross. From 80,000 on it is 200 lines per pool, the largest value in the grid (the grid searched 50, 100, 150 and 200). From 80,000 to 125,000 the optimum keeps \(c = 3\) and raises plots per cross from 2 to 3 to 4; at 150,000 and 200,000 the 3,000-plot field cap binds, the optimum is identical (\(c = 5\), 3 plots per cross, response 8.086, cost 132,300), and the extra money buys nothing. Response per 1,000 currency units falls from 0.102 to 0.061. Interpretation. Within this grid, once the candidate set is at its maximum of 200 lines, additional money is spent on plots per cross until the field cap binds and then buys nothing. Whether more money would then be worth a larger candidate set cannot be read from the table, because the grid stops at 200 lines, the size of the running example’s pools. The preference for sparse designs is a statement about the cost model, in which a reciprocal tester plan needs about twice the crosses of a sparse plan with the same \(c\), and which cannot credit bulk tester seed (above); the optimiser sees no accuracy difference between the families, because it scores both with the same least-squares formula. “No tester is optimal” is therefore conditional on that cost model and on that formula, not a result about accuracy, and the ordering of \(c\) along the frontier (\(c = 3\) to 5) rests on a score that is optimistic for sparse designs: the sweep, not the optimiser, is the evidence on \(c\).
The published allocation results come from other designs and scales and are not tested by this grid; they are cited as context, not as confirmation. A training population of 500 at one replicate was only 4 % more accurate than 125 at four, and a second replicate added 0.09 correlation points (Lorenz 2013); selection gain levels off quickly with budget, so additional money is better spent on more populations than on deeper testing (Riedelsheimer and Melchinger 2013); and the optimum number of testers, locations and stages is a joint decision (C. F. H. Longin et al. 2006; C. Longin et al. 2006; Mi et al. 2014; Marulanda et al. 2016).
