text:
18.8 A decision framework
The chapter collapses into a procedure a breeder can apply in a planning meeting.








Figure 18.8: A decision procedure for the crossing plan of a two-pool programme. Each question is answered by a section of this chapter.






Can you fit a mixed model? If not, avoid the sparsest layouts (\(c \le 3\) per line, circulant \(c = 5\)): under least squares at 2,000 plots they are worse than the best tester (Table 18.11). Designs with \(c = 10\) or NC II sets exceeded that tester in the cached sweep (the circulant \(c = 10\) row is not reproduced in-repo), and a tester loses little to least squares (Table 18.10); if the field holds only two or three crosses per line, a tester with \(k\) from the curve of Figure 18.2 is the safe choice. Markers are not needed at this step; they enter at step 4.
How many candidates must be ranked, and can the field hold a cross for each? If it can hold \(c \ge 2\) crosses per candidate, prefer a connected sparse factorial (Table 18.6).
Choose \(c\) from the objective. \(c = 2\) ranks lines; \(c \ge 3\) is required before any statement about SCA variance. Do not take \(c\) from the optimiser of Table 18.17, whose score is optimistic for sparse designs (Table 18.2); read it from the accuracy of the sweep (Figure 18.4). Build the layout, do not sample it, and confirm with design_diagnostics() that it is one component.
Choose the line set, not just the crosses. When the field cannot hold every candidate, GBLUP is the only route to the lines left out (Table 18.12). Which lines to field is a separate choice; in this sweep CDmean sets did not raise the genomic accuracy above random sets (Table 18.14), so the decision rests on other grounds than the sweep.
Check the nursery before committing: ears, rows and isolation blocks, not just plots (Table 18.16).
Re-estimate every cycle. Published SCA shares differ between cycles (Lorenzi et al. 2024), and the pools drift (Section 18.11).

text:
18.9 Open problems
Five gaps remain, each defined by the evidence that would close it.

Seed production as an explicit constraint. None of the cost studies cited here (Marulanda et al. 2016; Longin et al. 2015) models seed yield per pollination, isolation capacity or seed per plot inside the optimisation of a mating design; they carry hybrid-seed production as a scalar (no systematic search beyond them was made). cross_cost() gives the structure; the levels are missing.
Joint sparsity in crosses and environments. The cross-sparsity literature (Lorenzi et al. 2022; Melchinger et al. 2023) holds the environment design fixed; the environment-sparsity literature (Jarquin et al. 2020; Atanda et al. 2022; Montesinos-López et al. 2023) works with line or testcross entries. Thomsen et al. (2026) is the closest to a joint treatment, and it is observational. Chapter 20 takes this gap up.
Connectivity reported, structured layouts compared. The tools are seventy years old (Weeks and Williams 1964; Fernando et al. 1983); design papers rarely report the connectivity of the layouts they use. Table 18.8 closes the matched-\(c\) comparison in simulation only.
Tropical maize. Under-represented relative to its share of breeding effort; Fritsche-Neto et al. (2021) and Chaingeni et al. (2025) are the main exceptions.
Multi-cycle validation. The long-term consequences of genomics-driven cross selection for pool divergence are modelled (Gorjanc et al. 2018; Allier et al. 2019; Melchinger and Frisch 2023) but not validated over real cycles, and the SCA shares that differ between cycles in Lorenzi et al. (2024) are the warning case. The design of the crossing plan across cycles is also not treated in Chapter 23, which evaluates every \(A \times B\) hybrid in each cycle and has no crossing design.

18.10 Reproducibility and assumptions
What runs live. Every table and figure above built from design_*(), design_diagnostics(), fit_gca(), cross_cost() or gca_accuracy_theory() is computed at render, from base R, at the full 200 x 200 scale. The package’s tests (tests/testthat/test-mating.R) assert the rank rule for every design family, the NC II estimability result, the \(k = 1\) saturation, the Sprague-Tatum error variance by Monte Carlo, and that BLUP converges to least squares as the GCA variance grows.
What is cached. The 24-design x 3-budget sweep, the REML variance components, the genomic results and the optimiser frontier come from the external sparsex study and are not reproducible from this repository. Its validation file records 37 checks, all marked PASS against the study’s own tolerances. The observed maxima are: closed form against AlphaSimR’s genotypic values 5.7e-14 (absolute); sampling-variance and accuracy expressions (V3, V4) 1.47 % against tolerances of 6, 8, 10 %; REML recovery of the variance components (V5) 8.1 % against 25 %; in-house REML against sommer (V6) 1.4e-05 relative error; and the rank rule for every family. The phenotypic core of that sweep is re-run in-repo by Rscript book/scripts/regenerate.R mating (seed 4242, 30 replicates per cell, a new factorial and a new design draw in each replicate), with the package’s i.i.d. model and the variance components held at their true values (typed to three decimals in the script; the chapter reads them from the validation file at full precision, a difference far below the standard errors). Both are compared at 2,000 plots, on each cell’s mean and standard error:


Show code
cr <- subset(core, budget_plots == 2000)
ca <- subset(sm, budget_plots == 2000 & model %in% c("LS", "BLUP"))
ca$method <- tolower(ca$model)
cmp <- merge(cr, ca[, c("scenario", "method", "acc_gca_all", "se_acc_gca_all")],
             by = c("scenario", "method"))
cmp$z <- (cmp$acc_mean - cmp$acc_gca_all) / sqrt(cmp$acc_se^2 + cmp$se_acc_gca_all^2)
rep_tab <- reshape(data.frame(design = cmp$scenario, method = cmp$method,
                              inrepo = cmp$acc_mean, cached = cmp$acc_gca_all, z = cmp$z),
                   idvar = "design", timevar = "method", direction = "wide")
rep_tab <- rep_tab[order(rep_tab$inrepo.blup), ]
rownames(rep_tab) <- NULL
cmp_out <- cmp[abs(cmp$z) >= 3, ]
fmt(rep_tab, 3)

Result. Of the 22 in-repo against cached comparisons, 20 have \(|z| < 3\) and 2 do not: circulant c=10 by ls (0.615 in-repo against 0.707, z = -5.2); NC II 10x10 sets by ls (0.756 in-repo against 0.737, z = 3.8). All the BLUP comparisons are within \(|z| =\) 2.6. The qualitative claims of the chapter – sparse ahead of tester at equal plots, circulant ahead of random at low \(c\), a least-squares penalty that is large at low \(c\) and negligible for testers – hold in both. Interpretation. The two sweeps therefore do not agree to sampling error in every cell, and the disagreement is largest in least squares at \(c = 10\) (NC II, the other exception, also has one plot per cross), where every cross has the same weight, so the least-squares estimate does not depend on the variance components at all: a difference in how the components were estimated (REML against known values) cannot explain it. The remaining differences between the two runs – the external study’s coalescent founders, linkage and finite QTL (described by the study; the validation file’s V2 note mentions linkage disequilibrium among QTL), and a realised factorial against an i.i.d. draw – are candidate explanations, none tested here, because the external run cannot be repeated from this repository.
Assumptions, stated in the chapter rather than a footnote.

Thirty replicates per cell. Every row of the cached sweep has n_rep =

Whether a cached replicate is a new founder set or new phenotypes on one founder set is not recorded in this repository, and the z-scores of this chapter are unpaired (Table 18.6, Table 18.8, Table 18.12); they are conservative if arms share the replicate’s truth. The standard error of a cell mean ranges from 0.0014 to 0.018 (median 0.0042), so a fixed width in correlation points is not a threshold: this chapter calls a difference resolved when its unpaired z exceeds 3, and says where one does not. The single cached run is the unit; none of the cross-budget or cross-design results is replicated across founder sets.

One trait, one marker density (1,000 markers, as described by the sparsex study; not checkable here), no epistasis, no selection during line development, no spatial trend, no missing plots.
Genotype x location is folded into plot error. An extra location and an extra replicate are treated as equivalent, which is exact under that assumption and optimistic when G x L variance is large. Chapter 19 did not compare a location with a replicate. With G x L in the model, its result 2 (Section 19.11.3) held two plots per hybrid fixed and found that spreading them over more trial locations, 2 to 10, raised accuracy: once G x L exists, the number of environments a trial samples matters, which this assumption cannot represent.
Unrelated candidate panel. The DH lines come from two pools described by the sparsex study as diverged for 100 generations, with no family structure; this is a candidate reason for the low genomic T0 accuracy, not a tested one.
Placeholder costs. Every level in cross_cost_par().
Integer budgets. Replication is floor(plots / crosses) capped at three, with the remainder spread at random, so “budget” is not a continuous axis: a one-tester design with 399 crosses stops at 1,197 plots.

title: 18  How few hybrids are enough? Mating designs for a two-pool programme
text:
18.11 Where this connects
This chapter settled which crosses to make with the field held fixed: a connected sparse factorial, analysed by BLUP, with \(c\) chosen by the objective (from the sweep, not from the optimiser, Section 18.7). It left the field itself – how many locations each cross is planted in, and which – to Chapter 19, and the trade between crosses and locations under one budget to Chapter 20.
What the Optimisation part receives. Chapter 15, Chapter 16 and Chapter 17 take the values of the whole \(A \times B\) factorial as known. A sparse plan fields 1 to 5 % of it, so the rest are predictions, with the accuracies measured here (all-lines GCA accuracy from 0.52 to 0.83 across the 200-line designs at the three budgets; genomic accuracy for hybrids of untested lines, T0, about 0.14). Which values a sparse plan passes on for the unfielded cells – the GCA sum without SCA, or a genomic prediction – is a choice this chapter does not make, and none of the selection problems of that part accounts for the prediction error; Chapter 14 and the Finding 5 of Section 12.5 are where the two meet.
A hypothesis, not a result: the diversity of the line set. The crossing plan decides which lines are seen. A design that fields 50 lines per pool selected by CDmean ranks those 50, so the next cycle’s parents may in practice come from them, and a loss of gene diversity of the kind that Chapter 13 tracks across the pipeline would then start at the choice of lines (line selection, stage S3 of Table 1.1, which Chapter 13 already measures), not at the later selection of hybrids. No diversity metric of a design – \(GD\), \(\theta\), alleles retained – is computed in this chapter, so this is the book’s subject offered as a question about nursery plans, not a finding of the sweep. A sparse factorial that crosses every candidate keeps every candidate line in the field, which is a statement about which lines are tested, not about the diversity of the hybrids fielded; the latter depends on which cells are filled, and the identities of Section 1.2 that tie it to \(GD_T + GD_{BS}\) are stated for the complete factorial.
Section 5.11 is where the dominance part of the GCA and SCA used here was derived from allele frequencies, and Section 5.13.6 is the finite-tester version of Figure 18.2. Chapter 5 reports, under neutral divergence and dominance only, a share of SCA in the heterosis variance that falls as the pools diverge – a different statistic from the SCA:GCA ratio of this chapter, defined above, and under narrower assumptions – so the direction suggests that the number of testers and the crosses per line a programme needs are not constants of the crop, without giving their value. Chapter 14 fits an additive GBLUP on a trait with no SCA; it does not fit the pool-specific or SCA kernels, and the genomic accuracies of this chapter come from the cached sparsex study (Section 18.10), not from that chapter. Chapter 23 evaluates every \(A \times B\) hybrid in each cycle and has no crossing design: how a design chosen once behaves while the pools drift is not tested there, and not in this book. The contributions of Chapter 15 attach to hybrids; the literature on optimal cross selection (Gorjanc et al. 2018) concerns within-pool crosses, and nothing in this book implements it.

title: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations
text:
19.1 The allocation problem of stage 1
A hybrid programme’s first field stage concentrates most of its selection pressure where it has the least information. It typically has thousands of testcrosses, seed for one or two plots of each, a handful of locations, and almost no replication. Chapter 18 compared which crosses to make from two pools – connected sparse factorials against tester designs, analysed by best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP), with results that are conditional on the design and field size it states – but held the field fixed and folded genotype x location into plot error. This chapter takes the crosses as given and asks the next question: which locations should each one be planted in?
Sparse testing is the strategy that the six primary studies of Table 19.5 examine, on different axes and with different conclusions about overlap (Section 19.6). Not every hybrid is grown at every location. Different subsets go to different environments, and the missing hybrid x environment cells are predicted, not discarded, with a relationship matrix connecting what the field left unconnected. In Chapter 18 the sparsity was in the female x male grid. Here it is in the hybrid x environment grid. Real programmes face both at once, the joint problem Section 18.9 lists as its second gap.
The chapter covers the quantitative basis, the history and a taxonomy of the designs, the validation schemes used to judge them, and the empirical record across crops, including its main controversy. It then measures the question with a simulation that the primary literature had not run. The results it defends:
Scope. Every simulated result below refers to one configuration: a 20 x 20 female x male factorial of which 80 % of the hybrids are planted at random (each line is a parent of about 16 planted crosses), 400 hybrids, at most ten locations, one plot per cell, and the calibration of sparse_vc(). It is a dense factorial, in which parents are shared by construction. The sparse factorials of Chapter 18 (a few crosses per line out of 200 candidates per pool) and the 2,000-lines-per-pool pipeline of Figure 19.1 are different regimes, and none of the results was measured there. The cached study is one study, and the contrasts and bias figures quoted from it cannot be recomputed in this repository.
The numbering is that of Section 19.11.3, which the rest of the book cites.

title: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations
text:
19.1.1 The economics of the first stage
Stage 1 is where a plot costs least and a decision is worth most. Early-stage testing typically evaluates a large number of candidates at one or a few experimental sites (Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. 2025). Two shifts are taken here as premises of the chapter, not as results measured in it or taken from a cited source:

Genotyping is no longer the bottleneck. Phenotyping is. The cost of a marker datum is taken to be small against the cost of a yield plot.
Doubled haploids (DH) reversed the constraint. A programme can now make more candidates than it can evaluate. Allocating plots, not creating variation, is then the limiting factor.

What is left is the classical trade-off. More genotypes at fewer locations buys selection intensity and costs accuracy. Fewer genotypes at more locations does the opposite. At stage 1 the scarce resource is the plot, so the question is not how much to test but how to spread what can already be tested (Li et al. 2026).








Figure 19.1: A two-pool hybrid pipeline. Population improvement (left) feeds product development (right). Candidate numbers fall by an order of magnitude per stage while plots per candidate rise. Sparse testing applies where the plots per candidate are fewest: the first testcross trial. The numbers are schematic; the simulation of this chapter has 400 hybrids.







19.1.2 The breeder’s equation as the decision criterion
The gain per unit time,
\[
\Delta G_T = \frac{i \, \rho \, \sigma_A}{T},
\tag{19.1}\]
has four terms. \(\rho\) is the accuracy of the selection criterion – the \(r\) of Chapter 4; this Part keeps \(r\) for plots, as Chapter 18 does. \(\sigma_A\) is the additive standard deviation of Chapter 4 (written \(\sigma_g\) in Chapter 18). The accuracy reported by the simulation below is a correlation with the value of a hybrid, defined in Section 19.11.3; it is not the GCA accuracy of Chapter 18, which is a correlation over lines. A trial design moves at least three of the terms of Equation 19.1 together (Table 19.1):

intensity \(i\), through the number of candidates;
accuracy \(\rho\), through plots, locations, and how well the locations sample the target population of environments (TPE);
cycle length \(T\), when parents can be recycled from stage 1.

What a gain measured on a research station is worth depends on the genetic correlation between the selection environment and the TPE (Atlin et al. 2000, 2001). No design is better in the abstract. A design is better according to whichever term limits that programme (Werner, Zaman-Allah, et al. 2025; Riedelsheimer and Melchinger 2013).






NoteBox 1 – Where each term of the breeder’s equation meets the trial design






Table 19.1: The terms of Equation 19.1 and the design decisions that move each.









Term
Design decision that moves it




\(i\) (intensity)
number of candidates tested at a fixed plot budget


\(\rho\) (accuracy)
plots per candidate, locations per candidate, use of a relationship matrix


\(\rho\) (relevance)
how well the chosen locations sample the TPE


\(\sigma_A\)
indirectly: which parents are recycled, and how related they are (Chapter 15)


\(T\) (cycle length)
whether stage-1 GCA predictions are good enough to recycle parents immediately

title: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations
text:
19.2 Foundations

19.2.1 The hybrid model: GCA, SCA, and what sparsity threatens
The value of the single cross between female \(i\) and male \(j\) – a pool-A and a pool-B line in the notation of Chapter 18 – splits as
\[
g_{ij} = \mathrm{GCA}^f_i + \mathrm{GCA}^m_j + \mathrm{SCA}_{ij}
\tag{19.2}\]
This split (Equation 19.2) is classically attributed to Sprague and Tatum (1942) (not checked at page level here). Section 5.11 derives it from allele frequencies. Its consequence for this chapter is that a line’s GCA includes dominance effects weighted by the opposite pool’s frequencies. A GCA is therefore specific to the tester pool, not a property of the line alone (González-Diéguez et al. 2021; Legarra et al. 2023). The ratio \(\sigma^2_s/\sigma^2_g\) of Chapter 18 (symbols defined below) is a design parameter of the simulation. In the dominance-only model of Section 5.11 the corresponding quantity grows with the mean degree of dominance and with how close the pools are; Chapter 18 notes that this is a different statistic from its own ratio, under narrower assumptions, so the statement is not transferred to the ratio used here. In simulated maize the ratio of González-Diéguez et al. (2026), in that paper’s own definition, was 0.05, 0.23 and 0.50 at cycle 1 for mean dominance degrees of 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9.
GCA is expected to survive sparsity better than SCA, because it is mostly additive and is averaged over many crosses. This is an expectation, not a result of this chapter. The one supporting number is from Li et al. (2026), who recovered GCA from a prediction-completed 50 % trial with correlations of 0.94 to 0.97 against the complete data, while phenotypic prediction accuracy over the same scenarios was 0.43 to 0.59. The chapter has no SCA comparator for that correlation, and its own simulation measures the bias of the SCA variance, not the robustness of SCA prediction (see its limitations). If stage 1 is used to recycle parents, GCA is what it has to estimate; whether GCA is the part of the model most robust to missing cells, and therefore the reason sparse testing works in hybrids, is not tested here.






NoteQuick glossary




GCA: a line’s average performance in crosses with the opposite pool.
SCA: the deviation of a particular cross from the sum of its parents’ GCAs.
Mid-parent heterosis: the hybrid’s advantage over the mean of its parents (Chapter 5).
Heterotic pool: a group of lines bred to cross well with another group.
Tester: a line of the opposite pool used to evaluate candidates.
TPE: the target population of environments the product is sold into.





19.2.2 Hybrid relationship matrices
With female and male relationship matrices \(\mathbf{A}_f\) and \(\mathbf{A}_m\), the three hybrid terms are distributed as
\[
\mathrm{GCA}^f \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf A_f\sigma^2_{f}), \quad
\mathrm{GCA}^m \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf A_m\sigma^2_{m}), \quad
\mathrm{SCA}   \sim N(\mathbf 0, (\mathbf A_f\otimes\mathbf A_m)\sigma^2_{s})
\tag{19.3}\]
(Bernardo 1994, 1996; Technow et al. 2012). In Equation 19.3, \(\sigma^2_f\) and \(\sigma^2_m\) are the GCA variances of the female (pool-A) and male (pool-B) lines. They are the \(\sigma^2_{gA}\) and \(\sigma^2_{gB}\) of Chapter 18, whose \(\sigma^2_g\) is their mean, \(\sigma^2_g = (\sigma^2_f + \sigma^2_m)/2\); \(\sigma^2_s\) is the SCA variance of Chapter 18, also written \(\sigma^2_{SCA}\) in this chapter. The effects \(\mathrm{GCA}^f_i\), \(\mathrm{GCA}^m_j\) and \(\mathrm{SCA}_{ij}\) are the \(g^A_i\), \(g^B_j\) and \(s_{ij}\) of Chapter 18. Two sums are used below and each is defined here once. The genetic variance of a hybrid’s value in the target population of environments is \(\sigma^2_G = \sigma^2_f + \sigma^2_m + \sigma^2_s\) (2.25 in sparse_vc(), where it is Vg); it is not the \(\sigma^2_g\) of Chapter 18. Each of the three terms interacts with location, with variances \(\sigma^2_{f\ell}\), \(\sigma^2_{m\ell}\) and \(\sigma^2_{s\ell}\) (s2fl, s2ml, s2sl; the last is also written \(\sigma^2_{SCA\times L}\) below), and \(\sigma^2_{GE} = \sigma^2_{f\ell} + \sigma^2_{m\ell} + \sigma^2_{s\ell}\) (1.125 in sparse_vc(), where it is VgxE). \(\sigma^2_e\) is the plot error.
The practical point is that the hybrid itself never needs genotyping: its covariance is a Kronecker product of the parental matrices. Replacing pedigree \(\mathbf A\) by marker \(\mathbf G\) (VanRaden 2008) gives the genomic version. Chapter 14 fits a single additive genomic BLUP (GBLUP) over all hybrids, with no pool split, no SCA kernel and no Kronecker product, so the kernels of this section are not fitted there. The live code of this chapter uses the pedigree matrices of relmat_halfsib(), and the cached genomic layer comes from the external study. There are two ways to write the additive and dominance effects: the “biological” form and the “statistical” form, which is orthogonal at the population’s frequencies. Pool-specific marker effects are a third option (Vitezica et al. 2013; González-Diéguez et al. 2021). All of them lead to the same covariance structure.
The relationship matrix is what makes a sparse design analysable. It is the only link between cells that the field did not link. A hybrid with no plot gets a BLUP only because its parents are related to parents that do have plots. Without it, a sparse design yields comparisons that are not fair.


19.2.3 Multi-environment trials and mixed models
How many parameters the between-environment covariance spends ranges widely:

identity, diagonal, or compound symmetry;
heterogeneous first-order autoregressive, AR(1);
unstructured;
factor-analytic (Smith et al. 2001; Smith et al. 2005; Kelly et al. 2007; Smith and Cullis 2018).

Factor-analytic models carry most of the information of the unstructured matrix at a fraction of its parameters, and extend directly to genomic relationships (Oakey et al. 2016; Tolhurst et al. 2019; Burgueño et al. 2012). Reaction-norm and marker x environment models are cheaper alternatives (Jarquin et al. 2013; Lopez-Cruz et al. 2015). Only crossover genotype x environment (G x E) interaction changes selection decisions. A scale effect does not.
In a sparse design the between-environment covariance stops being a statistical detail and becomes part of the design. It decides how much one environment can tell us about another. Two-stage analyses that carry the first-stage error forward are now as efficient as one-stage ones (Piepho et al. 2012; Endelman 2023). Unreplicated trials still need spatial correction and checks (Robbins et al. 2012; Cullis et al. 2006). Table 19.2 sets the heritability-type quantities that can be reported side by side.






WarningBox 2 – Which heritability to report in a sparse trial






Table 19.2: Four heritability-type quantities and their behaviour under sparsity.











Quantity
Formula
What it answers
Behaviour under sparsity




Plot-level \(h^2\)
\(\sigma^2_G / (\sigma^2_G + \sigma^2_{GE} + \sigma^2_e)\)
how informative one plot is
design-independent; it is what the simulations of Section 19.11.3 fix


Entry-mean \(H^2\)
\(\sigma^2_G / (\sigma^2_G + \sigma^2_{GE}/L + \sigma^2_e/(rL))\)
how informative an entry mean is, if every entry had \(L\) locations and \(r\) reps
undefined when entries have different \(L\), i.e. in every sparse design


Per-genotype reliability
\(1 - \overline{\mathrm{PEV}} / \sigma^2_G\), with \(\overline{\mathrm{PEV}}\) the mean prediction error variance (PEV) of the target values
the squared correlation of the BLUP with the true value of one genotype, in expectation over repeated draws, if the components are right; the realised correlation over a finite set of hybrids differs (Box 4)
the quantity Box 4 computes; it uses the actual PEVs


Generalised (Cullis) \(H^2\)
\(1 - \bar v_\Delta / (2\sigma^2_G)\), with \(\bar v_\Delta\) the mean variance of the difference between two BLUPs (Cullis et al. 2006; Piepho and Mohring 2007)
how well the analysed design ranks entries
also uses the actual variances; not computed in this chapter. In an unbalanced design \(\bar v_\Delta\) is not twice the mean PEV, so it is a different number from the reliability above






The entry-mean formula silently assumes balance. In a sparse trial, report a quantity that uses the actual PEVs: Cullis’ \(H^2\) or the per-genotype reliability. The two are different numbers, and this chapter computes only the second.

section: 19.3 What sparse testing is, and where it came from
text:
19.3 What sparse testing is, and where it came from

19.3.1 Definition and genealogy
Definition. A trial is sparse when not every genotype is evaluated in every environment and the missing cells are predicted rather than discarded. The literature’s environment is a location in a year; the simulations of this Part have one season, so their environments are locations, and the two words are used in those two senses. The idea developed in four steps:

Incomplete blocks and lattices. These already accepted partial evaluation within a location.
Partially replicated designs (p-rep) and augmented p-rep. These replaced replication of each entry with replicated checks and partial replication (Cullis et al. 2006; Williams et al. 2011).
The genomic relationship replacing replication (Endelman et al. 2014). With markers, the replicated unit is no longer the genotype but the haplotype, shared among relatives.
Genomic sparse testing across environments, formalised (Jarquin et al. 2020). The design was later framed explicitly as a balanced incomplete block design in which the block is the environment (Montesinos-López et al. 2023).

Farm-as-incomplete-block is the limiting case. Each farmer’s field is an incomplete block holding a handful of entries, and the TPE is sampled through hundreds of them (Werner, Zaman-Allah, et al. 2025; Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. 2025; Atlin et al. 2001).
Sparse testing is not a new method. It is incomplete-block design applied at the scale of many environments, made workable by genomic relationships acting as the connecting mechanism. The classical theory of incomplete blocks therefore carries over. Figure 19.2 draws the four steps as genotype x environment matrices.








Figure 19.2: The genealogy of sparse testing, drawn as genotype (rows) x environment (columns) matrices; dark = observed. From the complete trial, to incomplete blocks within locations, to p-rep (a few entries and checks replicated), to genomic sparse testing (each entry in a subset of environments, connected through relationships), to farm-as-incomplete-block (many environments, very few entries each). Schematic, not simulated data: four of the five panels are drawn by hand; the fourth of the five (genomic sparse testing) is one random draw of sparse_alloc() for 12 hybrids in 4 locations with 2 locations per hybrid.







19.3.2 A taxonomy of sparse designs
The designs can be classified along three independent axes. Figure 19.3 draws six allocations and Table 19.3 maps them onto the literature.
Axis of sparsity.

Environments: the classical case.
Testers: sparse testcrossing (Section 19.8).
Female x male combinations: the incomplete factorials of Section 18.4.
Any combination of these.

Overlap structure.

full overlap, with a common core in every environment;
no overlap;
partial overlap, with a fixed core plus entries unique to each environment;
unrestricted random allocation;
restricted random allocation, for example keeping full-sibs out of the same location (Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. 2025);
allocation optimised against a formal criterion (Isidro y Sanchez and Akdemir 2021; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al. 2023).

Replicated unit. Genotype, family, or haplotype.


Show code

  M <- matrix(0L, 32, 6); M[seq_len(n_core), ] <- 1L
  rest <- setdiff(1:32, seq_len(n_core))
  M[cbind(rest, rep_len(1:6, length(rest)))] <- 1L; M
}

WarningA naming collision to watch for



Li et al. (2026) use “CV1” to “CV5” as names of allocation strategies, not of the classical validation schemes of Section 19.4. Their “CV1” is the full-overlap design: 44 of the 264 genotypes are evaluated in all six environments. Their introduction states that CV1 “is used to predict entirely new genotypes”, and in their Methods only those 44 genotypes carry records, so for CV1 the prediction task is the “new genotype” one of Burgueño et al. (2012). Their CV2 and CV3 retain at least one record per genotype (Methods, Section 2.4, and the legend of their Fig. 1), so the cells predicted are unobserved cells of observed genotypes. For CV4 and CV5 the text read does not state that every genotype is observed, and the correspondence is not asserted here. What the label collision does is more modest: the same labels name a design in one literature and a validation task in the other, and reading the two together without noticing this produces wrong comparisons.
A second collision is inside this book, and it has three parts. Section 14.4 uses CV2 / CV1 / CV0 for hybrids with both / one / neither parent seen in training – the T2 / T1 / T0 of Section 18.6. Here, as in Burgueño et al. (2012), the labels classify genotype x environment cells. A hybrid that is CV1 here (never planted) is CV2 in Section 14.4 when both its parents are planted in other crosses, CV1 there when one parent is not, and CV0 there when neither is. Section 14.4’s CV1 (one parent unseen) therefore has no counterpart label in this chapter, and this chapter’s CV0 (a new environment) shares only the label with that chapter’s CV0. In this chapter’s simulation every parent is planted (a 20 x 20 factorial with 20 % of the hybrids dropped at random), so every CV1 hybrid here is a T2 / CV2 hybrid in those terms. That is a property of the simulated design, not of the definition, which also admits T1 and T0 hybrids.

19.4 Validation schemes: what each one answers
The classical cross-validation (CV) schemes are defined by two questions. Has the genotype been observed anywhere? Has the environment been observed for anyone? (Burgueño et al. 2012; Jarquin et al. 2020) Figure 19.4 draws the four schemes as a grid.

CV2: the genotype is observed in some environments and missing in others. The task is to complete the table.
CV1: the genotype is new, never observed anywhere. The task is to predict an unseen candidate.
CV0: the environment is new (next year, say) and the genotypes are known. The task is to extrapolate to an untested environment.
CV00: both the genotype and the environment are new. This is the hardest case, and the most realistic for long-run decisions.

Table 19.4 arranges the four by what is new. The schemes pose different prediction tasks, so accuracies obtained under different schemes are not comparable like for like. In the cached cells of this chapter acc_cv1 exceeds acc_cv2 in 114 of the 165 scenario cells where both exist (median difference +0.026): neither is above the other in general, and the two also differ in target (see the estimands in Section 19.11.3). The correlation is not the only metric:

top-\(x\) % coincidence: top 20 % by a Smith-Hazel index in Atanda et al. (2022), top 50 % in Li et al. (2026);
mean squared error (MSE) (Lubanga et al. 2025);
Kendall’s \(\tau\) (Hild Aono and Chawade 2026);
PEV and reliability, and the dispersion slope \(b_1\) of truth on prediction.

At stage 1 the operationally relevant number is the rate of wrongly discarded superior candidates. The correlation is only a proxy for it.








Figure 19.4: The four validation schemes as a 2 x 2 by whether the genotype (rows) and the environment (columns) were observed. Blue: training cells. Orange: the cells to be predicted. Schematic: 8 genotypes x 5 environments, not simulated data.

The anchor numbers are as follows.

Maize (Li et al. 2026). Mean accuracy was 0.418 under full overlap and 0.479 to 0.504 under every other allocation. Returns diminish beyond about 50 % coverage: going from 50 % to 67 % cost 33 % more phenotyping and returned 3.5 to 5.4 % accuracy. Top-50 % coincidence was above 61.9 % in all 25 strategies.
Wheat (Atanda et al. 2022). Going from 0 to 50 % common lines raised predictive ability by 42 % to 989 %, depending on the environment. Plot \(h^2\) was 0.18 in the worst environment. Genetic correlations between environments in the same year ranged from \(-0.04\) to \(0.67\).
Cassava (Lubanga et al. 2025). With 20 % of records per environment, predictive ability was moderate (maxima of 0.53 for dry matter and 0.47 for fresh root yield). Phenotyping cost could be cut by up to 80 %.
Potato (Hild Aono and Chawade 2026). For pairs of environments at 50 % completeness, \(r^2\) was 0.995 to 0.997 with an image-derived environment kernel, against 0.612 to 0.798 with the genomic kernel. Section 19.10 covers the caveat.

The common denominator is the genetic correlation between environments, and the size and diversity of the training set. Together they explain most of the spread. In Atanda et al. (2022), the environment with low heritability and weak correlations stayed poorly predicted under every design. In Li et al. (2026), plant height was the trait with the strongest between-environment correlations (0.36 to 0.67) and the best predicted. Grain yield had no strong correlations and was predicted worst. The record on modelling G x E explicitly is mixed. Lubanga et al. (2025) report higher predictive ability and lower MSE for the G x E model across their sparse designs, with 20 % of records per environment; in Li et al. (2026) the reaction-norm model, which has a main genomic effect and an environment-specific deviation, had the highest accuracy of the four models compared (Table 2, S1 and CV1, and, by their text, averaged by region group over the 25 strategies); in Hild Aono and Chawade (2026) the G x E term gave results comparable to the model without it at 66 % of the data per environment, and performance fell when it was included at higher proportions of missing data, which the authors attribute to too few individuals to estimate it. The studies differ in crop, data, kernels and sparsity, and none compares the same models across the same range, so the chapter draws no rule from them. Cutting phenotyping by 50 to 80 % without losing accuracy is feasible. The exact cut depends on the programme’s own between-environment correlations, and does not transfer between programmes.

title: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations
text:
19.6 The minimum-overlap controversy
The literature disagrees openly on how much overlap is needed:

Atanda et al. (2022) conclude that “a substantial overlap between lines across environments should be used to achieve optimal prediction accuracy”.
Crespo-Herrera et al. (2021) suggest 30 to 50 common lines.
Persa et al. (2023) report a gain with as few as 10.
Lubanga et al. (2025) find that more overlap made prediction worse: predictive ability fell and MSE rose monotonically with the number of overlapping genotypes, and the fully non-overlapping design was the best.
Li et al. (2026) sit in between. Full overlap was the worst design, and the four partial or non-overlapping designs tied.
Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025) and González-Diéguez et al. (2026) do without overlap altogether. All of their connectivity comes from relationships.

A proposed reconciliation, offered here as a hypothesis. The designs are not comparable because they confound overlap with the size and diversity of the training set:

In Lubanga et al. (2025) the training set per environment is fixed in size. More overlap therefore means fewer distinct genotypes observed.
In Atanda et al. (2022) more overlap means a larger calibration set per environment, growing from 46-47 lines to as many as 165.

A second factor is family structure. Families of 1 to 9 individuals (Atanda et al. 2022) give the relationship matrix little to work with, so physical overlap has to carry the connection. Families of 20 to 50 (Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. 2025; González-Diéguez et al. 2026) let the relationship matrix carry all of it.
The first half of the hypothesis can be examined with the package, but only in part (see below). The experiment uses four locations and a training set fixed at 80 hybrids per location out of 400. A fraction of the 80 is a core common to all four locations, and the rest are unique to each location. Family size runs from unrelated lines to half-sib families of 10 (regenerate.R sparse, part c; 30 replicates per point; known components; plot \(h^2 = 0.4\)). Figure 19.5 shows the result.


Show code
ov <- subset(core, part == "overlap")
fs <- sort(unique(ov$family_size))
cols <- c("grey40", "#1b9e77", "#d95f02")[seq_along(fs)]
op <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3.2, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = range(ov$acc_all - 2 * ov$acc_all_se, ov$acc_all + 2 * ov$acc_all_se),
     xlab = "Overlap: fraction of each location's plots in the common core",
     ylab = "Accuracy, all hybrids")
for (i in seq_along(fs)) {
  d <- ov[ov$family_size == fs[i], ]; d <- d[order(d$overlap), ]
  lines(d$overlap, d$acc_all, type = "b", pch = 19, col = cols[i])
  arrows(d$overlap, d$acc_all - 2 * d$acc_all_se, d$overlap, d$acc_all + 2 * d$acc_all_se,
         angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.03, col = cols[i])
}
d0 <- ov[ov$family_size == fs[1], ]; d0 <- d0[order(d0$overlap), ]
axis(3, at = d0$overlap, labels = d0$n_distinct, cex.axis = 0.8)
mtext("distinct hybrids observed", 3, line = 2, cex = 0.8)
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = cols,
       legend = ifelse(fs == 1, "unrelated lines", paste("half-sib families of", fs)))
par(op)








Figure 19.5: Accuracy over all 400 hybrids against the fraction of each location’s 80 plots taken by a core common to all four locations, by half-sib family size. The training size is held fixed, so more overlap means fewer distinct hybrids observed (top axis). Error bars span the mean plus and minus two standard errors over 30 replicates. In-repo sweep, known variance components.





With the training size held fixed, accuracy falls as overlap rises: it is 0.023 to 0.059 lower under full overlap than under none, 1.6 to 4.7 standard errors of the difference depending on family size. The drop exceeds two standard errors for family size 1 and 10 (1 is unrelated lines) and not for family size 4 (1.6 standard errors), whose curve has the same direction. Every hybrid moved into the common core is one fewer distinct hybrid observed (top axis), so in this design overlap and the number of distinct hybrids move together by construction, and no arm varies one with the other fixed. The fall in accuracy is the pattern Lubanga et al. (2025) reported and the one the confound hypothesis predicts, but this experiment cannot attribute it to the fall in distinct hybrids rather than to overlap as such.
The second half of the hypothesis is not supported at this scale. The family-size curves cross, and they differ by at most 2.2 standard errors at any one overlap: of the 15 pairs compared (every pair of family sizes at every overlap, with no correction for multiple comparisons), 1 exceeded two standard errors and 0 exceeded three. A possible reason, not tested here, is structural. In this factorial every line is a parent of 20 hybrids, of which on average 16 (no overlap) to 4 (full overlap) are observed, so the factorial may carry much of the connectivity before any relationship among lines is added, and half-sib families would add relatively little on top of that. In a line-breeding programme like Atanda et al. (2022), each entry is its own genotype and no parent links them, so family structure should matter far more. This experiment cannot test that case. The experiment also holds the training size fixed, so it does not reproduce Atanda et al. (2022)’s design, in which more overlap also meant a larger calibration set and the two effects pull in opposite directions.
What to do with this. The right question is not “how many common genotypes?”. It is “how much effective connectivity does the design have, counting both physical overlap and relationships?”. The experiment of Figure 19.5 did not resolve an effect of relationships between lines at this scale, so it does not show that physical overlap and relationships substitute for each other. Atanda et al. (2022) found both the genetic correlation between environments and the genomic relationship of lines across them among the drivers of sparse-testing accuracy. In a factorial as dense as the simulated one, shared parents may already supply much of the relationship side (a hypothesis, not tested here).

text:
19.7 Connectivity and checks
Connectivity is not the same as overlap. Two designs with the same number of common genotypes can be connected very differently, depending on how those genotypes are distributed. Hybrids add a dimension. There is female x male connectivity, the subject of Section 18.2.3. There is genotype x location connectivity. And there is female x male x location, for which no metric is agreed (Section 19.13); Section 20.4 gives a necessary screen and a counter-example to sufficiency, and leaves the metric open. The available tools are:

the rank of the incidence matrix;
the PEV of pairwise contrasts, and the reliability derived from it;
the connected components of the genotype-environment graph.

Checks do three jobs:

anchor connectivity;
estimate within-environment error in unreplicated trials, as in the augmented design of Li et al. (2026);
control spatial trend (Cullis et al. 2006; Williams et al. 2011).

Restricted randomisation is a cheap connectivity tool. Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025) kept full-sibs apart within a location, but did not measure the restriction against unrestricted randomisation. Section 19.11.3 does measure a structured layout against unrestricted randomisation.
Connectivity can be checked before planting. Compute it at the planning stage, rather than finding out from a model that does not converge.






TipBox 4 – Computing the connectivity of a design before planting it




Build the genotype x environment incidence matrix.
Check the connected components of the bipartite graph. Every location should share hybrids, or at least parents, with every other.
Compute the mean PEV of the target values under the intended model, with provisional variance components.
Convert it to the per-genotype reliability \(1 - \overline{\mathrm{PEV}}/\sigma^2_G\), with \(\overline{\mathrm{PEV}}\) the mean over hybrids of the prediction error variance of the target value and \(\sigma^2_G\) the genetic variance of

This is not Cullis’ \(H^2\) (Box 2), which uses the variance of differences.

Compare candidate designs on the same metric.



Show code
set.seed(8)
nF <- 20; nM <- 20; L <- 6
Af <- relmat_halfsib(nF, 5); Am <- relmat_halfsib(nM, 5)
vc <- sparse_vc(0.3)
pev_of <- function(M, y = 0) {
  cells <- which(M == 1L, arr.ind = TRUE)
  ph <- data.frame(y = y, hyb = cells[, 1], loc = cells[, 2])
  sparse_blup(ph, nF, nM, L, vc, Af, Am)$pev
}
recipe <- function(M) {
  cn <- sparse_connectivity(M, nF, nM)                        # steps 1-2
  c(plots = sum(M), fem_cover = cn$fem_cover, disconnected_pairs = cn$frac_disconn,
    reliability = 1 - mean(pev_of(M)) / vc$Vg)                # steps 3-4
}
rec <- rbind(complete_2loc = recipe(sparse_alloc(nF, nM, 2, strategy = "complete")),
             random_k2     = recipe(sparse_alloc(nF, nM, L, 2, "random")),
             parentage_k2  = recipe(sparse_alloc(nF, nM, L, 2, "parentage")))

All three designs cost 800 plots (Table 19.6). In that one draw the reliability is 0.703 for random allocation and 0.705 for parentage, against 0.625 for the complete design in two locations. Over ten further layouts of each strategy (seeds 101 to 110) the reliability is 0.7025 (s.d. 0.0004) for random allocation and 0.7050 (s.d. 0.0001) for parentage. The PEV depends only on the design and the components, not on the data (the stopifnot() above), which makes it a design tool and not only an evaluation metric.
The level is not the squared accuracy. In the in-repo sweep, the realised acc_all\(^2\) exceeds this reliability by a mean of +0.038 at \(h^2 = 0.2\) and +0.051 at \(h^2 = 0.4\) (range -0.0004 to +0.080), and the cause of the offset is not investigated here. The rank correlation of the reliability with acc_all over the 26 cells is 0.97. Use it to rank designs at fixed components, not to predict the correlation.

19.8 Sparse testcrossing and the number of testers
The central idea of González-Diéguez et al. (2026) is to treat the tester as an “environment”. Each line is crossed to one tester, but full-sibs go to different testers. What gets evaluated against several testers is therefore the haplotype, not the genotype. This removes a real logistical constraint. The more accurate alternative, an incomplete factorial among candidates (Section 18.4), needs hand pollination at scale and synchronised flowering between pools. Figure 19.6 shows the layout and Table 19.7 the gains the authors report.








Figure 19.6: Sparse testcrossing. A biparental cross yields 20 DH lines; each line is crossed to one of four testers, so the family – not the line – meets every tester. The relationship matrix connects the full-sibs, and through them the four testers. Schematic.








Table 19.7: Sparse testcrossing in González-Diéguez et al. (2026): accuracy and gain against a single tester at an equal number of testcrosses. A dash means that no figure of that kind is tabulated here; the 5.3 % and 0.7 % are genetic gain in the hybrid at cycle 15, not GCA accuracy. Every sparse layout beat the single tester, and gains plateau at 5 to 10 testers; 3 to 5 is the practical recommendation.










Testers (1,200 testcrosses per pool)

Gain in hybrid genetic gain, cycle 15

–

+3 % / +11 % / +23 %

The advantage is largest in early cycles, while the pools are still close. That does not confine the method to emerging programmes. González-Diéguez et al. (2026) report a minimum Nei distance of 0.17 from the public maize programme of the University of Hohenheim, a figure they attribute to Legarra et al. (2023), and place it in their simulated cycles 3 to 4. The \(F_{ST}\) of 0.223 of Kadoumi et al. (2025), from a private programme, is placed by the same reading at about cycle 2. Both figures are second-hand here: the original of Legarra et al. (2023) was not read for this chapter.
A useful side effect is that sparse testcrossing slowed the erosion of within-pool variance. It stops selection from piling onto closely related lines that happen to nick with one tester. The authors recommend combining it with optimum contribution selection (Chapter 15; Santantonio and Robbins (2020)).
The advocates of incomplete factorials (Seye et al. 2020; Lorenzi et al. 2022; Lorenzi et al. 2024; Melchinger and Frisch 2023) reach a different conclusion. In González-Diéguez et al. (2026), an approximate incomplete factorial matched 3 to 5 testers, with much heavier logistics. Two costs were not modelled. Five testers need ten isolation blocks. And in many public programmes hand pollination is already routine, which lowers the extra cost of the factorial.






NoteBox 5 – Choosing testers: theory against practice



The classical recommendation is a low-performing tester, or one carrying recessive alleles at the loci of interest. Such a tester discriminates among candidates best (a recommendation classically attributed to Hull (1945) and Rawlings and Thompson (1962), not checked at page level here). Commercial practice uses elite testers, chosen for seed production and per se performance, because the testcross may itself become a product. The consequence follows from Section 5.11: GCA is measured against the tester’s allele frequencies. An elite tester carries the favourable allele at many loci and shrinks the visible differences there, so a few elite testers sample the opposite pool’s frequencies poorly. Several testers spread across the pool, the sparse-testcross recipe, sample them better (C. Longin et al. 2006; Jong et al. 2023).

section: 19.9 What sparsity does to variance components and to the BLUP
text:
19.9 What sparsity does to variance components and to the BLUP
Two questions are often merged in the literature, and they should be kept separate:

Do the predictions stay accurate?
Do the variance-component estimates stay unbiased?

The second is barely covered. None of the six primary studies reports bias in the GCA, SCA or G x E variances (\(\sigma^2_f\), \(\sigma^2_m\), \(\sigma^2_s\), \(\sigma^2_{GE}\)) under sparsity. The indirect evidence is thin:

In Hild Aono and Chawade (2026) the G x E term degraded prediction in the scenarios with less than 66 % of the data per environment (it was comparable at 66 %), which the authors attribute, without testing it, to too few individuals to estimate it. They then used models without the term.
In Li et al. (2026) propagating prediction uncertainty barely changed the GCA estimates (correlation 0.9974 to 0.9998 with the point estimates). That is a sensitivity of GCA, not of the variance components.

Two diagnostics separate the questions.

The dispersion slope \(b_1\), from regressing truth on prediction. \(b_1 = 1\) means no scale bias. \(b_1 < 1\) means the predictions are too spread out, and \(b_1 > 1\) means they are over-shrunk.
PEV and reliability. These can be computed before any data exist (Box 4), so they serve as design tools.

Accuracy and estimation quality do not degrade at the same rate. A design can rank candidates well and still estimate the SCA and G x E variances badly (Cullis et al. 2006; Piepho and Mohring 2007; Smith and Cullis 2018; Tolhurst et al. 2019). The simulation of Section 19.11.3 measures this directly. That is the gap in the primary literature it was designed to fill.

title: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations
text:
19.10 Sparse testing with phenomics
Phenomic data pose a specific problem. Markers can be read from a seedling whatever happens in the field. Sensor data exist only for plots that were actually grown, so they cannot serve as a covariate for an individual that was never observed. There are three ways out:

multi-trait models with image indices as secondary traits;
kernel regression on the indices;
the proposal of Hild Aono and Chawade (2026): use the images to build an environment kernel.

The environment kernel is built in three steps (Figure 19.7). A principal component analysis (PCA) of the image traits is run within each environment. The first-component eigenvector of each environment is extracted. The kernel entries are the correlations between those eigenvectors.
At 30 % data availability the comparison varied with the combination of environments. Across all scenarios with at least 33 % complete data per environment, the environment kernel matched or outperformed the genomic kernel, reaching \(r^2 = 0.997\) on pairs of environments. At 10 and 20 % “no consistent trend emerged; however, the G kernel generally performed better in most scenarios” (Hild Aono and Chawade 2026), that is, the genomic kernel, not the image-derived one. The authors warn of possible information leakage, because the kernel came from the same trial that supplied training and validation. The result should be reported with that caveat.








Figure 19.7: Building an environment kernel from images, after Hild Aono and Chawade (2026). The dashed box marks where training and validation share information – the leakage the authors flag.





The approach is attractive for programmes without routine genotyping. It is also promising for maize, where sensor phenotyping exists but has not been tested in this arrangement with hybrids. It connects to envirotyping. When locations are close together, coarse-grid weather covariates discriminate poorly, and images capture differences that the weather data miss (Costa-Neto et al. 2020; Crossa et al. 2021; Rincent et al. 2017). near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS)-based phenomic prediction in maize points the same way, in a non-sparse setting (DeSalvio et al. 2024).
Sensor data enter sparse testing as descriptors of environments, not of genotypes. This inversion solves the availability problem. In programmes that genotype little, it can partly replace the genomic matrix.

19.11 Simulation as a sizing tool

19.11.1 Why simulate before designing
None of the published numbers transfers directly to another programme. Each one depends on the between-environment correlations, the family structure, the \(\sigma^2_{SCA}/\sigma^2_{GCA}\) ratio and the heritability of the programme that produced it, and the authors say so themselves (Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. 2025; González-Diéguez et al. 2026). A simulation can do three things an experiment cannot:

it knows the true values;
it can rerun the programme a hundred times;
it can isolate one factor at a time.

The tools exist. AlphaSimR covers the genetics , Chapter 9, FieldSimR covers plots and G x E (Werner et al. 2024), and sommer or BGLR fit the models (Covarrubias-Pazaran 2016). Staged-allocation theory provides the deterministic cross-check (Mi et al. 2014; C. F. H. Longin et al. 2006). Simulation does not replace the experiment. It replaces guessing at the design of the experiment.

Two features of real data a simulation must respect:

Environmental variance exceeds genetic variance by an order of magnitude. For maize grain yield, the ratio of environment to genotype variance is about 8.1 (1.13 / 0.14, in the notation of Li et al. (2026); their genotype variance is not the \(\sigma^2_g\) of Chapter 18) (Li et al. 2026).
Between-environment correlations for yield are often weak. Scenarios should be anchored on measured parameters, not chosen for numerical convenience.



19.11.3 What the simulation finds
The model. The study simulated a female x male factorial of single crosses, tested with one plot per hybrid x location cell. The phenotype is
\[
y = \mu + \text{loc} + \mathrm{GCA}^f + \mathrm{GCA}^m + \mathrm{SCA}
  + \mathrm{GCA}^f{\times}\text{loc} + \mathrm{GCA}^m{\times}\text{loc}
  + \mathrm{SCA}{\times}\text{loc} + e .
\tag{19.4}\]
In Equation 19.4 the target is the value in the TPE, \(\mathrm{GCA}^f + \mathrm{GCA}^m +
\mathrm{SCA}\). In every replicate, 20 % of the hybrids get no plot at all. These are the CV1 hybrids, predicted only through relationships.
The estimands. Three accuracies are reported, and they are three different correlations, computed within a replicate and then averaged over replicates. acc_all is the Pearson correlation between a hybrid’s BLUP and its true TPE value \(\mathrm{GCA}^f + \mathrm{GCA}^m + \mathrm{SCA}\), over all 400 hybrids of the factorial, planted or not. acc_cv1 is the same correlation over the hybrids with no plot. acc_cv2 is the correlation, over the missing cells of planted hybrids, between the location-specific prediction and the location-specific true value (which includes the interactions with location, among them \(\mathrm{SCA}\times\text{loc}\), which the analysis model cannot carry). None of the three is the acc_gca_all of Chapter 18, a correlation of GCA estimates with true GCA over lines. For the in-repo sweep these definitions are those of one_fit() in regenerate.R; for the cached REML study they are assumed to be the same, and the code of that study is not in this repository.
The planted share. In the in-repo sweep the 80 % of hybrids that are planted are drawn at random from the 20 x 20 factorial (the cached study is described as leaving 20 % untested, and its mechanism is assumed to be the same), so every line stays a parent of about 16 planted crosses. That makes the “CV1 is T2” correspondence of the callout in Section 19.3 true here, and it makes shared parents abundant. Both are properties of this configuration (see Scope).
The calibration is sparse_vc():

\(\sigma^2_f = \sigma^2_m = 1\) and \(\sigma^2_s = \sigma^2_{SCA} = 0.25\), so that \(\sigma^2_G = 2.25\) and \(\sigma^2_s/\sigma^2_g = 0.25\);
every interaction with location is half its main effect, so that \(\sigma^2_{GE} = 1.125\);
plot \(h^2 = \sigma^2_G/(\sigma^2_G + \sigma^2_{GE} + \sigma^2_e)\) of 0.20 or 0.40, which fixes \(\sigma^2_e\).

In sparse_vc() the components are s2f, s2m, s2s (\(\sigma^2_{SCA}\)), s2fl, s2ml (the two GCA x location variances), s2sl (\(\sigma^2_{SCA\times L}\), written \(\sigma^2_{s\ell}\) in Section 20.2) and s2e; s2res is the residual of the analysis model, \(\sigma^2_{res} = \sigma^2_{SCA\times L} + \sigma^2_e\).
These choices imply a genetic correlation between locations of \(\sigma^2_G/(\sigma^2_G+\sigma^2_{GE}) = 0.667\). That sits inside the 0.36 to 0.67 measured for plant height in maize (Li et al. 2026) and close to the 0.60 of Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025). The ratio \(\sigma^2_s/\sigma^2_g\) of 0.25 lies among the values reported by González-Diéguez et al. (2026) for their own ratio. The plot heritabilities 0.2 and 0.4 lie above the 0.10 of Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025)’s founder population. The 0.30 of González-Diéguez et al. (2026) is a broad-sense \(H^2\) over all hybrids, a different quantity from the plot-level \(h^2\) of Box 2, so it does not bracket the values here. Plot heritability is also defined differently in the other chapters: in Chapter 18 the interaction with location is folded into the plot error, and in Chapter 14 it is the heritability in a single environment. The three values are not on one scale.
The four strategies, all at the same cost of \(k\) locations per hybrid out of \(L\) in the trial (\(k\) is not the testers per pool of Chapter 18):

complete;
random: each hybrid goes to \(k\) locations drawn at random;
optimised blocks: an exchange algorithm on the mixed-model coefficient matrix, with replicated checks;
parentage: the factorial is cut into cyclic groups, each holding every female and every male, and groups are dealt to locations so that every location receives both whole pools (Chapter 20’s coverage is the closest analogue, not the same allocation: it has no term for the hybrids two locations share).

The last is sparse_alloc(strategy = "parentage").
Validation of the estimator. Before any comparison, the estimator was checked on the complete design, where REML must recover the true components (Table 19.9).

For every component except SCA, \(|t| \le\) 1.3. For \(\sigma^2_{SCA}\) the relative bias is +39.9 % (\(t\) = 2.16, two-sided \(p\) = 0.039 on 29 degrees of freedom, taking the 30 replicates of the caption) at \(h^2 = 0.2\) and +21.3 % (\(t\) = 1.02, \(p\) = 0.32) at \(h^2 = 0.4\). The table therefore does not establish an upward bias of the SCA variance in the complete design: the sign agrees in the two cells, and the size is unresolved (30 replicates per cell; the s.e. of the relative bias is 18.5 % and 20.9 %). Right: accuracy at a FIXED cost of two plots per hybrid, spread over 2 to 10 locations, random allocation, both heritabilities. Points are cell means; no error bars are drawn. Cached study, REML components, 15 replicates.





Take 400 hybrids at \(h^2 = 0.4\). The complete design over ten locations (3,200 plots) reaches an accuracy of 0.941. The cheapest allocation within 5 % of that is the parentage design with 2 locations per hybrid. It uses 640 plots, 20 % of the budget, and reaches 0.897, which is 95.3 % of the reference. Coincidence with the true top 5 % falls from 70.0 % to 65.7 %. At \(h^2 = 0.2\) the cheapest cell within 5 % is the random design with 5 locations per hybrid, 1600 plots, 50 % of the budget. Table 19.10 lists every scenario.
How thin this is. The margin of the 400-hybrid cell over the 95 % line is 0.0033 accuracy units, against a standard error of 0.0060 for that difference, so it passes by 0.5 standard errors (the cell at \(h^2 = 0.2\) passes by 1.1). Each is the cheapest passing cell among 12 candidates at ten locations, selected on the same cached means that are then reported, so the relative accuracy of the selected cell is optimistic by a winner’s-curse amount that is not estimated here. The fall in coincidence with the true top 5 % (20 of the 400 hybrids) is -4.3 \(\pm\) 2.7 percentage points over 15 replicates. No interval is attached to the relative accuracy or the relative cost of the table. The statement “wider at higher heritability” compares one selected cell per heritability, at one number of locations, without replicate-level dispersion for the comparison. The qualitative reading, that a layout using about a fifth to a half of the plots comes close to the complete design, rests on those two cells and is not a general margin.

19.11.3.2 2. At fixed cost, spreading plots over locations beats concentrating them
This is the most actionable result (Figure 19.8, right). Each planted hybrid keeps two plots (the 80 % of the factorial that is planted, so 640 plots in every design of the panel), the cost of a two-location trial of those hybrids. At \(h^2 = 0.4\), accuracy rises from 0.831 with both plots in the same two locations to 0.860, 0.883 and 0.892 as those plots are spread across 4, 6 and 10 locations. At \(h^2 = 0.2\) it rises from 0.733 to 0.819. The standard errors of the unpaired differences from the two-location trial are, at \(h^2 = 0.4\), 0.0127, 0.0111 and 0.0094 for 4, 6 and 10 locations (\(z\) = 2.3, 4.7 and 6.4), and at \(h^2 = 0.2\) 0.0236, 0.0235 and 0.0256 (\(z\) = 1.2, 3.5 and 3.3). The step from six to ten locations is +0.008 (s.e. 0.010, \(z\) = 0.82) at \(h^2 = 0.4\) and +0.003 (s.e. 0.021, \(z\) = 0.15) at \(h^2 = 0.2\). Not one extra plot is spent, and no planted hybrid gains a location: each is still in two. What grows is the number of environments the trial samples, and with it the number of locations over which each parent’s crosses, and so its GCA, are spread. The gain from two locations to six or ten is beyond two standard errors at both heritabilities (with no correction for the several steps shown). The gain from six to ten is not, so these data show no further gain beyond six; they do not show that it is absent, since a difference of a few hundredths is within the standard errors printed above. The figure’s right panel carries no error bars; the standard errors are those of the cached acc_all_se (15 replicates per cell), and the difference is treated as unpaired, because the file does not record pairing. This slice never varied the locations per hybrid and never traded a location against a replicate, so it measures only the value of sampling more trial sites at a fixed number of plots – the “broader sampling of trial sites” of Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025) – not a trade against replication.


19.11.3.3 3. Parentage minus random allocation is small, and not resolved after correction
The cached study provides 22 contrasts against random allocation, and Table 19.11 lists all of them: that is the family. The multiplicity rule is Bonferroni over the family, a threshold of 0.0023 on \(p\) (the column \(p_{Bonf}\) is \(p\) times 22, capped at 1). The contrasts are not independent (the metrics are correlated, and the same replicates enter every row), so the rule is conservative. The rows for \(k \le 2\) exist for acc_cv1 only; they are exploratory: the file does not record whether that subset was specified before the data were seen, and it was not computed for the other metrics.


Show code

In the fast layer, parentage minus random is +0.0051 \(\pm\) 0.0029 on acc_all (\(p\) = 0.077), +0.0086 \(\pm\) 0.0039 on acc_cv1 (\(p\) = 0.026), +0.0077 \(\pm\) 0.0026 on acc_cv2 (\(p\) = 0.0031), and +0.0046 \(\pm\) 0.0069 on coinc_t5_truth (\(p\) = 0.50). The coincidence is the operational metric of the validation section, the rate at which the true top 5 % is not wrongly discarded; it shows nothing, for parentage or for the optimised blocks (+0.0094 \(\pm\) 0.0064, \(p\) = 0.14). The smallest \(p\) of the family is 0.0031, above the Bonferroni threshold, so no contrast is resolved after correction. In the exploratory subset \(k \le 2\), parentage minus random on acc_cv1 is +0.0187 \(\pm\) 0.0069 (\(p\) = 0.007) and the optimised blocks give -0.0012 \(\pm\) 0.0079. In the genomic layer (Figure 19.9; marker relationships, real dominance, 32 pairs) the parentage difference on acc_all is +0.023 \(\pm\) 0.009 (\(p\) = 0.014, \(p_{Bonf}\) = 0.30).
Interpretation, with its limits. Parentage minus random is positive on all four fast-layer metrics, by 0.005 to 0.009 in correlation units, and is resolved at the uncorrected 5 % level on acc_cv1 and acc_cv2 only. Because acc_cv2 (missing cells of planted hybrids) shows a difference as resolved as acc_cv1 (never-planted hybrids), the advantage is not limited to hybrids the field never saw. The effect, if real, is small, and the metric on which a breeder’s decision rests does not show it. Three limits apply to all of this. (i) The cached parentage arm comes from the search whose criterion returned \(-\infty\) for a disconnected start (1), so these contrasts concern that allocation and not sparse_alloc("parentage") of this repository. (ii) The replicate-level file is not in the repository: the pairing, the unit of replication and the standard errors cannot be rechecked, and the 791 pairs pool heterogeneous cells. (iii) At \(k = 1\) the in-repo sweep does not resolve the difference either (1).
Li et al. (2026) compared random sampling of cells (their CV2) with genotype-balanced (CV3), environment-balanced (CV4) and partially overlapping (CV5) allocations and found no consistently superior scheme among them. Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025) used restricted randomisation without a random control. In my reading of the six texts for this specific contrast, none compares an allocation built to put every parent in every location with a random allocation of the same size; that is a statement about those six papers, not a search of the literature. The comparison was made here for the hybrid case, with the result above: a small advantage, not resolved after multiplicity correction, in the one dense configuration simulated.

Result. At ten locations with two per hybrid and \(h^2 = 0.4\), the accuracies are 0.897 for parentage (s.e. 0.005), 0.892 for random allocation (0.006) and 0.887 for the optimised blocks (0.009). The parentage design shares no hybrid between 61.8 % of the location pairs, against a structural minimum of 55.6 % (twenty groups at two locations each touch at most 20 of the 45 pairs); its female coverage is 0.999, against 0.965 for random allocation. The optimised blocks have the highest concurrence (26.7 hybrids per pair of locations, against 5.5 for random) and female coverage 0.992, and are not more accurate than random allocation (-0.0044, \(z\) = -0.42). The pooled paired contrast of result 3 for parentage on acc_all is +0.0051 \(\pm\) 0.0029 (\(p\) = 0.077).
Interpretation, with its limits. The account that fits parentage alone is that a layout keeping both pools in every location connects the trial through shared parents, and does not need shared hybrids. The optimised blocks, which have nearly the same coverage and the most shared hybrids, gain nothing over random allocation, so high coverage together with high overlap did not help in this cell. Across the three arms coverage and concurrence are not varied independently: no arm varies one with the other fixed, so these data cannot separate “parent coverage, not shared hybrids” from the opposite reading, and the effect that parentage shows is itself not resolved. The cached parentage arm is the one from the search with the defective criterion (1), so the fraction of disconnected pairs above is for that layout and sits above the structural minimum. The in-repo overlap sweep (Section 19.6) has no coverage arm either. Finally, in this 80 % planted 20 x 20 factorial every line is a parent of about 16 planted crosses, so parents are shared by construction; in the sparse factorials of Chapter 18 (two to ten crosses per line out of 200 candidates per pool) they are not, and a coverage rule does not come for free there. Whether coverage accounts for the Atanda et al. (2022) versus Lubanga et al. (2025) disagreement remains a hypothesis (Section 19.6).

NoteBox – REML at one location per hybrid: a hypothesis, not a measurement



With \(k = 1\) each hybrid contributes a single plot in a single location, and REML converged in 42.6 % of the cached fits, against 88.5 % at \(k = 2\). A candidate explanation, which nothing in this chapter or in the cached files tests, is that the data then carry no within-hybrid information to separate a hybrid’s GCA from its GCA x location deviation, so that the likelihood is flat along that direction and the optimiser stops at the boundary of the parameter space or short of its criterion. It would be tested by examining the likelihood surface, or by summarising the converged and non-converged fits separately; the cached file holds scenario means over both and does not allow the second.
What the cached file does show is limited. The median dispersion slope at \(k = 1\) is 0.968 with outliers (Figure 19.10, right), so that the BLUPs of non-converged fits are usable is not established by it either. The median bias of the female GCA variance at \(k = 1\) is -2.0 % (interquartile range -10 to +7 %), pooled over converged and non-converged fits, which is not what an unusable estimate looks like in a median, while that of the SCA variance is +220 %. A report of components from a one-location-per-hybrid trial should state the convergence status of the fit, because the pooled summaries here cannot say which estimates to trust.




19.11.3.6 6. Two stages: covering more candidates sparsely gave more gain at the same budget (four replicates)
The two-stage scenario works as follows:

A pool of 400 candidate hybrids is available.
Stage 1 tests \(N_1\) of them sparsely and keeps the top \(q\) by BLUP.
Stage 2 tests the survivors densely in new locations.
The final analysis is joint.

The metric is the realised gain: the mean true value of the ten hybrids finally chosen, in genetic standard deviations. The cached file has four replicates at every setting. The three values of \(N_1\) span different budgets (130 to 560, 260 to 1,120, 520 to 2,240 total plots for \(N_1\) = 100, 200 and 400), so a mean over all the cells of each \(N_1\) compares different budgets and is not reported. Result and reading. At the same total plots, a larger \(N_1\) gave a larger realised gain in every one of the eight comparisons, resolved at the uncorrected level from 100 to 200 candidates and not from 200 to 400 (the latter is the step to covering every candidate of the pool). A reading is that stage 1 should cover more candidates with fewer plots each rather than a subset with many; at four replicates, with an uncontrolled mixture of strategies, this is a direction and not an established margin. The cached grid also varies the stage-1 locations, the sparsity, the stage-2 locations and the fraction kept. Picking its best cell is a post-hoc search over many cells at four replicates, and no such cell is reported as a result.


19.11.3.7 Limitations of the simulation
The simulation has eight limitations.

One plot per cell. SCA x location then has the same incidence as plot error, and the analysis model absorbs it into an i.i.d. residual that estimates \(\sigma^2_{SCA\times L} + \sigma^2_e\). Equal incidence alone does not make the two inseparable: drawn with the kernel \(\mathbf A_f \otimes \mathbf A_m\), as sparse_simulate() draws it, SCA x location is correlated between related crosses in one location and could be carried as a structured term; Section 20.2 measures what that buys in one configuration. Within-location replication was not simulated.
G x E is full-rank and symmetric in the fast layer, and rank one in the genomic layer. Neither layer has the factor-analytic structure of real trials or a crossover/non-crossover split (Burgueño et al. 2012; Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. 2025).
The pools are symmetric and unselected. There are no cycles of reciprocal recurrent selection, so the simulation says nothing about long-run pool trajectories (Chapter 23) or about unbalanced pools.
Cost is counted in plots, not money. Opening a location costs more than adding plots to an existing one. The advice to spread plots assumes the marginal location is moderately priced (Section 18.7 has the cost structure).
The grid is reduced. It has at most 15 replicates per cell, no 200-hybrid level, and the high-SCA block run separately. The two-stage layer has 4 replicates and the genomic layer 8.
Components are checked by mean bias only. No per-replicate confidence intervals were computed for them, and none for the contrasts of result 3, the two-stage comparison of result 6 or the minimal allocation of result 1 beyond the standard errors printed with each.
A dense factorial, planted at random. The 20 x 20 factorial has 80 % of its hybrids planted, so every line is a parent of about 16 planted crosses. Parents are shared by construction. The sparse factorials of Chapter 18 (a few crosses per line out of 200 candidates per pool, where connectivity binds) and the 2,000-lines-per-pool pipeline of Figure 19.1 are different regimes. Results 2 to 4, and the “CV1 is T2” correspondence of the callout in Section 19.3, depend on this density and were not measured at another.
The cached parentage arm comes from a defective search. Its criterion returned \(-\infty\) for any disconnected start (1), so results 3 and 4 concern that layout, not sparse_alloc("parentage") of this repository.
