title: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations
text:
19.12 Practical recommendations by stage
Stage 1 (first agronomic testcross trial).
Each item below carries its basis: a result of this chapter, a cited study, or neither (“not tested here”, design reasoning only).

Give priority to the number of candidates and the number of locations in the trial. At fixed plots per hybrid, spread them over more locations: in result 2 accuracy rose from two to six locations and showed no resolved further gain from six to ten (one configuration; 0.8 and 0.1 standard errors).
Use 3 to 5 testers in sparse testcrossing, with full-sibs spread across testers (basis: González-Diéguez et al. (2026), a simulation of reciprocal recurrent selection; not tested here).
Use low partial replication with checks replicated in every block (basis: a p-rep of 0.1 in Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025); no p-rep value, 0.1 or 0.2, is compared in this chapter, so the level is not tested here).
When plots per hybrid fall to one or two, a layout that puts both pools in every location is cheap to adopt and was not worse than random allocation in the cached grid; its advantage there was small and not resolved after multiplicity correction (results 3 and 4).
The estimation target is GCA. In the cached grid the SCA variance had an upward median bias at small \(k\) whose cause these data do not separate, so treat an SCA estimate from a stage-1 trial as unverified (result 5).

Stage 2 (pre-commercial hybrids).

Test fewer candidates, and raise replication and environmental coverage (not tested here: the simulation covers stage 1 and one stage-2 step in result 6).
Keep a common core large enough to estimate the between-environment genetic correlations (not tested here, and set against the overlap sweep of Section 19.6, where at a fixed training size a larger common core lowered accuracy over all hybrids; the item concerns estimating the correlations, which that sweep did not examine).
The estimation target is now specific performance and stability, so SCA and G x E matter (design reasoning; see 2).

Decisions that span both stages.

Genotype the parents, not the hybrids.
Check connectivity before planting (Box 4).
Match the between-environment covariance to the amount of data. Do not force an unstructured matrix on a very sparse design.
Advance on GBLUP rather than best linear unbiased estimation (BLUE) when heritability is low to moderate and locations are few (Atanda et al. 2022; Endelman et al. 2014).

What not to do.

Put everything in one location, however many candidates that allows. It gave the most variable gain in Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025), with replicates of negative gain.
Use one tester at stage 1 when there is infrastructure for three.
Transfer a sparsity percentage from another crop or programme without your own simulation.
Assume that a G x E term helps under extreme sparsity: Hild Aono and Chawade (2026) found that it degraded prediction when less than 66 % of the data per environment were available, whereas Lubanga et al. (2025) found that it raised predictive ability at 20 % of records per environment. The two used different data and models, and this chapter has not compared them.

The right sparse design changes from stage to stage because the parameter of interest changes: GCA in stage 1, specific performance and stability in stage 2.






TipBox 6 – A checklist for designing a sparse trial




Define the TPE and the market segment.
Estimate the genetic correlations between candidate locations from historical data.
Fix the budget in plots.
Choose the axis of sparsity: environments, testers, or both.
Fix the number of testers.
Fix the partial-replication rate.
Choose the checks and how often they appear.
Generate the allocation by restricted randomisation or a formal criterion. Where plots per hybrid are fewest, consider keeping both pools in every location (results 3 and 4: a small advantage, not resolved after correction).
Compute connectivity and the expected PEV before planting (Box 4).
Simulate the design with the programme’s own parameters (sparse_vc(), sparse_simulate(), sparse_blup()).
Fix the analysis model and the covariance structure a priori.
Fix the decision metric and the cut-off a priori.

section: 19.13 Limitations of the evidence, and perspectives
text:
19.13 Limitations of the evidence, and perspectives
The authors of the primary studies declare their own limitations:

Li et al. (2026): a narrow genetic base and a single year.
Atanda et al. (2022): no way to identify the optimal overlap, and families of 1 to 9.
Werner, Covarrubias-Pazaran, et al. (2025): no cost model, and no hybrid structure.
Lubanga et al. (2025): a training set that was not optimised.
González-Diéguez et al. (2026): no G x E, no epistasis, no diversity management, and the logistic cost ignored.
Hild Aono and Chawade (2026): possible information leakage, and very similar environments.

As a research agenda, the open gaps are these.

SCA estimation, and prediction of specific hybrids, under sparsity. In the cached grid the SCA variance had an upward median bias of +12 %, +24 % and +30 % at \(k = 4\), 3 and 2 and +220 % at \(k = 1\) (with 42.6 % convergence). Its coverage and precision, and a comparison with product-development designs, were not measured, so whether it is recoverable at stage 1 is open. The accuracy of specific unseen crosses is also unmeasured.
A three-dimensional connectivity metric, female x male x location. It would join Section 18.2.3 to Box 4. Section 20.4 defines a pair of counts for it.
The long-run effect on pool divergence and within-pool variance, in interaction with optimum contribution selection (Chapter 23; Chapter 15; Santantonio and Robbins (2020)).
Phenomics-assisted sparse testing in maize hybrids.
Pools unequal in size and breeding level, which is the usual commercial case.
Cost-accuracy frontiers in money, including isolation blocks and hand pollination.
The rate of wrongly discarded candidates as the evaluation metric, in place of the correlation.
Prospective empirical validation. Almost all the evidence for sparse testing comes from resampling complete data or from simulation, not from trials designed sparse from the start (Alemu et al. 2024; Crossa et al. 2017).

Sparse testing changes the stage-1 question. It is no longer “which genotypes can I evaluate well?”. It becomes “which haplotypes can I evaluate well, and against what sample of the opposite pool?”. The evidence reviewed supports considering sparse designs at stage 1; it does not support adopting them with confidence. Almost all of it comes from resampling or simulation (above). In this chapter’s own simulation a sparse allocation came within 5 % of the complete design in one cell by a margin of 0.5 standard errors (result 1), the structured allocation was not resolved against random after correction (result 3), the two-stage comparison has four replicates (result 6), and every simulated result comes from one dense factorial (limitation 7). The result least in doubt is that, at a fixed number of plots, more locations raised accuracy up to about six (result 2): the differences of the six- and ten-location trials from the two-location trial are beyond two standard errors at both heritabilities, and the four-location step has \(z\) = 2.3 at \(h^2 = 0.4\) and 1.2 at \(h^2 = 0.2\). It is not sufficient to prescribe a universal sparsity level. That decision remains specific to each programme, and should be sized by the programme’s own simulation.

19.14 Reproducibility and assumptions
regenerate.R sparse reruns the phenotypic core of the cached study with R/17_sparse_testing.R. The scale and calibration are the same: 20 x 20 hybrids, half-sib families of four, and 20 % of hybrids untested. There are two differences:

the variance components are known, not estimated by REML;
the parentage allocation’s exchange search minimises the number of disconnected location pairs before the harmonic concurrence. The cached study’s criterion returned \(-\infty\) for any disconnected start, which left its search no gradient.

Table 19.16 compares the two sweeps cell by cell.


Show code
cr <- subset(core, part %in% c("spread", "k1"))
cr$cached <- mapply(function(L, k, s, h) {
  x <- s4$acc_all_mean[s4$nLoc == L & s4$k == k & s4$strategy == s & s4$h2_plot == h]
  if (length(x)) x[1] else NA
}, cr$nLoc, cr$k, cr$strategy, cr$h2_plot)
cr$cached_se <- mapply(function(L, k, s, h) {
  x <- s4$acc_all_se[s4$nLoc == L & s4$k == k & s4$strategy == s & s4$h2_plot == h]
  if (length(x)) x[1] else NA
}, cr$nLoc, cr$k, cr$strategy, cr$h2_plot)
cr$z <- (cr$acc_all - cr$cached) / sqrt(cr$acc_all_se^2 + cr$cached_se^2)
cr <- cr[order(cr$h2_plot, cr$k, cr$nLoc, cr$strategy), ]
knitr::kable(fmt(cr[, c("h2_plot", "nLoc", "k", "strategy", "acc_all", "cached", "z", "b1")], 3),
             row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Plot h2", "Locations", "k", "Strategy", "In-repo acc.", "Cached acc.",

dk <- tapply(cr$acc_all - cr$cached, cr$k, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

At \(k = 2\) the mean difference is +0.006, and 1 of the 14 cells differs by more than two standard errors (the largest, 4.1); the gain from spreading the same plots over more locations reproduces. At \(k = 1\) the known-component values are higher by +0.017 on average over the 8 comparable cells, with \(z\) (in-repo minus cached) of 0.7, 1.1, 1.9, 0.0, 2.2, 0.6, -0.3, 0.6: 7 positive and 1 beyond two standard errors. The mean difference was not tested. The cost of estimating the components, where REML mostly fails to converge (result 5), is one possible reason; the two arms also differ in the parentage search and in the number of replicates, so the difference is not attributed here. The in-repo dispersion slopes all sit near 1. The in-repo sweep does not resolve the parentage-versus-random difference at \(k = 1\): its 30 unpaired replicates per cell have standard errors near 0.01, the same size as the effect. The cached paired contrasts of Table 19.11, which pool 791 pairs (385 for the exploratory \(k \le 2\) subset), are the evidence for result 3.


Show code
set.seed(3)
nF2 <- 4; nM2 <- 3; L2 <- 3
Af2 <- relmat_halfsib(nF2, 2); Am2 <- diag(nM2) * 0.8 + 0.2
vc2 <- sparse_vc(0.4)
M2 <- sparse_alloc(nF2, nM2, L2, 2, "random"); M2[c(2, 7), ] <- 0L   # two hybrids never planted
sim2  <- sparse_simulate(M2, nF2, nM2, vc2, Af2, Am2)
fast2 <- sparse_blup(sim2$pheno, nF2, nM2, L2, vc2, Af2, Am2)
ref2  <- ref_sparse_blup(sim2$pheno, nF2, nM2, L2, vc2, Af2, Am2)
dev_blup <- max(abs(fast2$blup - ref2$blup)); dev_pev <- max(abs(fast2$pev - ref2$pev))
stopifnot(dev_blup < 1e-8, dev_pev < 1e-8)


One draw is checked in this chapter (a 4 x 3 factorial, three locations, two hybrids never planted): the largest deviation of sparse_blup() from the literal GLS form of ref_sparse_blup() is \(1.5 \times 10^{-13}\) for the BLUP and \(1.8 \times 10^{-15}\) for the PEV. The other live functions are verified in tests/testthat/test-sparse.R (the list of tests is in Appendix C):

sparse_blup() equals the literal GLS form of ref_sparse_blup() to \(10^{-8}\), including untested hybrids, and so do its PEVs.
Every allocation puts each hybrid in exactly \(k\) locations.
The parentage design covers both pools in every location.
The dispersion slope of the known-component BLUP averages 1.

The cached numbers carry the assumptions listed in the limitations of the simulation (Section 19.11.3). Treat them as findings of that configuration, not as constants; the cached ones cannot be reproduced from this repository.

title: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations
text:
19.15 Where this connects

Chapter 18 compared designs of which crosses to make. This chapter asked where to plant them, mostly with the factorial taken as given (80 % of it planted at random). Result 6 traded locations per candidate against a smaller stage-1 factorial at equal plots; what it leaves is the version in which every line stays in the data and the unmade crosses are predicted, so that an extra location per hybrid costs a cross rather than a parent. Result 2 never varied the locations per hybrid; it held two plots per hybrid and widened the trial. The joint problem, Section 18.9’s second gap, is Chapter 20.
The GCA/SCA decomposition and the tester-frequency argument behind Box 5 are derived in Section 5.11.
The relationship matrices that make sparse designs analysable are the pedigree matrices of relmat_halfsib() here, and marker matrices in the cached genomic layer. Chapter 14 fits one additive GBLUP and does not fit the pool-specific or SCA kernels of this chapter.
The staged-trial trade-off of Chapter 22 (a later chapter, in the Evidence and practice part) is an analogy to result 6, not a replication of it: in that chapter a replicate is an independent draw of plot error only, and the genotype-by-environment deviate is one draw per phenotyping call shared by all entries, so its replicates are not locations, whereas result 6 uses a genetic correlation between locations of 0.667.
Spreading testers and parents to slow within-pool erosion is the same concern as Chapter 15 and Chapter 23. Sparse testcrossing does by design what a diversity constraint does by optimisation.

crumbs: 19  Sparse testing: which hybrids go to which locations

title: 20  Which crosses, at which locations? Joint sparse allocation
text:
20.1 Why the two decisions are one
Chapter 18 chose which crosses to make from two pools, with the field design held fixed. Chapter 19 chose which locations each hybrid goes to, with the crossing plan taken as given (a 20 x 20 factorial of which 80 % of the hybrids were planted). A programme makes both decisions out of one budget, in the same season, and each changes what the other can do: a cross that is not made cannot be planted anywhere, and a cross planted in one location says nothing about the others except through its parents. This chapter treats the two as one decision.
The search reported in Section 20.3 found strong methods for each half but none that chooses the crosses and their locations together for a two-pool hybrid programme – an absence of evidence from one search, not a proof of absence. The nearest treatments optimise the crosses and leave the environments to the trial manager (Heslot and Feoktistov 2020; Kadam et al. 2021), or optimise the environments for a fixed entry list (Cullis et al. 2020; Montesinos-López et al. 2022). This is the second gap of Section 18.9, and it needs the female x male x location connectivity metric Section 19.13 asked for.
The results this chapter defends:
Write \(n_F\) and \(n_M\) for the female and male lines – the pool-A and pool-B candidates, \(n_A\) and \(n_B\), of Chapter 18 – \(n_c\) for the number of distinct crosses made, \(L\) for the locations, \(k\) for the number of locations each cross is planted in (as in Chapter 19; not the testers per pool of Chapter 18, which appear in this chapter only in the label tester k=2 of Figure 20.1), and \(r\) for plots per cross per location (not the plots a cross received in total, as in Chapter 18, which differs by the factor \(k\)). Two letters are reused from other parts of the book: \(n_c\) is the DH lines per cross in Chapter 13, and \(L\) the parent lines in Chapter 14; here \(n_c\) counts crosses and \(L\) counts locations (Appendix A). The field budget is
\[
B = n_c \, k \, r .
\tag{20.1}\]
Chapter 18 varied \(n_c\) (through the crosses per line \(c\), \(n_c = c\,n_F\) for a circulant plan) at fixed \(k\); Chapter 19 varied \(k\) and the layout at fixed \(n_c\) (80 % of \(n_F n_M\), that is 320 of 400 hybrids planted). At \(r = 1\) – the value used throughout the sweep below; unreplicated stage-1 trials exist, for instance the alpha-lattice design without replications of Thomsen et al. (2026), but this chapter does not claim it is the norm – fixing \(B\) ties the two together: halving the crosses doubles the locations each one can see. The nearest earlier look at this trade is result 6 of Section 19.11.3, which at equal plots compared testing every candidate at few locations against a smaller factorial at more, and found the first better in the point estimates, with four replicates and no step resolved after multiplicity correction. There the excluded candidates are a smaller factorial, so their parents leave the data, and a second stage with selection follows. Here every line stays in the data, the unmade crosses are predicted from it, and the comparison is of stage-1 accuracy alone. Result 1 (Section 20.5.1) points the same way as result 6.
The two terms buy different things. More crosses sample more of the factorial (in the circulant plans every line is in the data at every split; in the random sparse plans of Section 20.5 it is not, Section 20.4), which is what predicts the crosses never made (Section 18.6; Melchinger et al. (2023)). More locations per cross average that cross’s genotype x location deviations, \((g^f\ell)\), \((g^m\ell)\) and \((s\ell)\) in Equation 20.2, over more environments, which is what sharpens the estimate of a cross that was made. That is the expectation under the model of Section 20.2, not a result of Chapter 19: its result 2 held the locations per hybrid fixed while widening the trial (the difference from raising \(k\) is drawn in Section 20.5), and its result 6 measured selection after two stages, not the estimate of each made cross. A parent’s GCA is averaged over the locations of all its crosses, which an allocation can widen without adding locations per cross. Which term matters more depends on the SCA:GCA variance ratio, the genotype x location share of the genetic variance and how well the relationship matrix links lines across families – the quantities a programme knows least about at stage 1.

title: 20  Which crosses, at which locations? Joint sparse allocation
text:
20.2 The joint model
The model is Chapter 19’s, unchanged:
\[
y_{ijl} = \mu + \ell_l + g^f_i + g^m_j + s_{ij}
        + (g^f\ell)_{il} + (g^m\ell)_{jl} + (s\ell)_{ijl} + e_{ijl},
\tag{20.2}\]
where \(g^f_i\), \(g^m_j\) and \(s_{ij}\) are the \(\mathrm{GCA}^f_i\), \(\mathrm{GCA}^m_j\) and \(\mathrm{SCA}_{ij}\) of Section 19.2 (the \(g^A_i\), \(g^B_j\) and \(s_{ij}\) of Chapter 18, with the female pool as A; Appendix A), \(\ell_l\) is the fixed effect of location \(l\), \(g^f \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf A_f\sigma^2_f)\), \(g^m \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf A_m\sigma^2_m)\), \(s \sim N(\mathbf 0, (\mathbf A_f \otimes \mathbf A_m)\sigma^2_s)\), and the three interactions with location carry the same kernels crossed with the identity \(\mathbf I_L\) over locations: \((g^f\ell) \sim N(\mathbf 0, (\mathbf A_f \otimes \mathbf I_L)\sigma^2_{f\ell})\), \((g^m\ell) \sim N(\mathbf 0, (\mathbf A_m \otimes \mathbf I_L)\sigma^2_{m\ell})\), \((s\ell) \sim N(\mathbf 0, (\mathbf A_f \otimes \mathbf A_m \otimes \mathbf I_L)\sigma^2_{s\ell})\), and \(e_{ijl} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_e)\) i.i.d. In sparse_vc() these are s2f, s2m, s2s, s2fl, s2ml, s2sl and s2e. \(\sigma^2_f\) and \(\sigma^2_m\) are the \(\sigma^2_{gA}\) and \(\sigma^2_{gB}\) of Chapter 18 and \(\sigma^2_s\) its \(\sigma^2_s\) (the mapping is in Section 19.2 and in Appendix A). The target is the value in the target population of environments, \(g^f_i + g^m_j + s_{ij}\).
One simplification is inherited from Chapter 19. With one plot per cross per location, \((s\ell)_{ijl}\) and \(e_{ijl}\) have the same incidence, but the simulator draws \((s\ell)\) with the kernel of Equation 20.2, correlated between related crosses in one location, so a model could carry it as a structured term. The analysis model does not: it absorbs it into an i.i.d. residual of variance \(\sigma^2_{s\ell} + \sigma^2_e\) (vc$s2res). The best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) and every PEV below are therefore exact for the analysis model, not for the generating one. With known components the cost is measured directly, by a literal generalised least squares (GLS) solve that carries the structured kernel, in the configuration of Table 20.5 (Table 20.1).


Show code
# Literal GLS BLUP of the target g^f + g^m + s, with (s l) given the kernel
# Ksl over the hybrids within a location: A_f x A_m as simulated, or I as
# analysed. Circulant c = 4, 20 x 20 half-sib pools, 8 locations, k = 2,
# plot h2 = 0.4; 30 paired replicates per SCA level.
ms <- local({
  n <- 20; nLoc <- 8; A <- relmat_halfsib(n, 5); AA <- kronecker(A, A)
  pf <- rep(seq_len(n), each = n); pm <- rep(seq_len(n), n)    # male fastest
  set.seed(41)
  M <- joint_alloc(design_circulant(n, n, c = 4), n, n, nLoc, k = 2,
                   strategy = "coverage")
  gls <- function(ph, vc, Ksl) {
    f <- pf[ph$hyb]; m <- pm[ph$hyb]; h <- ph$hyb
    same <- outer(ph$loc, ph$loc, "==")
    V <- vc$s2f * A[f, f] + vc$s2m * A[m, m] + vc$s2s * AA[h, h] +
      same * (vc$s2fl * A[f, f] + vc$s2ml * A[m, m] + vc$s2sl * Ksl[h, h]) +
      diag(vc$s2e, nrow(ph))
    X <- model.matrix(~ factor(ph$loc)); Vi <- solve(V)
    b <- solve(crossprod(X, Vi %*% X), crossprod(X, Vi %*% ph$y))
    C <- vc$s2f * A[pf, f] + vc$s2m * A[pm, m] + vc$s2s * AA[, h]
    drop(C %*% Vi %*% (ph$y - X %*% b))
  }
  vapply(c(low = "low", high = "high"), function(sca) {
    vc <- sparse_vc(0.4, sca)
    set.seed(42)
    d <- vapply(seq_len(30), function(r) {
      s <- sparse_simulate(M, n, n, vc, A, A)
      mis <- gls(s$pheno, vc, diag(n * n))
      # The I-kernel GLS is the analysis model: it must equal sparse_blup().
      if (r == 1) stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(mis,
        sparse_blup(s$pheno, n, n, nLoc, vc, A, A)$blup, tolerance = 1e-8)))
      cor(gls(s$pheno, vc, AA), s$g_target) - cor(mis, s$g_target)
    }, 0)
    c(diff = mean(d), se = sd(d) / sqrt(length(d)))
  }, c(diff = 0, se = 0))
})
knitr::kable(data.frame(SCA = colnames(ms), fmt(t(ms), 6), row.names = NULL),
             col.names = c("SCA level", "Mean difference", "SE"))

Circulant plan, 4 crosses per line, 20 x 20 pools in half-sib families of four, 8 locations, 2 locations per cross, coverage allocation, plot \(h^2 = 0.4\), known components. Live.

Carrying the structured kernel changes accuracy over all hybrids by -0.00002 (SE 0.00002) at low SCA and -0.00006 (SE 0.00005) at high SCA: nothing detectable, because \(\sigma^2_{s\ell}\) is a small share of the residual (5 % and 14 %) and half-sib relationships of 0.25 give the kernel off-diagonals of at most 0.25. The check covers one plan at \(h^2 = 0.4\); stronger relationships or a larger \(\sigma^2_{s\ell}\) would need it repeated.
What is new is only the incidence. A crossing plan \(P \subset \{1..n_F\} \times
\{1..n_M\}\) and an allocation give a 0/1 matrix \(M\) of size \(n_F n_M \times L\) whose row is zero when \((i, j) \notin P\) and sums to \(k\) otherwise. The R/17 functions take such an \(M\) directly; unmade crosses are predicted through \(\mathbf A_f\), \(\mathbf A_m\) and the GCA they share with made crosses – the prediction of never-planted hybrids that Section 19.4 calls CV1 (T2 of Section 18.6 when both parents are in made crosses, T1 or T0 otherwise, as in the callout of Section 19.3; Chapter 14 calls the T2 case CV2), produced by the plan rather than by a mask. This chapter names the class by its T-level. In the circulant plans every line is crossed, so every unmade cross is T2 (the Not made column of Table 20.6); the random sparse plans can leave a line uncrossed, and their unmade crosses then include T1 and T0.


Show code
p <- design_circulant(6, 6, c = 2)            # 12 of 36 possible crosses
set.seed(21)
M <- joint_alloc(p, 6, 6, nLoc = 3, k = 1, strategy = "coverage")
stopifnot(sum(M) == nrow(p) * 1, all(rowSums(M) %in% c(0, 1)))  # N_P = n_c k
c(crosses_made = sum(rowSums(M) > 0), plots = sum(M), per_location = colSums(M))
#>  crosses_made         plots per_location1 per_location2 per_location3 
#>            12            12             4             4             4

20.3 What the literature offers
Two searches were run: in October 2026 the Consensus index (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, PubMed), Crossref and a general web search, reaching bioRxiv and the Crop Science / Plant Genome literature; on 20 October 2026, PubMed directly. Terms combined sparse testing, multi-environment trial, allocation of genotypes / hybrids to environments, incomplete factorial, mating design, training set optimisation, CDmean, A-optimality and genetic relatedness, with and without hybrid and maize, then genotype-based allocation (stratified or representative allocation, population structure in training-set and trial design, anticlustering). Nine families emerge (Table 20.2); none was built for the joint problem and each supplies a piece. The training-set optimisation tools of Akdemir et al. (2021) and Isidro y Sanchez and Akdemir (2021) could in principle select genotype-environment pairs, but none of the papers found does so for a crossing plan.

Optimising the field for a given entry list (rows 1, 2, 5, 6) supplies the criterion. Cullis et al. (2020) build model-based designs for multi-environment trials, with the genetic relationship between entries in the model and analysed on 34 trials; the A-optimality criterion that this chapter takes from Butler et al. (2014) is stated here from the general design literature, not from a reading of the full text, and neither the comparison with designs built for unrelated entries nor Butler’s pairwise-difference A-value (below) was verified for this book; Lisle et al. (2021) propose D-optimality as a diagnostic that better forecasts the precision of the variance-parameter estimates under restricted maximum likelihood (REML); Rio et al. (2022) extend CDmean, the mean coefficient of determination (Rincent et al. 2012), to genotype x environment (G x E) models, so reliability can be forecast before planting. The criterion of this chapter is that framework restricted to GCA. Incomplete-block allocation of lines to locations beat random allocation by 1.4 to 26.5 % in mean squared error (Montesinos-López et al. 2022) and was best with random close behind (Osval A. Montesinos-López et al. 2023); two of four allocation methods were slightly better, with accuracy barely lower at a 15:85 training-testing split (O. A. Montesinos-López et al. 2023); and at equal environments per line incomplete blocks performed better than random and were less variable (Montesinos-López et al. 2024) – the second a worst-case property a mean accuracy does not show. Lell et al. (2021) (1,604 wheat hybrids) found equal subgroups in overlapping subsets of environments one promising design, with high accuracy and low variability; Mothukuri et al. (2025) guided the split by relatedness to fully tested maize lines, with a weak correlation (0.20 to 0.31) between relatedness and accuracy. The overlap question is Section 19.6’s (Jarquin et al. 2020; Crespo-Herrera et al. 2021; Lubanga et al. 2025; Atanda et al. 2022). Which environments to sample is a further choice: sets chosen with a crop-growth-model criterion estimated wheat phenology parameters better than random sets twice as large (Rincent et al. 2017), a moderate mega-environmental allocation could potentially raise selection response by up to 43 % for the same resources (González-Barrios et al. 2019), and Hoefler and Gutierrez (2026) optimise its replication and sparsity by simulation. The locations here are exchangeable, which a real target population of environments is not.
Choosing entries and crosses for given environments (rows 3, 4, 7) supplies the search and the coverage logic. Kadam et al. (2021) report that optimising PEV or CDmean over all possible single crosses, not only those made, raised the expected prediction accuracy of the training set (a model forecast, not a realised accuracy) and conclude that it may be worthwhile; Heslot and Feoktistov (2020), the closest methodological precedent, choose which hybrid combinations to create and phenotype under a budget, and extend the choice to designing a population before crossing (their published abstract; the maize application and the differential-evolution optimiser are those of its preprint title and were not verified in the published version); Guo et al. (2019) chose hybrid training sets from the parents’ genotypes: the designs beat random sampling and PEV- or CD-based methods on 276 maize hybrids and were validated on wheat and rice, with training sets of 2 to 13 % of the hybrids (abstract; full text not read). Endelman et al. (2014) asked the budget question within fixed biparental barley and maize families, choosing no cross: an unbalanced design over several locations predicted better than every entry in one, and up to 250 yield-plot equivalents per family the optimum did not genotype more progeny than were phenotyped (its relation to result 1 is in Section 20.5.1). Sparse factorials trained hybrid prediction as well as tester designs, and for some traits better (Seye et al. 2020; Lorenzi et al. 2022). How many crosses per line to allow depends on what is predicted: Lorenzi et al. (2022) reduce the hybrids per line, Seye et al. (2020) report a small effect of the contribution number, and Melchinger et al. (2023) find that one cross per line gives the highest accuracy for hybrids with neither parent yet crossed (their H0) and for the GCA of lines never crossed, and the lowest for hybrids with one or both parents already crossed (H1 and H2) and for the GCA of lines already crossed, with an optimum that depends on the size and resources of the programme (abstracts; the same trade-off that result 1 turns on). González-Diéguez et al. (2026) instead spread three to five testers sparsely among full-sibs (sparse testcrossing), which beat a single tester at an equal number of testcrosses and was matched, not beaten, by an approximate incomplete factorial (Section 19.8). Thomsen et al. (2026) is observational: sparse, unreplicated multi-environment data from a commercial winter oilseed rape hybrid programme, covering 1.67 % of mother x father combinations, which a GCA + SCA model still predicted (Section 18.4). Schoemaker et al. (2024), trading testers against environments in maize, found three to five well-chosen environments match ten random ones – the closest empirical look at one corner of the joint budget.
Representing genetic structure (rows 8, 9) supplies the balancing objective. For training sets, stratified sampling suited strong structure (rice) and CDmean, or CDmean within subpopulations, mild structure [wheat, all traits but test weight and heading date; Isidro et al. (2015)]; uniform sampling of the genetic space beat stratified and random sampling and matched maximising CD in maize and wheat, with all methods alike in strongly structured rice (Bustos-Korts et al. 2016); and stratified sampling with a marker-effect-weighted relationship matrix was best for forward prediction (Berro et al. 2019). Ou and Liao (2019) derived a new optimality criterion from Pearson’s correlation between the genomic estimated breeding values and the phenotypic values of a test set, under a ridge-regression whole-genome model, applicable to data with varying degrees of population structure; they illustrate it on rice (strong structure) and wheat (mild structure), implement it in the R package TSDFGS, and report it advantageous over existing methods. Akdemir and Isidro-Sánchez (2019) compared targeted training sets, optimised using the genotypes of the test set, with untargeted ones, and found the targeted sets gave the highest accuracies. Core Hunter (De Beukelaer et al. 2018) selects subsets on allele-frequency and distance criteria. All of these choose which candidates to phenotype.
Representation per environment has one precedent. Atanda et al. (2021) chose by CDmean which members of each full-sib family go to each environment, so that every biparental population is represented everywhere (their CV2), against predicting new populations tested in some environments only (CV1). Accuracy was similar. Their case for CV2 is about the data (every family phenotyped everywhere, a complete historical record), and their gain from grouping environments by growing and management conditions is a finding about the environments. Nor is CV1 against CV2 a controlled test of representation: the two differ in what is predicted (new populations against the unphenotyped half of phenotyped families) as well as in how families are spread. The formal object behind balancing is k-means anticlustering (Papenberg and Klau 2021), partitioning a set into groups of prescribed size that are as alike as possible.
Why balance at all is therefore this chapter’s own inference, with no direct empirical test in either direction. Genomic prediction across a maize hybrid diversity panel came mostly from differences in mean between breeding populations [predicting each from the others gave 0.12 for grain yield; Windhausen et al. (2012)], so subgroup means are much of what is predicted. Under the model of Section 20.2, with fixed location effects and a connected design, concentrating one subgroup’s crosses in a few locations does not bias the BLUP of its mean; it inflates the PEV of contrasts between subgroups, which pass through the effects of locations they do not share. Bias needs a systematic subgroup x location interaction the analysis model does not carry: the GCA x location terms, correlated within a family through \(A_f\), carry a random family x location interaction with mean zero, not a systematic one. Against the presumption, Fernandez-Gonzalez et al. (2023) found in a benchmark of training-set optimisers that a diverse training set made prediction robust to structure and clustering information was less effective. None of these papers allocates a crossing plan.
The gap is therefore precise. The criteria (PEV and CD with relatedness) and the search methods (exchange algorithms, differential evolution) exist, and each half has been optimised separately. Missing is the object that holds the crossing plan and the allocation under one budget, and evidence on how to split it.

title: 20  Which crosses, at which locations? Joint sparse allocation
text:
20.4 Design criteria computable before planting
Two quantities can be read off \(M\) before a seed is sown.
The mean PEV of GCA. The left-hand side of the mixed-model equations depends on the design alone, so the prediction error variance of every GCA effect is known before any phenotype exists. joint_pev() returns its mean over the \(n_F + n_M\) GCA effects, the trace of the GCA block of the inverted coefficient matrix divided by its order, exact for the analysis model of Section 20.2 with known components. It is not the criterion of Box 4 of Section 19.7, which is the mean PEV of the hybrids’ target values converted to a reliability; this one is the mean over the GCA effects, needs the plan, and is the one the sweep below ranks. It is an A-type criterion on the effects themselves, not the mean PEV of pairwise differences between effects used as the A-value in model-based design (Butler et al. 2014); the two differ by the covariance terms and need not rank designs identically. Table 20.4 shows it ranking allocations of one plan. It is blind to SCA and to the difference between predicting made and unmade crosses.
Two component counts. A single graph with females, males and locations as nodes is the obvious female x male x location metric, and it is wrong: a location node joins every parent planted there, so at one location it reports one component for any plan, two disconnected North Carolina design II (NC II) blocks included (the design is attributed to Comstock and Robinson (1948), an attribution not verified for this book, as in Section 1.1 and Chapter 18). A shared location links only sums of GCA. joint_connectivity() therefore returns two counts alongside the R/17 diagnostics:

n_comp_cross, the components of the female x male graph of the crosses that receive a plot, pooled over locations. At one location it is exactly the bipartite count of Section 18.2.3.
n_comp_loc, the components of the location graph in which two locations are joined when they share a parent, over the locations that receive at least one plot: a location with no plot is not a node of that graph, so neither count flags an empty location.

Both equal to 1 is necessary for GCA and location contrasts to be linked by data, and the pair is not two independent conditions: n_comp_cross = 1 implies n_comp_loc = 1 (over the locations that have a plot). Locations split into two sets sharing no parent would put each planted cross wholly in one set, disconnecting the cross graph. So n_comp_loc > 1 occurs only with n_comp_cross > 1, and what n_comp_loc adds is where such a split runs: along locations (n_comp_loc > 1, blocks grown apart) or within them. Neither count is sufficient, and the pair does not detect confounding of GCA with location. With 2 x 2 pools, two locations and \(k = 1\), the crosses (1,1) and (1,2) at location 1 and (2,1) and (2,2) at location 2 give n_comp_cross = 1 and n_comp_loc = 1, yet the female contrast is the location contrast: the fixed-effects matrix of location, female and male is rank-deficient by one (Table 20.3; a third, empty location added to that example leaves both counts at 1, checked in the same chunk). A check that would detect this is the rank of that matrix over the planted plots; joint_connectivity() does not compute it. The two counts are therefore a screen, not the female x male x location metric Section 19.13 asked for, which remains open.


Show code
pix <- list(f = rep(1:2, each = 2), m = rep(1:2, 2))  # male fastest, as in R/17
Ma <- cbind(loc1 = as.integer(pix$f == 1), loc2 = as.integer(pix$f == 2))
cn <- joint_connectivity(Ma, 2, 2)
cells <- which(Ma == 1L, arr.ind = TRUE)
Xa <- model.matrix(~ loc + f + m,
                   data.frame(loc = factor(cells[, 2]), f = factor(pix$f[cells[, 1]]),
                              m = factor(pix$m[cells[, 1]])))
rk <- qr(Xa)$rank
stopifnot(cn[["n_comp_cross"]] == 1, cn[["n_comp_loc"]] == 1, rk == ncol(Xa) - 1)
# A third location with no plot is not a node: both counts stay at 1.
ce <- joint_connectivity(cbind(Ma, loc3 = 0L), 2, 2)
stopifnot(ce[["n_comp_cross"]] == 1, ce[["n_comp_loc"]] == 1)
knitr::kable(data.frame(female = pix$f, male = pix$m, Ma), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Female", "Male", "Location 1", "Location 2"))

Show code
# Share of random sparse plans (20 x 20) with at least one uncrossed line.
uncrossed <- function(p, n) {
  any(tabulate(p[["parent1"]], n) == 0 | tabulate(p[["parent2"]], n) == 0)
}
n_unc <- 20000
unc <- c(c4 = NA, c8 = NA)
set.seed(21)
unc[["c4"]] <- mean(replicate(n_unc, uncrossed(design_random_sparse(20, 20, c = 4), 20)))
set.seed(22)
unc[["c8"]] <- mean(replicate(n_unc, uncrossed(design_random_sparse(20, 20, c = 8), 20)))
# A c = 4 plan with an uncrossed line passes both counts.
set.seed(23)
repeat {
  pu <- design_random_sparse(20, 20, c = 4)
  du <- design_diagnostics(pu, 20, 20)
  if (uncrossed(pu, 20) && du[["components"]] == 1) break
}
cn_u <- joint_connectivity(joint_alloc(pu, 20, 20, nLoc = 8, k = 2, strategy = "coverage"),
                           20, 20)
stopifnot(cn_u[["n_comp_cross"]] == 1, cn_u[["n_comp_loc"]] == 1, !du[["connected"]])


Neither count sees a line that receives no cross. design_random_sparse() draws \(\mathrm{round}(c\,n_F)\) cells of the factorial without a per-line guarantee, so a line can go uncrossed; design_components() labels it unused and both counts are taken over the lines in use. In 20,000 random sparse plans on the 20 x 20 pools of Section 20.5, the share with at least one uncrossed line was 0.348 at 4 crosses per line and 0.001 at 8 (Table 18.8 reports the same quantity for 200 x 200 pools and 2 to 10 crosses per line). One c = 4 plan with an uncrossed line, allocated by coverage to eight locations at two per cross, returns n_comp_cross = 1 and n_comp_loc = 1. design_diagnostics() flags it (connected is FALSE because lines_A or lines_B falls short of the pool). Within the random family, therefore, moving from 8 to 4 crosses per line changes the number of lines in the data as well as the split, and the two random configurations of Section 20.5 do not isolate the split; the circulant plans, which cross every line \(c\) times, do.


Show code
set.seed(11)
vc <- sparse_vc(0.3); A <- relmat_halfsib(10, 2)
p <- design_circulant(10, 10, c = 3)
live <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(strat_col), function(s) {
  M <- joint_alloc(p, 10, 10, nLoc = 4, k = 2, strategy = s, vc = vc,
                   Af = A, Am = A, n_iter = 100)
  cn <- joint_connectivity(M, 10, 10)
  data.frame(strategy = s, plots = sum(M), pev_gca = joint_pev(M, 10, 10, vc, A, A),
             fem_cover = cn$fem_cover, male_cover = cn$male_cover,
             n_comp_cross = cn$n_comp_cross, n_comp_loc = cn$n_comp_loc)
}))

20.4.1 Allele frequencies per location
Neither criterion of Section 20.4 reads a genotype. A plan can be connected and low in PEV and still send most crosses of one subgroup to a few locations, which costs precision in subgroup contrasts, or bias under a subgroup x location interaction the model omits (Section 20.3 gives the argument and the evidence on both sides). The quantity that sees the imbalance is computed from the hybrids’ marker genotypes, and its algebra is exact.
The decomposition. Let \(\mathbf X_P\) be the hybrid marker matrix of the planted plots: one row \(\mathbf x_u\) per plot \(u\) (a cross planted at \(k\) locations appears \(k\) times) and \(N_{SNP}\) markers coded 0/0.5/1 as everywhere in this book (\(N_{SNP}\) is the symbol of Meuwissen et al. (2020), used as a second symbol for the number of markers because \(m\) marks the male pool; Appendix A). It has \(N_P = n_c k r\) rows, the budget in plots. Write \(n_l\) for the plots at location \(l\), \(\bar{\mathbf p}_l\) for their allele frequencies (column means) and \(\bar{\mathbf p}\) for those of all planted plots. Summing the one-way analysis-of-variance identity over markers,
\[
\sum_u \lVert \mathbf x_u - \bar{\mathbf p} \rVert^2
= \sum_l \sum_{u \in l} \lVert \mathbf x_u - \bar{\mathbf p}_l \rVert^2
+ SS_B,
\qquad
SS_B = \sum_l n_l \lVert \bar{\mathbf p}_l - \bar{\mathbf p} \rVert^2 ,
\tag{20.3}\]
with \(SS_B\) the between-location sum of squares, summed over markers.
The plan and \(k\) fix the rows of \(\mathbf X_P\), hence the left-hand side; an allocation only decides which location each row goes to. Minimising \(SS_B\) is therefore maximising the within-location sum, the k-means objective, which is what Papenberg and Klau (2021) call k-means anticlustering: groups of prescribed size (which carries the loads \(n_l\)) made as alike as possible. What their formulation does not carry is the item structure: here each cross enters as exactly \(k\) copies that must go to \(k\) different locations, whereas anticlustering assigns every item once and independently.
On \(\mathbf X_P\), \(SS_B/(N_P N_{SNP})\) is the plot-weighted mean squared deviation of a location’s allele frequencies from the pooled ones. On a 0/1 matrix \(\mathbf Z\) with one column per subgroup (a family, a heterotic subgroup, a female-family x male-family class) the column means are subgroup shares, and minimising \(SS_B\) equalises them. The two objectives differ; Table 20.5 measures both.
The diversity lens. The gene diversity of location \(l\)’s plots, \(GD_l = 1 - \theta_l\) over the molecular coancestry of Section 2.3, is \(\frac{1}{N_{SNP}} \sum_v 2\bar p_{lv}(1 - \bar p_{lv})\) over markers \(v\), Nei’s gene diversity at the location’s frequencies (Section 11.2; Nei (1973), abstract level: the equation was not read in the original). Because \(2p(1-p)\) is quadratic in \(p\), the decomposition carries over exactly:
\[
\sum_l \frac{n_l}{N_P}\, GD_l \;=\; GD_P - \frac{2\,SS_B}{N_P\, N_{SNP}},
\tag{20.4}\]
with \(GD_P\) the gene diversity of all planted plots. Take the locations as the subpopulations of Chapter 3 and weight them, as that chapter weights the subpopulations of Caballero and Toro (2002), by their share \(N_i/N_T = n_l/N_P\) of the plots. Then \(GD_P\) is \(GD_T = 1 - \bar f\), the left-hand side is \(GD_{WS} = 1 - \tilde f\), and
\[
\frac{2\,SS_B}{N_P\, N_{SNP}} = GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f
\tag{20.5}\]
exactly, for any loads; it is also the \(\bar D\) in Chapter 3’s \(F_{ST}\), and, by the standard definition, Nei’s \(D_{ST} = H_T - H_S\) (Nei 1973) with \(H_S\) the plot-weighted mean of the location diversities (the plain mean under equal loads). \(SS_B\) differs from all of these only by the factor \(N_P N_{SNP}/2\). Between heterotic pools this component is the heterosis engine, to be preserved; between the locations of one trial it is a nuisance, to be minimised.
The base. \(SS_B\) is centred on \(\bar{\mathbf p}\), the planted set’s own frequencies, not on a frozen base \(\mathbf p_0\) (Section 10.7.1). Against \(\mathbf p_0\) – here the frequencies of the complete factorial of candidate lines –
\[
\sum_l n_l \lVert \bar{\mathbf p}_l - \mathbf p_0 \rVert^2
= SS_B + N_P \lVert \bar{\mathbf p} - \mathbf p_0 \rVert^2 ,
\tag{20.6}\]
and the second term is fixed by the crossing plan, so with the plan fixed the two bases rank allocations identically. That term is the plan’s departure from the pool in the drift lens: \(\lVert \bar{\mathbf p} - \mathbf p_0 \rVert^2\) is the numerator of \(F_{drift}\) (Section 10.7.2; Meuwissen et al. (2020)) before each marker is standardised by \(p_{0}(1 - p_{0})\), with the planted set in the place of cycle \(t\). It is not a loss of gene diversity, which the book keeps in the other lens: per marker \(GD(p_0) - GD(\bar p) = 2(p_0 - \bar p)(1 - p_0 - \bar p)\), whose sign depends on which side of \(1/2\) the two frequencies sit. \(SS_B\) belongs to the allocation, the drift term to the crossing plan (Section 18.11).
Table 20.5 computes all of this for one plan at the scale of the sweep of Section 20.5, under four allocations: random; coverage; an exchange search that swaps two plots between locations when \(SS_B\) falls (loads and \(k\) unchanged); and the same search on \([\mathbf X_P,\; w\mathbf Z]\), the markers with the female-family x male-family indicators appended and \(w\) set so that both blocks carry the same total sum of squares over the planted plots. Rows: between_pct, \(100\,SS_B\) over the marker sum of squares; rms_dp, \(\sqrt{SS_B/(N_P N_{SNP})}\); gd_short_pct, the shortfall of the plot-weighted mean \(GD_l\) from \(GD_P\), in % of \(GD_P\); groups_between_pct, between_pct on \(\mathbf Z\); families and family_pairs, the share of each pool’s parent families, and of the plan’s family classes, present per location; fem_cover and pev_gca as in Table 20.4. The chunk asserts the decomposition (Equation 20.3), the \(GD\) identity (Equation 20.4) on \(\mathbf f\) and \(GD_{BS} = 2\,SS_B/(N_P N_{SNP})\) (Equation 20.5) for every allocation, and the change of base (Equation 20.6), which has power only on the random sparse plan checked after the table (a circulant plan uses every line equally often, so its drift term is zero). No accuracy is computed. The marker panel is simulated for this table alone: each pool is a mixture of a family-founder allele and an unrelated gamete at independent loci with \(q \sim U(0.1, 0.9)\) per pool and no control of the divergence between pools; it is not the generator of Chapter 6.


Show code
nF <- 20; nM <- 20; nLoc <- 8; nfam <- 5; n_snp <- 500
fam <- rep(seq_len(nfam), each = nF / nfam)
# A DH line carries its family's common parent at each marker with probability
# 1/2, else an unrelated gamete; a hybrid is the mean of its two parents (0/0.5/1).
dh_pool <- function(q) {
  par <- matrix(rbinom(nfam * n_snp, 1, rep(q, each = nfam)), nfam)
  ifelse(matrix(runif(nF * n_snp) < 0.5, nF), par[fam, ],
         matrix(rbinom(nF * n_snp, 1, rep(q, each = nF)), nF))
}
set.seed(31)
U <- dh_pool(runif(n_snp, 0.1, 0.9)); V <- dh_pool(runif(n_snp, 0.1, 0.9))
pix <- list(f = rep(seq_len(nF), each = nM), m = rep(seq_len(nM), nF))  # male fastest
Xh <- (U[pix$f, ] + V[pix$m, ]) / 2
p0 <- colMeans(Xh)                      # frozen base: the complete factorial
pl <- design_circulant(nF, nM, c = 4)
A <- relmat_halfsib(nF, nfam); vc <- sparse_vc(0.3)
ss <- function(Z) sum(sweep(Z, 2, colMeans(Z))^2)
between <- function(Z, g) {             # SS_B for the rows of Z grouped by location g
  n <- tabulate(g, nLoc)
  sum(n * rowSums(sweep(rowsum(Z, g) / n, 2, colMeans(Z))^2))
}
freq_terms <- function(M) {
  cl <- which(M == 1L, arr.ind = TRUE); X <- Xh[cl[, 1], ]; g <- cl[, 2]
  n <- tabulate(g, nLoc); NP <- nrow(X); SSB <- between(X, g)
  W <- sum(vapply(split(seq_len(NP), g), function(r) ss(X[r, , drop = FALSE]), 0))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ss(X), W + SSB, tolerance = 1e-12)))
  # Plot-weighted mean GD_l = GD_P - 2 SS_B / (N_P N_SNP), computed on f itself.
  f <- molecular_coancestry(X)
  fll <- vapply(seq_len(nLoc), function(l) vapply(seq_len(nLoc), function(j)
    mean(f[g == l, g == j]), 0), numeric(nLoc))   # mean coancestry between locations
  gd_l <- 1 - diag(fll); gd_P <- 1 - mean(f); w <- n / NP
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(w * gd_l), gd_P - 2 * SSB / (NP * n_snp))))
  # Caballero & Toro (2002) with weights N_i / N_T = n_l / N_P: GD_BS = f_til -
  # f_bar = D_bar (mean Nei distance) = 2 SS_B / (N_P N_SNP), for any loads.
  Dij <- outer(diag(fll), diag(fll), "+") / 2 - fll
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(w * diag(fll)) - mean(f), 2 * SSB / (NP * n_snp))),
            isTRUE(all.equal(drop(w %*% Dij %*% w), 2 * SSB / (NP * n_snp))))
  # Change of base to p0: the extra term depends on the plan, not the allocation.
  SSB0 <- sum(n * rowSums(sweep(rowsum(X, g) / n, 2, p0)^2))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(SSB0, SSB + NP * sum((colMeans(X) - p0)^2))))
  gp <- paste(fam[pix$f[cl[, 1]]], fam[pix$m[cl[, 1]]])
  nu <- function(z) mean(tapply(z, g, function(v) length(unique(v))))
  c(between_pct = 100 * SSB / ss(X), rms_dp = sqrt(SSB / (NP * n_snp)),
    gd_short_pct = 100 * 2 * SSB / (NP * n_snp) / gd_P,
    groups_between_pct = 100 * between(model.matrix(~ gp - 1), g) /
      ss(model.matrix(~ gp - 1)),
    families = (nu(fam[pix$f[cl[, 1]]]) + nu(fam[pix$m[cl[, 1]]])) / (2 * nfam),
    family_pairs = nu(gp) / length(unique(gp)),
    fem_cover = joint_connectivity(M, nF, nM)$fem_cover,
    pev_gca = joint_pev(M, nF, nM, vc, A, A))
}
# Swap the locations of two plots when SS_B of Y falls: loads and k fixed.
# Y has one row per hybrid, as Xh; Y = Xh balances marker frequencies.
freq_balance <- function(M, Y, n_iter = 5000) {
  cl <- which(M == 1L, arr.ind = TRUE)
  S <- rowsum(Y[cl[, 1], , drop = FALSE], cl[, 2]); n <- colSums(M)
  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    i <- sample.int(nrow(cl), 2); x <- cl[i[1], 1]; y <- cl[i[2], 1]
    a <- cl[i[1], 2]; b <- cl[i[2], 2]
    if (a == b || M[x, b] == 1L || M[y, a] == 1L) next
    d <- Y[y, ] - Y[x, ]
    if (sum((S[a, ] + d)^2 - S[a, ]^2) / n[a] + sum((S[b, ] - d)^2 - S[b, ]^2) / n[b] < 0) {
      S[a, ] <- S[a, ] + d; S[b, ] <- S[b, ] - d
      M[x, c(a, b)] <- c(0L, 1L); M[y, c(b, a)] <- c(0L, 1L)
      cl[i, 2] <- c(b, a)
    }
  }
  M
}
# Family-class indicators Z (one column per female-family x male-family class),
# weighted so that Z and the markers carry the same total SS over the planted
# plots (fixed by the plan and k, whatever the allocation).
Zh <- model.matrix(~ factor(paste(fam[pix$f], fam[pix$m])) - 1)
rP <- rep((pl$parent1 - 1) * nM + pl$parent2, 2)        # planted rows, k = 2
wZ <- sqrt(ss(Xh[rP, ]) / ss(Zh[rP, ]))
set.seed(32)
fr_a <- replicate(5, {
  Mc <- joint_alloc(pl, nF, nM, nLoc, k = 2, strategy = "coverage")
  stopifnot(sum(Mc) == 2 * nrow(pl))                 # N_P = n_c k, used as NP below
  sapply(list(random = joint_alloc(pl, nF, nM, nLoc, k = 2, strategy = "random"),
              coverage = Mc, freq_balanced = freq_balance(Mc, Xh),
              freq_family_balanced = freq_balance(Mc, cbind(Xh, wZ * Zh))),
         freq_terms)
})
fr <- data.frame(strategy = dimnames(fr_a)[[2]], t(apply(fr_a, 1:2, mean)), row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(fmt(apply(fr_a, 1:2, mean), 4))   # = t(fr): metrics as rows

Result. Over five allocations of the same plan, the between-location share of the marker sum of squares is 3.97 % (SD 0.30) under random placement, 1.08 % (SD 0.10) under the coverage rule, 0.55 % (SD 0.04) after the exchange search on markers and 1.26 % after the search on markers and family classes (\(w =\) 6.86); a random partition of the same plots into eight locations, ignoring that the copies of a cross must be apart, gives \((L-1)/(N_P-1) =\) 4.40 % in expectation. The mean location falls short of \(GD_P\) by 1.66 %, 0.45 %, 0.23 % and 0.53 %. The share of each pool’s parent families present per location is 0.985 to 1.000 under every strategy. Female-family x male-family classes are present at 0.57 to 0.60 per location under the first three strategies, with a between-location share (groups_between_pct) of 3.6 to 4.1 %, and at 0.79, share 0.9 %, under the fourth, against a ceiling of 0.80 (20 plots per location for 25 classes). Female coverage is 0.891 under the coverage rule and 0.860 under the fourth strategy; mean PEV of GCA is 0.504, 0.494, 0.492 and 0.495. On a random sparse plan with the same mean of four crosses per line, whose lines enter 1 to 8 crosses, the drift term \(N_P \lVert \bar{\mathbf p} - \mathbf
p_0 \rVert^2\) is 23.6 % of the \(\mathbf p_0\)-centred sum, \(F_{drift}\) of the planted set is 0.0043, the change of base holds, and the planted set’s gene diversity is above that of \(\mathbf p_0\) at 42 % of markers and below it at the rest.
Interpretation. Balancing parents per location balances their alleles: the coverage rule removes most of the frequency imbalance, and the marker search a further 49 % of what remains, at no cost in PEV of GCA here. Marker balance harmonises allele frequencies but not subgroup shares: under it the family classes stay at the level of random placement. Putting the class indicators into the criterion raises class presence from 0.60 at its coverage start to 0.79, close to the 0.80 ceiling, and pays for it in the marker term (1.26 % against 0.55 % for the marker-only search), in female coverage and a little in PEV – a trade-off set by \(w\), which was fixed by the equal-sum-of-squares rule, not tuned. Family presence barely separates the strategies, because half-sib families reach nearly every location under any of them. The limits, which hold wherever this section is used later: the search is first-improvement over 5,000 random pair swaps with no convergence test, so its rows bound what 5,000 proposals buy, not the minimum of \(SS_B\); one plan at one scale was examined; and no accuracy was computed, so whether a smaller \(SS_B\) on either block improves prediction, or protects subgroup contrasts against a subgroup x location interaction, is untested (Section 20.7).
The share needs no package function. For a 0/1 plan M (one row per hybrid, one column per location, as joint_alloc() returns) and a hybrid marker matrix X in the same row order it is three lines of base R; with X replaced by 0/1 subgroup indicators it gives groups_between_pct. On the random sparse plan above, checked against the chunk’s own between():

M <- M_r; X <- Xh
cl <- which(M == 1L, arr.ind = TRUE); XP <- X[cl[, 1], , drop = FALSE]; g <- cl[, 2]
SSB <- sum(table(g) * rowSums(sweep(rowsum(XP, g) / c(table(g)), 2, colMeans(XP))^2))
100 * SSB / sum(sweep(XP, 2, colMeans(XP))^2)   # between-location share, %
#> [1] 3.332507
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(SSB, between(XP, g))))
crumbs: 20  Which crosses, at which locations? Joint sparse allocation

title: 20  Which crosses, at which locations? Joint sparse allocation
text:
20.5 What the simulation finds
The sweep crosses six configurations that all spend 160 plots (the tester design 152) – circulant plans with 8, 4 and 2 crosses per line at 1, 2 and 4 locations per cross, random sparse plans with 8 and 4, and a two-tester design at two locations – with the allocation strategies, two plot heritabilities and two SCA levels (sparse_vc(): SCA a quarter of, or equal to, a GCA variance; genotype x location half of each main effect, so a genetic correlation of 2/3 between locations). Plot \(h^2\) is \(\sigma^2_G/(\sigma^2_G + \sigma^2_{GE} + \sigma^2_e)\) with the \(\sigma^2_e\) of Chapter 19 (Appendix A); it is not the single-plant \(h^2\) of Chapter 18, whose error absorbs the interaction with location (Section 19.11.3). Pools are 20 x 20 in half-sib families of four; eight locations; 30 replicates per cell (Figure 20.1).
Comparisons between strategies are paired; those between configurations are not. Within one configuration and scenario each replicate draws one plan, random and coverage allocate it, and both are simulated from the same seed, so they share the true genetic values (sparse_simulate() draws every effect before it looks at the allocation). Each configuration draws its own seeds, so the budget-split comparisons of result 1 are between independent cells, with both cells’ standard errors combined. The exchange search is too slow to repeat per replicate: per cell one plan gets a coverage allocation (start) and a search from it, and those two fixed designs are simulated in every replicate with the same seed, pairing optimised with its own start.
The evidence bar. A difference is detected past two standard errors of the difference. Chapter 18 calls a difference resolved only past three; a quantity between two and three is flagged where it appears. The “resolved” of Chapter 19 is a different bar, survival of a Bonferroni correction over its family of tests; where this chapter cites it, it says so.

20.5.1 1. The budget split: crosses against locations


Show code
lev <- c("circulant c=8, 1 loc", "circulant c=4, 2 loc", "circulant c=2, 4 loc",
         "random c=8, 1 loc", "random c=4, 2 loc", "tester k=2, 2 loc")
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(7.5, 4, 2, 0.5), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0))
for (sc in c("low", "high")) for (h in c(0.2, 0.4)) {
  d <- js[js$sca == sc & js$h2_plot == h, ]
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, length(lev) + 0.5),
       ylim = range(js$acc_all - 2 * js$acc_all_se, js$acc_all + 2 * js$acc_all_se),
       xaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "Accuracy, all hybrids",
       main = bquote(italic(h)^2 == .(h) * ", " * .(sc) ~ "SCA"), cex.main = 0.95,
       font.main = 1)
  axis(1, at = seq_along(lev), labels = lev, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.75)
  title(xlab = "Configuration", line = 6.3)
  for (j in seq_along(strat_col)) {
    e <- d[d$strategy == names(strat_col)[j], ]
    x <- match(e$label, lev) + (j - 2) * 0.2
    arrows(x, e$acc_all - 2 * e$acc_all_se, x, e$acc_all + 2 * e$acc_all_se,
           angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.02, col = strat_col[j])
    points(x, e$acc_all, pch = 19, col = strat_col[j])
  }
  if (sc == "high" && h == 0.2)
    legend("topright", legend = names(strat_col), col = strat_col, pch = 19,
           bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}

Figure 20.1: Accuracy (correlation between predicted and true genetic value) over all 400 possible hybrids at a budget of 160 plots (tester design 152), by configuration (plan, crosses per line \(c\), locations per cross) and allocation strategy; one panel per plot heritability \(h^2\) and SCA level. Points are cell means over 30 replicates, error bars span plus or minus two standard errors. optimised is one fixed design per cell. 20 x 20 pools in half-sib families of four, eight locations, known variance components; in-repo sweep (regenerate.R joint).





Figure 20.1 reads left to right along the budget identity (Equation 20.1). Within the circulant family, with the coverage allocation, 160 crosses at one location each reach 0.787 at \(h^2 = 0.4\) and low SCA, 80 crosses at two locations 0.767, and 40 at four 0.700. With high SCA the point estimates are 0.682, 0.636, 0.535, larger steps at this \(h^2\); that is not a detected dependence on the SCA variance: the difference between the 160-against-40 gaps has z = 1.98 here and 0.86 at \(h^2 = 0.2\), where the 80-against-40 step is smaller with high SCA (0.013 against 0.052). The order holds in all four scenarios, unevenly: the step from 80 to 160 crosses is 0.5 to 3.4 standard errors of the difference, the step from 40 to 80 0.5 to 4.4. Of the 8 steps, 4 – 160 versus 80 at \(h^2 = 0.2\), low SCA; 160 versus 80 at \(h^2 = 0.4\), low SCA; 80 versus 40 at \(h^2 = 0.2\), low SCA; 80 versus 40 at \(h^2 = 0.2\), high SCA – are under two standard errors, and 160 versus 80 at \(h^2 = 0.4\), high SCA, at 2.14, is under Chapter 18’s three; only their direction agrees with the rest. The two-tester design, with 76 crosses at two locations, sits below the circulant plan with 80 crosses at two locations in every scenario and strategy, at nearly the same budget (152 against 160 plots). The 16 pairs (four scenarios, four strategies) are unpaired and differ by 2.1 to 3.8 standard errors of the difference, all in the same direction. The plans differ in more than the testers (76 against 80 crosses, and the line structure), so no causal reading to the tester structure is made. Chapter 18 compared the two families in another regime (unrelated lines, 200 x 200 pools, no relationship matrix, one location, accuracy of line GCA), and conditions its result on the crosses per line, the layout and the estimator; the direction here agrees, which is all that is claimed.
For the crosses that were made the comparison reverses (Table 20.6). Forty crosses at four locations estimate those crosses at 0.845, against 0.807 for 160 crosses at one location (\(h^2 = 0.4\), low SCA; z = 2.67, under Chapter 18’s three). A gain from averaging each made cross over four locations rather than one fits this, but the contrast does not test it: the crosses and the locations per cross change together, and the made crosses are different subsets of the 400 hybrids at each split (160, 80 and 40), so these correlations are not on one estimand. Across scenarios this difference is 1.2 to 6.0 standard errors; the smallest, 1.2 at \(h^2 = 0.2\) and low SCA, is not resolved. Nor is the reversal visibly monotone: at \(h^2 = 0.2\) and high SCA, 80 crosses at two locations reach 0.610 against 0.618 for 160 at one (z = -0.32, not resolved). A programme that picks parents on GCA, or will choose among all possible single crosses with a prediction model, should spend the budget on distinct crosses. One that will advance only crosses it has made estimates them better from more locations, but then chooses among 40 candidates instead of 160, and the response to selection depends on that intensity as well as on accuracy, which this chapter does not model.

This does not contradict result 2 of Section 19.11.3, which varied something else: there \(k = 2\), one plot per cell and the planted 80 % of the factorial were held fixed and the trial was widened from 2 to 10 locations, so the plots per hybrid stayed the same and only the environments sampled grew. Here \(L = 8\) is fixed and \(k\) rises, so each location added per cross is one more plot for that cross, paid for with a cross. Endelman et al. (2014) is the line-breeding analogue of the first operation (entries and plots fixed, spread over more locations). Widening the trial at fixed plots per entry raised accuracy in both; adding locations per cross at a fixed budget lowered all-hybrid accuracy here. That was measured at one genetic correlation between locations, 2/3; a lower one makes each location say less about the others and would be expected to move the optimum toward more locations per cross, which this sweep did not test.


20.5.2 2. Allocation strategy, with the plan fixed
With the plan and \(k\) fixed, the strategies are close (Figure 20.1). The paired contrasts (Table 20.8) resolve what the cell means cannot. Coverage (a greedy parent-presence rule, the closest analogue of the parentage allocation of Chapter 19 and not the same rule, as the check below shows) does what it is built to do: in the factorial plans the share of females present per location rises from 0.676 under random placement to 0.874. Paired against random placement of the same plan, the accuracy difference over all hybrids, averaged over the 24 cells, is +0.0057 \(\pm\) 0.0033 (z = 1.7; 16 of 24 cells positive). That is below the two-standard-error bar, so the gain is not detected overall. Within the random sparse plans alone it is +0.0119 \(\pm\) 0.0052 (z = 2.29, past two standard errors but not Chapter 18’s three), one of three families tested, with no correction for that. Only 2 of the 24 cells differ by more than two standard errors on their own (z = 2.32 and 2.68, all under three), about what chance gives. The tester design is the exception in the other direction: there coverage moves the share of females present per location only from 0.494 to 0.549, within 0.001 of the ceiling: a non-tester female has two crosses, so at two locations per cross it reaches at most four of the eight locations, and with the two female testers present everywhere the mean is at most \((18 \times 4/8 + 2)/20 =\) 0.55. Over the 4 tester cells the paired difference is -0.012 \(\pm\) 0.011, not detected.


Show code
# Complete 20 x 20 factorial, 8 locations, k = 2: coverage against parentage.
full <- data.frame(parent1 = rep(1:20, each = 20), parent2 = rep(1:20, 20))
pcmp <- t(vapply(1:20, function(s) {
  set.seed(s); Mp <- sparse_alloc(20, 20, 8, k = 2, strategy = "parentage")
  set.seed(s); Mc <- joint_alloc(full, 20, 20, 8, k = 2, strategy = "coverage")
  cp <- sparse_connectivity(Mp, 20, 20); cc <- joint_connectivity(Mc, 20, 20)
  c(same = all(Mc == Mp), disc_p = cp$frac_disconn, disc_c = cc$frac_disconn,
    conc_p = cp$conc_hmean, conc_c = cc$conc_hmean,
    cover = min(cp$fem_cover, cp$male_cover, cc$fem_cover, cc$male_cover),
    load_range = max(diff(range(colSums(Mp))), diff(range(colSums(Mc)))))
}, numeric(7)))
stopifnot(all(pcmp[, "same"] == 0), all(pcmp[, "cover"] == 1), all(pcmp[, "load_range"] == 0),
          all(pcmp[, "disc_c"] == 0), all(abs(pcmp[, "disc_p"] - 8 / 28) < 1e-9),
          20 * choose(2, 2) < choose(8, 2))      # n_M groups x one pair each < pairs


What coverage is, and is not. It places the crosses one at a time in random order, each in the \(k\) locations where its female and male are still absent, ties broken by the lightest load, and aims at a cap of \(\lceil n_c k / L \rceil\) plots per location. It has no term for the hybrids two locations share. Chapter 19’s parentage cuts the complete factorial into \(n_M\) cyclic groups and optimises the concurrence between locations. On the complete 20 x 20 factorial at eight locations and \(k = 2\) (seeds 1 to 20) the two allocations differ in 20 of 20 draws; both give female and male coverage 1 and equal loads, but the fraction of location pairs sharing no hybrid is 0.000 under coverage and 0.286 under parentage in all 20 draws, and the harmonic-mean concurrence is 13.4 against 0. This is structural: each of the \(n_M = 20\) groups is planted at \(k = 2\) locations and so links one pair, and 20 groups link at most 20 of the \(\binom{8}{2} = 28\) pairs. The two agree on parent coverage and differ on shared hybrids, which is the distinction result 4 of Section 19.11.3 leaves open; the contrast of this section therefore varies both at once (Section 20.9).
The cap itself is not guaranteed. When fewer than \(k\) locations are below the cap the rule still takes the \(k\) best, so a location can end one plot above it. Table 20.7 counts the draws, with the sweep’s configurations and plan draws, over seeds 1 to 100 and 101 to 200, with the maximum excess in plots. The sweep above probably contains such draws (an inference: the per-replicate allocations are not stored, and at the rates of Table 20.7 for circulant \(c = 2\), \(k = 4\) it would be near certain that some are); their effect, one extra plot at one location, was not separated from the rest.

                      c = c(8, 4, 2, 8, 4, 2), k = c(1, 2, 4, 1, 2, 2))
cap_exc <- function(i, s) {
  set.seed(s)
  pl <- switch(cap_cfg$plan[i], circulant = design_circulant(20, 20, cap_cfg$c[i]),
               random = design_random_sparse(20, 20, cap_cfg$c[i]),
               tester = design_tester(20, 20, cap_cfg$c[i]))
  M <- joint_alloc(pl, 20, 20, 8, cap_cfg$k[i], "coverage")
  max(colSums(M)) - ceiling(nrow(pl) * cap_cfg$k[i] / 8)
}

The pooled contrast is not detected and one family of three passes two standard errors. The direction agrees with the finding of Chapter 19 that a structured layout’s advantage over random allocation is small and not resolved after multiplicity correction (the larger difference at \(k \le 2\) there is an exploratory subset). It is not a replication: coverage is not that chapter’s parentage layout, and its bar (Bonferroni) is not the two standard errors used here. It sits with the mixed record of incomplete-block allocation (Montesinos-López et al. (2022) and Montesinos-López et al. (2024) better than random, Osval A. Montesinos-López et al. (2023) close). When every line appears in several crosses spread over eight locations, random placement already puts most parents in most locations; whatever coverage adds – about +0.006 correlation points overall on the point estimate, at most +0.012 within a plan family – is small next to the budget split.


20.5.3 3. What the criterion can and cannot see


Show code
jp <- js[js$strategy %in% names(strat_col), ]
op <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1, 1))
plot(jp$pev_gca, jp$acc_all, pch = 19, col = strat_col[jp$strategy],
     xlab = "Mean PEV of GCA (before planting)", ylab = "Accuracy, all hybrids")
legend("topright", legend = names(strat_col), col = strat_col, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(op)
r_pev <- cor(jp$pev_gca, jp$acc_all)
# Rank agreement between PEV and accuracy over the six configurations, per scenario.
cvr <- js[js$strategy == "coverage", ]
rho <- sapply(split(cvr, paste(cvr$h2_plot, cvr$sca)),
              function(d) cor(d$pev_gca, d$acc_all, method = "spearman"))
rho_made <- sapply(split(cvr, paste(cvr$h2_plot, cvr$sca)),
                   function(d) cor(d$pev_gca, d$acc_made, method = "spearman"))
# Exact two-sided permutation p of Spearman's rho at n = 6 (all 720 orders).
stopifnot(all(table(paste(cvr$h2_plot, cvr$sca)) == 6),
          !anyDuplicated(paste(cvr$h2_plot, cvr$sca, cvr$pev_gca)))
pm <- as.matrix(expand.grid(rep(list(seq_len(6)), 6)))
pm <- pm[apply(pm, 1, anyDuplicated) == 0, ]
rho0 <- 1 - 6 * rowSums((pm - col(pm))^2) / (6 * (6^2 - 1))
p_rho <- function(r) mean(abs(rho0) >= abs(r) - 1e-9)
rho_crit <- min(abs(rho0)[vapply(abs(rho0), p_rho, 0) <= 0.05])
p_all <- vapply(rho, p_rho, 0); p_made <- vapply(rho_made, p_rho, 0)
g300 <- median(1 - jo$pev_300 / jo$pev_start)
g600 <- median(1 - jo$pev_600 / jo$pev_start)
spread <- sapply(split(jp, paste(jp$label, jp$h2_plot, jp$sca)),
                 function(d) diff(range(d$pev_gca)) / min(d$pev_gca))
second <- (jo$pev_300 - jo$pev_600) / (jo$pev_start - jo$pev_300)
pot <- pooled("optimised - start", by = "plan")
pot <- pot[pot$group == "tester", ]
spread_circ <- spread[startsWith(names(spread), "circulant")]
# Cost of one allocation and of one PEV evaluation at the sweep's scale, this machine.
tm <- local({
  set.seed(1); pl <- design_circulant(20, 20, 4); A <- relmat_halfsib(20, 5)
  M <- joint_alloc(pl, 20, 20, 8, 2, "coverage")
  c(cov = 1000 * system.time(for (i in 1:20) joint_alloc(pl, 20, 20, 8, 2, "coverage"))[["elapsed"]] / 20,
    pev = 1000 * system.time(for (i in 1:3) joint_pev(M, 20, 20, sparse_vc(0.3), A, A))[["elapsed"]] / 3)
})








Figure 20.2: Mean PEV of GCA, computed from the design before planting, against realised accuracy (correlation between predicted and true genetic value) over all 400 hybrids. One point per configuration x allocation strategy x variance scenario, each the mean of 30 replicates; colour is the strategy. 20 x 20 pools, eight locations, 160 plots (tester design 152), known variance components; in-repo sweep (regenerate.R joint).





Across all cells the mean PEV of GCA correlates with accuracy over all hybrids at -0.96 (Figure 20.2; lower PEV, higher accuracy). Almost all of that comes from the plan and the scenario: the clusters are configurations, and within a cluster the strategies differ by 0.3 to 4.7 % in PEV (median 1.8 %). In the circulant clusters the plan is the same for every strategy and the spread is the strategy alone (0.3 to 4.7 %); in the random sparse and tester clusters the optimised row is one plan against the means over 30 plans for random and coverage, so plan-to-plan variation is mixed in. Over the six configurations of one scenario, the rank correlation between PEV and all-hybrid accuracy is -1.00 to -0.89 (exact permutation p 0.003 to 0.033; at \(n = 6\) a two-sided \(p \le 0.05\) needs \(|\rho| \ge\) 0.89). The criterion is therefore a usable screen for which plan and how many locations per cross – it can be computed for every split of a budget in seconds – but only for that objective. Against accuracy on the crosses that were made its rank correlation is 0.20 to 0.66, positive (higher PEV, higher made-cross accuracy) in all four scenarios but with p 0.17 to 0.71: there is no evidence that the PEV ranking agrees with made-cross accuracy, and weak, non-significant evidence that it runs opposite.
As a guide to fine placement it is weak, and the exchange search shows it from the other side (Table 20.9). From the coverage start, 300 proposals lowered PEV by a median 0.10 % and 600 by 0.15 %, at about 47 seconds per design against 0.8 ms for the greedy start (one joint_pev() call takes 92 ms; timings on the machine that rendered this page). Paired against its own start the optimised design changed accuracy by +0.0027 \(\pm\) 0.0022 overall. The one family that stands out is the tester design, +0.019 \(\pm\) 0.007 (z = 2.71, under Chapter 18’s three) with 4 of 4 cells positive, where the search also found the largest PEV reductions. It is tentative: each cell is one optimised design from one plan, in one of three plan families, with no correction for that. The search, first improvement with no convergence test, had not converged: the second 300 proposals added a median 40 % of what the first 300 achieved, and in 8 of 24 cells 65 % or more (that cut-off was chosen after the data and is descriptive). These results say what 600 proposals buy, not what a converged placement optimiser would buy. The optimised-block design of the external study behind Chapter 19 showed the same absence of gain on untested hybrids.

The component counts were 1 in almost every replicate. The exception is informative: the draw split the factorial into two components in 2 of the 120 random sparse plans with 4 crosses per line (in 2 scenarios, appearing under both strategies that share the plan) – a defect of the plan that no allocation can repair, visible before a seed is sown. Location connectivity (n_comp_loc) was 1 throughout: with several crosses per line over eight locations, locations always shared parents.


20.5.4 Limitations of the simulation

Known variance components. The criterion and the BLUP use the true values; restricted maximum likelihood (REML) on a sparse trial is the weak point of Section 19.11.3 (result 5).
A misspecified analysis model: \((s\ell)\) is absorbed into an i.i.d. residual, checked for one plan only (Section 20.2).
Exchangeable locations, genetic correlation 2/3 between every pair. Mega-environment structure (González-Barrios et al. 2019; Hoefler and Gutierrez 2026) would favour allocations that sample each mega-environment, which the coverage rule does not see.
Half-sib relationships, one plot per cell, no markers, spatial trend or replicated checks in the sweep; the marker term of Section 20.4.1 comes from a separate live simulation, not scored for accuracy.
One budget, one scale: 160 plots, 20 x 20 pools, eight locations.
Accuracy, not response. Selection intensity differs between 40 and 160 candidates and is not modelled.

title: 20  Which crosses, at which locations? Joint sparse allocation
text:
20.6 Practical recommendations






TipA checklist for a joint crossing and testing plan




Fix the budget in plots, \(B = n_c k r\), and the locations available.
Decide what will be selected. Parents on GCA, or any single cross by prediction: favour distinct crosses (result 1, Section 20.5.1). Only crosses already made: more locations per cross estimate them better, at a cost in selection intensity.
Screen candidate splits with the mean PEV of GCA (joint_pev()), using the previous cycle’s relationship matrix and components, for the GCA / all-hybrid objective only.
Treat one location per cross with caution. It was best with known components. REML converged in under half of the cached fits at one location per hybrid (Section 19.11.3, result 5); that chapter proposes little information on the variance components as the reason, a hypothesis it did not test, so two locations per cross is offered as a precaution, not as a measured floor.
Place crosses with the coverage rule (joint_alloc(strategy = "coverage")): it costs nothing and raises parent coverage, though its accuracy gain was not detected (result 2, 1). With known subgroups, read the between-location shares of markers and subgroup indicators before planting, and balance on the indicators if subgroup shares must be equal; neither marker nor indicator balancing has been shown to raise accuracy (Section 20.4.1, including its limits).
Check n_comp_cross == 1 and n_comp_loc == 1 before planting, and separately that every location receives plots (an empty location is not counted by either). A disconnected plan needs a new plan, not a new allocation. Passing is necessary, not sufficient: it does not exclude GCA aliased with location (Section 20.4).
Reserve exchange optimisation of the placement for tester designs, as provisional (result 3, Section 20.5.3), and run it well beyond 600 proposals. The evidence is four cells with one optimised design each, past two standard errors but not three, and its standard error carries no design-to-design variance.

title: 20  Which crosses, at which locations? Joint sparse allocation
text:
20.7 Open problems

A joint optimiser over the plan itself. Here the plan family was enumerated and only the placement optimised. Searching crosses and locations in one binary space is the problem Heslot and Feoktistov (2020) solved for crosses alone.
A criterion that sees SCA and the selection objective: one on the target values of the candidates that will actually be selected among, with intensity.
Non-exchangeable environments. Joining mega-environments (González-Barrios et al. 2019) or a choice of environments (Rincent et al. 2017) to a crossing plan, and finding the genetic correlation between locations at which the optimum moves toward more locations per cross.
Estimated components. How much of the budget split survives REML, and whether the PEV screen should use a prior or the previous cycle’s estimates (Lisle et al. 2021).
Seed as a constraint. A cross planted at \(k\) locations needs \(k\) plots of seed; cross_cost() (Section 18.7) has not been joined to the allocation.
Frequency-balanced allocation and accuracy. A test of Section 20.4.1’s criterion (Papenberg and Klau 2021) needs pools whose subgroups differ in mean, as the breeding populations of Windhausen et al. (2012) did, and in genotype x location; an analysis model without that interaction; estimated components; a sweep over \(w\); and a paired comparison against the coverage rule. Why the answer should not be presumed is in Section 20.3.
Prospective validation. No trial has been designed jointly sparse from the start and compared against a conventional plan.
