title: 20  Which crosses, at which locations? Joint sparse allocation
text:
20.9 Where this connects

Chapter 18 chose the crosses with the field fixed and Chapter 19 the field with the crosses fixed; under one budget the crossing plan is the larger lever.
The coverage rule is the nearest allocation rule here to the hypothesis of result 4 of Section 19.11.3 – that parent coverage, not shared hybrids, connects a sparse trial, which the data there do not decide. Its accuracy gain over random placement was not detected (z = 1.7), and the contrast moves parent coverage and shared-hybrid concurrence together at fixed plan, \(k\) and loads, so a non-detection is not a test of that hypothesis.
In plans where a line could go uncrossed, distinct crosses might also keep more lines in the data. Section 18.11 states the next step, that a line never crossed is one the next cycle may in practice not use, as a hypothesis and not a result; Chapter 23 has no crossing design and does not test it. The only quantity measured here is the plan-level drift term of one random sparse plan (Section 20.4.1). The circulant comparison of result 1 holds every line in the data at every split, so it does not measure this effect.
The PEV screen is the mixed-model machinery of Chapter 14, read before planting instead of after harvest.
The frequency term of Section 20.4.1 is the partition of Chapter 3 with locations in place of pools.

This closes the Part. The crossing plan and its field decide which hybrids, and which lines, are seen at all. What it hands on is the budget-split result under known components, the two screens (mean PEV of GCA; the component counts, necessary and not sufficient) and the open question of allele frequencies per location. The Evidence and practice part that follows does not use them: it starts from the metrics of Chapter 12 and asks what the applied literature reports, beginning with Chapter 21.

title: 21  What the plant literature establishes
text:
21.1 The corpus, and what it can support
Chapter 12 derived a recommendation from the book’s own simulations. This chapter, the first of the Evidence and practice part, asks what the applied literature reports about the same quantities: where it agrees, and where it is silent. It follows the Mating and testing design part (Chapter 18, Chapter 19, Chapter 20) without using it. The corpus (Section 21.1) was screened for diversity metrics, heterotic structure, genetic resources and optimisation (Appendix D), not for crossing or testing design, so nothing here bears on the literature of that part and no result of it is carried over.
Two cached files, both external literature screens with no producer in this repository (book/scripts/regenerate.R lists them as not regenerated here). Nothing computed from them is reproducible beyond what the shipped CSV contains. Each number in this chapter says which file it comes from.
The files are partly misfiled. The animal file holds plant studies (for example Yadav et al. (2025), wheat), and the plant file holds a record whose crop field reads “dairy cattle”. “In the plant file” and “in the animal file” in this chapter therefore describe a file, not a species. Appendix D describes both.
Both files carry one-line curator notes, not abstracts. The study-level numbers of this chapter are read from the abstracts of the papers cited by key, except that Kadoumi et al. (2025) and the final remark on Zhao et al. (2023) are read from the full text; they are not in the CSVs and were not recomputed. A sentence “not established in the retrieved set” is a statement about these two files, whose windows begin in 2017 (plant) and 2018 (animal) and so exclude earlier work such as Heerwaarden et al. (2012).
Two terms with more than one sense. Allelic richness is used in this chapter in four senses: \(A_{\text{ret}}\), the marker alleles retained by a set of inbred lines at biallelic markers (Equation 11.7, the book’s sense in Chapter 12 and Chapter 13); the figure a study reports under that name without saying how it is computed; the usage table’s merged category “Allelic richness / rare alleles”; and the expected number of alleles per locus at drift-mutation equilibrium at multiallelic loci. Each use says which. Status number in the literature is a count; on the book’s molecular \(\mathbf{f}\), \(N_s = 1/(2\theta) \in [1/2, 1]\) is a rescaling of \(\theta\) and not a head count (Section 11.3).

21.2 The headline qualification
Section 12.6 recommends, inside the homozygosity lens, for inbred parents and an index additive in the parents: two metrics inside the optimiser, the proportional loss \(\alpha\) of gene diversity against a same-size random-subset baseline (Chapter 15) and \(N_{e,\text{par}}\); three at validation, marker alleles retained \(A_{\text{ret}}\), the within/between-pool decomposition and \(N_s\); and \(F_{drift}\) and \(F_{hom}\) as monitoring against the random-subset null. That set was chosen by cost and by a residual criterion that Section 12.3 states is necessary and not sufficient. It is not claimed to be minimal, and the redundancy analysis behind it is cached external data with an unrecorded setting. This chapter compares those metrics with what the plant file reports.
On the screen’s own table (Table 21.1), the quantities from which the recommended metrics are built are reported unevenly, and none of the recommended metrics themselves has a category. The table is an external classification, which limits how far the statement can be pressed. The mapping of the recommended metrics to the table’s categories, given in this section, is this chapter’s, not the screen’s, and each pair is approximate.

\(\alpha\) is the proportional loss of \(GD = 1 - \theta\) against a random-subset baseline (Chapter 15). Its inner quantity, \(GD\), is Nei’s \(H_e\) computed on the group’s own frequencies (Section 11.2), so it maps to the category “Expected heterozygosity (He / gene diversity)”. The loss relative to a baseline has no category. \(\theta\) itself is a mean of the molecular coancestry \(\mathbf{f}\) over a usage vector, and only loosely the category “Marker coancestry / kinship / relatedness”, which holds pairwise kinship and relatedness of any kind.
\(N_{e,\text{par}}\), an effective number of parents of a usage vector, is nearest to “Effective population size / status number”, a different quantity.
\(A_{\text{ret}}\) is nearest to “Allelic richness / rare alleles”, the merged category of Section 21.1, not necessarily the same quantity.

Table 21.2 gives smaller counts than the usage table in every row. In the first four rows the table is 2.2 to 3.8 times the column; the column has 0 records with runs of homozygosity (ROH) and 1 effective-population-size record (1 maize) against 22 and 17. The gene-diversity pattern (row 7) finds 77 records against 101. The effective-size pattern does not contain the bare token “Ne”: the shipped column lists “effective alleles” in 7 records (2 of them as “(Ne)”), a per-locus allele count and not an effective population size, and the chunk of Table 21.2 asserts that none of them is matched. The shipped column lists coancestry, kinship or relatedness in 12 records (7 maize) where the usage table has 46 (22), and 0 records with runs of homozygosity where the table’s merged “Inbreeding coefficient / ROH” row has 22 (5 maize). The metric_used field is empty in 61 of the 687 records. The ROH query printed in Appendix D is the pattern of Table 21.2, anchored as a word, and returns 0 records. Unanchored, a case-insensitive “roh” returns 1 record, which matches the letters “roh” inside the word “microhaplotypes”, in an alfalfa record. The magnitudes of the usage table therefore cannot be reproduced from the shipped file, and I give them only as the curator’s classification. What the two sources share, among these six categories, is the order at the two ends: population structure and \(F_{ST}\) are well ahead of the other four in both, and runs of homozygosity and effective size are the two lowest in both. Allelic richness and coancestry tie in the table and are 18 against 12 records in the column counts. Expected heterozygosity is not in that order claim: it is third in the table and 77 records in the column. The statements in this chapter that rest on the usage table rest on the order, and not on the percentages.
Three observations follow.
Applied plant work often reports several metrics together. A panel of 376 elite sub-Saharan African inbreds reports, in one analysis, polymorphic information content (PIC) = 0.39, observed heterozygosity = 0.02, gene diversity = 0.37, minor allele frequency (MAF) = 0.29, Shannon = 6.86, Simpson = 949.09, allelic richness = 787.70 (the abstract does not say how it is computed) and an average genetic distance of 0.303 (Mukiti et al. 2025). The plant file’s annotation of that record lists “Rogers distance”; the abstract says “average genetic distance” and clusters on the identical-by-state (IBS) distance, so I write distance and not Rogers. The shipped metric_used column lists three or more items for 49% of the 687 screened records (44% of the 158 directly relevant ones), counting comma- or semicolon-separated annotation items. This is a count of annotation items, not a bound on how often several metric families are reported together: some items hold more than one family (splitting also on “/” and ” and ” gives 54% and 51%), and many items are not diversity metrics (“genetic gain”, “breeding value”, “QTL effects”). I did not define families.
The quantity inside \(\alpha\) is among the most reported; the other recommended metrics are not identified as categories of the screen. On the usage table (external classification), expected heterozygosity or gene diversity appears in 14.7% of screened records, rank 3 of 12; marker coancestry or kinship in 6.7%, allelic richness or rare alleles in 6.7%, and effective size or status number in 2.5%; against 44.1% for population structure, 17% for \(F_{ST}\) and 14.1% for PIC. By record count the coancestry and allelic-richness categories tie at rank 6, in the middle, and effective size ranks 12, the last. Under the mapping of Section 21.2, then, gene diversity itself has a category, and the baseline-relative loss and the effective number of parents are not identified as categories in the screen; \(A_{\text{ret}}\) maps only to the merged richness category, in the middle by record count. The absence of a category is not a measure of how often the papers report a quantity, which a screen of abstracts does not show. No category of the table corresponds to a proportional loss against a resampling baseline, the quantity \(\alpha\) constrains, or to an effective number of parents of a usage vector. The most reported categories describe structure. A screen of abstracts cannot see a constraint applied inside a selection programme, so “toward constraining” is not testable from it.
Nothing in either file computes \(\theta\) or \(N_s\) on a maize hybrid-usage vector. The formalism of Section 12.1 is not established in the retrieved set. That is a gap this work fills rather than a contradiction, but it means the approach has no published plant-breeding baseline to be validated against, which is a real limitation.






NoteThese are different jobs, not a conflict



For monitoring and description, the plant file shows many metrics reported together; why is not tested here. For constraining an optimiser, redundancy is a cost rather than a virtue.
Report the wide package to collaborators and in publications; constrain the optimiser on the two metrics of Section 12.6.

title: 21  What the plant literature establishes
section: 21.3 Why plant practice differs from animal breeding
text:
21.3 Why plant practice differs from animal breeding
Three structural facts separate the two literatures. They are reasons the animal methods do not transfer unchanged (Section 1.3), not a tested explanation of the metric choices in Table 21.1.
Lines are homozygous. Observed heterozygosity in an inbred panel is the residual heterozygosity of the lines, a measure of how far they are from fixation and not a descriptor of diversity: pearl millet parental lines report \(H_o = 0.031\) against \(H_e = 0.334\) (Kandarkar et al. 2024). Reading it as a purity control is this chapter’s, not the paper’s. Animal coancestry theory assumes a randomly mating heterozygous population; the plant analogue computes \(\theta\) directly on line genotypes, which is the setting where the line-level collapse of Section 12.1 applies, for inbred parents and an index additive in the parents.
The product is the F1, not the line. Diversity is tracked separately for each parental pool and for cross-pool complementarity, a structure with no livestock analogue. Association models are now built to partition additive and dominance effects by the heterotic group of origin of the allele (Beugnot et al. 2023).
Diversity is partitioned into two objects, not one. Chapter 3 gives the partition of gene diversity into within-pool and between-pool terms, and Section 1.1 derives that under drift alone in two closed pools of equal weight the within-pool term falls while the between-pool term rises. That derivation does not cover selection; the rise of \(GD_{BS}\) under run_cycles() is a simulation result (Chapter 23) with drift and selection acting together. A single pool-wide statistic sees the sum, which is why the book partitions it.

21.3.1 Distance measures, and the absence of a standard
The usage table’s row “Modified Rogers / genetic distance” has 83 records over all crops, of which 36 are maize. It is a merged category covering any genetic distance, not a share of modified Rogers distance (MRD) among the distance measures: the string “Rogers” appears in 6 metric_used cells of the plant file (5 maize). A 2025 methods paper is annotated in the plant file as a unified framework relating diversity metrics to distance (Cendoya et al. 2025); I have not read it beyond that note.
For inbred lines coded 0/1, \(f_{ij} = 1 - \text{MRD}_{ij}^2\), and the book checks it numerically to \(10^{-12}\) on simulated lines (Trap 1 of Chapter 13). It is not claimed for hybrids, and a reported MRD equals \(1 - f\) only for inbred lines on the same markers coded 0/1.
One result is worth carrying into practice. In 298 African highland maize inbreds, nearly 91% of pairs differ at 30-36% of the scored alleles, but only 32% have a relative kinship coefficient below 0.050; the authors read the gap as redundancy in allelic composition from repeated use of few source germplasm backgrounds (Wegary et al. 2019).
That is the study’s result. The following is an inference, and it limits what the result supports. On 0/1 inbred lines a pair differing at a fraction \(d\) of loci has \(f = 1 - d\), so if “scored alleles” means loci that differ, 91% of these pairs sit at \(f\) between 0.64 and 0.70 on the book’s definition. The “relative kinship coefficient” is on another scale, presumably relative to the sample, with unrelated pairs near zero; the abstract gives no estimator and the definition is in no versioned file. The two figures are therefore not a contrast between the book’s \(f\) and a distance: on inbred 0/1 lines \(f\) is a monotone function of the distance. Whether a reading from state and a reading relative to the sample disagree about redundancy is this chapter’s inference, not the study’s: the abstract gives no threshold on either scale at which a pair counts as redundant, compares the two figures nowhere, and the authors read both as evidence of redundancy. The book’s constraint is on state-based \(f\), which is the first reading. Whether \(\alpha\), \(N_{e,\text{par}}\) and \(A_{\text{ret}}\) would flag a panel like this one is not tested here, and the study is not an argument for a coancestry constraint over a distance constraint.
Other calibration benchmarks, all from abstracts: 329 North American ex-PVP (expired Plant Variety Protection) dent inbreds resolve into eight admixture subgroups reflecting heterotic patterns and company of origin (White et al. 2020); in China summer maize (490 inbreds, 525,141 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)), 66.05% of pairs show relative kinship near zero (Shu et al. 2021); sweet corn shows lower diversity, PIC and MAF than field corn across 514 versus 181 lines (Yang et al. 2024).

title: 21  What the plant literature establishes
text:
21.4 Heterotic groups

21.4.1 Assignment is not a solved problem
Records that compare ways of assigning lines to groups report different winners. In 41 early-maturing yellow inbreds crossed to five testers, the HSGCA method (heterotic-group-specific and general combining ability) was more effective than the alternatives compared, which the abstract does not list (Annor et al. 2020). In a 19-line diallel, crosses between groups formed on simple sequence repeat (SSR) markers linked to yield-contributing traits showed no superiority, whereas inter-group crosses formed on random SSRs were superior to intra-group crosses (Kumar et al. 2022). In the 376-line panel of Mukiti et al. (2025), the IBS distance with average-linkage clustering gave the highest cophenetic correlation among the methods compared and yielded three groups (Mukiti et al. 2025); a cophenetic correlation measures the fit of a tree to a distance matrix, not agreement with testcross performance. These are three records on panels of 19 to 376 lines with different criteria. They do not show a consistent winner, but I did not tabulate winners across the plant file, so “no consistent winner” is not a finding of the corpus.
This matters for the pipeline: the line-level collapse assumes pool structure is given. Group assignment is itself contested, so the pool-balance constraint inherits whatever uncertainty the assignment method carries. Treat it as an uncertain input, not a fixed given.


21.4.2 A longitudinal programme, and what it can and cannot show
Kadoumi et al. (2025) analysed forty years of breeding data and about 84,000 genotypes from one private European dent maize programme. Their abstract states that differentiation between Stiff Stalk (SS) and Non-Stiff Stalk (NSS) groups increased significantly over time while genetic diversity within both groups declined. Their results are narrower. \(F_{ST}\) between the groups rose from 0.178 to 0.223. \(H_e\) fell from 0.371 to 0.279 in NSS, while \(H_e\) of SS remained stable (0.278 to 0.281), but in the full text the proportion of SS markers with \(\text{MAF} < 0.05\) “also increased by 20.76 %, reaching 22.3 % of SNPs in era 4”, so the stability of \(H_e\) in SS does not mean an unchanged allele-frequency spectrum. The abstract states that marker fixation and linkage disequilibrium increased; I did not locate an SS-specific linkage-disequilibrium result and claim none. The mean between-group Hamming distance fell slightly, from 0.430 to 0.420. The authors attribute the main germplasm-wide loss to the merging and homogenisation of the Iodent and Lancaster groups into NSS, so NSS was not a closed pool. They call the changes “not critical” and say they “only suggest that increased caution in diversity management is now needed”. They write that, without phenotypic information, they “can only speculate” that selection caused the rise in divergence. Before the genomic-selection era (eras 0-2) the dataset holds only the inbreds that fed the modern programme, a survivor sample whose bias in the early diversity estimates they call uncertain in order of magnitude and direction. They recommend enhancing group divergence while preserving diversity across selection cycles. Section 1.1 gives the same numbers with their limits; Heerwaarden et al. (2012), outside this corpus’s window, report increasing separation of breeding pools across the history of North American maize lines and attribute little of the genome-wide pattern to selection.
This is one company’s programme, observed, with a merger and a survivor sample, and no counterfactual. It shows that falling diversity in one group and rising \(F_{ST}\) occurred together in a commercial programme. It does not show that a constraint is needed, and it does not isolate drift or selection as the cause. The between-group Hamming distance, the quantity nearest the hybrid’s heterozygosity (Section 1.1), fell while \(F_{ST}\) rose, and it is not a column of the panel s1_monitor() logs (Table 13.3). The paper is one programme with both movements, not a test of that panel (Chapter 13).
What the plant literature adds on why divergence is held, not maximised, is narrower than the book’s argument. Beugnot et al. (2023), in a Dent-by-Flint factorial and a diallel of admixed lines, report additive and dominance quantitative trait locus (QTL) effects for hybrid performance that are background-specific, depending on the heterotic group of origin of the allele, and say that group complementarity and differentiation increase over time. That supports background-specific effects. That divergence is not a bonus is the book’s argument: under drift, with a dominance coefficient drawn independently of the frequencies, expected heterosis is invariant to the divergence of the pools (\(F_{BN}\)), and under selection what happens to it can go either way (Section 5.8, Section 5.9). That is Trap 3 of Chapter 13: the prescription agrees, by a different mechanism from the one the QTL result suggests.
Crossing across the heterotic boundary for germplasm enhancement generated usable variation: in a connected population from four heterotic groups, 10.8% of the hybrids of one population (POP5/C229) exceeded the high-yielding check ND678 (Cheng et al. 2025). One population and one check bear on pre-breeding; they do not bear on whether the commercial hybrid-parent pools should be crossed. My reading is that the boundary is maintained for hybrid-parent pools and porous for pre-breeding.

title: 21  What the plant literature establishes
text:
21.5 Selecting within the pool

21.5.1 The constraint alone is not sufficient
Optimal cross selection under a diversity constraint is simulated in a crop in a two-part programme with rapid recurrent genomic selection by Gorjanc et al. (2018) (animal file). In a simulation of a global programme with bridging and elite components, Sanchez et al. (2023) conclude that, with realistic plant breeding population sizes, diversity depletion in closed programmes “appears ineluctable”, calling for the introduction of relevant diversity donors; bridging populations made by crossing genetic resources to elite lines, taking 25% of experimental resources, appear highly beneficial in their simulations, with optimal cross selection maintaining a constant diversity to incorporate improved donors.

Inference, from one simulation under its assumptions: a constraint on the existing pool can slow the loss of diversity but may not stop it. Plan periodic external injections rather than treating the line pool as closed. Chapter 23 simulates an injection in the book’s own setting; that is not an operating programme.



21.5.2 Cycle length, and what goes unreported
Shortening cycles is reported with gain-rate benefits in simulation and in one breeding programme:

In a simulation of a sorghum programme in Haiti, genomic-assisted recurrent selection at two or three cycles a year had a maximum relative genetic gain advantage over phenotypic recurrent selection at one cycle a year of 12-88% for an oligogenic architecture and 26-165% for a polygenic one, observed for the oligogenic case only in the first few cycles. Prediction accuracy declined substantially after several cycles, and for small populations and oligogenic traits the cost per unit gain was lower under phenotypic selection (Muleta et al. 2019).
In intermediate wheatgrass, genomic selection from 2017 cut the generation time from 2-5 years to one cycle a year. About 100 of about 4,000 seedlings were chosen as parents on their genomic estimated breeding value (GEBV); the genomic relationship matrix was used to represent genetic diversity in the 1,000-1,200-genet validation populations that train the model, not in parent selection (Crain et al. 2021).
In simulation, two-cycle genomewide selection in maize gave 124-178% of the largest gain from phenotypic selection at the same cost and time; the abstract reports no diversity metric (Bernardo 2021).

The diversity cost per unit of cycle-time reduction is not established in the plant file. It is addressed only in part elsewhere. Gorjanc et al. (2018) (animal file) simulates optimal cross selection under rapid recurrent genomic selection, and Chapter 22 measures the relative loss of gene diversity from year 1 to year 15 in paired simulated runs with genomic selection switched on in year 6, in an inbred-line, wheat-type programme, and reports the mean cycle length of each arm beside it; that is a stock after fifteen years, not a cost per unit of cycle-time reduction, which Chapter 22 does not compute. Neither is a hybrid maize programme, so the item stays open as worded.
Simulation of reciprocal recurrent selection in hybrid rice finds that larger population sizes give the highest rates of improvement and the smallest decrease in additive genetic variance due to drift (Fritsche-Neto et al. 2023). That study predicts single-cross performance rather than shortening cycles, and its abstract says nothing about how diversity is managed.


21.5.3 What is hybrid-specific, and what is not
This distinction decides which literature transfers. Of the records the screen scored, every usefulness-criterion and progeny-variance study I found operates upstream, at inbred-line development: usefulness criterion with parental contributions for multi-parental crosses (Allier et al. 2019), barley validation against realised populations (Neyhart and Smith 2019), soybean family mean and variance prediction (Wartha and Lorenz 2024), wheat cross-progeny variance (Oget-Ebrad et al. 2024). None of them, in the abstracts and notes, operates on F1 hybrids of fixed inbreds. That is a negative on abstracts, and a paper that does so without saying it in the abstract is invisible to it.
That fits the book’s decision to drop the progeny-variance term for hybrids: all F1 hybrids of one pair of fixed inbreds are genetically identical, so there is no within-cross variance to predict after fixation, and the term is real only before it. It is why usefulness_criterion() belongs at S2 and nowhere else (Chapter 13).
One caution is hybrid-specific, and it concerns the mean, not diversity. Where dominance is present, the expected value of an F1 is not the mean of its parents’ additive values, and an additive-only index misses the specific combining ability (SCA) part (Section 5.11); the index of Chapter 14 is additive by construction, with no SCA. Two consequences are the book’s, not the corpus’s. The diversity side of the collapse (Section 12.1) holds whatever the index, but the mean index is a function of the line-usage vector only if it is additive in the parents. And the line merit of the rounded route of Chapter 17 is a general combining ability (GCA) against the opposite pool, a property of the line against that tester pool. So line-usage optimisation on \(\alpha\) should not be conflated with mean-performance ranking of the same crosses. I attach no source to the claim that hybrid-mean prediction gains from additive-plus-dominance models: the plant file holds records on hybrid prediction with dominance modelled (for example 10.3835/plantgenome2018.10.0082), which I have not read to a conclusion, and the book fits no dominance model in prediction.

title: 21  What the plant literature establishes
text:
21.6 Genebanks, core collections and introgression
Core-subset construction converges on a shared objective, maximising retained diversity at minimum accession count, but diverges on method: GenoCore selecting 310 from 3,333 sorghum accessions (Mufumbo et al. 2022); rice cores of 247 (core) and 30 from 2,242 accessions (Choudhury et al. 2021); a lettuce core of 268 from 811 accessions capturing 99.4% of total variation (Huo et al. 2025); cassava core collections built by two strategies (two plant-file records).
The quantitatively strongest result: in Arabidopsis, Populus and sorghum panels, marker-based subsets captured 3-78-fold more haplotypic diversity than subsets from geographic or environmental data (Reeves et al. 2020). For cores assembled in those settings, assemble them on markers.
Maize-specific core-collection algorithm choice is not established in the retrieved set. Maize genetic-resource work in it is oriented toward bridging and targeted introgression instead:

DNA-pool genotyping of 156 landraces (2,340 individuals) against 327 elite lines spanning the 20th century gave two indicators of a landrace’s genomic contribution to elite germplasm (Arca et al. 2023). The abstract reports that lines derived from landraces with limited contributions enriched the haplotype diversity of the reference lines more than those from high-contribution landraces.
Haplotype mining in about 1,000 landrace-derived doubled haploids (DH) found landrace haplotypes outperforming breeding-line alternatives, stable across populations and environments (Mayer et al. 2020).
Rapid-cycling genomic selection within a landrace population (899 DH lines for training, 600K array) improves donor material before it contacts the elite pool; the abstract also reports that prediction accuracies declined across cycles (Polzer et al. 2025).
For capturing landrace variation, the doubled-haploid route beats gamete capture in prediction accuracy (Hölker et al. 2022).

A \(\theta\)- or \(N_s\)-based accounting of introgression cost against a same-size resampling baseline is not established in the retrieved set.

title: 21  What the plant literature establishes
text:
21.7 Matrix choice: the animal file
The animal file tags 163 records with the theme “Coancestry / relationship matrix choice”. In the records read for this chapter the optimal-contribution selection (OCS, Chapter 15) or optimal-cross framework is common ground and the matrix placed inside it is not settled. The records differ in species, criterion and design:

Drift-, homozygosity- and identity-by-descent (IBD)-based inbreeding could differ substantially in genomic OCS unless diversity management was based upon IBD , Chapter 10.
A deviation-based coancestry matrix retained more genetic variability, while VanRaden’s kept allele frequencies closer to those of the base population (Morales-González et al. 2021). The criteria differ, so this is a trade-off between variability kept and frequency change.
A linkage-and-pedigree-informed matrix had the highest correlation with the true IBD, the most accurate rate of inbreeding \(\Delta F\), and was the only scheme to stay below the inbreeding target while minimising frequency change at neutral loci (Wæge et al. 2026).
In pigs, genomic mating limited inbreeding accumulation better than other mating approaches at the same expected gain, and ROH-based relatedness in genomic mating gave faster gain than SNP-based relatedness (Zhao et al. 2023). That is a mate-allocation study, not OCS, and in the full text the authors saw no trend using ROH-based inbreeding coefficients to assess the inbreeding trend.

These records do not rank the matrices, and this book relies on no ranking (Section 12.6, caveats): a table of Chapter 10 reports that in the nine schemes of Meuwissen et al. (2020) the homozygosity-based matrix, to which the book’s \(\mathbf{f}\) is affine, misses the drift target by the widest margin. The line-level collapse of Section 12.1 is algebra for any symmetric line-level \(\mathbf{f}^L\), given that the hybrid-level matrix is defined by Equation 12.1; whether that definition is right for a centred VanRaden matrix is not established there, and managing on molecular coancestry controls homozygosity, not drift. So the open choice of matrix does not change the cost and identity results of Chapter 12 and does change what the constraint controls.
On allelic variation, Allendorf et al. (2024) write about the expected number of alleles per locus at drift-mutation equilibrium in a species-conservation setting, which is the fourth sense of allelic richness (Section 21.1) and not \(A_{\text{ret}}\). They report that allelic variation is much more sensitive to bottlenecks than heterozygosity, that the usual adjustments of \(N_e\) for departures from the ideal population do not predict the loss of allelic variation well, that the expected number of alleles at equilibrium is linearly related to the reduction of the census size, and they recommend extending the guideline of long-term \(N_e > 500\) to allelic variation. Those results concern multiallelic loci. The book has not shown that they transfer to \(A_{\text{ret}}\) on biallelic SNPs of inbred lines, Section 11.5 declines the transfer, and Chapter 12 says that whether the MAF-threshold loss and allelic richness carry the same information was not examined. The paper is a reason to expect allele counts and heterozygosity to respond differently to a bottleneck, which is why \(A_{\text{ret}}\) is reported beside \(\alpha\). It does not test the recommendation.
On effective size, Toro et al. (2020) report in their abstract that under optimal molecular management the rate-based \(N_e = 1/(2\Delta F)\) takes negative values in early generations and reaches no asymptote in the long term (abstract only, as in Section 11.3). Allendorf et al. (2024) is a statement about \(N_e\) as a predictor of allelic loss. The first cautions against reading a rate-based \(N_e\) off a managed population, and the second is a separate limit of \(N_e\); Section 12.6 says not to report a rate-based \(N_e\) under active management, and reports \(N_s\) as a descriptor of a plan. That is not a recommendation to stop measuring \(\Delta F\): Chapter 12 monitors \(F_{drift}\) and \(F_{hom}\) against the random-subset null, and Chapter 23 measures \(\Delta F\) from the trajectory of \(F_{\text{drift}}\) with a diagnostic for a saturating series.

title: 21  What the plant literature establishes
text:
21.8 Optimisation machinery reported in plants
This is where the corpus is thinnest. In the abstracts and notes the screen read:

Optimal contribution methods in plant records (for example Sanchez et al. (2023)) do not state solver type, runtime or complexity class.
Core-subset search is greedy or distance-based heuristic; only input and output set sizes are reported, not runtime.
Evolutionary and metaheuristic algorithms are applied in plants, to other objectives. Yadav et al. (2025) (animal file) compare a genetic algorithm (GA), differential evolution (DE), particle swarm optimisation (PSO) and simulated annealing (SA) for choosing parents under Optimal Haplotype Selection and Optimal Population Value (OPV), on 583 wheat lines with 29,972 SNPs scored for stripe rust. Yadav et al. (2026) (animal file) use a genetic algorithm to select 50 donor parents for introgression into one elite cultivar. Villiers et al. (2024) (plant file), titled “Evolutionary computing to assemble standing genetic diversity …”, compare optimal haplotype stacking, optimal population value, truncation and OCS over 100 generations in a wheat simulation: OCS and truncation had exhausted diversity while considerable diversity remained under haplotype stacking. A plant-file record optimises breeding-programme design by stochastic simulation with evolutionary algorithms (10.1093/g3journal/jkae248); I have not read it beyond its note.
Problem sizes are reported as candidate-cross counts (330,078 possible barley parent combinations, Neyhart and Smith (2019)) or collection sizes, never as optimiser performance.

In neither file does a record apply DE or another metaheuristic to a diversity-constrained selection of hybrids, or report a runtime or complexity comparison against quadratic-programming OCS solvers. The tasks of the records in this section are haplotype stacking and introgression, not selection under a coancestry constraint. That is a statement about notes and abstracts.
AlphaMate (Gorjanc and Hickey 2018), whose note in the animal file says it optimises with an evolutionary algorithm, has 58 citations at screening, rank 9 of 324 by citations in that file, so the file does not support calling it the most cited tool.
The ranking in Yadav et al. (2025) is of algorithms on one problem. As Chapter 17 reads it, the order by convergence area under the curve (AUC) for the OPV objective is GA 0.879, DE 0.860, PSO 0.820 and SA 0.769, with DE comparable in final fitness; the abstract says GA “consistently achieved high fitness and rapid convergence” and DE “showed robustness but required longer runtime and careful tuning”. The AUC values and the 583 are not in either CSV, whose note for the record only says that it compares DE, GA, PSO and SA, and are in no versioned file here. This is evidence about algorithms on a haplotype objective. It is not evidence about encodings: Finding 4 of Section 12.4 is a verdict on the N-dimensional key encoding at one budget (three seeds, one setup, four restrictions), and Chapter 17 finds sel_de() ahead of the line-encoded DE only without a cap and a swap local search ahead of both at equal wall-clock. For this book’s problem the algorithm and its move structure matter as well as the encoding. The wheat study tests neither claim: it has a different objective, no OCS and no swap local search.

title: 21  What the plant literature establishes
text:
21.9 What remains unestablished
Stated strictly, from the screened abstracts and notes. The distinction that matters is between unestablished in the literature, the claim of this chapter, and unaddressed in this book. Table 21.3 lists the items and, for each, the answer the book gives. Those answers are simulations and measurements under stated assumptions, none from an operating programme; they narrow what the book leaves open and do not change what the corpus establishes. The third and seventh rows rest on Chapter 23 and Chapter 22, which had no final review record when this chapter was reviewed; read them as conditional on those chapters. The seventh row’s answer is a year-15 stock beside the arms’ mean cycle lengths, not a rate per unit of cycle-time reduction.



Table 21.3: Items unestablished in the retrieved set, and where the book answers each in simulation or measurement.









Item (not in the retrieved set)
What the book gives, and its limits




DE or any metaheuristic on a \(\theta\)-constrained line-usage selection in maize
Line-encoded DE and a swap local search on simulated pools (Chapter 17); not maize data


Runtime or complexity comparison of OCS quadratic solvers and metaheuristics, any plant problem
Quadratic-programming OCS (Chapter 15) against metaheuristics on simulated data, at book and production scale (Chapter 17)


Proportional diversity loss against a same-size resampling baseline in an operating maize programme
None from a programme. Chapter 23 simulates the multi-cycle consequence and finds a gain crossover


Joint longitudinal reporting of \(A_{\text{ret}}\) with \(\theta\) or \(N_s\) in one hybrid programme
Reported together on simulated plans (Section 12.6); not longitudinal


Coancestry optimisation at the hybrid genome level, F1 maize
\(N \times N\) hybrid matrix in Chapter 15; its collapse to lines for inbred parents and an additive index in Section 12.1


Whether a dominance-informed term changes optimal-cross outcomes against the mean-only approach
Chapter 5 derives the term: expected heterosis is invariant to \(F_{BN}\) under neutral divergence, for a dominance coefficient independent of the frequencies, and a mean is not a ranking. Realised outcomes in a programme are untested either way


Diversity cost per unit of cycle-time reduction, rapid-cycling hybrid maize
Relative loss of gene diversity from year 1 to year 15 in an inbred-line, wheat-type simulated programme, with each arm’s mean cycle length (Chapter 22): a stock, not a per-cycle or per-year rate; not hybrid maize


ROH-based diversity metrics applied to maize hybrid pools
None. The usage table lists 22 records in its merged “Inbreeding coefficient / ROH” row, 5 in maize (external classification); the shipped metric_used column has 0 ROH records. Neither supports a hybrid-pool application


Per-evaluation computational cost of diversity metrics, in either file
Measured in Section 12.2 (cached external data) and in Chapter 17


Diversity metrics defined on hybrids rather than on lines
Hybrid-level \(\mathbf{f}\) in Chapter 11 and Section 1.2


Combinatorial equal-contribution (0/1) selection against continuous-contribution designs
Relaxation and rounding against the bound in Chapter 15 and Chapter 17

title: 21  What the plant literature establishes
text:
21.10 Consequences for the pipeline

Keep the two metrics of Section 12.6 inside the optimiser and report the wide package outside it.
Plan for periodic germplasm injection. On the one simulation reviewed (Sanchez et al. 2023), a closed elite pool depletes however well the within-pool constraint is managed.
Bridging, rather than direct introduction, for exotic material is the recommendation of the Sanchez et al. (2023) abstract, which I could not confirm against a direct-introduction arm; I read it as a hypothesis for this book, not as an established comparison. Sanchez et al. (2023) select donors on phenotype, not on genomic predictions calibrated on the ongoing programme. The choice of donor criterion is not established: Arca et al. (2023) report that lines derived from landraces with limited contributions enriched the haplotype diversity of the reference lines more than those from high-contribution landraces, and compare no ranking by contribution with a ranking by raw diversity.
Treat heterotic-group assignment as an uncertain input: the pool-balance constraint is only as good as the assignment behind it.
Hold between-pool divergence in a band rather than maximising it (Trap 3 of Chapter 13); the width of the band is a programme decision.
Do not conflate the diversity constraint with mean prediction. The diversity side is a function of line usage and needs no dominance model; the mean index needs one wherever dominance is present (a consequence of Section 5.11, not a corpus result).
Report the diversity cost per cycle explicitly when shortening cycles (Chapter 22 reports the year-15 stock and the cycle length, not a per-cycle rate).
If assembling a core or donor set, do it on markers rather than passport data, within the settings of Reeves et al. (2020).
Do not read a high marker-based distance as the absence of redundancy: a constraint on state-based \(f\) is a constraint on distance for inbred lines (Trap 1 of Chapter 13). In the 298-line study (Wegary et al. 2019) a large share of pairs is distant on the state scale while a majority is above 0.050 on the relative-kinship scale; the authors read both as redundancy. That the two scales disagree is this chapter’s inference, not a result of the study.
Validate on real genotypes the redundancy result of Section 12.3, which is cached external data with an unrecorded setting, before treating it as settled.

title: 22  A complete plant breeding programme, and what it costs in diversity
text:
22.1 The scheme
The seventh consequence for the pipeline drawn in Chapter 21 is to report the diversity cost per cycle explicitly whenever cycles are shortened. This chapter measures that cost in a whole programme, but as a stock: the change in gene diversity after 15 years, for arms whose cycle lengths in years it also states. It does not report a rate per cycle, because the cycles of the programme overlap (Section 22.7).
Chapter 9, built back in the Simulation part, assembled AlphaSimR’s primitives into a hybrid scheme: two heterotic pools, reciprocal testers, a commercial cross at the end. This chapter assembles the same primitives into the other kind of programme – an inbred-line pipeline, where the product is a variety rather than a hybrid, and where the organising problem is not which cross to sell but how many genotypes to carry through how many stages of field testing.
The scheme is the staged wheat programme of Gaynor et al. (2017), as reduced for the AlphaSimR course vignette (Gorjanc et al. (2022), week 5 C) and reduced further here (the configuration, and how it differs from both, is stated in Section 22.1). It is a stylised inbred-line programme, not a survey of programmes in use. It is worth building because it exposes something the hybrid chapter cannot: the trade between the number of genotypes tested and the precision with which each is measured. A breeder has a fixed number of plots. Spending them on more entries scored once or fewer entries scored with eight replicates (the course calls replicates “locations”; they are not locations here, see Section 22.1.1) is the same budget spent two ways, and the staged trial is the standard compromise. This chapter sets that trade up but does not measure it: it never varies the number of entries against the replication at a fixed number of plots. The Mating and testing design part measures allocation of plots between crosses and locations, for hybrids, in Chapter 18, Chapter 19 and Chapter 20; none of those chapters is a measurement on this inbred-line programme.
Then the chapter does what the course vignette does not (it reports the genetic mean and variance only): it puts the book’s diversity machinery over the result, and asks what the faster programme spends to be faster.
The configuration. It is the author’s own reduction, not the course’s and not Gaynor et al.’s. Gaynor et al. (Table 1 and the Methods, pp. 2375-2377) start from 50 founders and run 100 crosses a year, 100 doubled-haploid (DH) lines per cross, 10,000 headrows, 500 lines in the preliminary trial, 50 in the advanced trial and 10 in the elite trial. The course vignette reduces that to 30 founders on 21 chromosomes, 30 crosses, 50 DH lines per cross (1500 headrows), at most 10 lines per cross into the preliminary trial and 300, 25 and 5 entries in the three trials, with 50 causal sites (quantitative trait loci, QTL) per chromosome. The values below (sch) reduce it again; Figure 22.1 draws the stages.
Show code
sch <- list(
  n_founders = 40, n_chr = 10, n_qtl = 60,   # founder genomes
  n_neutral = 0,                             # neutral sites per chromosome (0 = every site is a QTL)
  n_crosses  = 20, n_dh = 20, fam_max = 5,   # crossing and DH production
  n_pyt = 60, n_ayt = 12, n_eyt = 4,         # entries per yield trial
  rep_hdrw = 1/4, rep_pyt = 1, rep_ayt = 4, rep_eyt = 8,   # replicates per stage
  var_e = 0.4, gs_boost = 3, n_burn = 7, n_years = 15,
  gs_from = 6                                # first year a genomic arm switches on
)
n_hdrw <- sch$n_crosses * sch$n_dh           # every DH line is scored in the headrows
fx <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf("%.*f", d, x)   # fixed decimals for inline numbers
n_probe <- 48                                # seeds of the neutral-locus probe
Figure 22.1: The staged inbred-line programme at the scale of sch. Entries fall at every stage while replication – the number of replicates (reps) each entry is scored with – rises. Parents for the next cycle are recycled from the late trials (solid) or, in the arms with lever 2 and in the phenotype-only control of Section 22.4, from the preliminary trial as well (dashed). DH: doubled haploid; PYT, AYT, EYT: preliminary, advanced and elite yield trial.
Seven stages (Figure 22.1), and the logic connecting them is a single idea: at every step, entries fall and replication rises. 400 doubled-haploid lines are scored once, cheaply, in unreplicated headrows; 60 survive into a preliminary yield trial (PYT) with 1 replicate; 12 into an advanced trial (AYT) with 4; 4 into an elite trial (EYT) with 8. The number of entries falls by factors of 6.7, 5.0 and 3.0 over the three steps, not by a constant factor.
rep_hdrw = 1/4 is the course’s device for a stage less precise than a single plot: headrows are scored visually on a short row, which carries less information than one replicated plot, so the plot-error variance is multiplied by four. fam_max caps how many DH lines any one cross may contribute to the preliminary trial – selectWithinFam() from Chapter 9’s Step 6, holding the genetic base open against a truncation that would otherwise take the whole trial from the two best crosses.
crumbs: 22  A complete plant breeding programme, and what it costs in diversity

title: 22  A complete plant breeding programme, and what it costs in diversity
text:
22.1.1 What reps does, and what it does not
reps in setPheno() is the argument Chapter 9’s Step 2 flagged as the plant idiom, and the course calls its values “locations”. It divides the plot-error variance varE by the number of replicates and nothing else. The genotype-by-environment (GxE) term enters a phenotype differently. In AlphaSimR 2.1.0 the trait of addTraitAG(varGxE = ) gives each entry a deviate \(g_i\) of variance varGxE, and a setPheno() call multiplies every \(g_i\) by one standard-normal draw \(z\) made for that call and shared by all entries of the call; reps does not average it. The chunk checks that structure by its consequence, in two parts. With varE = 0, the departures of the phenotypes from the genetic values over four calls (two with reps = 1, two with reps = 8) are one vector scaled four times, so the matrix has rank one: one shared deviate per call. That check is blind to a rescaling of each call, so it cannot say whether reps divides the GxE term; the second part measures it directly, as the mean squared departure over 2000 calls at reps = 1 and at reps = 8, which would fall eight-fold at reps = 8 if reps averaged GxE. The chunk then measures the accuracy of an entry mean (Table 22.1), \(r = \text{cor}(\text{genetic value}, \text{phenotype})\) over the 40 founders, as the number of replicates grows, with and without the GxE term.


Show code
set.seed(7)
fg_acc <- quickHaplo(nInd = 40, nChr = 10, segSites = 60, inbred = TRUE)
mk <- function(vg) {
  SP <- SimParam$new(fg_acc)
  SP$addTraitAG(nQtlPerChr = 60, mean = 4, var = 0.1, varGxE = vg)
  list(SP = SP, pop = newPop(fg_acc, simParam = SP))
}
# GxE enters as g_i * z, one z per call: varE = 0 leaves a rank-one residual matrix
m <- mk(0.2)
res <- sapply(c(1, 1, 8, 8), function(r)
  setPheno(m$pop, varE = 0, reps = r, onlyPheno = TRUE, simParam = m$SP)[, 1] -
    gv(m$pop)[, 1])
sv <- svd(res)[["d"]]
stopifnot(sv[2] < 1e-8 * sv[1])
set.seed(5)
msq <- sapply(c(1, 8), function(r) mean(replicate(2000,
  (setPheno(m$pop, varE = 0, reps = r, onlyPheno = TRUE, simParam = m$SP)[, 1] -
     gv(m$pop)[, 1])^2)))
stopifnot(msq[2] / msq[1] > 0.5)          # eight-fold division would give 0.125
acc <- function(vg, r, seed = 11) {
  m <- mk(vg); set.seed(seed)
  a <- replicate(300, cor(gv(m$pop)[, 1],
                          setPheno(m$pop, varE = sch$var_e, reps = r,
                                   onlyPheno = TRUE, simParam = m$SP)[, 1]))
  c(mean(a), stats::sd(a))
}
reps_grid <- c(0.25, 1, 3, 4, 8)

The mean squared departure of the phenotype from the genetic value, with varE = 0, is 0.202 at reps = 1 and 0.200 at reps = 8, against varGxE = 0.2: reps does not divide the GxE term (it would give 0.025 at 8 if it did). The founders’ additive variance is 0.103 (var = 0.1), so the GxE variance of 0.2 is about twice it. Eight replicates raise the accuracy of an entry mean from 0.40 to 0.63 with the GxE term, against 0.45 to 0.82 without it, and the standard deviation across calls stays at 0.18 where the GxE term is present against 0.04 where it is not. Selection accuracy at the last stage is higher because the plot-error variance has been divided by eight, not because the trait became more heritable; but it is bounded by a GxE term that replication does not reduce and that changes from call to call. What the chapter exposes is therefore the trade between entries and plot-error precision under one shared, random environmental shift per setPheno() call, and not between entries and independent locations. section: 22.2 Why a breeding programme needs a burn-in
crumbs: 22  A complete plant breeding programme, and what it costs in diversity

title: 22  A complete plant breeding programme, and what it costs in diversity
text:
22.3 One programme, fifteen years
The whole scheme is one function. It is written out rather than packaged because the loop is the thing being taught, and because a reader adapting it to their own programme will edit the loop, not call it. Its argument arm selects one of five programmes, all sharing the burn-in and the stage sizes of sch:

"ps", the phenotypic programme: selection on phenotype throughout; parents are all n_eyt + n_ayt lines of the EYT and the AYT, so there is no truncation at the parents’ step.
"l1", lever 1 alone: from year gs_from, the PYT-to-AYT step uses a surrogate genomic value; parents as in "ps".
"l2", lever 2 alone: from year gs_from, parents are the best n_eyt + n_ayt of the n_eyt + n_ayt + n_pyt lines of EYT, AYT and PYT by the surrogate genomic value (raw phenotype for the EYT and AYT lines, the surrogate for the PYT lines); the PYT-to-AYT step is phenotypic.
"gs", both levers.
"ctl", a control for lever 2: parents are the best n_eyt + n_ayt of the same n_eyt + n_ayt + n_pyt lines, truncated by plain phenotype, with no surrogate anywhere.

The surrogate genomic value is a phenotype of the same line simulated at gs_boost times the PYT replication, in a separate setPheno() call; its accuracy is the row 3 of Table 22.1 (0.54 with GxE, 0.66 without), and it is a phenotypic correlation, not a prediction accuracy fitted from markers. In "l2" and "ctl" the candidates come from different cohorts and different setPheno() calls, so the selection criterion compares lines measured with unequal precision and under different GxE deviates; this is part of what the arms do, and the control inherits it.


Show code
gd_of <- function(pop, SP, loci = c("qtl", "neutral")) {
  loci <- match.arg(loci)
  g <- pullSegSiteGeno(pop, simParam = SP)
  is_q <- colnames(g) %in% colnames(pullQtlGeno(pop, simParam = SP))
  1 - mean(molecular_coancestry(
    g[, if (loci == "qtl") is_q else !is_q, drop = FALSE] / 2))
}

run_programme <- function(cfg, seed, arm = c("ps", "l1", "l2", "gs", "ctl")) {
  arm <- match.arg(arm)
  lever1 <- arm %in% c("l1", "gs")   # surrogate genomic value for PYT -> AYT
  lever2 <- arm %in% c("l2", "gs")   # parents from c(EYT, AYT, PYT)
  stopifnot(cfg$n_burn >= 7)
  # founders: re-drawn per arm from the same seed (quickHaplo() is deterministic)
  set.seed(seed)
  fg <- quickHaplo(nInd = cfg$n_founders, nChr = cfg$n_chr,
                   segSites = cfg$n_qtl + cfg$n_neutral, inbred = TRUE)
  SP <- SimParam$new(fg)
  SP$addTraitAG(nQtlPerChr = cfg$n_qtl, mean = 4, var = 0.1, varGxE = 0.2)
  ph <- function(p, r) setPheno(p, varE = cfg$var_e, reps = r, simParam = SP)

  # --- burn-in: fill every stage with a cohort of the right age ---
  Parents <- newPop(fg, simParam = SP)
  gd_founders <- gd_of(Parents, SP)
  nb <- cfg$n_burn
  for (year in 1:nb) {
    F1 <- randCross(Parents, cfg$n_crosses, simParam = SP)
    if (year < nb)     DH   <- makeDH(F1, cfg$n_dh, simParam = SP)
    if (year < nb - 1) HDRW <- ph(DH, cfg$rep_hdrw)
    if (year < nb - 2) {
      PYT <- selectWithinFam(HDRW, nInd = cfg$fam_max, use = "pheno", simParam = SP)
      PYT <- ph(selectInd(PYT, nInd = cfg$n_pyt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
                cfg$rep_pyt)
    }
    if (year < nb - 3)
      AYT <- ph(selectInd(PYT, nInd = cfg$n_ayt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
                cfg$rep_ayt)
    if (year < nb - 4)
      EYT <- ph(selectInd(AYT, nInd = cfg$n_eyt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
                cfg$rep_eyt)
  }

  # --- advancing years, last stage first so each reads the previous cohort ---
  out <- data.frame(year = 1:cfg$n_years, meanG = NA_real_, varG = NA_real_,
                    acc_pyt = NA_real_, gd_pyt = NA_real_, gd_parents = NA_real_,
                    gd_pyt_neutral = NA_real_, par_eyt = NA_integer_,
                    par_ayt = NA_integer_, par_pyt = NA_integer_)
  for (year in 1:cfg$n_years) {
    on <- year >= cfg$gs_from          # the switch of the arm is on from this year

    # (the released variety, the best EYT entry, is not tracked: the chapter
    #  measures the pipeline, not the released line)
    EYT <- ph(selectInd(AYT, nInd = cfg$n_eyt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
              cfg$rep_eyt)

    if (lever1 && on) {  # lever 1: a more accurate criterion at the PYT stage
      PYT@ebv <- setPheno(PYT, varE = cfg$var_e,
                          reps = cfg$rep_pyt * cfg$gs_boost,
                          onlyPheno = TRUE, simParam = SP)
      AYT <- ph(selectInd(PYT, nInd = cfg$n_ayt, use = "ebv", simParam = SP),
                cfg$rep_ayt)
    } else {
      AYT <- ph(selectInd(PYT, nInd = cfg$n_ayt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
                cfg$rep_ayt)
    }

    PYT <- selectWithinFam(HDRW, nInd = cfg$fam_max, use = "pheno", simParam = SP)
    PYT <- ph(selectInd(PYT, nInd = cfg$n_pyt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
              cfg$rep_pyt)
    HDRW <- ph(DH, cfg$rep_hdrw)
    DH   <- makeDH(F1, cfg$n_dh, simParam = SP)

    if (lever2 && on) {  # lever 2: recycle parents a year earlier, from the PYT
      PYT@ebv <- setPheno(PYT, varE = cfg$var_e,
                          reps = cfg$rep_pyt * cfg$gs_boost,
                          onlyPheno = TRUE, simParam = SP)
      EYT@ebv <- pheno(EYT); AYT@ebv <- pheno(AYT)
      Parents <- selectInd(c(EYT, AYT, PYT), nInd = cfg$n_eyt + cfg$n_ayt,
                           use = "ebv", simParam = SP)
    } else if (arm == "ctl" && on) {   # control: the same wider set, plain phenotype
      Parents <- selectInd(c(EYT, AYT, PYT), nInd = cfg$n_eyt + cfg$n_ayt,
                           use = "pheno", simParam = SP)
    } else {
      Parents <- c(EYT, AYT)
    }
    F1 <- randCross(Parents, cfg$n_crosses, simParam = SP)

    out$meanG[year]      <- meanG(PYT)
    out$varG[year]       <- varG(PYT)
    out$acc_pyt[year]    <- stats::cor(PYT@gv[, 1], PYT@pheno[, 1])
    out$gd_pyt[year]     <- gd_of(PYT, SP)
    out$gd_parents[year] <- gd_of(Parents, SP)
    if (cfg$n_neutral > 0) out$gd_pyt_neutral[year] <- gd_of(PYT, SP, "neutral")
    out$par_eyt[year] <- sum(Parents@id %in% EYT@id)
    out$par_ayt[year] <- sum(Parents@id %in% AYT@id)
    out$par_pyt[year] <- sum(Parents@id %in% PYT@id)
  }
  out$gd_founders <- gd_founders
  out
}


Two details are worth pausing on.
The advancing loop runs backwards. The elite trial is filled before the advanced trial is refilled, which is before the preliminary trial is refilled. Written in the other order, EYT would be selected from an AYT that had already been overwritten with this year’s cohort, and the programme would advance two stages per year without anyone noticing. Ordering is the whole correctness argument of a staged simulation.
Progress is reported at the PYT. It is the first stage with a yield phenotype and the last with enough entries for a variance to mean anything – meanG on four elite lines is noise. This is the course’s choice and it is the right one.
The phenotypic arm on seed 1 is the first run (Table 22.2).

Genetic mean rises, genetic variance falls, and gene diversity of the preliminary trial falls with it. Nothing here is surprising; what matters is that all three are now being measured on the same run.






ImportantThese numbers are reproducible



The founders come from quickHaplo(), which is seeded by set.seed(), so run_programme(sch, seed = 1) returns the same data frame every time – unlike Chapter 9’s Step 8, whose runMacs2() founders are not reproducible. That is what makes the paired comparison below legitimate: the phenotypic and genomic arms are run from the same seed, so they share founders, and every difference between them is attributable to the scheme.
This is a documented exception to rule 1 of Chapter 9’s Step 1 (found the founders once and branch every arm off that object): each arm here re-draws its founders from the same seed. It is safe only because quickHaplo() is plain R sampling; the design chunk below asserts, for every seed, that years 1 to 5 (burn-in and the years before the arms differ) are identical across the five arms, which they could not be if the founders differed.

title: 22  A complete plant breeding programme, and what it costs in diversity
text:
22.4 Genomic selection: two levers, separated
Genomic selection is usually described as buying accuracy. In a staged programme it can buy two things, and the arms above have a switch for each:

Accuracy earlier in the cycle (lever 1). A prediction is available on a line that has been genotyped but barely phenotyped, so the advance from preliminary to advanced trial can be made on better information than one replicate of yield.
A shorter generation interval (lever 2). Parents can be recycled from the preliminary trial instead of waiting for the elite trial. Define the cycle length \(T\) of a parent as the years from the crossing that produced its cohort to the crossing that uses it. By the loop above a cross in year \(t\) gives DH lines in year \(t+1\), headrows in \(t+2\), the PYT in \(t+3\), the AYT in \(t+4\) and the EYT in \(t+5\), and the parents are chosen in the year their cohort is in the trial: \(T = 3\), \(4\), \(5\) years for a parent taken from the PYT, the AYT and the EYT.

The breeder’s equation of Chapter 4, \(R = i\,r\,\sigma_A\) (Equation 4.1), is the response to one round of selection: \(i\) the intensity, \(r\) the accuracy and \(\sigma_A\) the additive standard deviation. A response per year is that response divided by the years \(T\) a round takes. That division is the chapter’s own bookkeeping, not an equation of Chapter 4, and it assumes discrete rounds of a common length (assumption A4 of Chapter 10), which this overlapping programme, with parents of three different lengths, only approximates. It is used below to read a direction, not to predict a number.
Two statements in the literature are about these levers, and neither transfers as a ratio. Gaynor et al. (2017) report, in their simulations, that a genomic programme that changes accuracy only gained 1.21 (95 % confidence interval, CI, 1.18-1.25) to 1.39 times the gain of the conventional programme, and the two-part programmes, which also shorten the cycle, 2.36 to 2.47 times (p. 2379; the ranges span their genotype-by-year variance settings, 0 and 10); they write that in the two-part programmes “the shortening of breeding cycle time was the major driver of increased genetic gain” (p. 2381). Their genomic programmes are cost-matched (fewer DH lines per cross to pay for genotyping, Table 1), whereas the genomic arms here are free. And Meuwissen et al. (2001) state in their abstract that marker-based selection could substantially increase the rate of genetic gain, especially if combined with reproductive techniques that shorten the generation interval (the full text was not consulted for this chapter). That the second lever is the larger is thus reported for one simulated design; what follows measures it for this one.
This chapter mimics the prediction rather than fitting one: ebv is filled with a phenotype simulated at gs_boost times the replication, which is a stand-in for a genomic prediction of the corresponding accuracy. Chapter 14 is where the book actually fits prediction models and measures what accuracy is attainable; the honest statement here is that this chapter assumes an accuracy (gs_boost = 3, the row 3 of Table 22.1) and studies its consequences, rather than earning it.

text:
22.5 The comparison, replicated
One run of one seed is an anecdote. Five arms are cheap enough to replicate. The design runs all five arms on 120 seeds (600 programme runs, several minutes to execute); the seeds are read in five batches of 24, because 24 seeds is a size a single experiment of this kind can easily have and the batches show how far such an experiment moves.


Show code
arms <- c(ps = "phenotypic", l1 = "lever 1 alone", l2 = "lever 2 alone",
          gs = "both levers", ctl = "control (phenotype-only truncation)")
seeds   <- 1:120
n_batch <- 24
batch   <- rep(seq_len(length(seeds) / n_batch), each = n_batch)
stopifnot(length(seeds) == 120, n_batch == 24, n_probe == 48)  # constants typed in captions
runs <- lapply(setNames(names(arms), names(arms)), function(a)
  lapply(seeds, function(s) run_programme(sch, s, a)))

# The pairing rests on identical history: years 1-5 equal across arms, every seed
for (a in names(arms)[-1]) for (i in seq_along(seeds))
  stopifnot(identical(runs[[a]][[i]][1:5, ], runs[["ps"]][[i]][1:5, ]))
stopifnot(identical(ps1, runs[["ps"]][[1]]), identical(gs1, runs[["gs"]][[1]]))

last <- sch$n_years
rate <- function(d)                       # slope of PYT genetic mean on year
  unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(meanG ~ year,
                               data = d[d$year >= sch$gs_from, ]))[2])
per_seed <- function(f) sapply(runs, function(r) vapply(r, f, numeric(1)))
S <- list(
  gain   = per_seed(rate),
  gd_pyt = per_seed(function(d) d[["gd_pyt"]][last]),
  gd_par = per_seed(function(d) d[["gd_parents"]][last]),
  par_eyt = per_seed(function(d) mean(d[["par_eyt"]][d$year >= sch$gs_from])),
  par_ayt = per_seed(function(d) mean(d[["par_ayt"]][d$year >= sch$gs_from])),
  par_pyt = per_seed(function(d) mean(d[["par_pyt"]][d$year >= sch$gs_from])))
# cycle length T (years) of the parents: 5, 4, 3 for EYT, AYT, PYT (see above)
S[["Tcyc"]] <- (5 * S[["par_eyt"]] + 4 * S[["par_ayt"]] + 3 * S[["par_pyt"]]) /
  (sch$n_eyt + sch$n_ayt)

se <- function(x) stats::sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))
contrast <- function(v, a, b, i = seq_along(seeds)) {
  d <- (S[[v]][, b] - S[[v]][, a])[i]
  c(diff = mean(d), se = se(d), t = mean(d) / se(d))
}
pairs <- list(c("ps", "l1"), c("ps", "l2"), c("ps", "gs"), c("ps", "ctl"),
              c("l1", "gs"), c("l2", "gs"), c("l2", "ctl"))
cx <- do.call(rbind, lapply(pairs, function(p) {
  g <- contrast("gain", p[1], p[2]); d <- contrast("gd_pyt", p[1], p[2])
  q <- contrast("gd_par", p[1], p[2])
  data.frame(gain_d = g[["diff"]], gain_se = g[["se"]], gain_t = g[["t"]],
             gdp_d = d[["diff"]], gdp_se = d[["se"]], gdp_t = d[["t"]],
             gdq_d = q[["diff"]], gdq_se = q[["se"]], gdq_t = q[["t"]])
}))
rownames(cx) <- vapply(pairs, function(p) paste(p[2], "-", p[1]), "")
K <- function(r, c, d = 4) fx(cx[r, c], d)     # inline accessor
t_crit_pooled <- stats::qt(0.975, length(seeds) - 1)
t_crit_batch  <- stats::qt(0.975, n_batch - 1)

# the same comparison, both levers against phenotypic, batch by batch
bt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(batch), function(b) {
  i <- batch == b
  g <- contrast("gain", "ps", "gs", i); d <- contrast("gd_pyt", "ps", "gs", i)
  q <- contrast("gd_par", "ps", "gs", i)
  data.frame(batch = as.character(b), seeds = paste(range(seeds[i]), collapse = "-"),
             gain_ratio = mean(S[["gain"]][i, "gs"]) / mean(S[["gain"]][i, "ps"]),
             gain_t = g[["t"]], gdp_d = d[["diff"]], gdp_t = d[["t"]],
             gdq_d = q[["diff"]], gdq_t = q[["t"]])
}))
pooled <- data.frame(batch = "pooled", seeds = paste(range(seeds), collapse = "-"),
  gain_ratio = mean(S[["gain"]][, "gs"]) / mean(S[["gain"]][, "ps"]),
  gain_t = cx["gs - ps", "gain_t"], gdp_d = cx["gs - ps", "gdp_d"],
  gdp_t = cx["gs - ps", "gdp_t"], gdq_d = cx["gs - ps", "gdq_d"],
  gdq_t = cx["gs - ps", "gdq_t"])


Table 22.4 gives each arm’s level, with the standard error over the 120 seeds; Table 22.5 gives the paired differences between arms, the mean over seeds of (second arm minus first arm), their standard errors, and \(t\) = mean/s.e. on 119 degrees of freedom (critical value 1.98 at the 5 % level, two-sided, for one comparison; seven comparisons are shown and none is corrected). The rate of gain is the slope of the genetic mean of the PYT on year over years 6 to 15; because a parent chosen in year 6 reaches the PYT three or more years later, that window includes years in which the arms have not yet diverged, so it is an average over a transient, not a steady-state rate. Figure 22.2 shows the genetic mean and the gene diversity of the PYT year by year.

Show code
# bootstrap over seeds (the unit of replication): ratios of mean gain against ps,
# and their excess over the ratio of mean cycle lengths, one resample for both
set.seed(1)
bres <- replicate(4000, {

    gap_ctl = g[["ctl"]] / g[["ps"]] - Tc[["ps"]] / Tc[["ctl"]])
})

gap <- c(l2 = g_all[["l2"]] / g_all[["ps"]] - Tc_all[["ps"]] / Tc_all[["l2"]],
         ctl = g_all[["ctl"]] / g_all[["ps"]] - Tc_all[["ps"]] / Tc_all[["ctl"]])
ci <- function(v, d = 2) paste(fx(bci[, v], d), collapse = " to ")
# the two statements the text makes about the intervals
stopifnot(bci[1, "gap_l2"] > 0, bci[1, "gap_ctl"] < 0, bci[2, "gap_ctl"] > 0)


Gain. The phenotypic arm gains 0.0575 (0.0013) per year (mean and s.e.). Relative to it, lever 1 alone adds 0.0086 (t = 7.2), lever 2 alone 0.0267 (t = 21.3) and both levers 0.0294 (t = 21.1); the ratio of the mean rates, both levers over phenotypic, is 1.51 (95 % bootstrap interval over seeds, 1.46 to 1.56). The two single effects add to 0.0353, more than the joint 0.0294, and adding lever 1 to lever 2 gives 0.0027 (t = 2.0). In this simulation, therefore, lever 2 contributes the larger part of the gain and lever 1 adds little once lever 2 is on. That is one configuration, with an assumed surrogate accuracy; it does not show that the second lever is normally the larger. Nor is it a statement about lever 1 in general: the PYT genetic mean that measures the gain is a lagged readout of a selection made one stage later, so lever 1 shows in it only through the parents.
The control recycles parents from the same wider set, but by plain phenotype. It gains 0.0184 per year over the phenotypic arm (t = 15.8), which is 69 % of lever 2’s gain, and differs from lever 2 alone by -0.0083 (t = -6.4). The mean cycle lengths \(T\) of Table 22.4 are 4.25 years for the phenotypic arm, 3.34 for lever 2 alone and 3.26 for the control. If \(i\,r\,\sigma_A\) per round were unchanged, the gain per year would scale as \(1/T\), by the ratio 1.27 for lever 2 alone and 1.30 for the control; the observed ratios of mean gains are 1.46 (95 % bootstrap interval over seeds, 1.42 to 1.51) and 1.32 (1.28 to 1.36). Lever 2’s ratio exceeds the ratio of cycle lengths by 0.19 (95 % interval, one resample of seeds for gains and cycle lengths, 0.14 to 0.24), an interval that excludes zero; the control’s exceeds it by 0.017 (-0.025 to 0.059), an interval that includes zero. The control’s ratio is therefore of the size of the shortening of the cycle, within this resolution; lever 2’s is larger. This is consistent with the surrogate genomic value in the parent choice adding to the accuracy \(r\) or the intensity \(i\) beyond what the shorter cycle gives, but neither \(i\) nor \(r\) is measured per round here, the rates are averages over a transient, and \(T\) is a mean of three parent sources; it is a reading, not a decomposition. The premise itself is a reference point, not a description of either arm: lever 2 and the control also change the intensity at the parent step, which takes the best 16 of 76 lines instead of all 16.
Diversity at year 15. Gene diversity of the PYT is 0.3660 (0.0020) in the phenotypic arm and 0.3438 (0.0030) with both levers (mean and s.e. over seeds). The paired difference is -0.0222 (s.e. 0.0035, t = -6.4), and the genomic arm is lower in 69 % of the seeds. Read in batches of 24 seeds (Table 22.6), the same difference has \(t\) between -4.8 and -1.3, and reaches the 5 % critical value (2.07 on 23 degrees of freedom) in 3 of 5 batches; the gain difference has \(t\) between 8.1 and 12.4 in every batch. The pooled sign of the diversity difference is therefore supported, and a 24-seed experiment is not enough to resolve it reliably: a single batch can show it as significant or not. The parent set (the population that actually transmits) has a pooled difference of -0.0286 (t = -8.1), beyond the batch critical value in 5 of 5 batches.

Which lever carries the loss. Lever 1 alone changes the PYT gene diversity at year 15 by -0.0035 (t = -1.3) and that of the parent set by -0.0124 (t = -4.9). Lever 2 alone changes them by -0.0242 (t = -6.5) and -0.0220 (t = -6.5). The control, with no genomic information at all, changes them by -0.0233 (t = -6.6) and -0.0286 (t = -7.9); against lever 2 alone the control differs by 0.0009 in the PYT (t = 0.2) and by -0.0066 in the parent set (t = -1.6). The year-15 loss of PYT diversity that goes with lever 2 is thus reproduced, within the resolution of 120 seeds (the standard error of the control-minus-lever-2 difference in the PYT is 0.0040), by truncating the same wider candidate set on plain phenotype. It does not need a genomic value. What it goes with is a different parent step: the phenotypic arm takes all 16 lines of the EYT and the AYT as parents, with no truncation, whereas the lever-2 arms and the control take the best 16 of 76, and 11.7 of them (lever 2) or 12.7 (control) come from the PYT. Lever 1 alone, whose parents are chosen as in the phenotypic arm, lowers the diversity of the parent set but its effect on the PYT is not resolved at this number of seeds; that is a statement about resolution, not about absence.
What was not measured is why. A natural hypothesis is that parents truncated from a wider set, and taken from a preliminary trial in which full sibs have not yet been separated by later trials, are more closely related to each other, and that a shorter interval accumulates coancestry faster per unit of time. This chapter does not test it: it records the gene diversity of the parent set, not the coancestry among the chosen parents, nor their family structure. Gaynor et al. (2017) give a different mechanism for the loss of genetic variance under genomic selection: the Bulmer effect of the increased selection accuracy in early stages, with effective population size, selection intensity, accuracy and the number of cycles per year as the factors of later changes (p. 2383). They name optimal contribution selection, with introgression, as an established remedy for the decline of genetic variance (p. 2382). That concerns variance, not molecular gene diversity, and supports the direction, not this mechanism.

22.6 The diversity ledger
The measurement above used gene diversity of the preliminary trial. The parent set is the population that actually transmits, and it is the one an optimal contribution scheme would act on. Table 22.7 gives both for the two extreme arms, averaged over the 120 seeds.


Show code
yrs <- c(1, 5, 10, 15)
lg <- function(a, v) sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)", avg(a, v)[yrs], avg_se(a, v)[yrs])
ledger <- data.frame(
  year       = yrs,
  gd_pyt_ps  = lg("ps", "gd_pyt"),  gd_pyt_gs  = lg("gs", "gd_pyt"),
  gd_par_ps  = lg("ps", "gd_parents"), gd_par_gs = lg("gs", "gd_parents"))
gd_found <- mean(vapply(runs[["ps"]], function(d) d[["gd_founders"]][1], numeric(1)))
# lines are DH (f_ii = 1), so theta = 1/n + (1 - 1/n) theta_off and GD = (1 - 1/n) GD_off,
# with GD_off = 1 - mean(f_ij, i != j): the gene diversity between distinct lines
gd_off <- function(gd, n) gd * n / (n - 1)
set.seed(1)
gchk <- matrix(rbinom(60 * 200, 1, 0.5), 60)          # 60 homozygous lines, 200 loci
fchk <- molecular_coancestry(gchk)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(gd_off(1 - mean(fchk), 60),
                           mean(1 - fchk[row(fchk) != col(fchk)]))))
n_of <- c(gd_pyt = sch$n_pyt, gd_parents = sch$n_eyt + sch$n_ayt)
off_found <- mean(vapply(runs[["ps"]], function(d)
  gd_off(d[["gd_founders"]][1], sch$n_founders), numeric(1)))
off_pyt1 <- mean(vapply(runs[["ps"]], function(d) gd_off(d[["gd_pyt"]][1], n_of[["gd_pyt"]]), numeric(1)))
off_par1 <- mean(vapply(runs[["ps"]], function(d) gd_off(d[["gd_parents"]][1], n_of[["gd_parents"]]), numeric(1)))
knitr::kable(ledger, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Year", "GD of PYT, ps", "GD of PYT, gs",
                           "GD of parents, ps", "GD of parents, gs"))

The base of these numbers is not the founders. The 40 founder lines have gene diversity 0.4875 (mean over seeds); by year 1, after the 7-year burn-in, the PYT is at 0.4682 and the parent set at 0.4435.






WarningGene diversity with the diagonal is not comparable across set sizes



These three levels are not on one scale: for fully homozygous lines the diagonal of \(f\) is 1, so that
\[
\theta = \frac{1}{n} + \Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{n}\Bigr)\theta_{\text{off}},
\qquad
GD = \Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{n}\Bigr)GD_{\text{off}},
\tag{22.1}\]
where \(\theta_{\text{off}}\) is the mean of \(f_{ij}\) over pairs of distinct lines and \(GD_{\text{off}} = 1 - \theta_{\text{off}}\) is the gene diversity between distinct lines (Equation 22.1 is checked in the chunk above on a random matrix of homozygous lines). \(GD_{\text{off}}\) does not carry the weight \(1/n\), which differs among \(n\) = 40 (founders), 60 (PYT) and 16 (parents). On that scale the founders are at 0.5000, the year-1 PYT at 0.4761 and the year-1 parent set at 0.4731. A part of the diversity of the founders has therefore gone before the first row of the table, by 0.027 for the parents on the \(GD_{\text{off}}\) scale, not by the 0.044 that the levels above suggest, 0.017 of which is the difference in diagonal weight between \(n\) = 40 and \(n\) = 16.


The loss is reported against both bases (Table 22.8), per seed, with the standard error over seeds.


Show code
loss <- function(a, v, base, off = TRUE) vapply(runs[[a]], function(d) {
  num <- d[[v]][last]
  den <- if (base == "year 1") d[[v]][1] else d[["gd_founders"]][1]
  if (off) {                                   # drop the diagonal of f before dividing
    num <- gd_off(num, n_of[[v]])
    den <- gd_off(den, if (base == "year 1") n_of[[v]] else sch$n_founders)
  }
  1 - num / den
}, numeric(1))
# against year 1 the numerator and denominator have the same n: the factor cancels
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(loss("gs", "gd_parents", "year 1"),
                           loss("gs", "gd_parents", "year 1", off = FALSE))))
ml <- function(a, v, base) { l <- loss(a, v, base); sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", mean(l), se(l)) }
tab_loss <- data.frame(
  arm = unname(arms),
  `PYT, year 1`      = vapply(names(arms), ml, "", v = "gd_pyt", base = "year 1"),
  `PYT, founders`    = vapply(names(arms), ml, "", v = "gd_pyt", base = "founders"),
  `parents, year 1`  = vapply(names(arms), ml, "", v = "gd_parents", base = "year 1"),
  `parents, founders` = vapply(names(arms), ml, "", v = "gd_parents", base = "founders"),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
tab_loss
