Result (Table 24.7). At cycle 5 the mean ratio is 0.64 (s.e. 0.04) for the unconstrained programme, 0.78 (0.07) for \(\alpha_{\max} = 0.02\) and 0.94 (0.06) for random selection: the realised variance is 36 %, 22 % and 6 % below the genic variance, the last being 1.0 standard errors from zero. Paired by founder draw, the constrained minus random ratio at cycle 5 is -0.16 (\(t =\) -1.43, 7 df). Over cycles 1 to 8 the ratios are 0.68 (0.03), 0.79 (0.05) and 1.00 (0.03).
Interpretation, and what limits it. Selection builds negative disequilibrium among unlinked loci in this simulation: the effect is negative in 6 of 8 seeds on the index scale and in 8 of 8 relative to genic variance. The seed-level tests carry the existence of the effect; the percentages of Table 24.7 carry its size, at eight seeds. What eight seeds do not resolve: the 6 % of the random arm at cycle 5 is within about one standard error of zero, and over cycles 1 to 8 the random arm shows no loss (1.00, s.e. 0.03), so the size of the loss in the control is not distinguished from none; the paired contrast of the constrained arm with the random arm at cycle 5 is not distinguished from zero either, so the difference between the percentages of those two arms at that cycle is not established (the constrained-minus-random effect over cycles 1 to 8 of Table 24.6, which averages eight cycles, is). The shrinking of the absolute gap in later cycles is consistent with the genic variance being used up, since the covariance term scales with the variance that remains (a reading, not tested separately).
On persistence: no trend of the relative effect is detected over cycles 1 to 8, but the slope has a 95 % interval that includes values at which the effect would reach zero near cycle 8.7 (from its mean at the middle of the window, cycle 4.5), so “no trend detected” is not evidence of no decay. What supports persistence is the late-window effect above (cycles 6 to 8), which is negative in the seeds counted above, and is itself post hoc. Late cycles of the relative measure beyond cycle 8 are ill-conditioned (the unconstrained genic variance is near zero by cycle 12) and are not interpreted. The early (1-4) against late (9-12) split on the index scale is exploratory (entered after the eight seeds had been seen); the twenty draws below were drawn after it was defined. These are eight seeds at one scale (625 candidates, 300 QTL, \(F_{ST} = 0.15\)); how the size of the effect moves with \(h^2\), \(N\), \(n_{sel}\) or the number of loci was not measured.
A replication on twenty founder draws the chapter had not used, run live (seeds 101 to 120; the random and unconstrained arms only; run_cycles() seeds each draw through its seed argument), together with a check that the cached file is reproducible from this repository:

                  selector = if (random) sel_rand else NULL)
  o$gap <- o$var_g - o$var_genic; o$regime <- if (random) "random" else "unconstrained"
  o$seed <- s; o
}

WarningUnlinked loci do not remove the covariance term



The measurement above shows that, with free recombination between loci, selection still builds a negative covariance term that the genic variance does not contain (Table 24.6). Assumption C1 of Chapter 23, that loci are unlinked, therefore cannot be read as the absence of that term. Its replacement is a statement about the size of the term, measured above at eight seeds. Whether the term decays to a negligible equilibrium at longer horizons is not shown either way: no decay is detected over cycles 1 to 8, and the data cannot exclude one (the slope interval above).




24.3.2 With real linkage
The same question with real meiosis behind it. Chapter 9’s reciprocal recurrent selection runs on a coalescent founder history with a genetic map, and AlphaSimR reports varA (which carries the disequilibrium) and genicVarA (which, for an additive trait, is the Hardy-Weinberg expectation with the average effect). This arm differs from the unlinked arm in more than linkage:


Show code
lk_cfg <- modifyList(rrs_config, list(n_cycles = 8))



genic variance: AlphaSimR’s genicVarA is \(\sum_k 2 p_k q_k \alpha_k^2\), not the package’s genic_var() of the matrix at hand; they coincide only for an additive trait in Hardy-Weinberg proportions (Chapter 9);
selection target and candidates: elite doubled-haploid lines per pool, chosen on a testcross phenotype with \(h^2 =\) 0.4 and dominance (mean dominance degree 0.4), 8 lines retained per pool from 3 doubled haploids per parent, against the hybrid index of 60 of 625 hybrids known without error;
size: 20 + 20 founders, 5 chromosomes of 100 segregating sites, all QTL, against 25 + 25 lines and 2000 markers;
cycles and replication: 8 cycles and four replicates, against 12 cycles and eight seeds.



Show code
lk$rel <- ((lk$varA_A - lk$genicVarA_A) + (lk$varA_B - lk$genicVarA_B)) /
          (lk$genicVarA_A + lk$genicVarA_B)
pl <- reshape(lk[, c("regime", "seed", "cycle", "rel")],
              idvar = c("seed", "cycle"), timevar = "regime", direction = "wide")
# both arms branch off one founder object per replicate, and replicates draw their own
c0l <- pl[pl$cycle == 0, ]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(c0l$rel.selected, c0l$rel.random)),
          length(unique(round(c0l$rel.selected, 10))) == nrow(c0l))
pl   <- pl[pl$cycle > 0, ]

NoteThe founders of the linked arm were not saved



alphasimr_founder_pools() draws the founder haplotypes with runMacs2(), which hands the coalescent to MaCS. Each replicate here sets its own seed (1 to 4) immediately before its founder draw, and both arms of a replicate branch off that one founder object, which is why cycle 0 is common to the two arms (asserted above); four replicates under four seeds gave four different cycle-0 states. The founders were not saved. Whether a second call of runMacs2() under the same seed returns the same founders was not measured in this chapter; Chapter 9 compares one pair of runMacs() calls per render and does not call runMacs2(). So limits_linked.csv is treated as a cached result, not as reproducible from this repository, and a re-run of regenerate.R limits is not known to reproduce it. One observation, not a rate: in the previous committed version of that file, cycle-0 varA_A of the replicates run under set.seed(1) was 0.4902 (replicate 1) and 0.5504 (replicates 2 to 4, equal to one another), against 1.2076 for replicate 1 under set.seed(1) in the present file; the code path of the earlier run is not documented here, so this is not evidence about whether runMacs2() is deterministic. The unlinked file is regenerated by the same call; the chunk above reproduces its seed 1.

title: 24  The limit, and what the metrics cannot see
text:
24.4 The two costs of selection
Result. In the unlinked arm the realised variance is, as a mean over eight seeds and cycles 1 to 8, 32 % below the genic variance for the unconstrained programme (s.e. 3 points) and 21 % for \(\alpha_{\max} = 0.02\) (5), against 0 % for random selection (3); no trend of the relative effect is detected over those cycles, with the interval of the slope given above. In the same simulation allele-frequency change is permanent: these runs have no mutation, migration or germplasm injection (inject is not used), and a fixed allele stays fixed.
Interpretation, and what limits it. Selection pays for gain in two currencies. It builds negative covariance between loci, a loss of usable variance that is charged every cycle while selection continues and that recombination reduces (here, at a measured balance that is not small); and it changes allele frequencies toward fixation, which only mutation or migration repays. The constraint of this book manages the second and does not see the first. Whether that is the right choice needs the two bills in a common unit (for example, response per cycle), and the chapter does not compute that: its two measurements are the unit-free ratio of the first and the short-horizon forecast of the second (Table 24.1). The ordering of the two bills is therefore not established here, and neither is whether the variance deficit lowers the response: no response was computed from it. The size of the covariance term may change with the genome (linkage, number of chromosomes, cycle time); that is a hypothesis with no source and no measurement in this chapter, and the four-replicate linked arm does not resolve it.
crumbs: 24  The limit, and what the metrics cannot see

title: 24  The limit, and what the metrics cannot see
text:
24.5 Where this connects
Chapter 4 supplies the variance decomposition (Equation 4.3) and the breeder’s equation this chapter runs forward. Chapter 23 supplies the trajectories and the assumption C1 tested above. Chapter 9 supplies the linked arm and the rules for founding pools that it follows. Three things are assumed that other chapters treat: the crossing plan behind the 625 hybrids (Chapter 18, Chapter 19, Chapter 20), the estimation of marker effects (Chapter 14), and the selector (Chapter 17). Two points of this chapter belong with the across-cycles items of Chapter 25: a projection from a fitted rate is not validated by the \(R^2\) of the \(\log(1 - F)\) regression, and the covariance term is outside every one-locus metric.

title: 25  End to end, and the operational checklist
section: 25.3 What this simulation cannot tell you
text:
25.3 What this simulation cannot tell you
Stated plainly, because the numbers above are precise and precision invites more confidence than the model supports.
The GEBVs carry no prediction error. The traits are built from known marker effects (Chapter 6). Chapter 12 Finding 5 measures what happens when they do not: the reported index is biased upward, and error correlated with relatedness costs several times the diversity that independent error of the same size does. The plans below should be read as an optimistic ceiling.
The model is additive. An additive \(\mathbf{G}\) misses heterosis and specific combining ability, which is precisely what a hybrid programme sells. The diversity constraint does not need a dominance model; the mean-performance ranking does (Chapter 5). Do not conflate them, and do not use these index values as performance predictions.
The pools are symmetric by construction. Both are simulated from the same ancestral frequencies at the same \(F_{ST}\). Real heterotic pools differ in size, history and internal structure, and a real programme will find one pool eroding faster than the other – which is why ne_lines_pool() is reported per pool.
\(N_s\) is not a drift projection. It is a static descriptor (Section 11.3). Do not extrapolate it forward.
One cycle, not a trajectory. Every result here is a single round of hybrid selection. Chapter 13 found, in 8 cached founder pools, that a diversity term on cross choice at S2 lowered the S2 loss and raised the S3 and S4 losses, and could not say whether it improved the effective number of parents or the alleles retained at the end of the pipeline – and the same question applies across cycles. A one-cycle constraint is not a multi-cycle policy: Chapter 23 runs fifteen of them and finds the unconstrained programme ahead of the \(\alpha_{\max} = 0.02\) programme, on the seed mean, for eight cycles and behind it for the rest.
\(p_0\) must be frozen. In this book it is set once in build_ctx(). In a real multi-cycle programme it must be the founder cycle’s frequencies, propagated forward – the single most common error in applying F_hom and F_drift (Chapter 10). Chapter 23 shows the failure directly: re-anchored, five generations of real drift are reported as exactly none.
crumbs: 25  End to end, and the operational checklist

title: 25  End to end, and the operational checklist
text:
25.4 The operational checklist

25.4.1 Setting up

The base \(p_0\) is frozen at the founding cycle and documented.
Diversity is computed on molecular coancestry f, never on a centered G. Check sum(G) == 0 once, to see why.
The marker panel’s MAF spectrum is known – it decides how severely the two lenses diverge.
Heterotic-group assignment is recorded, with the method that produced it, and treated as uncertain.



25.4.2 Choosing the budget

The attainable \(\alpha\) ceiling is computed before choosing \(\alpha_{\max}\). A budget above the ceiling constrains nothing.
Loss is measured against a same-size resampling baseline, never against the full pool.
The constraint is applied at the target set size, not incrementally.
The frontier is traced and the knee chosen, rather than a round number.



25.4.3 Running the optimiser

The search is encoded on line weights, not hybrid keys.
The differential evolution is warm-started from greedy solutions.
\(N_{e,\text{par}}\) is a second constraint, not a report line.
The per-line usage cap is enforced in the decoder, not by penalty.
The result is checked against the continuous relaxation. A large gap means the optimiser has not converged; a slack constraint means the search never reached the boundary.



25.4.4 Validating the plan

F_hom and F_drift are computed separately and reported together, with cov_diag as the diagnostic.
Allelic richness is computed on the returned plan – it is the one metric carrying information \(\theta\) does not.
The within/between pool decomposition confirms diversity was not preserved by degrading pool separation.
The number of selected parent lines is biologically plausible.
\(N_s\) is reported; a rate-based \(N_e\) is not, under active management.
Every metric is reported against the random null, in standard deviations.



25.4.5 Across cycles

The per-stage loss ledger is kept. DH induction, not hybrid mining, is usually where the diversity goes.
The regression of \(\log(1 - F)\) on cycle is checked for linearity. Curvature means a non-constant rate.
Periodic germplasm injection is planned. A closed elite pool depletes however well the constraint is managed.
The diversity cost per cycle is reported when cycle time is shortened.
crumbs: 25  End to end, and the operational checklist

title: 25  End to end, and the operational checklist
text:
25.5 Where to go next
Three extensions the material here supports but does not cover, each needing new work rather than new derivation:
Real data ingestion. load_data() is the single swap point and is currently a stub. A worked path from a VCF to the X/f/hybrids contract is what most readers will need first, and it is the one extension here that is pure engineering rather than new derivation.
Estimating the dominance deviations. Chapter 5 shows that expected heterosis depends on the alignment between divergence and \(d\), and that no frequency-based statistic can see \(d\). Everything downstream of that – ranking crosses on more than the mean, putting a number on the \(\lambda\) of Chapter 11 – waits on an estimate of \(d\) the book does not attempt.
Prediction error compounded across cycles. Chapter 12 Finding 5 measures it within one cycle and Chapter 23 assumes it away (C7). The two have not been run together, and the interaction is not obviously benign: correlated error concentrates the selection, and Chapter 23 shows concentration is what erodes the programme’s future.

A.1.3 The partition











Component
Definition
Meaning
In hybrid breeding




\(GD_T\)
\(1 - \bar f\)
total
the pool’s diversity


\(GD_{WI}\)
\(1 - \tilde s\)
within individuals
0 for inbred lines; use GD_WI_hyb for the F1s


\(GD_{BI}\)
\(\tilde s - \tilde f\)
between individuals, within subpopulation
segregating variation available to selection


\(GD_{WS}\)
\(1 - \tilde f\)
within subpopulations
within-pool diversity; equals \(GD_{BI}\) with inbred lines, the term recurrent selection erodes (Table 3.6)


\(GD_{BS}\)
\(\tilde f - \bar f\)
between subpopulations
the heterosis engine – maintain, do not maximise (Chapter 5)





with \(GD_T = GD_{WI} + GD_{BI} + GD_{BS}\) and \(F_{ST} = GD_{BS}/GD_T\).
That \(F_{ST}\) is a statistic computed on a set of genotypes. The Balding-Nichols parameter of the simulations, fst in the code and written \(F_{BN}\) here, is a different quantity: it is the variance of a pool’s allele frequency around the ancestral one, in units of \(p(1-p)\) (see Terms). Chapter 5, Chapter 12, Chapter 25 and Appendix C write that parameter as \(F_{ST}\) wherever it is a simulation setting or a Balding-Nichols expectation; read it there as \(F_{BN}\). With two pools of unbounded size the expected \(GD_{BS}\) per locus is \(F_{BN}\,p(1-p)\) and the expected \(GD_T\) is \((2 - F_{BN})\,p(1-p)\), so the statistic estimates approximately \(F_{BN}/(2 - F_{BN})\) (a ratio of expectations), not \(F_{BN}\): at \(F_{BN}\) = 0.15 that is 0.081, against 0.081 computed from simulated frequencies. On finite pools the statistic is larger again, because \(\tilde f\) includes each line’s self-coancestry: on the 25 + 25 lines that simulate_pools() draws at fst = 0.15 (seed 1), the \(F_{ST}\) of Chapter 3 is 0.102, and 0.084 once the diagonal is dropped from both \(\tilde f\) and \(\bar f\).

Expected heterosis splits as \(\sum_k d_k[\,2\bar p_k(1-\bar p_k) + y_k^2/2\,]\), whose two halves are \(GD_T\) and \(GD_{BS}\) when \(d_k \equiv 1\), and whose sum is \(1 - \theta_{AB}\) (Chapter 5). Over a complete factorial the realised values split orthogonally as \(H_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij}\).

title: Appendix A — Notation and glossary
text:
A.2 Conventions
Coancestry always includes the diagonal. Group coancestry in the sense of Cockerham. That is what makes \(1 - \theta\) exactly Nei’s \(H_e\) and makes the algebra close. Drop the diagonal and none of the identities hold.
Everything is computed per locus and then averaged over loci. Never average frequencies first.
Marker coding. Lines are 0/1 (or 0/2) because they are homozygous. Hybrids are 0/1/2 as dosage, rescaled to 0/0.5/1 as within-individual frequency. stage1_build() auto-detects and rescales.
f is never centered, G always is. A negative coancestry is a symptom of the wrong matrix.
Loss is always relative to a same-size random baseline. Never to the full pool.

title: Appendix A — Notation and glossary
text:
A.3 Terms
Balding-Nichols model. A Beta distribution with mean \(p\) and variance \(F_{BN}\,p(1-p)\), used to draw pool-specific allele frequencies from an ancestral frequency \(p\). \(F_{BN}\) (fst) is the expected divergence of each pool from the ancestral population; it is not the \(F_{ST}\) statistic of Chapter 3 computed on the pools (see the partition above).
Group coancestry. The probability that two alleles sampled at random from a whole set are identical in state, including the case of sampling the same individual twice.
Heterotic group / pool. A set of lines maintained as a breeding unit, crossed to lines of a complementary group to produce hybrids. Divergence between groups is where heterosis comes from – but only the divergence that coincides with dominance. Divergence produced by drift alone generates none, because it is paid for exactly out of the within-pool term. See Chapter 5.
Mid-parent heterosis. The F1’s value minus the mean of its two parents. With inbred parents the additive contributions cancel exactly, leaving only the dominance effects at the F1’s heterozygous loci.
General and specific combining ability (GCA, SCA). The two halves of a hybrid’s value that a two-way layout separates: what a line contributes to every cross it enters, and what depends on which two lines met. For heterosis both are exact functions of \(d\) and the pool frequencies, with GCA weighted by the opposite pool’s frequencies – so combining ability is a property of a line against a tester pool, never of the line alone. See Section 5.11.
Reciprocal recurrent selection. Selecting on performance in cross and recycling the winners within their own pool. Selection information crosses the pool boundary; germplasm does not. See Chapter 23.
Identity by state (IBS) vs by descent (IBD). IBS is what markers observe: two alleles are the same allele. IBD adds the requirement of common ancestry from a defined base. The gap between them is where Chapter 10’s whole argument lives.
Line-level collapse. The exact identity \(\theta_S = \mathbf{w}'
\mathbf{f}^L \mathbf{w}\) for F1 hybrids of homozygous lines, which removes the need for the \(N \times N\) hybrid matrix. See Section 12.1.
Status number. \(N_s = 1/(2\theta)\). A head count of unrelated non-inbred individuals only on coancestry measured against a base population; on molecular \(\mathbf{f}\), \(N_s \in [1/2, 1]\) and is a monotone rescaling of \(\theta\) (Section 11.3). A static descriptor.
Truncation selection. Take the top \(n\) by index, ignore everything else. The ceiling on gain and the floor on diversity.
Warm start. Seeding an optimiser’s initial population with heuristic solutions. Not optional here: without it the differential evolution finishes below a plain greedy.

title: Appendix A — Notation and glossary
text:
Reproduce this chapter
All the code of this chapter, in order and with the explanation kept as comments, is one script: 90-notation.R. Download it, install hybdiv, and run it top to bottom in an empty directory; cached results are fetched on first use.

title: Appendix B — The hybdiv package
text:
B.1 Installation
Every function used in this book lives in one package, whose source is the R/ directory of this repository. This appendix is the index.
Show code
install.packages(c("DEoptim", "quadprog"))
devtools::install(".")        # from the repository root
library(hybdiv)
Only DEoptim is a hard dependency, used solely by sel_de(). quadprog is suggested and needed only for optimal_contributions() and ocs_quadprog(). Everything else, including every plot, is base R.

B.3 The two-stage contract
Everything downstream of stage 1 talks only through three objects. This is the seam for swapping in real data.

#   $metrics    one row per scenario

Reproduce this chapter

title: Appendix C — Verification
text:
C.1 The method: slow oracles
A derivation the reader cannot re-run against a naive implementation is a claim, not a verification. This appendix says how each result in the book was checked, and how to re-run the checks.
Every fast route in the package has a deliberately slow, literal counterpart in R/09_reference.R that transcribes the definition with no algebraic shortcut. The fast route must match it to machine precision.
Show code
ref_theta
#> function(idx, ctx) mean(ctx[["f"]][idx, idx])
#> <bytecode: 0x7bb384b690>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>
theta_group
#> function(idx, ctx) {
#>   f <- ctx[["f"]]
#>   if (!is.matrix(f)) stop("ctx[[\"f\"]] (hybrid coancestry) is missing")
#>   mean(f[idx, idx])
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x7bb39195b0>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>
fast_theta
#> function(idx, ctx) {
#>   cnt <- line_counts(idx, ctx)
#>   u   <- which(cnt > 0L)                       # restrict to used lines
#>   cu  <- cnt[u]
#>   s   <- sum(cu)
#>   as.numeric(crossprod(cu, ctx$fL[u, u, drop = FALSE] %*% cu)) / (s * s)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x7bb3957738>
#> <environment: namespace:hybdiv>
Three implementations of one quantity: a literal mean over the submatrix, the packaged version, and the line-route collapse that never forms the submatrix at all. They must agree.
Show code
sim  <- simulate_pools(n_A = 20, n_B = 20, m = 1500, seed = 7)
ctxp <- ctx_from_pools(sim)
set.seed(3); sel <- sample.int(ctxp$N, 50)

c(oracle     = ref_theta(sel, ctxp),
  packaged   = theta_group(sel, ctxp),
  line_route = fast_theta(sel, ctxp),
  max_dev    = max(abs(c(theta_group(sel, ctxp), fast_theta(sel, ctxp)) -
                       ref_theta(sel, ctxp))))
#>       oracle     packaged   line_route      max_dev 
#> 6.708316e-01 6.708316e-01 6.708316e-01 1.110223e-16
The oracles exist so that this comparison is possible for a reader who does not trust the derivation – which is the correct posture.
Show code
fmt(rbind(
  he_nei       = c(oracle = ref_he_nei(sel, ctxp), packaged = he_nei(sel, ctxp)),
  theta_freq   = c(ref_theta_freq(sel, ctxp), theta_from_freq(sel, ctxp)),
  status_num   = c(ref_status_num(sel, ctxp), status_number(sel, ctxp)),
  ne_parents   = c(ref_ne_parents(sel, ctxp), ne_parents(sel, ctxp)),
  alleles_lost = c(ref_alleles_lost(sel, ctxp), alleles_lost(sel, ctxp)),
  ENE          = c(ref_ene(sel, ctxp), ene(sel, ctxp)),

title: Appendix C — Verification
text:
C.3 The test suite
The suite is tests/testthat/, run with devtools::test(). It takes about a minute. What it asserts, and why each check earns its place:









Check
If it fails




theta via submatrix == theta via allele frequencies
f is wrong: centered, rescaled, or the wrong marker coding


1 - theta == Nei’s He
the identity underpinning every ‘loss of X%’ statement is broken


f is bounded to [0, 1]
a centered matrix is being used as coancestry


sum(VanRaden G) == 0
the demonstration in Section 2.2 no longer holds on this data


theta and Ns analytical edge cases
the diagonal is being dropped somewhere


greedy < random < truncation on theta
there is no trade-off to optimise; the whole benchmark is pointless


decode() is unique, in range, deterministic
the DE fitness is noisy and cannot converge


fast line route == hybrid-matrix route
the collapse is broken; production scale becomes infeasible


incremental swap == full recomputation
any local search built on the state vector is wrong


popcount32 == naive bit count
allelic richness counts are wrong


F_hom and F_drift are 0 when the selection is the base
the base p0 is not frozen, or is being recomputed


cov_diag == F_hom - F_drift
one of the three lens formulas is wrong


max-diversity drives F_hom negative, F_drift positive
the two-lens argument of Chapter 10 does not reproduce


freq_metrics reproduces he_nei and alleles_lost
the consolidated marker sweep changed an existing number


the Caballero & Toro partition closes
the Eq. 8 algebra is broken


GD_WI == 0 for inbred lines, GD_WI_hyb large for their F1s
lines are not actually inbred, or the hybrid diagonal is wrong


eff_dim in (0, n - 1]
the double-centering was dropped and eff_dim re-measures theta


the two-stage output contract
downstream code reading $selection or $metrics will break


stage 2 runs without fL
the optional-fL path is broken


stage1_build accepts both marker codings
real data in the other coding would give different answers


genic_var == its literal oracle
the genic-variance route diverged from its definition


realised minus genic variance == the disequilibrium term
the disequilibrium decomposition of Chapter 4 is wrong


inbreeding depression == the shared term of the heterosis partition
Falconer’s symmetry is broken, or d is being applied inconsistently


inbreeding depression == simulated genotypes (Monte Carlo)
the closed form does not describe genotypes anyone could actually draw


the restricted index moves the restricted trait exactly zero
the restriction is a penalty, and the Chapter 15 analogy is wrong


no restriction reduces the restricted index to Smith-Hazel
the degenerate case silently returns something other than Smith-Hazel


MRD and coancestry are one statistic
Trap 1 of Chapter 13 no longer holds


Gst < Fst always, and Gst matches the classical route
Trap 2 is wrong, or the two definitions were conflated


the DH identities
the S2 algebra is wrong and crossing plans cannot be pre-evaluated


hybrid theta from usage == the hybrid matrix
Trap 5’s repair route is broken


constrained line selection meets its ceiling
the constrained selection silently returns an infeasible plan


the oracles agree with the packaged metrics
a fast route diverged from its definition


map length and Haldane spacing
the sizing chapter’s map is not the map it claims


heterozygosity halves per selfing
the simulator is not doing what selfing does


D == 1 - (1 - H)/N under neutrality
the identity every sizing number rests on is broken


n_equivalent inverts diversity_retained
N_eq is not the inverse it is described as


a Syn cycle adds half a map length of junctions
the intercrossing budget in Chapter 7 is wrong by 2x


distortion shifts ancestry away from 0.5
the distortion mechanism is inactive


f1_sizing halves the loss probability per plant
the F1 sizing argument is wrong


heterosis_value matches the literal oracle
the fast heterosis route diverged from its definition


additive effects cancel from the mid-parent difference
the derivation of Chapter 5 is wrong, or the parents are not inbred


shared and divergence == GD_T and GD_BS
the central identity of Chapter 5 is broken


2 * GD_WI_hyb == GD_T + GD_BS
the hybrid-level and line-level partitions have come apart


neutral divergence leaves expected heterosis unchanged
Chapter 5’s correction is wrong and F_ST would predict heterosis


alignment between d and divergence is what moves heterosis
the alignment result, and the argument for Chapter 23 with it, is wrong


GCA + SCA reconstruct heterosis exactly and are mean-zero
the combining-ability decomposition of Chapter 5 is not a decomposition


SCA is the interaction residual of the two-way additive fit
SCA is a proxy for the interaction, not the interaction – the section overclaims


the closed-form GCA and SCA variance components match
the variance-component result of Section 5.12 rests on a wrong closed form


uniform-d heterosis is the coancestry kernel, exactly
genetic distance no longer predicts heterosis under flat dominance


GD_T + GD_BS == 1 - theta_AB
the between-pool coancestry reading of the identity is wrong


pool_freqs reproduces what its callers computed inline
a pool frequency route diverged after the refactor


the DH draw is an unbiased gamete; selfing an inbred returns it
recycling fabricates or destroys diversity; every trajectory is wrong


p0 is frozen, not re-anchored, across cycles
both inbreeding lenses report no loss forever – the trap of Chapter 23


a closed programme loses diversity and gains index
the cycle loop is not selecting, or not recycling what it selected


the budget is respected; alpha_max = Inf is truncation
the budget is not binding across cycles


injection raises diversity relative to a closed run
injection is not actually introducing founder material


GCA rank == n’ - components for every design family
the connectivity argument of Chapter 18 is wrong, or a generator is


NC II: between-set GCA contrast not estimable
the estimability check accepts what it should reject


k = 1 tester leaves zero df for SCA
the tester saturation claim of Section 18.3 is wrong


LS GCA error == s2s/k + s2e/(k r)
the Sprague-Tatum closed form no longer describes fit_gca()


sparse_blup == literal GLS oracle (BLUP and PEV)
every live number of Chapter 19 is wrong: the MME are assembled incorrectly


each hybrid in exactly k locations; parentage covers both pools everywhere
the allocation comparison of Section 19.11.3 compares different budgets


known-component BLUP has dispersion slope ~ 1
the BLUP is mis-scaled; the dispersion claims of Section 19.9 fail

Rscript -e 'devtools::test()'

text:
C.4 Provenance of every figure and table
The book runs light examples live and reads heavy results from cache. This is the complete accounting.

C.4.1 Computed live at render









Chapter
Runs live




Chapter 1
the GCA-against-tester example, the observed-against-expected heterozygosity identities, the IBS-against-IBD example, a hybrid’s molecular inbreeding against its parents’ coancestry, the drift decay of a crossing block against a DH-derived pool

title: Appendix C — Verification
section: C.7 Known limitations of the verification
text:
C.7 Known limitations of the verification
Stated so they are not mistaken for oversights.
The oracles share the author’s understanding. They check that the fast route computes what the slow route computes. They cannot check that the slow route implements the right definition. That is what the reproduction of the published Caballero & Toro tables in Chapter 3 is for – an external check against numbers this project did not produce.
Monte Carlo checks have Monte Carlo error. Where a test asserts agreement with a simulated expectation rather than an algebraic identity, the tolerance is loose by necessity, and a genuinely small bias would pass.
Everything is verified on simulated data. The identities are algebraic and will hold on real genotypes. The empirical results – which metrics are redundant, how much index a constraint costs – were derived on simulated markers, and Chapter 12 says explicitly that the redundancy analysis rests on a cached file whose setting (\(F_{BN}\), number of lines and markers) is not recorded, and that it should be re-derived on real genotypes before being treated as settled.
One chapter’s headline results come from outside this repository. The mating-design sweep of Chapter 18 (mating_scenarios_summary.csv and its siblings) was produced by an external study whose code needs AlphaSimR and sommer; it shipped with its own 37-check validation report, summarised in that chapter, but it is not re-run by anything here. What is re-run is its phenotypic core (regenerate.R mating), and Section 18.10 compares the two.
The sparse-testing chapter (Chapter 19) has the same structure. Its REML grid, two-stage scenario and genomic layer are cached from an external study, which validated its own estimator on the complete design (Table 19.9). The in-repo regenerate.R sparse re-runs the known-component core, and Section 19.14 compares the two.
The joint-allocation chapter (Chapter 20) does not: its three data files are regenerated in this repository by regenerate.R joint (Section 20.8).

title: Appendix D — The bibliographic corpora
text:
D.6 Limitations
These are abstract screens. Relevance and the metric annotations were scored from titles and abstracts, not from full texts. A paper that computes a metric without naming it in the abstract is invisible to this table – which almost certainly understates how often coancestry is computed as an intermediate step.
The queries shaped the answer. 29 plant-breeding queries were run; a different query set would return a different landscape. The strong maize skew is by design, and the counts for other crops are too small to support a claim about those crops.
“Not established in the retrieved set” means exactly that. Every such statement in Chapter 21 is a claim about this corpus, not about the literature as a whole. It is a prompt to look further before assuming novelty, not a proof of it.
Citation counts are a snapshot at screening time and are already stale.
